general.) Here the two dots indicate a logical product; since two
dots do not occur anywhere else, the scope of these two dots extends
backwards to the beginning of the proposition, and forwards to the end.</p>

<p>"<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor q \ldotp \supset \colon\ldotp p \ldotp \lor \ldotp q \supset r : \supset \ldotp p \lor r\)" src="images/114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 27.905ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_114.svg">" will mean "if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_73"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_57"> is
true, then if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_74"> or '<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_58"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_10">' is true, it follows
that either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_75"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_11"> is true."<span class="pagenum" id="Page_11">[Pg 11]</span> If this is to be asserted, we
must put four dots after the assertion-sign, thus:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash \colon\colon p \lor q.\supset \colon\ldotp p. \lor .q \supset r \colon \supset .p \lor r.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/115.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 34.945ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_115.svg"></span>
(This proposition is proved in the body of the work; it is <a href="#_2_75" class="pginternal">*2·75</a>.) If
we wish to assert (what is equivalent to the above) the proposition:
"if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_76"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_59"> is true, and either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_77"> or '<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_60"> implies
<img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_12">' is true, then either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_78"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_13"> is true," we write
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash \colon\ldotp p \lor q \colon p. \lor .q \supset r \colon \supset .p \lor r.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/116.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 31.173ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_116.svg"></span>
Here the first pair of dots indicates a logical product, while the
second pair does not. Thus the scope of the second pair of dots passes
over the first pair, and back until we reach the three dots after the
assertion-sign.</p>

<p>Other uses of dots follow the same principles, and will be explained as
they are introduced. In reading a proposition, the dots should be noticed
first, as they show its structure. In a proposition containing several signs of
implication or equivalence, the one with the greatest number of dots before
or after it is the <i>principal</i> one: everything that goes before this one is stated
by the proposition to imply or be equivalent to everything that comes
after it.</p>

<p><i>Definitions</i>. A definition is a declaration that a certain
newly-introduced symbol or combination of symbols is to mean the same
as a certain other combination of symbols of which the meaning is
already known. Or, if the defining combination of symbols is one which
only acquires meaning when combined in a suitable manner with other
symbols<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_4" id="FNanchor_4">[4]</a>, what is meant is that any combination of symbols in which
the newly-defined symbol or combination of symbols occurs is to have
that meaning (if any) which results from substituting the defining
combination of symbols for the newly-defined symbol or combination
of symbols wherever the latter occurs. We will give the names of
<i>definiendum</i> and <i>definiens</i> respectively to what is defined
and to that which it is defined as meaning. We express a definition by
putting the <i>definiendum</i> to the left and the <i>definiens</i> to
the right, with the sign "=" between, and the letters "Df" to the right
of the <i>definiens</i>. It is to be understood that the sign "=" and
the letters "Df" are to be regarded as together forming one symbol. The
sign "=" without the letters "Df" will have a different meaning, to be
explained shortly.</p>

<p>An example of a definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ p \supset q \ldotp  = \ldotp  {\sim} p \lor q \qquad \text{Df.} \]" src="images/117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 22.996ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_117.svg"></span></p>

<p>It is to be observed that a definition is, strictly speaking, no part
of the subject in which it occurs. For a definition is concerned
wholly with the symbols, not with what they symbolise. Moreover it
is not true or false, being the expression of a volition, not of a
proposition. (For this reason,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_12">[Pg 12]</span> definitions are not preceded by the
assertion-sign.) Theoretically, it is unnecessary ever to give a
definition: we might always use the <i>definiens</i> instead, and thus
wholly dispense with the <i>definiendum</i>. Thus although we employ
definitions and do not define "definition," yet "definition" does
not appear among our primitive ideas, because the definitions are no
part of our subject, but are, strictly speaking, mere typographical
conveniences. Practically, of course, if we introduced no definitions,
our formulae would very soon become so lengthy as to be unmanageable;
but theoretically, all definitions are superfluous.</p>

<p>In spite of the fact that definitions are theoretically superfluous, it
is nevertheless true that they often convey more important information
than is contained in the propositions in which they are used. This
arises from two causes. First, a definition usually implies that
the <i>definiens</i> is worthy of careful consideration. Hence the
collection of definitions embodies our choice of subjects and our
judgment as to what is most important. Secondly, when what is defined
is (as often occurs) something already familiar, such as cardinal or
ordinal numbers, the definition contains an analysis of a common idea,
and may therefore express a notable advance. Cantor's definition of the
continuum illustrates this: his definition amounts to the statement
that what he is defining is the object which has the properties
commonly associated with the word "continuum," though what precisely
constitutes these properties had not before been known. In such cases,
a definition is a "making definite": it gives definiteness to an idea
which had previously been more or less vague.</p>

<p>For these reasons, it will be found, in what follows, that the
definitions are what is most important, and what most deserves the
reader's prolonged attention.</p>

<p>Some important remarks must be made respecting the variables occurring
in the <i>definiens</i> and the <i>definiendum</i>. But these will be
deferred till the notion of an "apparent variable" has been introduced,
when the subject can be considered as a whole.</p>

<p><i>Summary of preceding statements.</i> There are, in the above,
three primitive ideas which are not "defined" but only descriptively
explained. Their primitiveness is only relative to our exposition
of logical connection and is not absolute; though of course such an
exposition gains in importance according to the simplicity of its
primitive ideas. These ideas are symbolised by "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim} p\)" src="images/118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.898ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_118.svg">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor q\)" src="images/119.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.693ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_119.svg">," and by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\)" src="images/78.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.382ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_78.svg_4">" prefixed to a proposition.</p>

<p>Three definitions have been introduced:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} p \ldotp q \ldotp &amp;= \ldotp {\sim} ({\sim} p \lor {\sim} q) \quad &amp;\text{Df},\\ p \supset q \ldotp &amp;= \ldotp {\sim} p \lor q \quad &amp;\text{Df},\\ p \equiv q \ldotp &amp;= \ldotp p \supset q \ldotp q \supset p \quad &amp;\text{Df}. \\ \end{aligned} \]" src="images/120.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 30.791ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_120.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_13">[Pg 13]</span></p>

<p><i>Primitive propositions.</i> Some propositions must be assumed
without proof, since all inference proceeds from propositions
previously asserted. These, as far as they concern the functions
of propositions mentioned above, will be found stated in <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>, where
the formal and continuous exposition of the subject commences. Such
propositions will be called "primitive propositions." These, like the
primitive ideas, are to some extent a matter of arbitrary choice;
though, as in the previous case, a logical system grows in importance
according as the primitive propositions are few and simple. It will be
found that owing to the weakness of the imagination in dealing with
simple abstract ideas no very great stress can be laid upon their
obviousness. They are obvious to the instructed mind, but then so are
many propositions which cannot be quite true, as being disproved by
their contradictory consequences. The proof of a logical system is
its adequacy and its coherence. That is: (1) the system must embrace
among its deductions all those propositions which we believe to be
true and capable of deduction from logical premisses alone, though
possibly they may require some slight limitation in the form of an
increased stringency of enunciation; and (2) the system must lead to no
contradictions, namely in pursuing our inferences we must never be led
to assert both <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_79"> and not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_80">, <i>i.e.</i> both "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \ldotp p\)" src="images/121.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.526ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_121.svg">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \ldotp {\sim} p\)" src="images/122.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.287ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_122.svg">" cannot legitimately appear.</p>

<p>The following are the primitive propositions employed in the calculus
of propositions. The letters "Pp" stand for "primitive proposition."</p>

<p>(1) Anything implied by a true premiss is true Pp.</p>

<p>This is the rule which justifies inference.</p>

<p>(2) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p \lor p \ldotp \supset \ldotp p \quad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/123.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 17.15ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_123.svg">,</p>

<p class="nind">
<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_81"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_82"> is true, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_83"> is true.</p>

<p>(3) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon q \ldotp \supset \ldotp p \lor q \quad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/124.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 16.956ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_124.svg">,</p>

<p class="nind">
<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_61"> is true, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_84"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_62"> is true.</p>

<p>(4) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p \lor q \ldotp \supset \ldotp q \lor p \quad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/125.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.608ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_125.svg">,</p>

<p class="nind">
<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_85"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_63"> is true, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_64"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_86"> is true.</p>

<p>(5) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p \lor (q \lor r) \ldotp \supset \ldotp q \lor (p \lor r) \quad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/126.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.199ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_126.svg">,</p>

<p class="nind">
<i>i.e.</i> if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_87"> is true or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_65"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_14">" is true, then
either <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_66"> is true or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_88"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_15">" is true.</p>

<p>(6) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon \ldotp q \supset r \ldotp \supset \colon p \lor q \ldotp \supset \ldotp p \lor r \quad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/127.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 30.444ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_127.svg">,</p>

<p class="nind">
<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_67"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_16">, then "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_89"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_68">" implies
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_90"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_17">."</p>

<p>(7) Besides the above primitive propositions, we require a primitive
proposition called "the axiom of identification of real variables."
When we have separately asserted two different functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_1">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_2"> is undetermined, it is often important to know whether
we can identify the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_3"> in one<span class="pagenum" id="Page_14">[Pg 14]</span> assertion with the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_4"> in the
other. This will be the case—so our axiom allow us to infer—if both
assertions present x as the argument to some one function, that is
to say, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg"> is a constituent in both assertions (whatever
propositional function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_1"> may be), or, more generally, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x, y, z, \ldots)\)" src="images/129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.233ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_129.svg">
is a constituent in one assertion, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (x, u, v, \ldots)\)" src="images/130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.464ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_130.svg">
is a constituent in the other. This axiom introduces notions which
have not yet been explained; for a fuller account, see the remarks
accompanying <a href="#_3_03" class="pginternal">*3·03</a>, <a href="#_1_7" class="pginternal">*1·7</a>, <a href="#_1_71" class="pginternal">*1·71</a>, and <a href="#_1_72" class="pginternal">*1·72</a> (which is the statement of
this axiom) in the body of the work, as well as the explanation of
propositional functions and ambiguous assertion to be given shortly.</p>

<p><i>Some simple propositions</i>. In addition to the primitive
propositions we have already mentioned, the following are among the
most important of the elementary properties of propositions appearing
among the deductions.</p>

<p>The law of excluded middle:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash . p \lor {\sim}p. \]" src="images/131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.568ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_131.svg"></span>
This is <a href="#_2_11" class="pginternal">*2·11</a> below. We shall indicate in brackets the numbers given to
the following propositions in the body of the work.</p>

<p>The law of contradiction (<a href="#_3_24" class="pginternal">*3·24</a>):
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash . {\sim}(p.{\sim}p). \]" src="images/132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.58ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_132.svg"></span></p>

<p>The law of double negation (<a href="#_4_13" class="pginternal">*4·13</a>):
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash . p \equiv {\sim}({\sim}p). \]" src="images/133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.591ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_133.svg"></span></p>

<p>The principle of <i>transposition</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_91"> implies
<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_69">, then not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_70"> implies not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_92">," and vice versa: this
principle has various forms, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \text{(*4·1)}\qquad &amp;\vdash \colon p \supset q. \equiv .{\sim}q \supset {\sim}p,\\ \text{(*4·11)}\quad &amp;\vdash \colon p \equiv q. \equiv . {\sim}p \equiv {\sim}q,\\ \text{(*4·14)}\quad &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp p . q. \supset . r \equiv \colon p. {\sim}r . \supset. {\sim}q,\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/134.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 39.463ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_134.svg"></span>
as well as others which are variants of these.</p>

<p>The law of tautology, in the two forms:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \text{(*4·24)}\quad &amp;\vdash \colon p. \equiv .p\, . p,\\ \text{(*4·25)}\quad &amp;\vdash \colon p. \equiv .p \lor p,\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/135.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 24.157ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_135.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_93"> is true" is equivalent to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_94"> is true and <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_95">
is true," as well as to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_96"> is true or <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_97"> is true." From a formal
point of view, it is through the law of tautology and its consequences
that the algebra of logic is chiefly distinguished from ordinary
algebra.</p>

<p>The law of absorption :
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{(*4·24)}\qquad \vdash \colon\ldotp p \supset q. \equiv \colon p. \equiv . p . q, \]" src="images/136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.154ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_136.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_98"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_71">" is equivalent to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_99"> is equivalent
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(p . q\)" src="images/75.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.185ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_75.svg_2">." This is called the law of absorption because it shows
that the factor <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_72"> in the product is<span class="pagenum" id="Page_15">[Pg 15]</span> absorbed by the factor
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_100">, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_101"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_73">. This principle enables us to replace
an implication (<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \supset q\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.196ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_4">) by an equivalence (<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \ldotp \equiv\ldotp p \ldotp q)\)" src="images/137.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.975ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_137.svg">
whenever it is convenient to do so.</p>

<p>An analogous and very important principle is the following:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{(*4·73)}\qquad \vdash \colon \ldotp q \ldotp \supset \colon p \ldotp \equiv \ldotp p \ldotp q. \]" src="images/138.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.999ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_138.svg"></span></p>

<p>Logical addition and multiplication of propositions obey the
associative and commutative laws, and the distributive law in two
forms, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp;\text{(*4·4)} &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp p \ldotp q \lor r \ldotp \equiv \colon p \ldotp q \ldotp \lor \ldotp p \ldotp r\text{,}\\ &amp;\text{(*4·41)} &amp;\vdash \colon \ldotp p \ldotp \lor \ldotp q \ldotp r \colon \equiv \colon p \lor q \ldotp p \lor r\text{.}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/139.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 37.962ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_139.svg"></span>
The second of these distinguishes the relations of logical addition and
multiplication from those of arithmetical addition and multiplication.</p>

<p><i>Propositional functions.</i> Let <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg"> be a statement
containing a variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_5"> and such that it becomes a proposition
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_6"> is given any fixed determined meaning. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_1"> is
called a "propositional function"; it is not a proposition, since owing
to the ambiguity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_7"> it really makes no assertion at all. Thus
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_8"> is hurt" really makes no assertion at all, till we have settled
who <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_9"> is. Yet owing to the individuality retained by the ambiguous
variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_10">, it is an ambiguous example from the collection of
propositions arrived at by giving all possible determinations to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_11">
in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_12"> is hurt" which yield a proposition, true or false. Also if
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_13"> is hurt" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg"> is hurt" occur <i>in the same context</i>,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_1"> is another variable, then according to the determinations
given to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_2">, they can be settled to be (possibly) the same
proposition or (possibly) different propositions. But apart from some
determination given to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_15"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_3">, they retain in that context
their ambiguous differentiation. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_16"> is hurt" is an ambiguous
"value" of a propositional function. When we wish to speak of the
propositional function corresponding to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_17"> is hurt," we shall write
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg"> is hurt." Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_1"> is hurt" is the propositional
function and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_18"> is hurt" is an ambiguous value of that function.
Accordingly though "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_19"> is hurt" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_4"> is hurt" <i>occurring
in the same context</i> can be distinguished, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_2"> is hurt"
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}\)" src="images/143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_143.svg"> is hurt" convey no distinction of meaning at all.
More generally, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_2"> is an ambiguous value of the propositional
function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_2">, and when a definite signification <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg">
is substituted for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_20">, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}a\)" src="images/145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_145.svg"> is an unambiguous value of
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}\hat{x}\)" src="images/146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_146.svg">.</p>

<p>Propositional functions are the fundamental kind from which the more
usual kinds of function, such as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin x\)" src="images/147.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.449ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_147.svg">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\log x\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 4.563ex; height: 2.036ex;" id="img_images_148.svg">" or
"the father of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_21">," are derived. These derivative functions are
considered later, and are called "descriptive functions." The functions
of propositions considered above are a particular case of propositional
functions.</p>

<p><i>The range of values and total variation.</i> Thus corresponding
to any propositional function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_3">, there is a range, or
collection, of values, consisting of all the propositions (true or
false) which can be obtained by giving<span class="pagenum" id="Page_16">[Pg 16]</span> every possible determination to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_22"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_3">. A value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_23"> for which <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_4"> is true
will be said to "satisfy" <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_4">. Now in respect to the truth
or falsehood of propositions of this range three important cases must
be noted and symbolised. These cases are given by three propositions
of which one at least must be true. Either (1) all propositions of the
range are true, or (2) some propositions of the range are true, or (3)
no proposition of the range is true. The statement (1) is symbolised
by "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg">," and (2) is symbolised by "<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_150.svg">." No definition is given of these two symbols,
which accordingly embody two new primitive ideas in our system. The
symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_1">" may be read "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_5"> always," or
"<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_6"> is always true," or "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_7"> is true for all possible
values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_24">." The symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_151.svg">" may be
read "there exists an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_25"> for which <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_8"> is true," or "there
exists an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_26"> satisfying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_5">," and thus conforms to the
natural form of the expression of thought.</p>

<p>Proposition (3) can be expressed in terms of the fundamental ideas now
on hand. In order to do this, note that "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}{\phi}x\)" src="images/152.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.403ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_152.svg">" stands for
the contradictory of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_9">. Accordingly <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/153.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.031ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_153.svg"> is
another propositional function such that each value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_6">
contradicts a value of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/154.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.403ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_154.svg"> and vice versa. Hence
"<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\sim}{\phi}x\)" src="images/155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.463ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_155.svg">" symbolises the proposition that every
value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_7"> is untrue. This is number (3) as stated above.</p>

<p>It is an obvious error, though one easy to commit, to assume that
cases (1) and (3) are each other's contradictories. The symbolism
exposes this fallacy at once, for (1) is <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_2">, and
(3) is <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\sim}{\phi}x\)" src="images/155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.463ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_155.svg_1">, while the contradictory of (1) is
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\{(x) \ldotp {\phi}x\}\)" src="images/156.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.725ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_156.svg">. For the sake of brevity of symbolism
a definition is made, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\sim}(x) \ldotp {\phi}x \ldotp = \ldotp {\sim}\{(x) \ldotp {\phi}x\} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.273ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_157.svg"></span></p>

<p>Definitions of which the object is to gain some trivial advantage in
brevity by a slight adjustment of symbols will be said to be of "merely
symbolic import," in contradistinction to those definitions which
invite consideration of an important idea.</p>

<p>The proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_3"> is called the "total variation"
of the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_8">.</p>

<p>For reasons which will be explained in <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a>, we do not take
negation as a primitive idea when propositions of the forms <img alt="" data-tex="\((x)\ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/158.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_158.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_1"> are concerned, but
we <i>define</i> the negation of <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_4">, <i>i.e.</i>
of "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_10"> is always true," as being "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_11"> is sometimes
false," <i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp {\sim}{\phi}x\)" src="images/159.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.721ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_159.svg">," and
similarly we <i>define</i> the negation of <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_2">
as being <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\sim}{\phi}x\)" src="images/155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.463ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_155.svg_2">. Thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} {\sim}\{(x) \ldotp {\phi}x\} \ldotp = \ldotp (\exists x) \ldotp {\sim}{\phi}x \quad &amp;\text{Df}\text{,}\\ {\sim}\{(\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\} \ldotp = \ldotp (x) \ldotp {\sim}{\phi}x \quad &amp;\text{Df}\text{.}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/160.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 29.531ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_160.svg"></span></p>

<p>In like manner we define a disjunction in which one of the propositions
is of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_5">" or "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) \ldotp{\phi}x\)" src="images/161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_161.svg">"
in terms of a disjunction of propositions not of this form, putting
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x) \ldotp {\phi}x \ldotp \lor \ldotp p \colon = \ldotp (x) \ldotp {\phi}x \lor p \quad \text{Df}\text{,} \]" src="images/162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.802ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_162.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_17">[Pg 17]</span>
<i>i.e.</i> "either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_1"> is always true, or <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_102"> is true" is to
mean "'<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_2"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_103">' is always true," with similar definitions
in other cases. This subject is resumed in <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a>, and in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a> in the
body of the work.</p>

<p><i>Apparent variables</i>. The symbol "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg">" denotes one
definite proposition, and there is no distinction in meaning between
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_1">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\((y) . \phi y\)" src="images/164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.332ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_164.svg">" when they occur in the same
context. Thus the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_27">" in "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) . \phi x\)" src="images/165.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_165.svg">" is not an ambiguous
constituent of any expression in which "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_2">" occurs; and
such an expression does not cease to convey a determinate meaning by
reason of the ambiguity of the x in the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_3">." The symbol "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x). \phi x\)" src="images/166.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_166.svg">"
has some analogy to the symbol
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\int_a^{b} \phi(x) dx \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/167.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.044ex; width: 13.057ex; height: 5.616ex;" id="img_images_167.svg"></span>
for definite integration, since in neither case is the expression a
function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_28">.</p>

<p>The range of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_29"> in "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_3">" or "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . \phi x\)" src="images/168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_168.svg">"
extends over the complete field of the values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_30"> for
which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_4">" has meaning, and accordingly the meaning of "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x). \phi x\)" src="images/166.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_166.svg_1">"
or "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . \phi x\)" src="images/168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_168.svg_1">" involves the supposition
that such a field is determinate. The <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_31"> which occurs in "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) .\phi x\)" src="images/169.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_169.svg">"
or "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . \phi x\)" src="images/168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_168.svg_2">" is called (following Peano)
an "apparent variable." It follows from the meaning of "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x). \phi x\)" src="images/170.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_170.svg">"
that the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_32"> in this expression is also an apparent
variable. A proposition in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_33"> occurs as an apparent variable
is not a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_34">. Thus <i>e.g.</i> "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . x = x\)" src="images/171.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.786ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_171.svg">" will
mean "everything is equal to itself." This is an absolute constant,
not a function of a variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_35">. This is why the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_36"> is called an
apparent variable in such cases.</p>

<p>Besides the "<i>range</i>" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_37"> in "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_4">" or
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . \phi x\)" src="images/168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_168.svg_3">," which is the field of the values that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_38"> may have, we shall speak of the "<i>scope</i>" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_39">, meaning
the function of which all values or some value are being affirmed. If
we are asserting all values (or some value) of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_5">," "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_6">"
is the scope of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_40">; if we are asserting all values (or some
value) of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset p\)" src="images/172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.798ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_172.svg">," "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset p\)" src="images/172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.798ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_172.svg_1">" is the scope
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_41">; if we are asserting all values (or some value) of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_173.svg">,"
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_173.svg_1">" will be the scope of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_42">, and so on. The
scope of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_43"> is indicated by the number of dots after the "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_44">)"
or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x\)" src="images/174.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.552ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_174.svg">"; that is to say, the scope extends forwards until we
reach an equal number of dots not indicating a logical product, or a
greater number indicating a logical product, or the end of the asserted
proposition in which the "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_45">)" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x\)" src="images/174.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.552ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_174.svg_1">" occurs, whichever
of these happens first<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_5" id="FNanchor_5">[5]</a>. Thus <i>e.g.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(x) \colon \phi x . \supset . \psi x \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.505ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_175.svg"></span>
will mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_7"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg">," but
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(x) \colon \phi x . \supset . \psi x \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.505ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_175.svg_1"></span>
will mean "if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_8"> is always true, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_1"> is true for
the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_46">."</p>

<p>Note that in the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x) \colon \phi x . \supset . \psi x \]" src="images/177.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.242ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_177.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_18">[Pg 18]</span>
the two <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_47">'s have no connection with each other. Since only one dot
follows the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_48"> in brackets, the scope of the first <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_49"> is limited
to the "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_12">" immediately following the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_50"> in brackets. It
usually conduces to clearness to write
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp; (x) \ldotp {\phi}x \ldotp \supset \ldotp {\psi}y\\ \text{rather than} \quad &amp; (x) \ldotp {\psi}x \ldotp \supset \ldotp {\psi}x\text{,}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/178.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 27.398ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_178.svg"></span>
since the use of different letters emphasises the absence of connection
between the two variables; but there is no logical necessity to use
different letters, and it is <i>sometimes</i> convenient to use the
same letter.</p>

<p><i>Ambiguous assertion and the real variable.</i> Any value
"<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_13">" of the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_9"> can be asserted. Such an
assertion of an ambiguous member of the values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_10"> is
symbolised by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash \ldotp {\phi}x.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/179.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.928ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_179.svg"></span></p>

<p>Ambiguous assertion of this kind is a primitive idea, which cannot
be defined in terms of the assertion of propositions. This primitive
idea is the one which embodies the use of the variable. Apart from
ambiguous assertion, the consideration of "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_14">," which is an
ambiguous member of the values of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}\hat{x}\)" src="images/146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_146.svg_1">, would be of little
consequence. When we are considering or asserting "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_15">," the
variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_51"> is called a "real variable." Take, for example, the law
of excluded middle in the form which it has in traditional formal logic:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c} a\, \text{is either}\, b\, \text{or not}\, b.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 21.52ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_180.svg"></span>
Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg"> are real variables: as they vary, different
propositions are expressed, though all of them are true. While <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_2">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_1"> are undetermined, as in the above enunciation, no one
definite proposition is asserted, but what is asserted is <i>any</i>
value of the propositional function in question. This can only be
legitimately asserted if, whatever value may be chosen, that value is
true, <i>i.e.</i> if all the values are true. Thus the above form of
the law of excluded middle is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(a, b).a\, \text{is either}\, b\, \text{or not}\, b,\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/182.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.459ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_182.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> to "it is always true that <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_3"> is either <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_2"> or not
<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_3">." But these two, though equivalent, are not identical, and we
shall find it necessary to keep them distinguished.</p>

<p>When we assert something containing a real variable, as in <i>e.g.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash \ldotp x = x,\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/183.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 11.891ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_183.svg"></span>
we are asserting <i>any</i> value of a propositional function. When we
assert something containing an apparent variable, as in
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} \unicode{x201c}\vdash \ldotp (x) \ldotp x = x\unicode{x201d}\\ \text{or} \quad \unicode{x201c}\vdash \ldotp (\exists x) \ldotp x = x,\unicode{x201d} \end{align} \]" src="images/184.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 21.489ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_184.svg"></span>
we are asserting, in the first case <i>all</i> values, in the second
case <i>some</i> value (undetermined), of the propositional function in
question. It is plain that<span class="pagenum" id="Page_19">[Pg 19]</span> we can only legitimately assert "<i>any</i>
value" if <i>all</i> values are true; for otherwise, since the value of
the variable remains to be determined, it might be so determined as to
give a false proposition. Thus in the above instance, since we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp;\vdash \ldotp  x = x\\ \text{we may infer}\qquad\qquad &amp;\vdash \ldotp (x) \ldotp x = x. \end{align} \]" src="images/185.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 34.811ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_185.svg"></span>
And generally, given an assertion containing a real variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_52">, we
may transform the real variable into an apparent one by placing the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_53"> in brackets at the beginning, followed by as many dots as there
are after the assertion-sign.</p>

<p>When we assert something containing a real variable, we cannot strictly
be said to be asserting a <i>proposition</i>, for we only obtain a
definite proposition by assigning a value to the variable, and then our
assertion only applies to one definite case, so that it has not at all
the same force as before. When what we assert contains a real variable,
we are asserting a wholly undetermined one of all the propositions
that result from giving various values to the variable. It will be
convenient to speak of such assertions as <i>asserting a propositional
function</i>. The ordinary formulae of mathematics contain such
assertions; for example
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\text{sin}^{2} x + \text{cos}^{2} x = 1\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/186.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 19.545ex; height: 2.185ex;" id="img_images_186.svg"></span>
does not assert this or that particular case of the formula, nor does
it assert that the formula holds for <i>all</i> possible values of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_54">, though it is equivalent to this latter assertion; it simply
asserts that the formula holds, leaving <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_55"> wholly undetermined;
and it is able to do this legitimately, because, however <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_56"> may be
determined, a true proposition results.</p>

<p>Although an assertion containing a real variable does not, in
strictness, assert a proposition, yet it will be spoken of as asserting
a proposition except when the nature of the ambiguous assertion
involved is under discussion.</p>

<p><i>Definition and real variables.</i> When the <i>definiens</i>
contains one or more real variables, the <i>definiendum</i> must
also contain them. For in this case we have a function of the real
variables, and the <i>definiendum</i> must have the same meaning as the
<i>definiens</i> for all values of these variables, which requires that
the symbol which is the <i>definiendum</i> should contain the letters
representing the real variables. This rule is not always observed by
mathematicians, and its infringement has sometimes caused important
confusions of thought, notably in geometry and the philosophy of space.</p>

<p>In the definitions given above of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \ldotp q\)" src="images/60.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.185ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_60.svg_3">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \supset q\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.196ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_5">"
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \equiv q\)" src="images/73.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.196ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_73.svg_4">," <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_104"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_74"> are real variables, and
therefore appear on both sides of the definition. In the definition
of "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\{(x) \ldotp {\phi}x\}\)" src="images/156.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.725ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_156.svg_1">" only the function considered,
namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg">, is a real variable; thus so far as concerns the
rule in question, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_57"> need not appear on the left. But when a real
variable is a function, it is necessary to indicate<span class="pagenum" id="Page_20">[Pg 20]</span> how the argument
is to be supplied, and therefore there are objections to omitting an
apparent variable where (as in the case before us) this is the argument
to the function which is the real variable. This appears more plainly
if, instead of a general function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg">, we take some
particular function, say "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x} = a\)" src="images/189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 2.018ex;" id="img_images_189.svg">," and consider the definition
of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\{(x) . x = a\}\)" src="images/190.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.591ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_190.svg">. Our definition gives
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\sim}\{(x) . x = a\}. = .(\exists x). {\sim}(x = a) \qquad \text{Df.} \]" src="images/191.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.285ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_191.svg"></span>
But if we had adopted a notation in which the ambiguous value "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x = a\)" src="images/192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_192.svg">,"
containing the apparent variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_58">, did not occur in
the <i>definiendum</i>, we should have had to construct a notation
employing the function itself, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x} = a\)" src="images/189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 2.018ex;" id="img_images_189.svg_1">." This does not
involve an apparent variable, but would be clumsy in practice. In fact
we have found it convenient and possible—except in the explanatory
portions—to keep the explicit use of symbols of the type "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_11">,"
either as constants [<i>e.g.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x} = a\)" src="images/189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 2.018ex;" id="img_images_189.svg_2">] or as real variables,
almost entirely out of this work.</p>

<p><i>Propositions connecting real and apparent variables</i>. The most important
propositions connecting real and apparent variables are the following:</p>

<p>(1) "When a propositional function can be asserted, so can the
proposition that all values of the function are true." More briefly, if
less exactly, "what holds of any, however chosen, holds of all." This
translates itself into the rule that when a real variable occurs in
an assertion, we may turn it into an apparent variable by putting the
letter representing it in brackets immediately after the assertion-sign.</p>

<p>(2) "What holds of all, holds of any," <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon (x). \phi x . \supset . \phi y. \]" src="images/193.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.949ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_193.svg"></span>
This states "if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_9"> is always true, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg"> is true."</p>

<p>(3) "If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_1"> is true, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_10"> is sometimes true,"
<i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon \phi y . \supset . (\exists x). \phi x. \]" src="images/195.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.207ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_195.svg"></span>
An asserted proposition of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x). \phi x\)" src="images/196.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_196.svg">" expresses
an "existence-theorem," namely "there exists an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_59"> for which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_11"> is true." The above proposition gives what is in practice
the only way of proving existence-theorems: we always have to find
some particular <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_5"> for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_2"> holds, and thence to infer
"<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x). \phi x\)" src="images/196.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_196.svg_1">." If we were to assume what is called the
multiplicative axiom, or the equivalent axiom enunciated by Zermelo,
that would, in an important class of cases, give an existence-theorem
where no particular instance of its truth can be found.</p>

<p>In virtue of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon (x). \phi x . \supset . \phi y\)" src="images/197.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.321ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_197.svg">" and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon \phi y . \supset . (\exists x). \phi x\)" src="images/198.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.578ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_198.svg">," we have
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon (x) . \phi x . \supset . (\exists x). \phi x\)" src="images/199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.824ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_199.svg">,"
<i>i.e.</i> "what is always true is sometimes true." This would not
be the case if nothing existed; thus our assumptions contain the
assumption that there is something. This is involved in the principle<span class="pagenum" id="Page_21">[Pg 21]</span>
that what holds of all, holds of any; for this would not be true if
there were no "any."</p>

<p>(4) "If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_12"> is always true, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_2"> is always true, then
'<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x . \psi x\)" src="images/200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.416ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_200.svg">' is always true," <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp (x) . \phi x \colon (x) . \psi x : \supset . (x) . \phi x . \psi x. \]" src="images/201.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_201.svg"></span>
(This requires that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_1"> should be functions which
take arguments of the same <i>type</i>. We shall explain this requirement at a
later stage.) The converse also holds; <i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp (x) . \phi x . \psi x . \supset \colon (x) . \phi x : (x) . \psi x. \]" src="images/202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.688ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_202.svg"></span></p>

<p>It is to some extent optional which of the propositions connecting
real and apparent variables are taken as primitive propositions. The
primitive propositions assumed, on this subject, in the body of the
work (<a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>), are the following:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \text{(1)}\qquad \vdash \colon \phi x . \supset. (\exists z) . \phi z.\\ \text{(2)}\qquad \vdash \colon \phi x \lor \phi y. \supset . (\exists z) . \phi z, \end{array} \]" src="images/203.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 29.925ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_203.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_13"> is true, or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_3"> is true, then
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists z) . \phi z\)" src="images/204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.597ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_204.svg"> is true. (On the necessity for this primitive
proposition, see remarks on <a href="#_9_11" class="pginternal">*9·11</a> in the body of the work.)</p>

<p>(3) If we can assert <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_4">, where y is a real variable, then we
can assert <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) . \phi x\)" src="images/165.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_165.svg_1">; <i>i.e.</i> what holds of any, however
chosen, holds of all.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_22">[Pg 22]</span></p>

<p><i>Formal implication and formal equivalence</i>. When an implication,
say <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x . \supset . \psi x\)" src="images/205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.182ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_205.svg">, is said to hold always, <i>i.e.</i>
when <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \colon \phi x . \supset . \psi x\)" src="images/206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.242ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_206.svg">, we shall say that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_14"> <i>formally implies</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_3">; and propositions of the
form "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \colon \phi x . \supset . \psi x\)" src="images/206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.242ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_206.svg_1">" will be said to state
<i>formal implications</i>. In the usual instances of implication,
such as "'Socrates is a man' implies 'Socrates is mortal,'" we have
a proposition of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x . \supset . \psi x\)" src="images/205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.182ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_205.svg_1">" in a case
in which "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \colon \phi x . \supset . \psi x\)" src="images/206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.242ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_206.svg_2">" is true. In such
a case, we feel the implication as a particular case of a formal
implication. Thus it has come about that implications which are not
particular cases of formal implications have not been regarded as
implications at all. There is also a practical ground for the neglect
of such implications, for, speaking generally, they can only be
<i>known</i> when it is already known either that their hypothesis is
false or that their conclusion is true; and in neither of these cases
do they serve to make us know the conclusion, since in the first case
the conclusion need not be true, and in the second it is known already.
Thus such implications do not serve the purpose for which implications
are chiefly useful, namely that of making us know, by deduction,
conclusions of which we were previously ignorant. <i>Formal</i>
implications, on the contrary, do serve this purpose, owing to the
psychological fact that we often know "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \colon \phi x . \supset .\psi x\)" src="images/207.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.242ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_207.svg">"
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_5">, in cases where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi y\)" src="images/208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.581ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_208.svg"> (which follows from
