other use of <img alt="" data-tex="\(({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.814ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_314.svg_4">.</p>

<p>We now proceed to define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_315.svg_2">" so that it can
be read "the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_114"> satisfying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_24"> exists." (It will be observed
that this is a different meaning of existence from that which we
express by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists\)" src="images/317.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.258ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_317.svg">"). Its definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{E}! ({℩}x) (\phi x) . =: (\exists c): \phi x . \equiv_{x} . x = c\quad \text{Df,} \]" src="images/318.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.012ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_318.svg"></span>
<i>i.e</i>. "the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_115"> satisfying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_7"> exists" is to mean
"there is an object <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_25"> is true when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_116"> is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_1"> but not otherwise."</p>

<p>The following are equivalent forms:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash  \colon\ldotp \text{E}! ({℩}x) (\phi x) . \equiv : (\exists c) : \phi c : \phi x . \supset_{x} . x = c,\\ &amp;\vdash  \colon\ldotp \text{E}! ({℩}x) (\phi x) . \equiv : (\exists c) . \phi c : \phi x . \phi y . \supset_{x, y} . x = y,\\ &amp;\vdash  \colon\ldotp \text{E}! ({℩}x) (\phi x) . \equiv : (\exists c) : \phi c : x \neq c . \supset_{x} . \sim\phi x. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/320.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.558ex; width: 46.506ex; height: 8.247ex;" id="img_images_320.svg"></span></p>

<p>The last of these states that "the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_117"> satisfying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_8">
exists" is equivalent to "there is an object <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_2"> satisfying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_18">,
and every object other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_3"> does not satisfy <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_19">."</p>

<p>The kind of existence just defined covers a great many cases. Thus for
example "the most perfect Being exists" will mean:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists c): x\,\,\text{ is most perfect}. \equiv_{x} . x = c, \]" src="images/321.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.464ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_321.svg"></span>
which, taking the last of the above equivalences, is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists c) : c\text{ is most perfect}: x \neq c . \supset_{x} . x\,\,\text{ is not most perfect}. \]" src="images/322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.899ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_322.svg"></span></p>

<p>A proposition such as "Apollo exists" is really of the same logical
form, although it does not explicitly contain the word <i>the</i>. For
"Apollo" means really "the object having such-and-such properties,"
say "the object having the properties enumerated in the Classical
Dictionary<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_9" id="FNanchor_9">[9]</a>." If these properties make up the propositional function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_26">, then "Apollo" means "<img alt="" data-tex="\((℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/323.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.814ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_323.svg">," and "Apollo exists"
means "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_324.svg">." To take another illustration, "the
author of Waverley" means "the man who (or rather, the object which)
wrote Waverley." Thus "Scott is the author of Waverley" is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Scott} = ({℩}x)(x\,\text{ wrote Waverley}). \]" src="images/325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.682ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_325.svg"></span>
Here (as we observed before) the importance of <i>identity</i> in
connection with descriptions plainly appears.</p>

<p>The notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.814ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_314.svg_5">," which is long and inconvenient, is
seldom used, being chiefly required to lead up to another notation,
namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg">" meaning "the object having the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_9"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_28">." That is, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} Rʻy = ({℩}x) (xRy)\quad \text{Df.} \end{aligned} \]" src="images/327.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.804ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_327.svg"></span>
The inverted comma may be read "of." Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_1">" is read "the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_10">
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_29">." Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_11"> is the relation of father to son, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_2">"
means "the father of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_30">"; if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_12"> is the relation of son to father,
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_3">" means "the son of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_31">," which will<span class="pagenum" id="Page_33">[Pg 33]</span> only "exist" if <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_32">
has one son and no more. <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_4"> is a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_33">, but not a
propositional function; we shall call it a <i>descriptive</i> function.
All the ordinary functions of mathematics are of this kind, as will
appear more fully in the sequel. Thus in our notation, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin y\)" src="images/328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.264ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_328.svg">"
would be written "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin ʻy\)" src="images/329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.621ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_329.svg">," and "sin" would stand for the relation
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin ʻy\)" src="images/329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.621ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_329.svg_1"> has to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_34">. Instead of a variable descriptive
function <img alt="" data-tex="\(fy\)" src="images/330.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.353ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_330.svg">, we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_5">, where the variable relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_13">
takes the place of the variable function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_2">. A descriptive function
will in general exist while <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_35"> belongs to a certain domain, but not
outside that domain; thus if we are dealing with positive rationals,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\surd y\)" src="images/331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.038ex; height: 2.274ex;" id="img_images_331.svg"> will be significant if <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_36"> is a perfect square, but not
otherwise; if we are dealing with real numbers, and agree that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\surd y\)" src="images/331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.038ex; height: 2.274ex;" id="img_images_331.svg_1">"
is to mean the <i>positive</i> square root (or, is to mean the
negative square root), <img alt="" data-tex="\(\surd y\)" src="images/331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.038ex; height: 2.274ex;" id="img_images_331.svg_2"> will be significant provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_37">
is positive, but not otherwise; and so on. Thus every descriptive
function has what we may call a "domain of definition" or a "domain of
existence," which may be thus defined: If the function in question is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_6">, its domain of definition or of existence will be the class of
those arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_38"> for which we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.353ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_332.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>
for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}! (℩x) (xRy)\)" src="images/333.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.462ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_333.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> for which there is one
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_118">, and no more, having the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_14"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_39">.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_15"> is any relation, we will speak of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_7"> as the "associated
descriptive function." A great many of the constant relations which
we shall have occasion to introduce are only or chiefly important on
account of their associated descriptive functions. In such cases, it is
easier (though less correct) to begin by assigning the meaning of the
descriptive function, and to deduce the meaning of the relation from
that of the descriptive function. This will be done in the following
explanations of notation.</p>

<p><i>Various descriptive functions of relations.</i> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_16"> is any
relation, the <i>converse</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_17"> is the relation which holds
between <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_40"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_119"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_18"> holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_120"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_41">.
Thus <i>greater</i> is the converse of <i>less</i>, <i>before</i>
of <i>after</i>, <i>cause</i> of <i>effect</i>, <i>husband</i> of
<i>wife</i>, etc. The converse of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_19"> is written<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_10" id="FNanchor_10">[10]</a> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}ʻR\)" src="images/334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.161ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_334.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}\)" src="images/335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_335.svg">. The definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \breve{R} &amp;= \hat{x}\hat{y} (yRx) \quad &amp;\text{Df},\\ \text{Cnv}ʻR &amp;= \breve{R} \quad &amp;\text{Df}.\\ \end{aligned} \]" src="images/336.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.753ex; width: 28.298ex; height: 6.638ex;" id="img_images_336.svg"></span>
The second of these is not a formally correct definition, since we
ought to define "Cnv" and deduce the meaning of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}ʻR\)" src="images/334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.161ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_334.svg_1">. But
it is not worth while to adopt this plan in our present introductory
account, which aims at simplicity rather than formal correctness.</p>

<p>A relation is called <i>symmetrical</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R = \breve{R}\)" src="images/337.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.451ex; height: 2.6ex;" id="img_images_337.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> if it holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_42"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_121"> whenever it holds
between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_122"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_43"> (and therefore vice versa). Identity,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_34">[Pg 34]</span>
diversity, agreement or disagreement in any respect, are symmetrical
relations. A relation is called <i>asymmetrical</i> when it is
incompatible with its converse, <i>i.e.</i> when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \dot{\cap}\breve{R} = \dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/338.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.531ex; height: 2.6ex;" id="img_images_338.svg">, or, what is equivalent,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ xRy . \supset_{x, y} . \sim{(yRx)}. \]" src="images/339.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 19.121ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_339.svg"></span></p>

<p>Before and after, greater and less, ancestor and descendant, are
asymmetrical, as are all other relations of the sort that lead to
<i>series</i>. But there are many asymmetrical relations which do not
lead to series, for instance, that of wife's brother<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_11" id="FNanchor_11">[11]</a>. A relation
maybe neither symmetrical nor asymmetrical; for example, this holds of
the relation of inclusion between classes: <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset \beta\)" src="images/279.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_279.svg_3">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta \subset \alpha\)" src="images/340.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_340.svg"> will both be true if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = \beta\)" src="images/284.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_284.svg_1">,
but otherwise only one of them, at most, will be true. The relation
<i>brother</i> is neither symmetrical nor asymmetrical, for if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_123"> is
the brother of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_44">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_45"> may be either the brother or the sister of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_124">.</p>

<p>In the propositional function <img alt="" data-tex="\(xRy\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_266.svg_1">, we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_125"> the referent and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_46"> the relatum. The class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}(xRy)\)" src="images/341.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.174ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_341.svg">, consisting of all the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_126">'s which have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_20"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_47">, is called the class of
referents of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_48"> with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_21">; the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}(xRy)\)" src="images/342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.989ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_342.svg">,
consisting of all the <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_49">'s to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_127"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_22">,
is called the class of relata of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_128"> with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_23">. These
two classes are denoted respectively by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_343.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.102ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_344.svg">. Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \overrightarrow{R}ʻy \,= \hat{x}(xRy) \qquad \text{Df},\\ \overleftarrow{R}ʻx = \hat{y}(xRy) \qquad \text{Df}. \end{array} \]" src="images/345.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.643ex; width: 22.683ex; height: 8.416ex;" id="img_images_345.svg"></span>
The arrow runs towards <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_50"> in the first case, to show that we are
concerned with things having the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_24"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_51">; it runs away
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_129"> in the second case to show that the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_25"> goes
<i>from</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_130"> to the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.102ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_344.svg_1">. It runs in
fact <i>from</i> a referent and <i>towards</i> a relatum.</p>

<p>The notations <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_343.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.102ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_344.svg_2"> are
very important, and are used constantly. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_26"> is the relation of
parent to child, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_343.svg_2"> = the parents of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_52">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.102ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_344.svg_3"> = the children of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_131">. We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\vdash \colon x \in \overrightarrow{R}ʻy . \equiv . xRy\\ \text{and}\qquad\qquad &amp;\vdash \colon y \in \overleftarrow{R}ʻx . \equiv . xRy. \end{array} \]" src="images/346.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.643ex; width: 34.846ex; height: 8.416ex;" id="img_images_346.svg"></span>
These equivalences are often embodied in common language. For example,
we say indiscriminately "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_132"> is an inhabitant of London" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_133">
inhabits London." If we put "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_27">" for "inhabits," "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_134"> inhabits
London" is "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xR\)" src="images/347.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.011ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_347.svg"> London," while "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_135"> is an inhabitant of London" is
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \overrightarrow{R}ʻ\text{London}\)" src="images/348.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.585ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_348.svg">."</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_35">[Pg 35]</span></p>

<p>Instead of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_349.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}\)" src="images/350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.451ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_350.svg"> we
sometimes use <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sg}ʻR\)" src="images/351.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 5.097ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_351.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{gs}ʻR\)" src="images/352.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 5.097ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_352.svg">, where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sg}\)" src="images/353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_353.svg">"
stands for "sagitta," and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{gs}\)" src="images/354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_354.svg">" is "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sg}\)" src="images/353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_353.svg_1">" backwards.
Thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \text{sg}ʻR &amp;= \overrightarrow{R} \qquad \text{Df},\\ \text{gs}ʻR &amp;= \overleftarrow{R} \qquad \text{Df}. \end{array} \]" src="images/355.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.643ex; width: 19.774ex; height: 8.416ex;" id="img_images_355.svg"></span>
These notations are sometimes more convenient than an arrow when the
relation concerned is represented by a combination of letters, instead
of a single letter such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_28">. Thus <i>e.g.</i> we should write
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sg}ʻ(R \dot{\cap} S)\)" src="images/356.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.826ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_356.svg">, rather than put an arrow over the whole
length of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \dot{\cap} S\)" src="images/357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.686ex; height: 2.138ex;" id="img_images_357.svg">).</p>

<p>The class of all terms that have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_29"> to something or
other is called the <i>domain</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_30">. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_31"> is the
relation of parent and child, the domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_32"> will be the class of
parents. We represent the domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_33"> by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg">." Thus we
put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{D}ʻR = \hat{x} \{(\exists y) . xRy\} \qquad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.204ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_359.svg"></span>
Similarly the class of all terms to which something or other has the
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_34"> is called the <i>converse domain</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_35">; it is the
same as the domain of the converse of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_36">. The converse domain of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_37"> is represented by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg">"; thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \hat{y} \{(\exists x) . xRy\} \qquad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/361.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.833ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_361.svg"></span>
The sum of the domain and the converse domain is called the field, and
is represented by <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_362.svg">: thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ CʻR = \text{D}ʻR \cup \text{ᗡ}ʻR \qquad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/363.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.136ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_363.svg"></span></p>

<p>The <i>field</i> is chiefly important in connection with series. If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_38"> is the ordering relation of a series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_362.svg_1"> will be the class
of terms of the series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_1"> will be all the terms except
the last (if any), and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_1"> will be all the terms except
the first (if any). The first term, if it exists, is the only member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR \cap - \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.51ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_364.svg">, since it is the only term which
is a predecessor but not a follower. Similarly the last term (if any)
is the only member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR \cap - \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/365.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.51ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_365.svg">. The condition
that a series should have no end is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR \subset \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.252ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_366.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> "every follower is a predecessor"; the condition for no
beginning is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/367.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.252ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_367.svg">. These conditions are
equivalent respectively to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR = CʻR\)" src="images/368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.614ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_368.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR = CʻR\)" src="images/369.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.243ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_369.svg">.</p>

<p>The <i>relative product</i> of two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_39"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_2"> is
the relation which holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_136"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_4"> when there is an
intermediate term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_53"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_137"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_40"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_54">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_55"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_3"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_5">. The relative product of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_41"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_4"> is represented by <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg">; thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;R \mid S = \hat{x}\hat{z} \{(\exists y) . xRy. ySz\} \qquad \text{Df},\\ \text{whence}\qquad\qquad &amp;\vdash \colon x(R \mid S) z . \equiv . (\exists y) . xRy. ySz. \end{array} \]" src="images/371.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.217ex; width: 52.616ex; height: 5.566ex;" id="img_images_371.svg"></span>
Thus "paternal aunt" is the relative product of <i>sister</i> and
<i>father</i>; "paternal grandmother" is the relative product of
<i>mother</i> and <i>father</i>; "maternal<span class="pagenum" id="Page_36">[Pg 36]</span> grandfather" is the
relative product of <i>father</i> and <i>mother</i>. The relative
product is not commutative, but it obeys the associative law,
<i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \ldotp (P\mid Q)\mid R = P\mid (Q\mid R)\text{.} \]" src="images/372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.51ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_372.svg"></span>
It also obeys the distributive law with regard to the logical addition
of relations, <i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} \vdash \ldotp P\mid (Q \unicode{x228d} R) &amp;= (P\mid Q) \unicode{x228d} (P\mid R)\text{,}\\ \vdash \ldotp (Q \unicode{x228d} R) \mid P &amp;= (Q\mid P) \unicode{x228d} (R\mid P)\text{.}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/373.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 31.798ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_373.svg"></span></p>

<p>But with regard to the logical <i>product</i>, we have only
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} \vdash \ldotp P\mid (Q\dot{\cap}R)\unicode{x2abd}(P\mid Q)\dot{\cap}(P\mid R)\text{,}\\ \vdash \ldotp (Q\dot{\cap}R)\mid P\unicode{x2abd}(Q\mid P)\dot{\cap}(R\mid P)\text{.}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/374.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.428ex; width: 30.442ex; height: 5.986ex;" id="img_images_374.svg"></span></p>

<p>The relative product does not obey the law of tautology, <i>i.e.</i> we
do not have in general <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid R = R\)" src="images/375.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 10.055ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_375.svg">. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R^{2} = R\mid R \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/376.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 16.354ex; height: 2.563ex;" id="img_images_376.svg"></span>
Thus paternal grandfather = (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{father})^{2}\)" src="images/377.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.721ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_377.svg">,</p>

<p>maternal grandmother = (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{mother})^{2}\)" src="images/378.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.913ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_378.svg">.</p>

<p>A relation is called <i>transitive</i> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{2}\unicode{x2abd}R\)" src="images/379.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.78ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_379.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> when, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(xRy\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_266.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(yRz\)" src="images/380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.878ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_380.svg">, we always have <img alt="" data-tex="\(xRz\)" src="images/381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.063ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_381.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> when
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ xRy \ldotp yRz \ldotp \supset_{x, y, z} \ldotp xRz\text{.} \]" src="images/382.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 20.988ex; height: 2.213ex;" id="img_images_382.svg"></span>
Relations which generate series are always transitive; thus <i>e.g.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x \gt y \ldotp y \gt z \ldotp \supset_{x, y, z} \ldotp x \gt z\text{.} \]" src="images/383.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 24.888ex; height: 1.889ex;" id="img_images_383.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg"> is a relation which generates a series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_1"> may conveniently
be read "precedes"; thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy \ldotp yPz \ldotp \supset_{x, y, z}\ldotp xPz\)" src="images/385.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 20.305ex; height: 2.213ex;" id="img_images_385.svg">"
becomes "if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_138"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_56"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_57"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_6">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_139">
always precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_7">." The class of relations which generate series
are partially characterized by the fact that they are transitive and
asymmetrical, and never relate a term to itself.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_2"> is a relation which generates a series, and if we have not
merely <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}\unicode{x2abd}P\)" src="images/386.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.869ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_386.svg">, but <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2}=P\)" src="images/387.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.528ex; height: 2.072ex;" id="img_images_387.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_3"> generates a
series which is <i>compact</i> (<i>überall dicht</i>), <i>i.e.</i> such
that there are terms between any two. For in this case we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ xPz \ldotp \supset \ldotp (\exists y) \ldotp xPy \ldotp yPz\text{,} \]" src="images/388.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.547ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_388.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_140"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_8">, there is a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_58"> such that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_141"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_59"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_60"> precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_9">, <i>i.e.</i> there is
a term between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_142"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_10">. Thus among relations which generate
series, those which generate compact series are those for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2} = P\)" src="images/389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.528ex; height: 2.072ex;" id="img_images_389.svg">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_37">[Pg 37]</span></p>

<p>Many relations which do not generate series are transitive, for
example, identity, or the relation of inclusion between classes. Such
cases arise when the relations are not asymmetrical. Relations which
are transitive and symmetrical are an important class: they may be
regarded as consisting in the possession of some common property.</p>

<p><i>Plural descriptive functions.</i> The class of terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_143"> which
have the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_42"> to some member of a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_39"> is denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/391.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.777ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_391.svg">. The definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Rʻʻ\alpha = \hat{x}\{(\exists y) \ldotp y \in \alpha \ldotp xRy\} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.347ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_392.svg"></span>
Thus for example let <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_43"> be the relation of <i>inhabiting</i>, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_40"> the class of towns; then <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg_1"> = inhabitants of
towns. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_44"> be the relation "less than" among rationals, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_41"> the class of those rationals which are of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1 - 2^{-n}\)" src="images/393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.42ex; height: 1.939ex;" id="img_images_393.svg">, for integral values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg">; then <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg_2"> will be
all rationals less than some member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_42">, <i>i.e.</i> all
rationals less than <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_4"> is the generating relation of a
series, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_43"> is any class of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_396.svg">
will be predecessors of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_44">'s, <i>i.e.</i> the segment defined
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_45">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_6"> is a relation such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻy\)" src="images/397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.165ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_397.svg"> always exists
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \alpha\)" src="images/398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.323ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_398.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_396.svg_1"> will be the class of all terms of
the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻy\)" src="images/397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.165ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_397.svg_1"> for values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_61"> which are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_46">;
<i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Pʻʻ\alpha = \hat{x}\{(\exists y) \ldotp y \in \alpha \ldotp x = Pʻy\}\text{.} \]" src="images/399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.002ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_399.svg"></span>
Thus a member of the class "fathers of great men" will be the father
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_62">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_63"> is some great man. In other cases, this will
not hold; for instance, let <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_7"> be the relation of a number to any
number of which it is a factor; then <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ(\text{even numbers}) = \text{factors of even numbers}\)" src="images/400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.7ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_400.svg">,
but this class is not composed of terms of the form "<i>the</i> factor
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_144">," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_145"> is an even number, because numbers do not have
only one factor apiece.</p>

<p><i>Unit classes.</i> The class whose only member is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_146"> might be
thought to be identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_147">, but Peano and Frege have shown that
this is not the case. (The reasons why this is not the case will be
explained in a preliminary way in <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a> of the Introduction.) We
denote by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\)" src="images/401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_401.svg">" the class whose only member is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_148">: thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \iotaʻx = \hat{y}(y = x) \quad \text{Df}\text{,} \]" src="images/402.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.07ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_402.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\)" src="images/401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_401.svg_1">" means "the class of objects which are
identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_149">."</p>

<p>The class consisting of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_150"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_64"> will be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx \cup \iotaʻy\)" src="images/403.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_403.svg">; the class got by adding <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_151"> to a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_47"> will
be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \iotaʻx\)" src="images/404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.415ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_404.svg">; the class got by taking away <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_152"> from a
class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_48"> will be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha - \iotaʻx\)" src="images/405.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.666ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_405.svg">. (We write <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha - \beta\)" src="images/406.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_406.svg">
as an abbreviation for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap -\beta\)" src="images/407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.003ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_407.svg">.)</p>

<p>It will be observed that unit classes have been defined without
reference to the number <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_1">; in fact, we use unit classes to define
the number <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_2">. This number is defined as the class of unit classes,
<i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ 1 = \hat{\alpha} \{(\exists x) \ldotp \alpha = \iotaʻx\} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.407ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_408.svg"></span>
This leads to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \alpha \in 1 \ldotp \equiv \colon (\exists x) \colon y \in \alpha \ldotp \equiv_{y} \ldotp y = x\text{.} \]" src="images/409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 33.945ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_409.svg"></span>
From this it appears further that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp;\vdash \colon \alpha \in 1 \ldotp \equiv \ldotp \text{E}! ({℩}x) (x \in \alpha)\text{,}\\ \text{whence} &amp;\vdash \colon \hat{z} ({\phi}z) \in 1 \ldotp \equiv \ldotp \text{E}! ({℩}x) ({\phi}x)\text{,}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/410.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.104ex; width: 34.675ex; height: 5.339ex;" id="img_images_410.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}({\phi}z)\)" src="images/232.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_232.svg_1"> is a unit class" is equivalent to
"the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_153"> satisfying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_20"> exists."</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_38">[Pg 38]</span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in 1\)" src="images/411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.345ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_411.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_412.svg"> is the only member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_49">, for the only member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_50"> is the only term to
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_51"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_1">. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_413.svg">"
takes the place of "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({{℩}}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_414.svg">," if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_52"> stands for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg">. In practice, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_413.svg_1">" is a more
convenient notation than "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg">," and is generally used
instead of "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_1">."</p>

<p>The above account has explained most of the logical notation
employed in the present work. In the applications to various parts
of mathematics, other definitions are introduced; but the objects
defined by these later definitions belong, for the most part, rather
to mathematics than to logic. The reader who has mastered the symbols
explained above will find that any later formulae can be deciphered by
the help of comparatively few additional definitions.</p>

<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_39">[Pg 39]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="CHAPTER_II">CHAPTER II.<br>
THE THEORY OF LOGICAL TYPES.</h2>
</div>


<p>THE theory of logical types, to be explained in the present Chapter,
recommended itself to us in the first instance by its ability to solve
certain contradictions, of which the one best known to mathematicians
is Burali-Forti's concerning the greatest ordinal. But the theory in
question is not wholly dependent upon this indirect recommendation:
it has also a certain consonance with common sense which makes it
inherently credible. In what follows, we shall therefore first set
forth the theory on its own account, and then apply it to the solution
of the contradictions.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
I. <i>The Vicious-Circle Principle</i>.</p>


<p>An analysis of the paradoxes to be avoided shows that they all result
from a certain kind of vicious circle<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_12" id="FNanchor_12">[12]</a>. The vicious circles in
question arise from supposing that a collection of objects may contain
members which can only be defined by means of the collection as a
whole. Thus, for example, the collection of <i>propositions</i> will be
supposed to contain a proposition stating that "all propositions are
either true or false." It would seem, however, that such a statement
could not be legitimate unless "all propositions" referred to some
already definite collection, which it cannot do if new propositions are
created by statements about "all propositions." We shall, therefore,
have to say that statements about "all propositions" are meaningless.
More generally, given any set of objects such that, if we suppose the
set to have a total, it will contain members which presuppose this
total, then such a set cannot have a total. By saying that a set has
"no total," we mean, primarily, that no significant statement can be
made about "all its members." Propositions, as the above illustration
shows, must be a set having no total. The same is true, as we shall
shortly see, of propositional functions, even when these are restricted
to such as can significantly have as argument a given object <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_4">. In
such cases, it is necessary to break up our set into smaller sets, each
of which is capable of a total. This is what the theory of types aims
at effecting.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_40">[Pg 40]</span></p>

<p>The principle which enables us to avoid illegitimate totalities may
be stated as follows: "Whatever involves all of a collection must not
be one of the collection"; or, conversely: "If, provided a certain
collection had a total, it would have members only definable in terms
of that total, then the said collection has no total." We shall call
this the "vicious-circle principle," because it enables us to avoid the
vicious circles involved in the assumption of illegitimate totalities.
Arguments which are condemned by the vicious-circle principle will
be called "vicious-circle fallacies." Such arguments, in certain
circumstances, may lead to contradictions, but it often happens that
the conclusions to which they lead are in fact true, though the
arguments are fallacious. Take, for example, the law of excluded
middle, in the form "all propositions are true or false." If from this
law we argue that, because the law of excluded middle is a proposition,
therefore the law of excluded middle is true or false, we incur a
vicious-circle fallacy. "All propositions" must be in some way limited
before it becomes a legitimate totality, and any limitation which makes
it legitimate must make any statement about the totality fall outside
the totality. Similarly, the imaginary sceptic, who asserts that he
knows nothing, and is refuted by being asked if he knows that he knows
nothing, has asserted nonsense, and has been fallaciously refuted by
an argument which involves a vicious-circle fallacy. In order that
the sceptic's assertion may become significant, it is necessary to
place some limitation upon the things of which he is asserting his
ignorance, because the things of which it is possible to be ignorant
form an illegitimate totality. But as soon as a suitable limitation has
been placed by him upon the collection of propositions of which he is
asserting his ignorance, the proposition that he is ignorant of every
member of this collection must not itself be one of the collection.
Hence any significant scepticism is not open to the above form of
refutation.</p>

<p>The paradoxes of symbolic logic concern various sorts of objects:
propositions, classes, cardinal and ordinal numbers, etc. All these
sorts of objects, as we shall show, represent illegitimate totalities,
and are therefore capable of giving rise to vicious-circle fallacies.
But by means of the theory (to be explained in <a href="#CHAPTER_III" class="pginternal">Chapter III</a>) which
reduces statements that are verbally concerned with classes and
relations to statements that are concerned with propositional
functions, the paradoxes are reduced to such as are concerned with
propositions and propositional functions. The paradoxes that concern
propositions are only indirectly relevant to mathematics, while those
that more nearly concern the mathematician are all concerned with
<i>propositional functions</i>. We shall therefore proceed at once to
the consideration of propositional functions.</p>


<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_41">[Pg 41]</span></p>

<p class="nindc space-above2">
II. <i>The Nature of Propositional Functions.</i></p>


<p>By a "propositional function" we mean something which contains a
variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_157">, and expresses a <i>proposition</i> as soon as a value
is assigned to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_158">. That is to say, it differs from a proposition
solely by the fact that it is ambiguous: it contains a variable of
which the value is unassigned. It agrees with the ordinary functions
of mathematics in the fact of containing an unassigned variable:
where it differs is in the fact that the values of the function are
propositions. Thus <i>e.g.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_159"> is a man" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin x = 1\)" src="images/419.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 8.598ex; height: 1.699ex;" id="img_images_419.svg">"
is a propositional function. We shall find that it is possible to
incur a vicious-circle fallacy at the very outset, by admitting as
possible arguments to a propositional function terms which presuppose
the function. This form of the fallacy is very instructive, and its
avoidance leads, as we shall see, to the hierarchy of types.</p>

<p>The question as to the nature of a function<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_13" id="FNanchor_13">[13]</a> is by no means an easy
one. It would seem, however, that the essential characteristic of a
function is <i>ambiguity</i>. Take, for example, the law of identity
in the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_9"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_10">," which is the form in which it is usually
enunciated. It is plain that, regarded psychologically, we have here a
single judgment. But what are we to say of the object of the judgment?
We are not judging that Socrates is Socrates, nor that Plato is Plato,
nor any other of the definite judgments that are instances of the law
of identity. Yet each of these judgments is, in a sense, within the
scope of our judgment. We are in fact judging an ambiguous instance of
the propositional function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_11"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_12">." We appear to have a single
thought which does not have a definite object, but has as its object
an undetermined one of the values of the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_13"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_14">." It
is this kind of ambiguity that constitutes the essence of a function.
When we speak of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_29">" where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_160"> is not specified, we mean one
value of the function, but not a definite one. We may express this by
saying that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_30">" <i>ambiguously denotes</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi b\)" src="images/421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.319ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_421.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi c\)" src="images/422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.328ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_422.svg">, etc., where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi b\)" src="images/421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.319ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_421.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi c\)" src="images/422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.328ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_422.svg_1">, etc.,
are the various values of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_31">."</p>

<p>When we say that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_32">" ambiguously denotes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi b\)" src="images/423.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.319ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_423.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi c\)" src="images/422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.328ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_422.svg_2">, etc., we mean that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_33">" means one of the
objects <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi b\)" src="images/421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.319ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_421.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi c\)" src="images/422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.328ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_422.svg_3">, etc., though not a definite
one, but an undetermined one. It follows that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_34">" only has a
well-defined meaning (well-defined, that is to say, except in so far as
it is of its essence to be ambiguous) if the objects <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi b\)" src="images/421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.319ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_421.svg_3">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi c\)" src="images/422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.328ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_422.svg_4">, etc., are well-defined. That is to say, a function
is not a well-defined function unless all its values are already
well-defined. It follows from this that no function can have among
its values anything which presupposes the function, for if it had,
we could not regard the objects ambiguously denoted by the function
as definite until the function was definite, while conversely, as we
have just seen, the function cannot be<span class="pagenum" id="Page_42">[Pg 42]</span> definite until its values are
definite. This is a particular case, but perhaps the most fundamental
case, of the vicious-circle principle. A function is what ambiguously
denotes some one of a certain totality, namely the values of the
function; hence this totality cannot contain any members which involve
the function, since, if it did, it would contain members involving the
totality, which, by the vicious-circle principle, no totality can do.</p>

<p>It will be seen that, according to the above account, the values
of a function are presupposed by the function, not vice versa. It
is sufficiently obvious, in any particular case, that a value of
a function does not presuppose the function. Thus for example the
proposition "Socrates is human" can be perfectly apprehended without
regarding it as a value of the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_161"> is human." It is true
that, conversely, a function can be apprehended without its being
necessary to apprehend its values severally and individually. If this
were not the case, no function could be apprehended at all, since
the number of values (true and false) of a function is necessarily
infinite and there are necessarily possible arguments with which we are
unacquainted. What is necessary is not that the values should be given
individually and extensionally, but that the totality of the values
should be given intensionally, so that, concerning any assigned object,
it is at least theoretically determinate whether or not the said object
is a value of the function.</p>

<p>It is necessary practically to distinguish the function itself from
an undetermined value of the function. We may regard the function
itself as that which ambiguously denotes, while an undetermined
value of the function is that which is ambiguously denoted. If the
undetermined value is written "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_35">," we will write the function
itself "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_10">." (Any other letter may be used in place of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_162">.) Thus we should say "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_36"> is a proposition," but "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_21">
is a propositional function." When we say "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_37"> is
a proposition," we mean to state something which is true for every
possible value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_163">, though we do not decide what value <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_164"> is
to have. We are making an ambiguous statement about any value of the
function. But when we say "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_11"> is a function," we are not
making an ambiguous statement. It would be more correct to say that
we are making a statement about an ambiguity, taking the view that a
function is an ambiguity. The function itself, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_12">, is the
single thing which ambiguously denotes its many values; while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_38">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_165"> is not specified, is one of the denoted objects, with
the ambiguity belonging to the manner of denoting.</p>

<p>We have seen that, in accordance with the vicious-circle principle, the
values of a function cannot contain terms only definable in terms of
the function. Now given a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_13">, the values for the
function<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_14" id="FNanchor_14">[14]</a> are all propositions<span class="pagenum" id="Page_43">[Pg 43]</span> of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_39">. It follows
