that there must be no propositions, of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_40">, in which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_166"> has a value which involves <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_14">. (If this were the
case, the values of the function would not all be determinate until
the function was determinate, whereas we found that the function is
not determinate unless its values are previously determinate.) Hence
there must be no such thing as the value for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_15"> with the
argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_16">, or with any argument which involves <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_22">.
That is to say, the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\phi \hat{x})\)" src="images/424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.751ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_424.svg">" must not express a
proposition, as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_5">" does if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_6"> is a value for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_17">.
In fact "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\phi \hat{x})\)" src="images/424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.751ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_424.svg_1">" must be a symbol which does
not express anything: we may therefore say that it is not significant.
Thus given any function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_18">, there are arguments with
which the function has no value, as well as arguments with which it has
a value. We will call the arguments with which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_19"> has a
value "possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_167">." We will say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_20"> is
"significant with the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_168">" when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_21"> has a value
with the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_169">.</p>

<p>When it is said that <i>e.g.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\phi \hat{z})\)" src="images/425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.509ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_425.svg">" is
meaningless, and therefore neither true nor false, it is necessary to
avoid a misunderstanding. If "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\phi \hat{z})\)" src="images/425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.509ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_425.svg_1">" were interpreted
as meaning "the value for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_5"> with the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_6">
is true," that would be not meaningless, but false. It is
false for the same reason for which "the King of France is bald"
is false, namely because there is no such thing as "the value for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_6"> with the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_7">." But when, with
some argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_5">, we assert <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_7">, we are not meaning to assert
"the value for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_22"> with the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_6"> is true"; we are
meaning to assert the actual proposition which is the value for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_23">
with the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_7">. Thus for example if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_23">
is "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_3"> is a man," <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_3"> (Socrates) will be "Socrates is a
man," <i>not</i> "the value for the function '<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_4"> is a man,'
with the argument Socrates, is true." Thus in accordance with our
principle that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\phi \hat{z})\)" src="images/425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.509ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_425.svg_2">" is meaningless, we cannot
legitimately deny "the function '<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_5"> is a man' is a man,"
because this is nonsense, but we can legitimately deny "the value for
the function '<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_6"> is a man' with the argument '<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_7"> is a
man' is true," not on the ground that the value in question is false,
but on the ground that there is no such value for the function.</p>

<p>We will denote by the symbol "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg">" the proposition "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_427.svg"> always<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_15" id="FNanchor_15">[15]</a>," <i>i.e.</i> the proposition which asserts all the
values for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_24">. This proposition involves the function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_25">, not merely an ambiguous value of the function. The
assertion of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_41">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_170"> is unspecified, is a different
assertion from the one which asserts all values for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_26">,
for the former is an ambiguous assertion, whereas the latter is in no
sense ambiguous. It will be observed that "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_5">" does not
assert "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_42"> with all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_171">," because, as we have seen,
there must be values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_172"> with which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_43">" is meaningless.
What is asserted by "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_6">" is all propositions which are
values for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_27">; hence it is<span class="pagenum" id="Page_44">[Pg 44]</span> only with such values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_173"> as
make "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_44">" significant, <i>i.e.</i> with all possible arguments,
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_45"> is asserted when we assert "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_7">." Thus
a convenient way to read "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_8">" is "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_46"> is true
with all possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_174">." This is, however, a less accurate
reading than "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_47"> always," because the notion of truth is not
part of the content of what is judged. When we judge "all men are
mortal," we judge truly, but the notion of truth is not necessarily in
our minds, any more than it need be when we judge "Socrates is mortal."</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
III. <i>Definition and Systematic Ambiguity of Truth and Falsehood.</i></p>


<p>Since "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_9">" involves the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_28">, it
must, according to our principle, be impossible as an argument to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_4">. That is to say, the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \{(x) . \phi x\}\)" src="images/428.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.314ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_428.svg">" must
be meaningless. This principle would seem, at first sight, to have
certain exceptions. Take, for example, the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{p}\)" src="images/429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 2.271ex;" id="img_images_429.svg"> is
false," and consider the proposition "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(p) . p\)" src="images/430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.162ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_430.svg"> is false." This
should be a proposition asserting all propositions of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_105">
is false." Such a proposition, we should be inclined to say, must be
false, because "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_106"> is false" is not always true. Hence we should be
led to the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\{(p) . p\,\,  \text{is false}\}\, \text{is false},\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.575ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_431.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> we should be led to a proposition in which "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(p) . p\)" src="images/430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.162ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_430.svg_1"> is
false" is the argument to the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{p}\)" src="images/429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 2.271ex;" id="img_images_429.svg_1"> is false," which
we had declared to be impossible. Now it will be seen that "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(p) .p\)" src="images/432.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.162ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_432.svg">
is false," in the above, purports to be a proposition about all
propositions, and that, by the general form of the vicious-circle
principle, there must be no propositions about all propositions.
Nevertheless, it seems plain that, given any function, there is a
proposition (true or false) asserting all its values. Hence we are led
to the conclusion that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_107"> is false" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_75"> is false" must not
always be the values, with the arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_108"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_76">, for a single
function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{p}\)" src="images/429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 2.271ex;" id="img_images_429.svg_2"> is false." This, however, is only possible if
the word "false" really has many different meanings, appropriate to
propositions of different kinds.</p>

<p>That the words "true" and "false" have many different meanings,
according to the kind of proposition to which they are applied, is
not difficult to see. Let us take any function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_8">, and let
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_8"> be one of its values. Let us call the sort of truth which is
applicable to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_9"> "<i>first</i> truth." (This is not to assume
that this would be first truth in another context: it is merely to
indicate that it is the first sort of truth in our context.) Consider
now the proposition (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_10">. If this has truth of the sort
appropriate to it, that will mean that every value <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_48"> has
"first truth." Thus if we call the sort of truth that is appropriate to
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_11"> "<i>second</i> truth," we may define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\{(x) . \phi x\}\)" src="images/433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.965ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_433.svg">
has second truth" as meaning "every value for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_29">
has first truth," <i>i.e.</i> "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x)\)" src="images/434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 2.174ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_434.svg">.(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_49"> has first truth)."
Similarly, if we denote by "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . \phi x\)" src="images/168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_168.svg_4">" the proposition
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_50"> sometimes," <i>i.e.</i> as we may less accurately
express it, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_51"> with some value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_175">," we find that
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . \phi x\)" src="images/168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_168.svg_5"> has second truth if there is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_176"> with<span class="pagenum" id="Page_45">[Pg 45]</span>
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_52"> has first truth; thus we may define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\{(\exists x).\phi x\}\)" src="images/435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.223ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_435.svg">
has second truth" as meaning "some value for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_30"> has first
truth," <i>i.e.</i> "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . (\phi x\,\text{has first truth})\)" src="images/436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.773ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_436.svg">."
Similar remarks apply to falsehood. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\{(x).\phi x\}\)" src="images/437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.965ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_437.svg"> has
second falsehood" will mean "some value for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_31"> has first
falsehood," <i>i.e.</i> "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . (\phi x\, \text{has first falsehood})\)" src="images/438.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.737ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_438.svg">,"
while "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\{(\exists x).\phi x\}\)" src="images/435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.223ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_435.svg_1"> has second falsehood"
will mean "all values for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_32"> have first falsehood,"
<i>i.e.</i> "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x). (\phi x\, \text{has first falsehood})\)" src="images/439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.479ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_439.svg">." Thus the
sort of falsehood that can belong to a general proposition is different
from the sort that can belong to a particular proposition.</p>

<p>Applying these considerations to the proposition "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(p).p\)" src="images/440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.162ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_440.svg"> is false,"
we see that the kind of falsehood in question must be specified.
If, for example, first falsehood is meant, the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{p}\)" src="images/429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 2.271ex;" id="img_images_429.svg_3">
has first falsehood" is only significant when <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_109"> is the sort of
proposition which has first falsehood or first truth. Hence "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(p) . p\)" src="images/430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.162ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_430.svg_2">
is false" will be replaced by a statement which is equivalent to
"all propositions having either first truth or first falsehood have
first falsehood." This proposition has <i>second</i> falsehood, and is
not a possible argument to the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{p}\)" src="images/429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 2.271ex;" id="img_images_429.svg_4"> has <i>first</i>
falsehood." Thus the apparent exception to the principle that
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\{(x) . \phi x\}\)" src="images/441.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.314ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_441.svg">" must be meaningless disappears.</p>

<p>Similar considerations will enable us to deal with "not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_110">" and with
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_111"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_77">." It might seem as if these were functions in which
<i>any</i> proposition might appear as argument. But this is due to a
systematic ambiguity in the meanings of "not" and "or," by which they
adapt themselves to propositions of any order. To explain fully how
this occurs, it will be well to begin with a definition of the simplest
kind of <i>truth</i> and <i>falsehood</i>.</p>

<p>The universe consists of objects having various qualities and standing
in various relations. Some of the objects which occur in the universe
are complex. When an object is complex, it consists of interrelated
parts. Let us consider a complex object composed of two parts <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_8">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_4"> standing to each other in the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_45">. The complex
object "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_9">-in-the-relation-<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_46">-to-<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_5">" may be capable of being
<i>perceived</i>; when perceived, it is perceived as one object.
Attention may show that it is complex; we then <i>judge</i> that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_10"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_6"> stand in the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_47">. Such a judgment, being
derived from perception by mere attention, may be called a "judgment
of perception." This judgment of perception, considered as an actual
occurrence, is a relation of four terms, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_11"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_7"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_48"> and the percipient. The perception, on the contrary, is a
relation of two terms, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_12">-in-the-relation-<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_49">-to-<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_8">,"
and the percipient. Since an object of perception cannot be nothing,
we cannot perceive "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_13">-in-the-relation-<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_50">-to-<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_9">" unless a
is in the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_51"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_10">. Hence a judgment of perception,
according to the above definition, must be true. This does not
mean that, in a judgment which <i>appears</i> to us to be one of
perception, we are sure of not being in error, since we may err in
thinking that our judgment has really been derived merely by analysis
of<span class="pagenum" id="Page_46">[Pg 46]</span> what was perceived. But if our judgment has been so derived,
it must be true. In fact, we may define <i>truth</i>, where such
judgments are concerned, as consisting in the fact that there is a
complex <i>corresponding</i> to the discursive thought which is the
judgment. That is, when we judge "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_14"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_52"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_11">," our judgment is said to be <i>true</i> when there is a complex
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_15">-in-the-relation-<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_53">-to-<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_12">," and is said to be <i>false</i>
when this is not the case. This is a definition of truth and falsehood
in relation to judgments of this kind.</p>

<p>It will be seen that, according to the above account, a judgment does
not have a single object, namely the proposition, but has several
interrelated objects. That is to say, the relation which constitutes
judgment is not a relation of two terms, namely the judging mind
and the proposition, but is a relation of several terms, namely the
mind and what are called the constituents of the proposition. That
is, when we judge (say) "this is red," what occurs is a relation of
three terms, the mind, and "this," and red. On the other hand, when
we <i>perceive</i> "the redness of this," there is a relation of two
terms, namely the mind and the complex object "the redness of this."
When a judgment occurs, there is a certain complex entity, composed of
the mind and the various objects of the judgment. When the judgment
is <i>true</i>, in the case of the kind of judgments we have been
considering, there is a corresponding complex of the <i>objects</i>
of the judgment alone. Falsehood, in regard to our present class
of judgments, consists in the absence of a corresponding complex
composed of the objects alone. It follows from the above theory that
a "proposition," in the sense in which a proposition is supposed to
be <i>the</i> object of a judgment, is a false abstraction, because a
judgment has several objects, not one. It is the severalness of the
objects in judgment (as opposed to perception) which has led people to
speak of thought as "discursive," though they do not appear to have
realized clearly what was meant by this epithet.</p>

<p>Owing to the plurality of the objects of a single judgment, it follows
that what we call a "proposition" (in the sense in which this is
distinguished from the phrase expressing it) is not a single entity at
all. That is to say, the phrase which expresses a proposition is what
we call an "incomplete" symbol<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_16" id="FNanchor_16">[16]</a>; it does not have meaning in itself,
but requires some supplementation in order to acquire a complete
meaning. This fact is somewhat concealed by the circumstance that
judgment in itself supplies a sufficient supplement, and that judgment
in itself makes no <i>verbal</i> addition to the proposition. Thus "the
proposition 'Socrates is human'" uses "Socrates is human" in a way
which requires a supplement of some kind before it acquires a complete
meaning; but when I judge "Socrates is human," the meaning is completed
by the act of judging, and we no longer have an incomplete symbol.
The fact that propositions are "incomplete symbols"<span class="pagenum" id="Page_47">[Pg 47]</span> is important
philosophically, and is relevant at certain points in symbolic logic.</p>

<p>The judgments we have been dealing with hitherto are such as are of the
same form as judgments of perception, <i>i.e.</i> their subjects are
always particular and definite. But there are many judgments which are
not of this form. Such are "all men are mortal," "I met a man," "some
men are Greeks." Before dealing with such judgments, we will introduce
some technical terms.</p>

<p>We will give the name of "a <i>complex</i>" to any such object as
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_16"> in the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_54"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_13">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_17"> having the quality
<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_78">," or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_18"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_4"> standing in the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_5">."
Broadly speaking, a <i>complex</i> is anything which occurs in the
universe and is not simple. We will call a judgment <i>elementary</i>
when it merely asserts such things as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_19"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_55"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_15">," "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_20"> has the quality <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_79">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_21"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_16"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_5">
stand in the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_6">." Then an <i>elementary</i> judgment is
true when there is a corresponding complex, and false when there is no
corresponding complex.</p>

<p>But take now such a proposition as "all men are mortal." Here the
judgment does not correspond to <i>one</i> complex, but to many,
namely "Socrates is mortal," "Plato is mortal," "Aristotle is mortal,"
etc. (For the moment, it is unnecessary to inquire whether each of
these does not require further treatment before we reach the ultimate
complexes involved. For purposes of illustration, "Socrates is mortal"
is here treated as an elementary judgment, though it is in fact not
one, as will be explained later. Truly elementary judgments are not
very easily found.) We do not mean to deny that there may be some
relation of the concept <i>man</i> to the concept <i>mortal</i> which
may be <i>equivalent</i> to "all men are mortal," but in any case this
relation is not the same thing as what we affirm when we say that all
men are mortal. Our judgment that all men are mortal collects together
a number of elementary judgments. It is not, however, composed of
these, since (<i>e.g.</i>) the fact that Socrates is mortal is no
part of what we assert, as may be seen by considering the fact that
our assertion can be understood by a person who has never heard of
Socrates. In order to understand the judgment "all men are mortal," it
is not necessary to know what men there are. We must admit, therefore,
as a radically new kind of judgment, such general assertions as "all
men are mortal." We assert that, given that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_177"> is human, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_178"> is
always mortal. That is, we assert "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_179"> is mortal" of <i>every</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_180"> which is human. Thus we are able to judge (whether truly
or falsely) that <i>all</i> the objects which have some assigned
property also have some other assigned property. That is, given any
propositional functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_33"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi \hat{x}\)" src="images/223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_223.svg_1">, there
is a judgment asserting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_11"> with every <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_181"> for which we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_53">. Such judgments we will call <i>general judgments</i>.</p>

<p>It is evident (as explained above) that the definition of <i>truth</i>
is different<span class="pagenum" id="Page_48">[Pg 48]</span> in the case of general judgments from what it was in the
case of elementary judgments. Let us call the meaning of <i>truth</i>
which we gave for elementary judgments "elementary truth." Then when
we assert that it is true that all men are mortal, we shall mean that
all judgments of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_182"> is mortal," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_183"> is a man, have
elementary truth. We may define this as "truth of the second order" or
"second-order truth." Then if we express the proposition "all men are
mortal" in the form
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(x). x \, \text{is mortal, where}\, x\, \text{is a man}.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.718ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_442.svg"></span>
and call this judgment <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_112">, then "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_113"> is true" must be taken to
mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_114"> has second-order truth," which in turn means
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(x). \unicode{x2018}x \, \text{is mortal}\unicode{x2019}\, \text{has elementary truth, where}\, x \, \text{is a man}.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.806ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_443.svg"></span></p>

<p>In order to avoid the necessity for stating explicitly the limitation
to which our variable is subject, it is convenient to replace the
above interpretation of "all men are mortal" by a slightly different
interpretation. The proposition "all men are mortal" is equivalent to
"'<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_184"> is a man' implies '<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_185"> is mortal,' with all possible values
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_186">." Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_187"> is not restricted to such values as are men,
but may have any value with which "'<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_188"> is a man' implies '<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_189"> is
mortal'" is <i>significant</i>, <i>i.e.</i> either true or false. Such
a proposition is called a "formal implication." The advantage of this
form is that the values which the variable may take are given by the
function to which it is the argument: the values which the variable may
take are all those with which the function is significant.</p>

<p>We use the symbol "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_1">" to express the general judgment
which asserts all judgments of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_54">." Then the judgment
"all men are mortal" is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(x). \unicode{x2018}x \, \text{is a man}\unicode{x2019} \, \text{implies}\, \unicode{x2018}x\, \text{is a mortal},\unicode{x2019}\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.252ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_444.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> (in virtue of the definition of implication) to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(x) . x \,\text{is not a man or}\, x \, \text{is mortal}.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.155ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_445.svg"></span>
As we have just seen, the meaning of <i>truth</i> which is applicable
to this proposition is not the same as the meaning of <i>truth</i>
which is applicable to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_190"> is a man" or to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_191"> is mortal." And
generally, in any judgment (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_12">, the sense in which this
judgment is or may be true is not the same as that in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_55">
is or may be true. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_56"> is an elementary judgment, it is true
when it <i>points</i> to a corresponding complex. But (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_13">
does not point to a single corresponding complex: the corresponding
complexes are as numerous as the possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_192">.</p>

<p>It follows from the above that such a proposition as "all the judgments
made by Epimenides are true" will only be prima facie capable of truth
if all his judgments are of the same order. If they are of varying
orders, of which the nth is the highest, we may make n assertions of
the form "all the judgments of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg"> made by Epimenides are
true," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_1"> has all values<span class="pagenum" id="Page_49">[Pg 49]</span> up to <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_1">. But no such judgment
can include itself in its own scope, since such a judgment is always of
higher order than the judgments to which it refers.</p>

<p>Let us consider next what is meant by the negation of a proposition
of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_6">." We observe, to begin with,
that "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_23"> in some cases," or "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_24"> sometimes," is
a judgment which is on a par with "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_25"> in all cases," or
"<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_26"> always." The judgment "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_27"> sometimes" is true if
one or more values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_193"> exist for which <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_28"> is true. We
will express the proposition "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_29"> sometimes" by the notation
"<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_3">," where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists\)" src="images/317.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.258ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_317.svg_1">" stands for "there
exists," and the whole symbol may be read "there exists an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_194">
such that <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_30">." We take the two kinds of judgment expressed
by "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_7">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_4">" as
primitive ideas. We also take as a primitive idea the negation of an
<i>elementary</i> proposition. We can then define the negations of
<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_8"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_447.svg">. The negation
of any proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_115"> will be denoted by the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}p\)" src="images/58.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.898ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_58.svg_4">."
Then the negation of <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_9"> will be <i>defined</i> as
meaning
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x,\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.229ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_448.svg"></span>
and the negation of <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_151.svg_5"> will be
<i>defined</i> as meaning "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\sim}{\phi}x\)" src="images/155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.463ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_155.svg_3">." Thus, in
the traditional language of formal logic, the negation of a universal
affirmative is to be defined as the particular negative, and the
negation of the particular affirmative is to be defined as the
universal negative. Hence the meaning of negation for such propositions
is different from the meaning of negation for elementary propositions.</p>

<p>An analogous explanation will apply to disjunction. Consider the
statement "either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_116">, or <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_31"> always." We will denote the
disjunction of two propositions <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_117">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_80"> by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor q\)" src="images/59.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.693ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_59.svg_6">." Then
our statement is "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \ldotp \lor \ldotp (x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/449.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.362ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_449.svg">." We will
suppose that <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_118"> is an elementary proposition, and that <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_32">
is always an elementary proposition. We take the disjunction of
two elementary propositions as a primitive idea, and we wish to
<i>define</i> the disjunction
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}p \ldotp \lor \ldotp (x) \ldotp {\phi}x.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/450.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.63ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_450.svg"></span>
This may be defined as "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp p \lor {\phi}x\)" src="images/451.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.355ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_451.svg">," <i>i.e.</i>
"either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_119"> is true, or <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_33"> is always true" is to mean
"'<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_120"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_34">' is always true." Similarly we will define
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}p \ldotp \lor \ldotp (\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.882ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_452.svg"></span>
as meaning "<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x) \ldotp p \lor {\phi}x\)" src="images/453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.613ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_453.svg">," <i>i.e.</i> we
define "either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_121"> is true or there is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_195"> for which <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_35">
is true" as meaning "there is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_196"> for which either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_122"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_36"> is true." Similarly we can define a disjunction of two
universal propositions: "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x \ldotp \lor \ldotp (y)\ldotp {\psi}y\)" src="images/454.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.68ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_454.svg">"
will be defined as meaning "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x, y) \ldotp {\phi}x \lor {\psi}y\)" src="images/455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.914ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_455.svg">,"
<i>i.e.</i> "either <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_37"> is always true or
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}y\)" src="images/456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.581ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_456.svg"> is always true" is to mean "'<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_38"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}y\)" src="images/456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.581ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_456.svg_1">'
is always true." By this method we obtain definitions of disjunctions
containing propositions of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_10"> or
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_447.svg_1"> in terms of disjunctions of elementary
propositions; but the meaning of "disjunction" is not the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_50">[Pg 50]</span> same for
propositions of the forms (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . {\phi}x\)" src="images/457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_457.svg">, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x). {\phi}x\)" src="images/458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_458.svg">,
as it was for elementary propositions.</p>

<p>Similar explanations could be given for implication and conjunction,
but this is unnecessary, since these can be defined in terms of
negation and disjunction.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
IV. <i>Why a Given Function requires Arguments of a Certain Type.</i></p>


<p>The considerations so far adduced in favour of the view that a
function cannot significantly have as argument anything defined in
terms of the function itself have been more or less indirect. But a
direct consideration of the kinds of functions which have functions
as arguments and the kinds of functions which have arguments other
than functions will show, if we are not mistaken, that not only
is it impossible for a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_7"> to have itself or
anything derived from it as argument, but that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{z}\)" src="images/459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_459.svg"> is
another function such that there are arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_22"> with which both
"<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}a\)" src="images/145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_145.svg_1">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}a\)" src="images/460.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_460.svg">" are significant, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{z}\)" src="images/459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_459.svg_1">
and anything derived from it cannot significantly be argument to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_8">. This arises from the fact that a function is
essentially an ambiguity, and that, if it is to occur in a definite
proposition, it must occur in such a way that the ambiguity has
disappeared, and a wholly unambiguous statement has resulted. A few
illustrations will make this clear. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) . {\phi}x\)" src="images/461.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_461.svg">," which we
have already considered, is a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_24">; as soon as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_25"> is assigned, we have a definite proposition, wholly
free from ambiguity. But it is obvious that we cannot substitute for
the function something which is not a function: "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) . {\phi}x\)" src="images/461.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_461.svg_1">"
means "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_39"> in all cases," and depends for its significance
upon the fact that there are "cases" of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_40">, <i>i.e.</i> upon
the ambiguity which is characteristic of a function. This instance
illustrates the fact that, when a function can occur significantly as
argument, something which is not a function cannot occur significantly
as argument. But conversely, when something which is not a function can
occur significantly as argument, a function cannot occur significantly.
Take, <i>e.g.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_197"> is a man," and consider "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_26">
is a man." Here there is nothing to eliminate the ambiguity which
constitutes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_27">; there is thus nothing definite which
is said to be a man. A function, in fact, is not a definite object,
which could be or not be a man; it is a mere ambiguity awaiting
determination, and in order that it may occur significantly it must
receive the necessary determination, which it obviously does not
receive if it is merely substituted for something determinate in a
proposition<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_17" id="FNanchor_17">[17]</a>. This argument does not, however, apply directly as
against such a statement as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\{(x) . {\phi}x\}\)" src="images/462.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.965ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_462.svg"> is a man." Common
sense would pronounce such a statement to be meaningless, but it
cannot be condemned on the ground of ambiguity in its subject. We
need<span class="pagenum" id="Page_51">[Pg 51]</span> here a new objection, namely the following: A proposition is
not a single entity, but a relation of several; hence a statement in
which a proposition appears as subject will only be significant if
it can be reduced to a statement about the terms which appear in the
proposition. A proposition, like such phrases as "the so-and-so,"
where grammatically it appears as subject, must be broken up into its
constituents if we are to find the true subject or subjects<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_18" id="FNanchor_18">[18]</a>. But
in such a statement as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_123"> is a man," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_124"> is a proposition,
this is not possible. Hence "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\{(x) \ldotp \phi x\}\)" src="images/463.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.965ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_463.svg"> is a man" is
meaningless.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
V. <i>The Hierarchy of Functions and Propositions.</i></p>


<p>We are thus led to the conclusion, both from the vicious-circle
principle and from direct inspection, that the functions to which
a given object <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_23"> can be an argument are incapable of being
arguments to each other, and that they have no term in common with the
functions to which they can be arguments. We are thus led to construct
a hierarchy. Beginning with <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_24"> and the other terms which can be
arguments to the same functions to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_25"> can be argument, we come
next to functions to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_26"> is a possible argument, and then to
functions to which such functions are possible arguments, and so on.
But the hierarchy which has to be constructed is not so simple as might
at first appear. The functions which can take <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_27"> as argument form an
illegitimate totality, and themselves require division into a hierarchy
of functions. This is easily seen as follows. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi\hat{z}, x)\)" src="images/464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.705ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_464.svg">
be a function of the two variables <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_198">. Then if,
keeping <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_199"> fixed for the moment, we assert this with all possible
values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_5">, we obtain a proposition:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\phi) \ldotp f(\phi\hat{z}, x). \]" src="images/465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.449ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_465.svg"></span>
Here, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_200"> is variable, we have a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_201">; but as this
function involves a totality of values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_10"><a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_19" id="FNanchor_19">[19]</a>, it
cannot itself be one of the values included in the totality, by the
vicious-circle principle. It follows that the totality of values of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_11"> concerned in (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi) \ldotp f(\phi\hat{z}, x)\)" src="images/466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.94ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_466.svg"> is not
the totality of all functions in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_202"> can occur as argument, and
that there is no such totality as that of all functions in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_203">
can occur as argument.</p>

<p>It follows from the above that a function in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_12">
appears as argument requires that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_13">" should not stand
for <i>any</i> function which is capable of a given argument, but
must be restricted in such a way that none of the functions which are
possible values of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_14">" should involve any reference to
the totality of such functions. Let us take as an illustration the
definition of identity. We might attempt to define "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_204"> is identical
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_66">" as meaning "whatever is true of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_205"> is true of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_67">,"
<i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_57"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_6">." But here,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_52">[Pg 52]</span> since we
are concerned to assert all values of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_58"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_7">"
regarded as a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_6">, we shall be compelled to impose
upon <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_7"> some limitation which will prevent us from including
among values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_8"> values in which "all possible values of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_9">" are referred to. Thus for example "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_206"> is identical with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_28">" is a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_207">; hence, if it is a legitimate value of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_10"> in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_59"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_8">" we shall be able to
infer, by means of the above definition, that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_208"> is identical
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_29">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_209"> is identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_68">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_69"> is identical
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_30">. Although the conclusion is sound, the reasoning embodies
a vicious-circle fallacy, since we have taken "<img alt="" data-tex="\((\phi)\ldotp\phi x\)" src="images/467.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.757ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_467.svg">
implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_10">" as a possible value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_60">, which it cannot
be. If, however, we impose any limitation upon <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_11">, it may happen,
so far as appears at present, that with other values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_12"> we
might have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_61"> true and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_9"> false, so that our proposed
definition of identity would plainly be wrong. This difficulty is
avoided by the "axiom of reducibility," to be explained later. For the
present, it is only mentioned in order to illustrate the necessity and
the relevance of the hierarchy of functions of a given argument.</p>

<p>Let us give the name "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_31">-functions" to functions that are
significant for a given argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_32">. Then suppose we take any
selection of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_33">-functions, and consider the proposition "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_34">
satisfies all the functions belonging to the selection in question."
If we here replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_35"> by a variable, we obtain an <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_36">-function;
but by the vicious-circle principle this <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_37">-function cannot be a
member of our selection, since it refers to the whole of the selection.
Let the selection consist of all those functions which satisfy
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi\hat{z})\)" src="images/468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.405ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_468.svg">. Then our new function is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\phi) \ldotp \{f(\phi\hat{z}) \text{ implies } \phi x\}, \]" src="images/469.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.11ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_469.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_210"> is the argument. It thus appears that, whatever selection
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_38">-functions we may make, there will be other <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_39">-functions
that lie outside our selection. Such <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_40">-functions, as the above
instance illustrates, will always arise through taking a function of
two arguments, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_15"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_211">, and asserting all or some
of the values resulting from varying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_13">. What is necessary,
therefore, in order to avoid vicious-circle fallacies, is to divide our
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_41">-functions into "types," each of which contains no functions which
refer to the whole of that type.</p>

<p>When something is asserted or denied about all possible values or
about some (undetermined) possible values of a variable, that variable
is called <i>apparent</i>, after Peano. The presence of the words
<i>all</i> or <i>some</i> in a proposition indicates the presence of
