an apparent variable; but often an apparent variable is really present
where language does not at once indicate its presence. Thus for example
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_15"> is mortal" means "there is a time at which <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_16"> will die." Thus
a variable time occurs as apparent variable.</p>

<p>The clearest instances of propositions not containing apparent
variables are such as express immediate judgments of perception, such
as "this is red" or "this is painful," where "this" is something
immediately given. In other<span class="pagenum" id="Page_53">[Pg 53]</span> judgments, even where at first sight no
variable appears to be present, it often happens that there really is
one. Take (say) "Socrates is human." To Socrates himself, the word
"Socrates" no doubt stood for an object of which he was immediately
aware, and the judgment "Socrates is human" contained no apparent
variable. But to us, who only know Socrates by description, the
word "Socrates" cannot mean what it meant to him; it means rather
"the person having such-and-such properties," (say) "the Athenian
philosopher who drank the hemlock." Now in all propositions about "the
so-and-so" there is an apparent variable, as will be shown in <a href="#CHAPTER_III" class="pginternal">Chapter III</a>.
Thus in what <i>we</i> have in mind when we say "Socrates is
human" there is an apparent variable, though there was no apparent
variable in the corresponding judgment as made by Socrates, provided we
assume that there is such a thing as immediate awareness of oneself.</p>

<p>Whatever may be the instances of propositions not containing apparent
variables, it is obvious that propositional functions whose values do not
contain apparent variables are the source of propositions containing apparent
variables, in the sense in which the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_28"> is the source of the proposition
<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_11">. For the values for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_29"> do not contain the apparent variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_212">,
which appears in <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp {\phi}x\)" src="images/149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_149.svg_12">; if they contain an apparent variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_70">, this can be
similarly eliminated, and so on. This process must come to an end, since no
proposition which we can apprehend can contain more than a finite number
of apparent variables, on the ground that whatever we can apprehend must
be of finite complexity. Thus we must arrive at last at a function of as
many variables as there have been stages in reaching it from our original
proposition, and this function will be such that its values contain no apparent
variables. We may call this function the <i>matrix</i> of our original proposition
and of any other propositions and functions to be obtained by turning some
of the arguments to the function into apparent variables. Thus for example,
if we have a matrix-function whose values are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x, y)\)" src="images/470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_470.svg">, we shall derive from it</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\((y) \ldotp \phi(x, y)\)" src="images/471.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.392ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_471.svg">, which is a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_213">,</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\((x) \ldotp \phi(x, y)\)" src="images/472.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.578ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_472.svg">, which is a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_71">,</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\((x,y) \ldotp \phi(x, y)\)" src="images/473.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.692ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_473.svg">, meaning "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x, y)\)" src="images/470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_470.svg_1"> is true with
all possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_214"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_72">." This last is a proposition
containing no <i>real</i> variable, <i>i.e.</i> no variable except
apparent variables.</p>

<p>It is thus plain that all possible propositions and functions are
obtainable from matrices by the process of turning the arguments to the
matrices into apparent variables. In order to divide our propositions
and functions into types, we shall, therefore, start from matrices,
and consider how they are to be divided with a view to the avoidance
of vicious-circle fallacies in the definitions of the functions
concerned. For this purpose, we will use such letters as <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_42">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_17">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_6">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_215">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_73">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_12">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_1">, to denote objects which
are neither propositions nor functions. Such objects we shall call
<i>individuals</i>. Such objects will be<span class="pagenum" id="Page_54">[Pg 54]</span> constituents of propositions
or functions, and will be <i>genuine</i> constituents, in the sense
that they do not disappear on analysis, as (for example) classes do, or
phrases of the form "the so-and-so."</p>

<p>The first matrices that occur are those whose values are of the forms
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi x, \psi(x, y), \chi(x, y, z \ldots), \]" src="images/474.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.597ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_474.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> where the arguments, however many there may be, are
all individuals. The functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_14">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_1"> ...,
since (by definition) they contain no apparent variables, and have
no arguments except individuals, do not presuppose any totality of
functions. From the functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_2"> ... we may proceed
to form other functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_216">, such as (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y) . \psi(x, y)\)" src="images/475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.637ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_475.svg">,
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists y) . \psi(x y)\)" src="images/476.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.888ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_476.svg">, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y, z) . \chi(x, y, z)\)" src="images/477.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.696ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_477.svg">, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y) \colon (\exists z) . \chi(x, y, z)\)" src="images/478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.714ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_478.svg">, and so on. All these presuppose no
totality except that of individuals. We thus arrive at a certain
collection of functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_217">, characterized by the fact that they
involve no variables except individuals. Such functions we will call
"<i>first-order</i> functions."</p>

<p>We may now introduce a notation to express "any first-order function."
We will denote any first-order function by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{x}\)" src="images/479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_479.svg">" and
any value for such a function by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{x}\)" src="images/479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_479.svg_1">." Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi! \hat{x}\)" src="images/480.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_480.svg">"
stands for any value for any function which involves no
variables except individuals. It will be seen that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{x}\)" src="images/479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_479.svg_2">"
is itself a function of two variables, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_481.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_218">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{x}\)" src="images/479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_479.svg_3"> involves a variable which is not an
individual, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_481.svg_1">. Similarly "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x). \phi ! x\)" src="images/482.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.452ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_482.svg">"
is a function of the variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_481.svg_2">, and thus involves
a variable other than an individual. Again, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_43"> is a given
individual,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\phi ! x\,\, \text{implies}\, \phi !\,\, \text{a with all possible values of}\,\, \phi.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/483.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 45.809ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_483.svg"></span>
is a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_219">, but it is not a function of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi !x\)" src="images/484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_484.svg">,
because it involves an (apparent) variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_15"> which is not
an individual. Let us give the name "predicate" to any first-order
function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{x}\)" src="images/479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_479.svg_4"> (This use of the word "predicate" is
only proposed for the purposes of the present discussion.) Then the
statement "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! x\)" src="images/485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_485.svg"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! a\)" src="images/486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.174ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_486.svg"> with all possible values
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_16">" may be read "all the predicates of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_220"> are predicates of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_44">." This makes a statement about <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_221">, but does not attribute to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_222"> a <i>predicate</i> in the special sense just defined.</p>

<p>Owing to the introduction of the variable first-order function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi! \hat{z}\)" src="images/487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_487.svg">,
we now have a new set of matrices. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! x\)" src="images/485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_485.svg_1">" is
a function which contains no apparent variables, but contains the two
real variables <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_481.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_223">. (It should be observed
that when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_17"> is assigned, we may obtain a function whose values
do involve individuals as apparent variables, for example if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi! x\)" src="images/488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_488.svg">
is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y) . \psi(x, y)\)" src="images/475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.637ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_475.svg_1">. But so long as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_18"> is variable,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! x\)" src="images/485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_485.svg_2"> contains no apparent variables.) Again, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_45"> is a
definite individual, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! a\)" src="images/486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.174ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_486.svg_1"> is a function of the one variable
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_481.svg_4">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_46"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_18"> are definite individuals,
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! a\)" src="images/486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.174ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_486.svg_2"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi ! b\)" src="images/489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.072ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_489.svg">" is a function of the two variables
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_481.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_490.svg">, and so on. We are thus led to a
whole set of new matrices,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f(\phi ! \hat{z}),\, g(\phi ! \hat{z}, \psi ! \hat{z}),\, F(\phi ! \hat{z}, x),\, \text{and so on}. \]" src="images/491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.817ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_491.svg"></span>
These matrices contain individuals and first-order functions as
arguments, but<span class="pagenum" id="Page_55">[Pg 55]</span> (like all matrices) they contain no apparent variables.
Any such matrix, if it contains more than one variable, gives rise to
new functions of one variable by turning all its arguments except one
into apparent variables. Thus we obtain the functions
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} (\phi).g({\phi}!\hat{z},{\psi}!\hat{z})&amp;\text{, which is a function of}~ {\psi}!\hat{z}\text{.}\\ (x).F({\phi}!\hat{z}, x)&amp;\text{, which is a function of}~ {\phi}!\hat{z}\text{.}\\ (\phi).F({\phi}!\hat{z}, x)&amp;\text{, which is a function of}~ x\text{.}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/492.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.71ex; width: 40.317ex; height: 8.552ex;" id="img_images_492.svg"></span></p>

<p>We will give the name of <i>second-order matrices</i> to such matrices
as have first-order functions among their arguments, and have no
arguments except first-order functions and individuals. (It is not
<i>necessary</i> that they should have individuals among their
arguments.) We will give the name of <i>second-order functions</i>
to such as either are second-order matrices or are derived from such
matrices by turning some of the arguments into apparent variables. It
will be seen that either an individual or a first-order function may
appear as argument to a second-order function. Second-order functions
are such as contain variables which are first-order functions, but
contain no other variables except (possibly) individuals.</p>

<p>We now have various new classes of functions at our command. In the
first place, we have second-order functions which have one argument
which is a first-order function. We will denote a variable function of
this kind by the notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(f!(\hat{\phi}!\hat{z})\)" src="images/493.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.663ex; height: 2.968ex;" id="img_images_493.svg">, and any value
of such a function by <img alt="" data-tex="\(f!({\phi}!\hat{z})\)" src="images/494.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.663ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_494.svg">. Like <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!x\)" src="images/495.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_495.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f!({\phi}!\hat{z})\)" src="images/494.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.663ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_494.svg_1"> is a function of two variables, namely
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f!(\hat{\phi}!\hat{z})\)" src="images/493.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.663ex; height: 2.968ex;" id="img_images_493.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!\hat{z}\)" src="images/496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_496.svg">. Among possible
values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(f!({\phi}!\hat{z})\)" src="images/494.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.663ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_494.svg_2"> will be <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!a\)" src="images/497.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.174ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_497.svg"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_47">
is constant), <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).{\phi}!x\)" src="images/498.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.332ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_498.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x).{\phi}!x\)" src="images/499.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.59ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_499.svg">, and so on.
(These result from assigning a value to <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_3">, leaving <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_19"> to
be assigned.) We will call such functions "predicative functions of
first-order functions."</p>

<p>In the second place, we have second-order functions of two arguments,
one of which is a first-order function while the other is an
individual. Let us denote undetermined values of such functions by the
notation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f!({\phi}!\hat{z}, x). \]" src="images/500.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.592ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_500.svg"></span>
As soon as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_224"> is assigned, we shall have a predicative function of
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!\hat{z}\)" src="images/496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_496.svg_1">. If our function contains no first-order function
as apparent variable, we shall obtain a predicative function of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_225"> if we assign a value to <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!\hat{z}\)" src="images/496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_496.svg_2">. Thus, to take the
simplest possible case, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(f!({\phi}!\hat{z}, x)\)" src="images/501.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.963ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_501.svg"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!x\)" src="images/495.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_495.svg_1">,
the assignment of a value to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_20"> gives us a predicative function
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_226">, in virtue of the definition of "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!x\)" src="images/495.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_495.svg_2">." But if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f!({\phi}!\hat{z}, x)\)" src="images/501.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.963ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_501.svg_1"> contains a first-order function as apparent
variable, the assignment of a value to <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!\hat{z}\)" src="images/496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_496.svg_3"> gives us a
second-order function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_227">.</p>

<p>In the third place, we have second-order functions of
individuals. These will all be derived from functions of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f!({\phi}!\hat{z}, x)\)" src="images/501.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.963ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_501.svg_2"> by turning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_21"> into an apparent
variable. We do not, therefore, need a new notation for them.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_56">[Pg 56]</span></p>

<p>We have also second-order functions of two first-order functions, or of
two such functions and an individual, and so on.</p>

<p>We may now proceed in exactly the same way to third-order matrices,
which will be functions containing second-order functions as arguments,
and containing no apparent variables, and no arguments except
individuals and first-order functions and second-order functions.
Thence we shall proceed, as before, to third-order functions; and so we
can proceed indefinitely. If the highest order of variable occurring in
a function, whether as argument or as apparent variable, is a function
of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_2">th order, then the function in which it occurs is of the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(n + 1\)" src="images/502.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.254ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_502.svg">th order. We do not arrive at functions of an infinite order,
because the number of arguments and of apparent variables in a function
must be finite, and therefore every function must be of a finite order.
Since the orders of functions are only defined step by step, there
can be no process of "proceeding to the limit," and functions of an
infinite order cannot occur.</p>

<p>We will define a function of one variable as <i>predicative</i> when
it is of the next order above that of its argument, <i>i.e.</i> of the
lowest order compatible with its having that argument. If a function
has several arguments, and the highest order of function occurring
among the arguments is the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_3">th, we call the function predicative
if it is of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n + 1\)" src="images/502.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.254ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_502.svg_1">th order, <i>i.e.</i> again, if it is of
the lowest order compatible with its having the arguments it has. A
function of several arguments is predicative if there is one of its
arguments such that, when the other arguments have values assigned to
them, we obtain a predicative function of the one undetermined argument.</p>

<p>It is important to observe that all possible functions in the above
hierarchy can be obtained by means of predicative functions and
apparent variables. Thus, as we saw, second-order functions of an
individual <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_228"> are of the form
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\phi).f!(\phi ! \hat{z}, x)\, \text{or}\, (\exists \phi).f!(\phi ! \hat{z}, x) \text{or}\, (\phi, \psi).f!(\phi !\hat{z}, \psi !\hat{z}, x)\, \text{or etc.}, \]" src="images/503.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.408ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_503.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_4"> is a second-order predicative function. And speaking
generally, a non-predicative function of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_4">th order is
obtained from a predicative function of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_5">th order by turning
all the arguments of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n-1\)" src="images/504.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.254ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_504.svg">th order into apparent variables.
(Other arguments also may be turned into apparent variables.) Thus
we need not introduce as variables any functions except predicative
functions. Moreover, to obtain any function of one variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_229">,
we need not go beyond predicative functions of <i>two</i> variables.
For the function (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi).f!(\phi!\hat{z}, \psi !\hat{z}, x)\)" src="images/505.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.482ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_505.svg">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_5"> is given, is a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/506.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_506.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_230">, and is
predicative. Thus it is of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(F!(\phi !\hat{z}, x)\)" src="images/507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.413ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_507.svg">, and
therefore (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi, \psi).f!(\phi !\hat{z}, \psi !\hat{z}, x))\)" src="images/508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.716ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_508.svg"> is of
the form (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi).F!(\phi !\hat{z}, x)\)" src="images/509.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.648ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_509.svg">. Thus speaking generally,
by a succession of steps we find that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{u}\)" src="images/510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_510.svg"> is a
predicative function of a sufficiently high order, any assigned
non-predicative function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_231"> will be of one of the two forms
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\phi).F!(\phi !\hat{u}, x),\, (\exists \phi).F!(\phi !\hat{u}, x), \]" src="images/511.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.811ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_511.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(F\)" src="images/45.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.695ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_45.svg_2"> is a predicative function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{u}\)" src="images/510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_510.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_232">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_57">[Pg 57]</span></p>

<p>The nature of the above hierarchy of functions may be restated as
follows. A function, as we saw at an earlier stage, presupposes as
part of its meaning the totality of its values, or, what comes to the
same thing, the totality of its possible arguments. The arguments to
a function may be functions or propositions or individuals. (It will
be remembered that individuals were defined as whatever is neither a
proposition nor a function.) For the present we neglect the case in
which the argument to a function is a proposition. Consider a function
whose argument is an individual. This function presupposes the totality
of individuals; but unless it contains functions as apparent variables,
it does not presuppose any totality of functions. If, however, it does
contain a function as apparent variable, then it cannot be defined
until some totality of functions has been defined. It follows that we
must first define the totality of those functions that have individuals
as arguments and contain no functions as apparent variables. These
are the <i>predicative</i> functions of individuals. Generally, a
predicative function of a variable argument is one which involves no
totality except that of the possible values of the argument, and those
that are presupposed by any one of the possible arguments. Thus a
predicative function of a variable argument is any function which can
be specified without introducing new kinds of variables not necessarily
presupposed by the variable which is the argument.</p>

<p>A closely analogous treatment can be developed for propositions.
Propositions which contain no functions and no apparent variables may
be called <i>elementary propositions</i>. Propositions which are not
elementary, which contain no functions, and no apparent variables
except individuals, may be called <i>first-order propositions</i>. (It
should be observed that no variables except <i>apparent</i> variables
can occur in a proposition, since whatever contains a <i>real</i>
variable is a function, not a proposition.) Thus elementary and
first-order propositions will be values of first-order functions. (It
should be remembered that a function is not a constituent in one of its
values: thus for example the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_9"> is human" is not a
constituent of the proposition "Socrates is human.") Elementary and
first-order propositions presuppose no totality except (at most) the
totality of individuals. They are of one or other of the three forms
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi !x; (x). \phi !x; (\exists x).\phi !x, \]" src="images/512.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.834ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_512.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi !x\)" src="images/484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_484.svg_1"> is a predicative function of an individual. It
follows that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_125"> represents a variable elementary proposition
or a variable first-order proposition, a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(fp\)" src="images/513.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.382ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_513.svg"> is either
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi !x)\)" src="images/514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.276ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_514.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{(x).\phi !x\}\)" src="images/515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.839ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_515.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{(\exists x).\phi !x\}\)" src="images/516.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.097ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_516.svg">.
Thus a function of an elementary or a first-order proposition may
always be reduced to a function of a first-order function. It follows
that a proposition involving the totality of first-order propositions
may be reduced to one involving the totality of first-order functions;
and this obviously applies equally to higher<span class="pagenum" id="Page_58">[Pg 58]</span> orders. The propositional
hierarchy can, therefore, be derived from the functional hierarchy, and
we may define a proposition of the nth order as one which involves an
apparent variable of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n - 1\)" src="images/517.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.254ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_517.svg">th order in the functional hierarchy.
The propositional hierarchy is never required in practice, and is only
relevant for the solution of paradoxes; hence it is unnecessary to go
into further detail as to the types of propositions.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
VI. <i>The Axiom of Reducibility.</i></p>


<p>It remains to consider the "axiom of reducibility." It will be seen
that, according to the above hierarchy, no statement can be made
significantly about "all <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_48">-functions," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_49"> is some given
object. Thus such a notion as "all properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_50">," meaning
"all functions which are true with the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_51">," will be
illegitimate. We shall have to distinguish the order of function
concerned. We can speak of "all predicative properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_52">," "all
second-order properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_53">," and so on. (If <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_54"> is not an
individual, but an object of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_6">, "second-order properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_55">" will mean "functions of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n + 2\)" src="images/518.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.254ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_518.svg"> satisfied by <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_56">.")
But we cannot speak of "all properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_57">." In some cases, we can
see that some statement will hold of "all <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_7">th-order properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_58">," whatever value <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_8"> may have. In such cases, no practical harm
results from regarding the statement as being about "all properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_59">," provided we remember that it is really a number of statements,
and not a single statement which could be regarded as assigning another
property to <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_60">, over and above all properties. Such cases will
always involve some systematic ambiguity, such as that involved in
the meaning of the word "truth," as explained above. Owing to this
systematic ambiguity, it will be possible, sometimes, to combine
into a single verbal statement what are really a number of different
statements, corresponding to different orders in the hierarchy. This is
illustrated in the case of the liar, where the statement "all <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_17">'s
statements are false" should be broken up into different statements
referring to his statements of various orders, and attributing to each
the appropriate kind of falsehood.</p>

<p>The axiom of reducibility is introduced in order to legitimate a great
mass of reasoning, in which, prima facie, we are concerned with such
notions as "all properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_61">" or "all <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_62">-functions," and
in which, nevertheless, it seems scarcely possible to suspect any
substantial error. In order to state the axiom, we must first define
what is meant by "formal equivalence." Two functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_34">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi \hat{x}\)" src="images/223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_223.svg_2"> are said to be "formally equivalent" when, with
every possible argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_233">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_62"> is equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_12">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_63"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_13"> are either both true or
both false. Thus two functions are formally equivalent when they are
satisfied by the same set of arguments. The axiom of reducibility is
the assumption that, given any function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_35">, there is a
formally equivalent <i>predicative</i> function,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_59">[Pg 59]</span> <i>i.e.</i> there is
a predicative function which is true when <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_41"> is true and false
when <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_42"> is false. In symbols, the axiom is:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon (\exists \psi) \colon {\phi}x \ldotp \equiv_{x} \ldotp {\psi}!x\text{.} \]" src="images/519.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.428ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_519.svg"></span>
For two variables, we require a similar axiom, namely: Given any
function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\hat{x}, \hat{y})\)" src="images/520.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_520.svg">, there is a formally equivalent
<i>predicative</i> function, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon (\exists \psi) \colon \phi(x, y) \ldotp \equiv_{x, y} \ldotp \psi!(x, y)\text{.} \]" src="images/521.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 28.406ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_521.svg"></span></p>

<p>In order to explain the purposes of the axiom of reducibility, and the
nature of the grounds for supposing it true, we shall first illustrate
it by applying it to some particular cases.</p>

<p>If we call a <i>predicate</i> of an object a predicative function which
is true of that object, then the predicates of an object are only some
among its properties. Take for example such a proposition as "Napoleon
had all the qualities that make a great general." We may interpret this
as meaning "Napoleon had all the predicates that make a great general."
Here there is a predicate which is an apparent variable. If we put
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(f({\phi}!\hat{z})\)" src="images/522.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.034ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_522.svg">" for "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!\hat{z}\)" src="images/496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_496.svg_4"> is a predicate required
in a great general," our proposition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\phi) \colon f({\phi}!\hat{z}) ~\text{implies}~ {\phi}!(\text{Napoleon})\text{.} \]" src="images/523.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.811ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_523.svg"></span>
Since this refers to a totality of predicates, it is not itself a
predicate of Napoleon. It by no means follows, however, that there is
not some one predicate common and peculiar to great generals. In fact,
it is certain that there is such a predicate. For the number of great
generals is finite, and each of them certainly possessed some predicate
not possessed by any other human being—for example, the exact instant
of his birth. The disjunction of such predicates will constitute a
predicate common and peculiar to great generals<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_20" id="FNanchor_20">[20]</a>. If we call this
predicate <img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}!\hat{z}\)" src="images/524.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_524.svg">, the statement we made about Napoleon was
equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}!(\text{Napoleon})\)" src="images/525.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.102ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_525.svg">. And this equivalence holds
equally if we substitute any other individual for Napoleon. Thus we
have arrived at a predicate which is always equivalent to the property
we ascribed to Napoleon, <i>i.e.</i> it belongs to those objects which
have this property, and to no others. The axiom of reducibility states
that such a predicate always exists, <i>i.e.</i> that any property
of an object belongs to the same collection of objects as those that
possess some predicate.</p>

<p>We may next illustrate our principle by its application to
<i>identity</i>. In this connection, it has a certain affinity with
Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles. It is plain that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_234"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_74"> are identical, and <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_43"> is true, then <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}y\)" src="images/526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_526.svg"> is
true. Here it cannot matter what sort of function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_30"> may
be: the statement must hold for <i>any</i> function. But we cannot
say, conversely: "If, with all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_22">, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_44"> implies
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}y\)" src="images/526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_526.svg_1">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_235"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_75"> are identical"; because "all values
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_23">" is inadmissible. If we wish to speak of "all values of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_24">," we must confine ourselves to functions of one order. We may
confine <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_25"> to predicates, or to<span class="pagenum" id="Page_60">[Pg 60]</span> second-order functions, or to
functions of any order we please. But we must necessarily leave out
functions of all but one order. Thus we shall obtain, so to speak,
a hierarchy of different degrees of identity. We may say "all the
predicates of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_236"> belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_76">," "all second-order properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_237"> belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_77">," and so on. Each of these statements implies
all its predecessors: for example, if all second-order properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_238"> belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_78">, then all predicates of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_239"> belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_79">,
for to have all the predicates of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_240"> is a second-order property,
and this property belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_241">. But we cannot, without the help of
an axiom, argue conversely that if all the predicates of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_242"> belong
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_80">, all the second-order properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_243"> must also belong to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_81">. Thus we cannot, without the help of an axiom, be sure that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_244">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_82"> are identical if they have the same predicates. Leibniz's
identity of indiscernibles supplied this axiom. It should be observed
that by "indiscernibles" he cannot have meant two objects which agree
as to <i>all</i> their properties, for one of the properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_245">
is to be identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_246">, and therefore this property would
necessarily belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_83"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_247"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_84"> agreed in <i>all</i>
their properties. Some limitation of the common properties necessary to
make things indiscernible is therefore implied by the necessity of an
axiom. For purposes of illustration (not of interpreting Leibniz) we
may suppose the common properties required for indiscernibility to be
limited to predicates. Then the identity of indiscernibles will state
that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_248"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_85"> agree as to all their predicates, they are
identical. This can be proved if we assume the axiom of reducibility.
For, in that case, every property belongs to the same collection of
objects as is defined by some predicate. Hence there is some predicate
common and peculiar to the objects which are identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_249">. This
predicate belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_250">, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_251"> is identical with itself; hence
it belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_86">, since y has all the predicates of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_252">; hence y
is identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_253">. It follows that we may <i>define</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_254"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_87"> as identical when all the predicates of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_255"> belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_88">,
<i>i.e.</i> when (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi)\colon \phi !x . \supset . \phi !y\)" src="images/527.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.364ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_527.svg">. We
therefore adopt the following definition of identity<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_21" id="FNanchor_21">[21]</a>:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x = y . = \colon (\phi) \colon \phi !x . \supset . \phi !y \qquad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.011ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_528.svg"></span></p>

<p>But apart from the axiom of reducibility, or some axiom equivalent
in this connection, we should be compelled to regard identity as
indefinable, and to admit (what seems impossible) that two objects may
agree in all their predicates without being identical.</p>

<p>The axiom of reducibility is even more essential in the theory of
classes. It should be observed, in the first place, that if we assume
the existence of classes, the axiom of reducibility can be proved.
For in that case, given any function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_8"> of whatever
order, there is a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_53"> consisting of just those objects
which satisfy <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_9">. Hence "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_36">" is equivalent
to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_256"> belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_54">." But "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_257"> belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_55">"
is a statement containing no apparent variable, and is therefore a
predicative function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_258">. Hence if we assume the existence of<span class="pagenum" id="Page_61">[Pg 61]</span>
classes, the axiom of reducibility becomes unnecessary. The assumption
of the axiom of reducibility is therefore a smaller assumption than
the assumption that there are classes. This latter assumption has
hitherto been made unhesitatingly. However, both on the ground of the
contradictions, which require a more complicated treatment if classes
are assumed, and on the ground that it is always well to make the
smallest assumption required for proving our theorems, we prefer to
assume the axiom of reducibility rather than the existence of classes.
But in order to explain the use of the axiom in dealing with classes,
it is necessary first to explain the theory of classes, which is a
topic belonging to <a href="#CHAPTER_III" class="pginternal">Chapter III</a>. We therefore postpone to that Chapter
the explanation of the use of our axiom in dealing with classes.</p>

<p>It is worth while to note that all the purposes served by the axiom
of reducibility are equally well served if we assume that there is
always a function of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_9">th order (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_10"> is fixed) which
is formally equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_37">, whatever may be the order
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_38">. Here we shall mean by "a function of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_11">th
order" a function of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_12">th order relative to the arguments
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_39"><img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_40">; thus if these arguments are
absolutely of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_2">th order, we assume the existence of a function
formally equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_41"> whose absolute order is the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(m + n\)" src="images/529.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.11ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_529.svg">th. The axiom of reducibility in the form assumed above
takes <img alt="" data-tex="\(n = 1\)" src="images/530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.506ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_530.svg">, but this is not necessary to the use of the axiom.
It is also unnecessary that <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_13"> should be the same for different
values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_3">; what is necessary is that <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_14"> should be constant so
long as <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_4"> is constant. What is needed is that, where extensional
functions of functions are concerned, we should be able to deal with
any <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_63">-function by means of some formally equivalent function of a
given type, so as to be able to obtain results which would otherwise
require the illegitimate notion of "all <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_64">-functions"; but it does
not matter what the given type is. It does not appear, however, that
the axiom of reducibility is rendered appreciably more plausible by
being put in the above more general but more complicated form.</p>

<p>The axiom of reducibility is equivalent to the assumption that "any
combination or disjunction of predicates<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_22" id="FNanchor_22">[22]</a> is equivalent to a
single predicate," <i>i.e.</i> to the assumption that, if we assert
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_259"> has all the predicates that satisfy a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi !\hat{z})\)" src="images/531.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.034ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_531.svg">
there is some one predicate which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_260"> will have whenever
our assertion is true, and will not have whenever it is false, and
similarly if we assert that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_261"> has some one of the predicates that
satisfy a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.154ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_532.svg">). For by means of this
assumption, the order of a non-predicative function can be lowered by
one; hence, after some finite number of steps, we shall be able to get
from any non-predicative function to a formally equivalent predicative
function. It does not seem probable that<span class="pagenum" id="Page_62">[Pg 62]</span> the above assumption could
be substituted for the axiom of reducibility in symbolic deductions,
since its use would require the explicit introduction of the further
assumption that by a finite number of downward steps we can pass from
any function to a predicative function, and this assumption could not
well be made without developments that are scarcely possible at an
early stage. But on the above grounds it seems plain that in fact, if
the above alternative axiom is true, so is the axiom of reducibility.
The converse, which completes the proof of equivalence, is of course
evident.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
VII. <i>Reasons for Accepting the Axiom of Reducibility.</i></p>


<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_63">[Pg 63]</span></p>

<p>That the axiom of reducibility is self-evident is a proposition
which can hardly be maintained. But in fact self-evidence is never
more than a part of the reason for accepting an axiom, and is never
indispensable. The reason for accepting an axiom, as for accepting
any other proposition, is always largely inductive, namely that many
propositions which are nearly indubitable can be deduced from it, and
that no equally plausible way is known by which these propositions
could be true if the axiom were false, and nothing which is probably
false can be deduced from it. If the axiom is apparently self-evident,
that only means, practically, that it is nearly indubitable; for things
have been thought to be self-evident and have yet turned out to be
false. And if the axiom itself is nearly indubitable, that merely adds
to the inductive evidence derived from the fact that its consequences
are nearly indubitable: it does not provide new evidence of a radically
different kind. Infallibility is never attainable, and therefore some
element of doubt should always attach to every axiom and to all its
consequences. In formal logic, the element of doubt is less than in
most sciences, but it is not absent, as appears from the fact that
the paradoxes followed from premisses which were not previously known
to require limitations. In the case of the axiom of reducibility, the
inductive evidence in its favour is very strong, since the reasonings
which it permits and the results to which it leads are all such as
appear valid. But although it seems very improbable that the axiom
should turn out to be false, it is by no means improbable that it
should be found to be deducible from some other more fundamental and
more evident axiom. It is possible that the use of the vicious-circle
principle, as embodied in the above hierarchy of types, is more drastic
than it need be, and that by a less drastic use the necessity for
the axiom might be avoided. Such changes, however, would not render
anything false which had been asserted on the basis of the principles
explained above: they would merely provide easier proofs of the same
theorems. There would seem, therefore, to be but the slenderest ground
for fearing that the use of the axiom of reducibility may lead us into
error.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
VIII. <i>The Contradictions.</i></p>


<p>We are now in a position to show how the theory of types affects the
solution of the contradictions which have beset mathematical logic.
For this purpose, we shall begin by an enumeration of some of the more
important and illustrative of these contradictions, and shall then show
how they all embody vicious-circle fallacies, and are therefore all
avoided by the theory of types. It will be noticed that these paradoxes
do not relate exclusively to the ideas of number and quantity.
Accordingly no solution can be adequate which seeks to explain them
merely as the result of some illegitimate use of these ideas. The
solution must be sought in some such scrutiny of fundamental logical
ideas as has been attempted in the foregoing pages.</p>

<p>(1) The oldest contradiction of the kind in question is the
<i>Epimenides</i>. Epimenides the Cretan said that all Cretans were
liars, and all other statements made by Cretans were certainly lies.
Was this a lie? The simplest form of this contradiction is afforded
by the man who says "I am lying"; if he is lying, he is speaking the
truth, and vice versa.</p>

<p>(2) Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_2"> be the class of all those classes which are not members
of themselves. Then, whatever class <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_262"> may be, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_263"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_3">" is
equivalent to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_264"> is not an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_265">." Hence, giving to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_266"> the value
<img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_4">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_5"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_6">" is equivalent to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_7"> is not a <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_8">."</p>

<p>(3) Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg"> be the relation which subsists between two relations
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_56"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_7"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_57"> does not have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_58"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_8">. Then, whatever relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_59"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_9"> may be, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_60"> has the
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_1"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_10">" is equivalent to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_61"> does not have the
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_62"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_11">." Hence, giving the value <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_2"> to both <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_63">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_12">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_3"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_4"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_5">" is equivalent to
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_6"> does not have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_7"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_8">."</p>

<p>(4) Burali-Forti's contradiction<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_23" id="FNanchor_23">[23]</a> may be stated as follows: It can
be shown that every well-ordered series has an ordinal number, that the
series of ordinals up to and including any given ordinal exceeds the
given ordinal by one, and (on certain very natural assumptions) that
the series of all ordinals (in order of magnitude) is well-ordered.
It follows that the series of all ordinals has an ordinal number,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Omega\)" src="images/534.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.633ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_534.svg"> say. But in that case the series of all ordinals including
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Omega\)" src="images/534.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.633ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_534.svg_1"> has the ordinal number <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Omega + 1\)" src="images/535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.53ex; height: 1.778ex;" id="img_images_535.svg">, which must be greater
than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Omega\)" src="images/534.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.633ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_534.svg_2">. Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Omega\)" src="images/534.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.633ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_534.svg_3"> is not the ordinal number of all
ordinals.</p>

<p>(5) The number of syllables in the English names of finite integers
tends to increase as the integers grow larger, and must gradually
increase indefinitely, since only a finite number of names can be
made with a given finite number of syllables. Hence the names of some
integers must consist of at least nineteen syllables, and among these
there must be a least. Hence "the least integer not nameable in fewer
than nineteen syllables"<span class="pagenum" id="Page_64">[Pg 64]</span> must denote a definite integer; in fact, it
denotes 111,777. But "the least integer not nameable in fewer than
nineteen syllables" is itself a name consisting of eighteen syllables;
hence the least integer not nameable in fewer than nineteen syllables
can be named in eighteen syllables, which is a contradiction<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_24" id="FNanchor_24">[24]</a>.</p>

<p>(6) Among transfinite ordinals some can be defined, while
others can not; for the total number of possible definitions is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_536.svg"><a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_25" id="FNanchor_25">[25]</a>, while the number of transfinite ordinals exceeds
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_536.svg_1">. Hence there must be indefinable ordinals, and among
these there must be a least. But this is defined as "the least
indefinable ordinal," which is a contradiction<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_26" id="FNanchor_26">[26]</a>.</p>

<p>(7) Richard's paradox<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_27" id="FNanchor_27">[27]</a> is akin to that of the least indefinable
