the function '<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_18"> is a white man who claims to have reached
the North Pole,'" is not equivalent to "it is a strange coincidence
that two arguments should satisfy the function '<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_19"> is Dr Cook
or Commander Peary.'" Thus "it is a strange coincidence that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{x}\)" src="images/602.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_602.svg"> should be satisfied by two arguments" is an intensional
function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! \hat{x}\)" src="images/479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_479.svg_5">.</p>

<p>The above instances illustrate the fact that the functions of functions
with which mathematics is specially concerned are extensional, and that
intensional functions of functions only occur where non-mathematical
ideas are introduced, such as what somebody believes or affirms, or the
emotions aroused by some fact. Hence it is natural, in a mathematical
logic, to lay special stress on <i>extensional</i> functions of
functions.</p>

<p>When two functions are formally equivalent, we may say that they
<i>have the same extension</i>. In this definition, we are in close
agreement with usage. We do not assume that there is such a thing
as an extension: we merely define the whole phrase "having the same
extension." We may now say that an extensional function of a function
is one whose truth or falsehood depends only upon the extension of its
argument. In such a case, it is convenient to regard the statement
concerned as being about the extension. Since extensional functions are
many and important, it is natural to regard the extension as an object,
called a <i>class</i>, which is supposed to be the subject of all the
equivalent statements about various formally equivalent functions. Thus
<i>e.g.</i> if we say "there were twelve Apostles," it is natural to
regard this statement as attributing the property of being twelve to
a certain collection of men, namely those who were Apostles, rather
than as attributing the property of being satisfied by twelve arguments
to the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_20"> was an Apostle." This view is encouraged
by the feeling that there is something which is identical in the case
of two functions which "have the same extension." And if we take such
simple problems as "how many combinations can be made of <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_32"> things?"
it seems at first sight necessary that each "combination" should be a
single object which can be counted as one. This, however, is certainly
not necessary technically, and we see no reason to suppose that it is
true<span class="pagenum" id="Page_78">[Pg 78]</span> philosophically. The technical procedure by which the apparent
difficulty is overcome is as follows.</p>

<p>We have seen that an extensional function of a function may be regarded
as a function of the class determined by the argument-function, but
that an intensional function cannot be so regarded. In order to
obviate the necessity of giving different treatment to intensional
and extensional functions of functions, we construct an extensional
function derived from any function of a predicative function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_603.svg">,
and having the property of being equivalent to the function
from which it is derived, provided this function is extensional,
as well as the property of being significant (by the help of the
systematic ambiguity of equivalence) with any argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_10">
whose arguments are of the same type as those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_603.svg_1">. The
derived function, written "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg">," is defined as
follows: Given a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\psi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.278ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_605.svg">), our derived function
is to be "there is a predicative function which is formally equivalent
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_11"> and satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_7">." If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_12"> is a
predicative function, our derived function will be true whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.525ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_606.svg">) is true. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.525ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_606.svg_1">) is an extensional
function, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_13"> is a predicative function, our derived
function will not be true unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.525ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_606.svg_2">) is true; thus in
this case, our derived function is equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.525ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_606.svg_3">).
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.525ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_606.svg_4">) is not an extensional function, and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_14">
is a predicative function, our derived function may sometimes
be true when the original function is false. But in any case the
derived function is always extensional.</p>

<p>In order that the derived function should be significant for any
function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_15">, of whatever order, provided it takes
arguments of the right type, it is necessary and sufficient that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\psi \hat{z}\)" src="images/607.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.649ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_607.svg">) should be significant, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_603.svg_2">
is any <i>predicative</i> function. The reason of this is that we
only require, concerning an argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_16">, the hypothesis
that it is formally equivalent to some predicative function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/608.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_608.svg">, and formal equivalence has the same kind of systematic
ambiguity as to type that belongs to truth and falsehood, and can
therefore hold between functions of any two different orders,
provided the functions take arguments of the same type. Thus by means
of our derived function we have not merely provided extensional
functions everywhere in place of intensional functions, but we have
<i>practically</i> removed the necessity for considering differences of
type among functions whose arguments are of the same type. This effects
the same kind of simplification in our hierarchy as would result from
never considering any but predicative functions.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/609.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.278ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_609.svg">) can be built up by means of the primitive ideas
of disjunction, negation, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_2">, and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_610.svg">,
as is the case with all the functions of functions that explicitly
occur in the present work, it will be found that, in virtue of the
systematic ambiguity of the above primitive ideas, any function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_21">
whose arguments are of the same type as those of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_611.svg">
can significantly be substituted for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_603.svg_3">
in f without any other symbolic change. Thus in<span class="pagenum" id="Page_79">[Pg 79]</span> such a case what
is symbolically, though not really, the same function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_8"> can
receive as arguments functions of various different types. If, with
a given argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_17">, the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.525ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_606.svg_5">),
so interpreted, is equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/609.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.278ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_609.svg_1">) whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_490.svg_2"> is formally equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_18">, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_1"> is equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.525ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_606.svg_6">) provided
there is any predicative function formally equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/612.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_612.svg">. At this point, we make use of the axiom of reducibility,
according to which there always is a predicative function formally
equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_19">.</p>

<p>As was explained above, it is convenient to regard an extensional
function of a function as having for its argument not the function, but
the class determined by the function. Now we have seen that our derived
function is always extensional. Hence if our original function was
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\phi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/613.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.154ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_613.svg">), we write the derived function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_2">,
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg">)" may be read "the class of arguments
which satisfy <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_20">," or more simply "the class determined
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_21">." Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_3">" will mean:
"There is a predicative function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_603.svg_4"> which is formally
equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_22"> and is such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/609.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.278ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_609.svg_2">)
is true." This is in reality a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_23">, but we
treat it symbolically as if it had an argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_1">).
By the help of the axiom of reducibility, we find that the usual
properties of classes result. For example, two formally equivalent
functions determine the same class, and conversely, two functions which
determine the same class are formally equivalent. Also to say that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_286"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_2">), <i>i.e.</i> of the class
determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_24">, is true when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_66"> is true, and
false when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_67"> is false. Thus all the mathematical purposes for
which classes might seem to be required are fulfilled by the purely
symbolic objects <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_3">) provided we assume the axiom of
reducibility.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_80">[Pg 80]</span></p>

<p>In virtue of the axiom of reducibility, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_25"> is
any function, there is a formally equivalent predicative function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi ! \hat{z}\)" src="images/490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_490.svg_3">; then the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_4">) is identical
with the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi !z\)" src="images/615.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.086ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_615.svg">), so that every class can be
defined by a <i>predicative</i> function. Hence the totality of
the <i>classes</i> to which a given term can be significantly said
to belong or not to belong is a legitimate totality, although the
totality of <i>functions</i> which a given term can be significantly
said to satisfy or not to satisfy is not a legitimate totality. The
classes to which a given term <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_68"> belongs or does not belong are
the classes defined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_69">-functions; they are also the classes
defined by <i>predicative</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_70">-functions. Let us call them
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_71">-classes. Then "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_72">-classes" form a legitimate totality, derived
from that of predicative <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_73">-functions. Hence many kinds of general
statements become possible which would otherwise involve vicious-circle
paradoxes. These general statements are none of them such as lead to
contradictions, and many of them such as it is very hard to suppose
illegitimate. The fact that they are rendered possible by the axiom
of reducibility, and that they would otherwise be excluded by the
vicious-circle principle, is to be regarded as an argument in favour of
the axiom of reducibility.</p>

<p>The above definition of "the class defined by the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_22">,"
or rather, of any proposition in which this phrase occurs,
is, in symbols, as follows:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f{\hat{z}(\phi z)}.=\colon(\exists \psi)\colon \phi x.\equiv_{x}.\psi !x\colon f\{\psi !\hat{z}\}\,\quad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.997ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_616.svg"></span>
In order to recommend this definition, we shall enumerate five
requisites which a definition of classes must satisfy, and we shall
then show that the above definition satisfies these five requisites.</p>

<p>We require of classes, if they are to serve the purposes for which
they are commonly employed, that they shall have certain properties,
which may be enumerated as follows. (1) Every propositional function
must determine a class, which may be regarded as the collection of
all the arguments satisfying the function in question. This principle
must hold when the function is satisfied by an infinite number of
arguments as well as when it is satisfied by a finite number. It
must hold also when no arguments satisfy the function; <i>i.e.</i>
the "null-class" must be just as good a class as any other. (2) Two
propositional functions which are formally equivalent, <i>i.e.</i> such
that any argument which satisfies either satisfies the other, must
determine the same class; that is to say, a class must be something
wholly determined by its membership, so that <i>e.g.</i> the class
"featherless bipeds" is identical with the class "men," and the class
"even primes" is identical with the class "numbers identical with 2."
(3) Conversely, two propositional functions which determine the same
class must be formally equivalent; in other words, when the class is
given, the membership is determinate: two different sets of objects
cannot yield the same class. (4) In the same sense in which there are
classes (whatever this sense may be), or in some closely analogous
sense, there must also be classes of classes. Thus for example "the
combinations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_33"> things <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_5"> at a time," where the <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_34"> things
form a given class, is a class of classes; each combination of <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_6">
things is a class, and each such class is a member of the specified
set of combinations, which set is therefore a class whose members are
classes. Again, the class of unit classes, or of couples, is absolutely
indispensable; the former is the number 1, the latter the number 2.
Thus without classes of classes, arithmetic becomes impossible. (5)
It must under all circumstances be meaningless to suppose a class
identical with one of its own members. For if such a supposition
had any meaning, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \alpha\)" src="images/617.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.662ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_617.svg">" would be a significant
propositional function<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_33" id="FNanchor_33">[33]</a>, and so would "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \sim{\in \alpha}\)" src="images/618.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 8.051ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_618.svg">."
Hence, by (1) and (4), there would be a class of all classes satisfying
the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \sim{\in \alpha}\)" src="images/618.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 8.051ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_618.svg_1">." If we call this class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg">, we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \in \kappa.\equiv_{\alpha}. \alpha \sim{\in \alpha}. \]" src="images/620.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 19.18ex; height: 1.579ex;" id="img_images_620.svg"></span>
Since, by our hypothesis, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \in \kappa\)" src="images/621.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.372ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_621.svg">" is supposed
significant, the above equivalence, which holds with all possible
values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_59">, holds with the value <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_1">, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa \in \kappa.\equiv. \kappa \sim{\in \kappa}. \]" src="images/622.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 17.534ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_622.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_81">[Pg 81]</span>
But this is a contradiction<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_34" id="FNanchor_34">[34]</a>. Hence "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \alpha\)" src="images/617.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.662ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_617.svg_1">" and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \sim{\in \alpha}\)" src="images/618.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 8.051ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_618.svg_2">" must always be meaningless. In general,
there is nothing surprising about this conclusion, but it has two
consequences which deserve special notice. In the first place, a class
consisting of only one member must not be identical with that one
member, <i>i.e</i>. we must not have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx=x\)" src="images/623.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.764ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_623.svg">. For we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \iota ʻx\)" src="images/624.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.513ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_624.svg">,
and therefore, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x = \iota ʻx\)" src="images/625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.764ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_625.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx \in \iota ʻx\)" src="images/626.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.671ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_626.svg">,
which, we saw, must be meaningless. It follows that
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x = \iota ʻx\)" src="images/625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.764ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_625.svg_1">" must be absolutely meaningless, not simply false. In
the second place, it might appear as if the class of all classes were
a class, <i>i.e.</i> as if (writing "Cls" for "class") "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\,\in\, \text{Cls}\)" src="images/627.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 9.829ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_627.svg">"
were a true proposition. But this combination of symbols must be
meaningless; unless, indeed, an ambiguity exists in the meaning of
"Cls," so that, in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\, \in\, \text{Cls}\)" src="images/628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 9.829ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_628.svg">," the first "Cls"
can be supposed to have a different meaning from the second.</p>

<p>As regards the above requisites, it is plain, to begin with, that,
in accordance with our definition, every propositional function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_26"> determines a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_5">). Assuming
the axiom of reducibility, there must always be true propositions
about <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_6">), <i>i.e.</i> true propositions of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_4">. For suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_27"> is formally
equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_603.svg_5">, and suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_603.svg_6"> satisfies
some function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_9">. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_7">) also satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_10">.
Hence, given any function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_28">, there are true propositions
of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_5">, <i>i.e.</i> true propositions in
which "the class determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_29">" is grammatically the
subject. This shows that our definition fulfils the first of our five
requisites.</p>

<p>The second and third requisites together demand that the classes
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_8">) and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z\)" src="images/629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.457ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_629.svg">) should be identical when,
and only when, their defining functions are formally equivalent,
<i>i.e.</i> that we should have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{z}(\phi z)=\hat{z}(\psi z).\equiv\colon \phi x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x. \]" src="images/630.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.253ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_630.svg"></span>
Here the meaning of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_1"> = <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z)\)" src="images/631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.337ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_631.svg">" is to
be derived, by means of a two-fold application of the definition of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_6">, from the definition of
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[  \unicode{x201c}\chi !\hat{z} = \theta!\hat{z}, \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/632.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 12.125ex; height: 2.294ex;" id="img_images_632.svg"></span>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{which is}\quad \chi !\hat{z}= \theta!.\hat{z}=\colon (f)\colon f!\chi !\hat{z}.\supset.f!\theta !\hat{z}\, \quad\text{Df} \]" src="images/633.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.818ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_633.svg"></span>
by the general definition of identity.</p>

<p>In interpreting "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z = \hat{z}(\psi z)\)" src="images/634.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.687ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_634.svg">," we will adopt
the convention which we adopted in regard to (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x\)" src="images/635.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.054ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_635.svg">) and
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\psi x)\)" src="images/589.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_589.svg_3">, namely that the incomplete symbol which occurs
first is to have the larger scope. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z = \hat{z}(\psi z)\)" src="images/634.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.687ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_634.svg_1">
becomes, by our definition,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists \chi) \colon \phi x . \equiv_{x} . \chi !x \colon \chi ! \hat{z} = \hat{z}(\psi z), \]" src="images/636.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.384ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_636.svg"></span>
which, by eliminating <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z\)" src="images/629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.457ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_629.svg_1">), becomes
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists \chi) \colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi !x \colon\ldotp (\exists \theta)\colon \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\theta !x\colon \chi !\hat{z} = \theta !\hat{z}, \]" src="images/637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.518ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_637.svg"></span>
which is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists \chi , \theta)\colon \phi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi !x\colon \psi x.\equiv_{x}. \theta !x\colon \chi !\hat{z} = \theta !\hat{z}, \]" src="images/638.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.488ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_638.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_82">[Pg 82]</span>
which, again, is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists \chi) \colon \phi x \ldotp \equiv_{x} \ldotp \chi!x \colon \psi x \ldotp \equiv_{x} \ldotp \chi!x, \]" src="images/639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.914ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_639.svg"></span>
which, in virtue of the axiom of reducibility, is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi x \ldotp \equiv_{x} \ldotp \psi x. \]" src="images/640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.914ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_640.svg"></span>
Thus our definition of the use of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_2"> is such as to
satisfy the conditions (2) and (3) which we laid down for classes,
<i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \hat{z}(\phi z) = \hat{z}(\psi z) \ldotp \equiv \colon \phi x \ldotp \equiv_{x} \ldotp \psi x. \]" src="images/641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.647ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_641.svg"></span></p>

<p>Before considering classes of classes, it will be well to define
membership of a class, <i>i.e.</i> to define the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in\hat{z} (\phi z)\)" src="images/642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.273ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_642.svg">,"
which may be read "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_287"> is a member of the
class determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_23">." Since this is a function of the
form <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_7">, it must be derived, by means of our
general definition of such functions, from the corresponding function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\psi!\hat{z}\}\)" src="images/643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.661ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_643.svg">. We therefore put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x \in \psi!\hat{z} \ldotp = \ldotp \psi!x \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 19.694ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_644.svg"></span>
This definition is only needed in order to give a meaning to
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.273ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_645.svg">"; the meaning it gives is, in virtue of the
definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_8">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists\psi) \colon \phi y \ldotp \equiv_{y} \ldotp \psi!y \colon \psi!x. \]" src="images/646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 20.939ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_646.svg"></span>
It thus appears that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.273ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_647.svg">" implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_68">,
since it implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!x\)" src="images/648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.396ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_648.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!x\)" src="images/648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.396ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_648.svg_1"> is equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_69">;
also, in virtue of the axiom of reducibility, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_70"> implies
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.273ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_647.svg_1">," since there is a predicative function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_5"> formally equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_32">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_288"> must satisfy
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_6">, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_289"> (<i>ex hypothesi</i>) satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_33">. Thus in
virtue of the axiom of reducibility we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon x \in \hat{z}(\phi z) \ldotp \equiv \ldotp \phi x, \]" src="images/649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.705ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_649.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_290"> is a member of the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_3"> when,
and only when, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_291"> satisfies the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_34"> which defines the
class.</p>

<p>We have next to consider how to interpret a class of classes. As we
have defined <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_9">, we shall naturally regard a
class of classes as consisting of those values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_4">
which satisfy <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_10">. Let us write <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_60"> for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_5">; then we may write <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\alpha}(f\alpha)\)" src="images/650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.9ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_650.svg"> for
the class of values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_61"> which satisfy <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\alpha\)" src="images/651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.692ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_651.svg"><a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_35" id="FNanchor_35">[35]</a>. We
shall apply the same definition, and put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ F\{\hat{\alpha}(f\alpha)\} \ldotp = \colon (\exists g) \colon f\beta \ldotp \equiv_{\beta} \ldotp g!\beta \colon F\{g!\hat{\alpha}\} \quad \text{Df}, \]" src="images/652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 42.543ex; height: 2.482ex;" id="img_images_652.svg"></span>
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_16">" stands for any expression of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi!z)\)" src="images/653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.966ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_653.svg">.</p>

<p>Let us take "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma \in \hat{\alpha}(f\alpha)\)" src="images/654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.895ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_654.svg">" as an instance of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(F\{\hat{\alpha}(f\alpha)\}\)" src="images/655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.857ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_655.svg">. Then
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \gamma \in \hat{\alpha} (f\alpha) \ldotp \equiv \colon (\exists g) : f\beta \ldotp \equiv_{\beta} \ldotp g!\beta \colon \gamma\in g!\hat{\alpha}. \]" src="images/656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 42.209ex; height: 2.482ex;" id="img_images_656.svg"></span>
Just as we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x \in\psi! \hat{z} \ldotp = \ldotp \psi!x \quad \text{Df}, \]" src="images/657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 19.694ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_657.svg"></span>
so we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \gamma \in g! \hat{\alpha} \ldotp = \ldotp g!\gamma \quad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/658.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 19.172ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_658.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp \gamma \in \hat{\alpha} (f\alpha) \ldotp \equiv : (\exists g) : f\beta \ldotp \equiv_{\beta} \ldotp g!\beta : g!\gamma. \]" src="images/659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 39.127ex; height: 2.482ex;" id="img_images_659.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_83">[Pg 83]</span></p>

<p>If we now extend the axiom of reducibility so as to apply to functions
of functions, <i>i.e.</i> if we assume
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists g)\colon f(\psi !\hat{z}).\equiv_{\psi}.g!(\psi !\hat{z}), \]" src="images/660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 23.514ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_660.svg"></span>
we easily deduce
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\vdash\colon(\exists g)\colon f{\{\hat{z}(\psi !z)\}}.\equiv_{\psi}.g!\{\hat{z}(\psi !z)\},\\ \textit{i.e.}\quad &amp;\vdash\colon(\exists g)\colon f \beta .\equiv_{\beta}.g!\beta.\\ \text{Thus}\quad &amp;\vdash \colon \gamma \in \hat{\alpha}(f \alpha).\equiv.f \gamma. \end{array} \]" src="images/661.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.962ex; width: 42.097ex; height: 9.055ex;" id="img_images_661.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus every function which can take classes as arguments, <i>i.e.</i>
every function of functions, determines a class of classes, whose
members are those classes which satisfy the determining function. Thus
the theory of classes of classes offers no difficulty.</p>

<p>We have next to consider our fifth requisite, namely that
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\in \hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/662.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.311ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_662.svg">)" is to be meaningless. Applying
our definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_11">, we find that if this
collection of symbols had a meaning, it would mean
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists \psi)\colon \phi x.\equiv_{x}. \psi!x \colon \psi !\hat{z} \in \psi !\hat{z}, \]" src="images/663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.119ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_663.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> in virtue of the definition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;x \in \psi!\hat{z}.=. \psi !x \quad \text{Df},\\ \text{it would mean}\quad &amp;(\exists \psi)\colon \phi x.\equiv_{x}. \psi!x\colon \psi !(\psi !\hat{z}). \end{array} \]" src="images/664.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.285ex; width: 43.414ex; height: 5.701ex;" id="img_images_664.svg"></span>
But here the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!(\psi !\hat{z})\)" src="images/665.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.016ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_665.svg">" occurs, which assigns a
function as argument to itself. Such a symbol is always meaningless,
for the reasons explained at the beginning of Chapter II (<a href="#Page_41" class="pginternal">pp. 41</a>-<a href="#Page_43" class="pginternal">43</a>).
Hence "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z) \in \hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.191ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_666.svg">" is meaningless, and our
fifth and last requisite is fulfilled.</p>

<p>As in the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(f({℩}x)(\phi x\)" src="images/667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.179ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_667.svg">), so in that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_12">,
there is an ambiguity as to the scope of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_6">
if it occurs in a proposition which itself is part of a larger
proposition. But in the case of classes, since we always have the axiom
of reducibility, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists \psi) \colon \phi x.\equiv_{x}.\psi !x, \]" src="images/668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.04ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_668.svg"></span>
which takes the place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_324.svg_1">, it follows that the
truth-value of any proposition in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_7"> occurs is
the same whatever scope we may give to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_8">, provided
the proposition is an extensional function of whatever functions it
may contain. Hence we may adopt the convention that the scope is to be
always the smallest proposition enclosed in dots or brackets in which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_9"> occurs. If at any time a larger scope is required,
we may indicate it by "[<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_10">]" followed by dots, in the
same way as we did for <img alt="" data-tex="\([({℩}x)(\phi x)]\)" src="images/101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.072ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_101.svg_1">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_84">[Pg 84]</span></p>

<p>Similarly when two class symbols occur, <i>e.g.</i> in a proposition
of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z),\hat{z}(\psi z)\}\)" src="images/669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.063ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_669.svg">, we need not
remember rules for the scopes of the two symbols, since all choices
give equivalent results, as it is easy to prove. For the preliminary
propositions a rule is desirable, so we can decide that the class
symbol which occurs first in the order of writing is to have the larger
scope.</p>

<p>The representation of a class by a single letter <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \)" src="images/670.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_670.svg"> can now
be understood. For the denotation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \)" src="images/670.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_670.svg_1"> is ambiguous, in so
far as it is undecided as to which of the symbols <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_11">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z)\)" src="images/631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.337ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_631.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\chi z)\)" src="images/671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.281ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_671.svg">, etc. it is to stand for,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_30">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi \hat{z}\)" src="images/219.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_219.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi \hat{z}\)" src="images/672.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 2.468ex; height: 2.294ex;" id="img_images_672.svg">, etc. are
the various determining functions of the class. According to the choice
made, different propositions result. But all the resulting propositions
are equivalent by virtue of the easily proved proposition:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[  \unicode{x201c}\vdash :\phi x\equiv_{x}\psi x.\supset .f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\equiv f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}. \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/673.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.419ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_673.svg"></span>
Hence unless we wish to discuss the determining function itself,
so that the notion of a class is really not properly present, the
ambiguity in the denotation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_62"> is entirely immaterial,
though, as we shall see immediately, we are led to limit ourselves
to predicative determining functions. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\alpha)\)" src="images/674.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.452ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_674.svg">," where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_63"> is a variable class, is really "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_13">,"
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_35"> is a variable function, that is, it is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(\exists \psi ).\phi x\equiv_{x}\psi !x.f\{\psi !\hat{z}\}, \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/675.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.591ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_675.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_36"> is a variable function. But here a difficulty arises
which is removed by a limitation to our practice and by the axiom
of reducibility. For the determining functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{z}\)" src="images/218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_218.svg_31">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi \hat{z}\)" src="images/219.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_219.svg_3">, etc. will be of different types, though the axiom
of reducibility secures that some are predicative functions. Then, in
interpreting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_64"> as a variable in terms of the variation of any
determining function, we shall be led into errors unless we confine
ourselves to predicative determining functions. These errors especially
arise in the transition to total variation (cf. <a href="#Page_15" class="pginternal">pp. 15</a>, <a href="#Page_16" class="pginternal">16</a>). Accordingly
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f\alpha =.(\exists \psi ).\phi !x\equiv_{x}\psi !x.f\{\psi !\hat{z}\}\quad \text{Df.} \]" src="images/676.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.35ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_676.svg"></span>
It is the peculiarity of a definition of the use of a single letter
[viz. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_65">] for a variable incomplete symbol that it, though
in a sense a real variable, occurs only in the <i>definiendum</i>,
while "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \)" src="images/677.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_677.svg">," though a real variable, occurs only in the
<i>definiens</i>.</p>

<p>Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\hat{\alpha }\)" src="images/678.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.692ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_678.svg">" stands for
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(\exists \psi ).\hat{\phi }!x\equiv_{x}\psi !x.f\{\psi !\hat{z}\},\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/679.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.22ex; height: 2.968ex;" id="img_images_679.svg"></span>
and "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha).f\alpha\)" src="images/680.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.026ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_680.svg">" stands for
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[  \unicode{x201c}(\phi ):(\exists \psi ).\phi !x\equiv_{x}\psi !x.f\{\psi !\hat{z}\}. \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/681.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.214ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_681.svg"></span>
Accordingly, in mathematical reasoning, we can dismiss the whole
apparatus of functions and think only of classes as "quasi-things,"
capable of immediate representation by a single name. The advantages
are two-fold: (1) classes are determined by their membership, so that
to one set of members there is one class, (2) the "type" of a class is
entirely defined by the type of its members.</p>

<p>Also a predicative function of a class can be defined thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f!\alpha =.(\exists \psi ).\phi !x\equiv_{x}\psi !x.f!\{\psi !\hat{z}\}\quad \text{Df.} \]" src="images/682.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.608ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_682.svg"></span>
Thus a predicative function of a class is always a predicative function of any
predicative determining function of the class, though the converse does not
hold.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_85">[Pg 85]</span></p>

<p>(3) <i>Relations</i>. With regard to relations, we have a theory
strictly analogous to that which we have just explained as regards
classes. Relations in extension, like classes, are incomplete symbols.
We require a division of functions of two variables into predicative
and non-predicative functions, again for reasons which have been
explained in <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a>. We use the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi !(x,y)\)" src="images/683.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.146ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_683.svg">" for a
<i>predicative</i> function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_292"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_93">.</p>

<p>We use "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi !(\hat{x},\hat{z})\)" src="images/684.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.09ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_684.svg">" for the function as opposed to its
values; and we use "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi (x,y)\)" src="images/685.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.92ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_685.svg">" for the relation (in
extension) determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_6">. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f\{\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)\}.=\colon(\exists \psi)\colon \phi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi !(x,y)\colon f\{\psi!(\hat{x},\hat{y}\} \quad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/686.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 57.804ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_686.svg"></span>
Thus even when <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\psi !(\hat{x},\hat{y})\}\)" src="images/687.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.778ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_687.svg"> is not an extensional
function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_7">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)\}\)" src="images/688.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.427ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_688.svg"> is an
extensional function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_37">. Hence, just as in the case of
classes, we deduce
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y} \psi(x,y).\equiv\colon \phi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi(x,y), \]" src="images/689.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 48.04ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_689.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> a relation is determined by its extension, and vice versa.</p>

<p>On the analogy of the definition of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/690.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.214ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_690.svg">," we put<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_36" id="FNanchor_36">[36]</a>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x\{\psi!(\hat{x},\hat{y})\}y.=.\psi !(x,y) \quad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/691.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.291ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_691.svg"></span></p>

<p>This definition, like that of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/690.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.214ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_690.svg_1">," is not
introduced for its own sake, but in order to give a meaning to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x\{\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)\}y. \]" src="images/692.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.214ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_692.svg"></span>
This meaning, in virtue of our definitions, is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;(\exists \psi)\colon \phi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi !(x,y)\colon x\{\psi !(\hat{x},\hat{y})\}y,\\ \textit{i.e.}\quad &amp;(\exists \psi)\colon \phi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}. \psi !(x,y)\colon \psi !(x,y), \end{array} \]" src="images/693.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.319ex; width: 46.709ex; height: 5.769ex;" id="img_images_693.svg"></span>
and this, in virtue of the axiom of reducibility
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(\exists \psi)\colon \phi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}. \psi !(x,y),\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/694.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 28.657ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_694.svg"></span>
is equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_7">.</p>

<p>Thus we have always
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon x\{\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)\}y.\equiv.\phi(x,y). \]" src="images/695.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.892ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_695.svg"></span></p>

<p>Whenever the determining function of a relation is not relevant, we may
replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi (x,y)\)" src="images/685.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.92ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_685.svg_1"> by a single capital letter. In
virtue of the propositions given above,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp R=S.\equiv \colon xRy.\equiv_{x,y}.xSy,\\ &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp R=\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y).\equiv \colon xRy.\equiv_{x,y}.\phi(x,y),\\ \text{and}\quad &amp;\vdash .R=\hat{x}\hat{y}(xRy). \end{array} \]" src="images/696.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.97ex; width: 46.363ex; height: 9.072ex;" id="img_images_696.svg"></span></p>

<p>Classes of relations, and relations of relations, can be dealt with as
classes of classes were dealt with above.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_86">[Pg 86]</span></p>

<p>Just as a class must not be capable of being or not being a member
of itself, so a relation must neither be nor not be referent or
relatum with respect to itself. This turns out to be equivalent to the
assertion that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{x},\hat{y}\)" src="images/697.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.386ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_697.svg"> cannot significantly be either
of the arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_293"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_94"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!(x,y)\)" src="images/698.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.146ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_698.svg">. This principle, again,
results from the limitation to the possible arguments to a function
explained at the beginning of <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a>.</p>

<p>We may sum up this whole discussion on incomplete symbols as follows.</p>

<p>The use of the symbol "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_29">" as if in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_581.svg_6">"
it <i>directly</i> represented an argument to the function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\hat{z}\)" src="images/699.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.296ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_699.svg"> is rendered possible by the theorems
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x).\supset \colon (x).fx.\supset.f(℩x)(\phi x),\\ \vdash \colon(℩x)(\phi x)=(℩x)(\psi x).\supset.f(℩x)((\phi x)\equiv f(℩x)(\psi x),\\ \vdash \colon \text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x).\supset.(℩x)(\phi x)=(℩x)(\phi x),\\ \vdash \colon(℩x)(\phi x)=(℩x)(\psi x).\equiv.(℩x)(\psi x)=(℩x)(\phi x),\\ \vdash \colon(℩x)(\phi x)=(℩x)(\psi x).(℩x)(\psi x)=(℩x)(\chi x).\supset.(℩x)(\phi x)=(℩x)(\chi x). \end{array} \]" src="images/700.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 70.118ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_700.svg"></span></p>

<p>The use of the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}(\phi x)\)" src="images/316.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.697ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_316.svg_2">" (or of a single
letter, such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_66">, to represent such a symbol) as if, in
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{x}(\phi x)\}\)" src="images/701.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.204ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_701.svg">," it <i>directly</i> represented an argument
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_67"> to a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\hat{\alpha}\)" src="images/702.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.692ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_702.svg">, is rendered possible by the
theorems
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash \colon(\alpha).f_{\alpha}.\supset.f\{\hat{x}(\phi x)\},\\ \vdash \colon \hat{x}(\phi x)=\hat{x}(\psi x).\supset.f\{\hat{x}(\phi x)\}\equiv f\{\hat{x}(\psi x)\},\\ \vdash .\hat{x}(\phi x)=\hat{x}(\phi x),\\ \vdash \colon \hat{x}(\phi x)=\hat{x}(\psi x).\equiv.\hat{x}(\psi x)=\hat{x}(\phi x),\\ \vdash \colon \hat{x}(\phi x)=\hat{x}(\psi x).\hat{x}(\psi x)=\hat{x}(\chi x).\supset.\hat{x}(\phi x)=\hat{x}(\chi x). \end{array} \]" src="images/703.svg" style="vertical-align: -7.24ex; width: 51.413ex; height: 15.611ex;" id="img_images_703.svg"></span></p>

<p>Throughout these propositions the types must be supposed to be properly
adjusted, where ambiguity is possible.</p>

<p>The use of the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}\{\phi (x,y)\}\)" src="images/704.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.183ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_704.svg">"(or of a
single letter, such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_75">, to represent such a symbol) as if, in
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi (x,y)\}\)" src="images/705.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.427ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_705.svg">," it directly represented an
argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_76"> to a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\hat{R}\)" src="images/706.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.962ex; height: 2.842ex;" id="img_images_706.svg">, is rendered possible by the
theorems
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash \colon(R).fR.\supset.f\{\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)\},\\ \vdash \colon \hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y} \psi(x,y).\supset.f\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi (x,y)\}\equiv f\{\hat{x}\hat{y} \psi(x,y)\},\\ \vdash .\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y),\\ \vdash \colon \hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y} \psi(x,y).\equiv.\hat{x}\hat{y} \psi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y),\\ \vdash \colon \hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y} \psi(x,y).\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y} \chi(x,y).\\ \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\supset.\hat{x}\hat{y} \phi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y} \chi(x,y). \end{array} \]" src="images/707.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.891ex; width: 58.257ex; height: 18.914ex;" id="img_images_707.svg"></span>
Throughout these propositions the types must be supposed to be properly
adjusted where ambiguity is possible.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_87">[Pg 87]</span></p>

<p>It follows from these three groups of theorems that these incomplete
symbols are obedient to the same formal rules of identity as symbols
which directly represent objects, so long as we only consider the
<i>equivalence</i> of the resulting variable (or constant) values of
propositional functions and not their identity. This consideration
of the <i>identity</i> of propositions never enters into our formal
reasoning.</p>

<p>Similarly the <i>limitations</i> to the use of these symbols can be
summed up as follows. In the case of (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_30">, the chief way
in which its incompleteness is relevant is that we do not always have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x).fx.\supset.f({℩}x)(\phi x), \]" src="images/708.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_708.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> a function which is always true may nevertheless not be
true of (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_31">. This is possible because <img alt="" data-tex="\(f({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_581.svg_7">
is not a value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\hat{x}\)" src="images/709.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.538ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_709.svg">, so that even when all values
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\hat{x}\)" src="images/709.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.538ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_709.svg_1"> are true, <img alt="" data-tex="\(f({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_581.svg_8"> may not be true. This
happens when (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_32"> does not exist. Thus for example we
have (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).x=x\)" src="images/710.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.786ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_710.svg">, but we do not have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\text{the round square} = \text{the round square}.\\ \text{The inference} &amp;\qquad\qquad\quad(x).fx.\supset.f({℩}x)(\phi x) \end{array} \]" src="images/711.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 51.976ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_711.svg"></span>
is only valid when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_315.svg_3">. As soon as we know
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_315.svg_4">, the fact that (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x\)" src="images/635.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.054ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_635.svg_1">) is an
incomplete symbol becomes irrelevant so long as we confine ourselves
to truth-functions<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_37" id="FNanchor_37">[37]</a> of whatever proposition is its scope. But even
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_315.svg_5">, the incompleteness of (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_33">
may be relevant when we pass outside truth-functions. For example,
George IV wished to know whether Scott was the author of Waverley,
<i>i.e.</i> he wished to know whether a proposition of the form
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(c=({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/712.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.811ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_712.svg">" was true. But there was no proposition of the
form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(c=y\)" src="images/713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.105ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_713.svg">" concerning which he wished to know if it was true.</p>

<p>In regard to classes, the relevance of their incompleteness is somewhat
different. It may be illustrated by the fact that we may have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\hat{z}(\phi z)=\psi !\hat{z}.\hat{z}(\phi z)=\chi !\hat{z}\\ \text{without having} &amp;\qquad\qquad\quad \psi!\hat{z}=\chi!\hat{z}. \end{array} \]" src="images/714.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.285ex; width: 40.816ex; height: 5.701ex;" id="img_images_714.svg"></span>
For, by a direct application of the definitions, we find that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\hat{z}(\phi z)=\psi !\hat{z}.\equiv.\phi x\equiv_{x}\psi !x. \]" src="images/715.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.332ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_715.svg"></span>
Thus we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon \phi x\equiv_{x}\psi !x.\phi x\equiv_{x}\chi !x.\supset.\hat{z}(\phi z)=\psi !\hat{z}.\hat{z}(\phi z)=\chi !\hat{z}, \]" src="images/716.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 51.773ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_716.svg"></span>
but we shall not necessarily have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z} = \chi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/717.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.268ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_717.svg">
under these circumstances, for two functions may well be formally
equivalent without being identical; for example,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x=\text{Scott}.\equiv_{x}.x=\text{the author of Waverley}, \]" src="images/718.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 41.86ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_718.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_88">[Pg 88]</span>
but the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}\)" src="images/719.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_719.svg">=the author of Waverley" has the property
that George IV wished to know whether its value with the argument
"Scott" was true, whereas the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}\)" src="images/719.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_719.svg_1">=Scott" has no such
property, and therefore the two functions are not identical. Hence
there is a propositional function, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x=y.x=z.\supset.y=z, \]" src="images/720.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 21.368ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_720.svg"></span>
which holds without any exception, and yet does not hold when for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_294">
we substitute a class, and for <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_95"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_14"> we substitute functions.
This is only possible because a class is an incomplete symbol, and
therefore "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)=\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/721.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.384ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_721.svg">" is not a value of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y\)" src="images/722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_722.svg">."</p>

<p>It will be observed that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta!\hat{z}=\psi !\hat{z}\)" src="images/723.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.913ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_723.svg">" is not
an extensional function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_611.svg_1">. Thus the scope of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_9">) is relevant in interpreting the product
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{z}(\phi z)=\psi !\hat{z}.\hat{z}(\phi z)=\chi !\hat{z}. \]" src="images/724.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.346ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_724.svg"></span>
If we take the whole of the product as the scope of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_12">,
the product is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;(\exists \theta)\colon \phi x\equiv_{x}\theta !x.\theta !\hat{z}=\psi !\hat{z}.\theta!\hat{z}=\chi !\hat{z},\\ \text{and this}\, \textit{does}\, \text{imply} &amp;\psi !\hat{z}=\chi !\hat{z}. \end{array} \]" src="images/725.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.285ex; width: 56.116ex; height: 5.701ex;" id="img_images_725.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_89">[Pg 89]</span></p>

<p>We may say generally that the fact that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_10">) is an
incomplete symbol is not relevant so long as we confine ourselves to
extensional functions of functions, but is apt to become relevant for
other functions of functions.</p>

<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<h2 class="nobreak" id="PART_I">PART I.<br>
<br>
MATHEMATICAL LOGIC.</h2>
</div>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_91">[Pg 91]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SUMMARY_OF_PART_I"> <span class="allsmcap">SUMMARY OF PART I.</span></h2>
</div>


<p>IN this Part, we shall deal with such topics as belong traditionally
to symbolic logic, or deserve to belong to it in virtue of their
