generality. We shall, that is to say, establish such properties of
propositions, propositional functions, classes and relations as are
likely to be required in any mathematical reasoning, and not merely in
this or that branch of mathematics.</p>

<p>The subjects treated in Part I may be viewed in two aspects: (1) as
a deductive chain depending on the primitive propositions, (2) as
a formal calculus. Taking the first view first: We begin, in <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>,
with certain axioms as to deduction of one proposition or asserted
propositional function from another. From these primitive propositions,
in <a href="#SECTION_A_a" class="pginternal">Section A</a>, we deduce various propositions which are all concerned
with four ways of obtaining new propositions from given propositions,
namely negation, disjunction, joint assertion and implication, of which
the last two can be defined in terms of the first two. Throughout
this first section, although, as will be shown at the beginning of
<a href="#SECTION_B_a" class="pginternal">Section B</a>, our propositions, symbolically unchanged, will apply to any
propositions as values of our variables, yet it will be supposed that
our variable propositions are all what we shall call <i>elementary</i>
propositions, <i>i.e.</i> such as contain no reference, explicit or
implicit, to any totality. This restriction is imposed on account
of the distinction between different <i>types</i> of propositions,
explained in <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a> of the Introduction. Its importance and
purpose, however, are purely philosophical, and so long as only
mathematical purposes are considered, it is unnecessary to remember
this preliminary restriction to elementary propositions, which is
symbolically removed at the beginning of the next section.</p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_B_a" class="pginternal">Section B</a> deals, to begin with, with the relations of propositions
containing apparent variables (<i>i.e.</i> involving the notions of
"all" or "some") to each other and to propositions not containing
apparent variables. We show that, where propositions containing
apparent variables are concerned, we can define negation, disjunction,
joint assertion and implication in such a way that their properties
shall be exactly analogous to the properties of the corresponding ideas
as applied to elementary propositions. We show also that <i>formal
implication</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x) . {\phi}x \supset {\psi}x\)" src="images/727.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.487ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_727.svg">"
considered as a relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_33"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_1">, has
many properties analogous to those of <i>material implication</i>,
<i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \supset q\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.196ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_7">"<span class="pagenum" id="Page_92">[Pg 92]</span> considered as a relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_134">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_81">. We then consider <i>predicative</i> functions and the
axiom of <i>reducibility</i>, which are vital in the employment of
<i>functions</i> as apparent variables. An example of such employment
is afforded by <i>identity</i>, which is the next topic considered
in <a href="#SECTION_B_a" class="pginternal">Section B</a>. Finally, this section deals with <i>descriptions</i>,
<i>i.e.</i> phrases of the form "the so-and-so" (in the singular). It
is shown that the appearance of a grammatical subject "the so-and-so"
is deceptive, and that such propositions, fully stated, contain no such
subject, but contain instead an apparent variable.</p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_C_a" class="pginternal">Section C</a> deals with classes, and with relations in so far as they are
analogous to classes. Classes and relations, like descriptions, are
shown to be "incomplete symbols" (cf. Introduction, <a href="#CHAPTER_III" class="pginternal">Chapter III</a>), and
it is shown that a proposition which is grammatically about a class is
to be regarded as really concerned with a propositional function and
an apparent variable whose values are <i>predicative</i> propositional
functions (with a similar result for relations). The remainder of
<a href="#SECTION_C_a" class="pginternal">Section C</a> deals with the calculus of classes, and with the calculus of
relations in so far as it is analogous to that of classes.</p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_D_a" class="pginternal">Section D</a> deals with those properties of relations which have no
analogues for classes. In this section, a number of ideas and notations
are introduced which are constantly needed throughout the rest of the
work. Most of the properties of relations which have analogues in the
theory of classes are comparatively unimportant, while those that have
no such analogues are of the very greatest utility. It is partly for
this reason that emphasis on the calculus-aspect of symbolic logic has
proved a hindrance, hitherto, to the proper development of the theory
of relations.</p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_E_a" class="pginternal">Section E</a>, finally, extends the notions of the addition and
multiplication of classes or relations to cases where the summands or
factors are not individually given, but are given as the members of
some class. The advantage obtained by this extension is that it enables
us to deal with an infinite number of summands or factors.</p>

<p>Considered as a formal calculus, mathematical logic has three analogous
branches, namely (1) the calculus of propositions, (2) the calculus of
classes, (3) the calculus of relations. Of these, (1) is dealt with
in <a href="#SECTION_A_a" class="pginternal">Section A</a>, while (2) and (3), in so far as they are analogous, are
dealt with in <a href="#SECTION_C_a" class="pginternal">Section C</a>. We have, for each of the three, the four
analogous ideas of negation, addition, multiplication, and implication
or inclusion. Of these, negation is analogous to the negative in
ordinary algebra, and implication or inclusion is analogous to the
relation "less than or equal to" in ordinary algebra. But the analogy
must not be pressed, as it has important limitations. The sum of two
propositions is their disjunction, the sum of two classes is the
class of terms belonging to one or other, the sum of two relations
is the relation consisting in the fact that one or other of the two
relations holds. The sum of a class of classes is the class of all
terms belonging to some one or other of the classes, and the sum of a
class of relations is the relation consisting in the fact that some
one relation of the class holds. The product of two propositions is
their joint assertion, the product of two classes is their common
part, the product of two relations is the relation consisting in the
fact that both the relations hold. The product of a class of classes
is the part common to all of them, and the product of a class of
relations is the relation consisting in the fact that all relations
of the class in question hold. The inclusion of one class in another
consists in the fact that all members of the one are members of the
other, while the inclusion of one relation in another consists in the
fact that every pair of terms which has the one relation also has the
other relation. It is then shown that the properties of negation,
addition, multiplication and inclusion are exactly analogous for
classes and relations, and are, with certain exceptions, analogous to
the properties of negation, addition, multiplication and implication
for propositions. (The exceptions arise chiefly from the fact that
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_135"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_82">" is itself a proposition, and can therefore imply
and be implied, while "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_71"> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_18">," where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_72"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_19"> are classes, is not a class, and can therefore
neither contain nor be contained in another class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_2">.) But
classes have certain properties not possessed by propositions: these
arise from the fact that classes have not a <i>two-fold</i> division
corresponding to the division of propositions into true and false, but
a <i>threefold</i> division, namely into (1) the universal class, which
contains the whole of a certain type, (2) the null-class, which has
no members, (3) all other classes, which neither contain nothing nor
contain everything of the appropriate type. The resulting properties
of classes, which are not analogous to properties of propositions, are
dealt with in <a href="#_24" class="pginternal">*24</a>. And just as classes have properties not analogous
to any properties of propositions, so relations have properties not
analogous to any properties of classes, though all the properties of
classes have analogues among relations. The special properties of
relations are much more numerous and important than the properties
belonging to classes but not to propositions. These special properties
of relations therefore occupy a whole section, namely <a href="#SECTION_D_a" class="pginternal">Section D</a>.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_94">[Pg 94]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_A_a">SECTION A.<br>
<br>
THE THEORY OF DEDUCTION.</h2>
</div>


<p>THE purpose of the present section is to set forth the first stage
of the deduction of pure mathematics from its logical foundations.
This first stage is necessarily concerned with deduction itself,
<i>i.e.</i> with the principles by which conclusions are inferred from
premisses. If it is our purpose to make all our assumptions explicit,
and to effect the deduction of all our other propositions from these
assumptions, it is obvious that the first assumptions we need are those
that are required to make deduction possible. Symbolic logic is often
regarded as consisting of two coordinate parts, the theory of classes
and the theory of propositions. But from our point of view these two
parts are not coordinate; for in the theory of classes we deduce one
proposition from another by means of principles belonging to the theory
of propositions, whereas in the theory of propositions we nowhere
require the theory of classes. Hence, in a deductive system, the theory
of propositions necessarily precedes the theory of classes.</p>

<p>But the subject to be treated in what follows is not quite properly
described as the theory of <i>propositions</i>. It is in fact the
theory of how one proposition can be inferred from another. Now
in order that one proposition may be inferred from another, it is
necessary that the two should have that relation which makes the one
a consequence of the other. When a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_83"> is a consequence
of a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_136">, we say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_137"> <i>implies</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_84">. Thus
deduction depends upon the relation of implication, and every deductive
system must contain among its premisses as many of the properties of
implication as are necessary to legitimate the ordinary procedure of
deduction. In the present section, certain propositions will be stated
as premisses, and it will be shown that they are sufficient for all
common forms of inference. It will not be shown that they are all
<i>necessary</i>, and it is possible that the number of them might
be diminished. All that is affirmed concerning the premisses is (1)
that they are true, (2) that they are sufficient for the theory of
deduction, (3) that we do not know how to diminish their number. But
with regard to (2), there must always be some element of doubt, since
it is hard to be sure that one never uses some principle unconsciously.
The habit of being rigidly guided by formal symbolic rules is a
safeguard against unconscious assumptions; but even this safeguard is
not always adequate.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_95">[Pg 95]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_1">1. PRIMITIVE IDEAS AND PROPOSITIONS.</h2>
</div>

<p>Since all definitions of terms are effected by means of other terms,
every system of definitions which is not circular must start from a
certain apparatus of undefined terms. It is to some extent optional
what ideas we take as undefined in mathematics; the motives guiding
our choice will be (1) to make the number of undefined ideas as small
as possible, (2) as between two systems in which the number is equal,
to choose the one which seems the simpler and easier. We know no way
of proving that such and such a system of undefined ideas contains as
few as will give such and such results<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_38" id="FNanchor_38">[38]</a>. Hence we can only say that
such and such ideas are undefined in such and such a system, not that
they are indefinable. Following Peano, we shall call the undefined
ideas and the undemonstrated propositions <i>primitive</i> ideas
and <i>primitive</i> propositions respectively. The primitive ideas
are <i>explained</i> by means of descriptions intended to point out
to the reader what is meant; but the explanations do not constitute
definitions, because they really involve the ideas they explain.</p>

<p>In the present number, we shall first enumerate the primitive ideas
required in this section; then we shall define <i>implication</i>; and
then we shall enunciate the primitive propositions required in this
section. Every definition or proposition in the work has a number,
for purposes of reference. Following Peano, we use numbers having a
decimal as well as an integral part, in order to be able to insert
new propositions between any two. A change in the integral part of
the number will be used to correspond to a new chapter. Definitions
will generally have numbers whose decimal part is less than ·1, and
will be usually put at the beginning of chapters. In references, the
integral parts of the numbers of propositions will be distinguished
by being preceded by a star; thus "*1·01" will mean the definition
or proposition so numbered, and "*1" will mean the chapter in which
propositions have numbers whose integral part is 1, <i>i.e.</i> the
present chapter. Chapters will generally be called "numbers."</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
<span class="allsmcap">PRIMITIVE IDEAS.</span></p>

<p>(1) <i>Elementary propositions</i>. By an "elementary" proposition
we mean one which does not involve any variables, or, in other
language, one which does not involve such words as "all," "some,"
"the" or equivalents for such words. A proposition such as "this
is red," where "this" is something given<span class="pagenum" id="Page_96">[Pg 96]</span> in sensation, will be
elementary. Any combination of given elementary propositions by means
of negation, disjunction or conjunction (see below) will be elementary.
In the primitive propositions of the present number, and therefore
in the deductions from these primitive propositions in <a href="#_2" class="pginternal">*2</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a>, the
letters <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_138">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_85">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_18">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/40.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_40.svg_2"> will be used to denote elementary
propositions.</p>

<p>(2) <i>Elementary propositional functions</i>. By an "elementary
propositional function" we shall mean an expression containing an
undetermined constituent, <i>i.e.</i> a variable, or several such
constituents, and such that, when the undetermined constituent or
constituents are determined, <i>i.e.</i> when values are assigned to
the variable or variables, the resulting value of the expression in
question is an elementary proposition. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_139"> is an undetermined
elementary proposition, "not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_140">" is an elementary propositional
function.</p>

<p>We shall show in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a> how to extend the results of this and the following
numbers (<a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a>) to propositions which are not elementary.</p>

<p>(3) <i>Assertion</i>. Any proposition may be either asserted or
merely considered. If I say "Caesar died," I assert the proposition
"Caesar died," if I say "'Caesar died' is a proposition," I make a
different assertion, and "Caesar died" is no longer asserted, but
merely considered. Similarly in a hypothetical proposition, <i>e.g.</i>
"if <img alt="" data-tex="\(a = b\)" src="images/728.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.185ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_728.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(b = a\)" src="images/729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.185ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_729.svg">," we have two unasserted propositions,
namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a = b\)" src="images/728.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.185ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_728.svg_1">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(b = a\)" src="images/729.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.185ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_729.svg_1">," while what is asserted is that
the first of these implies the second. In language, we indicate
when a proposition is merely considered by "<i>if</i> so-and-so" or
"<i>that</i> so-and-so" or merely by inverted commas. In symbols, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_141"> is a proposition, <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_142"> by itself will stand for the unasserted
proposition, while the asserted proposition will be designated by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash.p.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.423ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_730.svg"></span>
The sign "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\)" src="images/78.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.382ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_78.svg_5">" is called the assertion-sign<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_39" id="FNanchor_39">[39]</a>; it may be read
"it is true that" (although philosophically this is not exactly what
it means). The dots after the assertion-sign indicate its range; that
is to say, everything following is asserted until we reach either an
equal number of dots preceding a sign of implication or the end of the
sentence. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p.\supset.q\)" src="images/731.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.339ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_731.svg">" means "it is true that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_143"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_86">," whereas "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.p.\supset\vdash.q\)" src="images/732.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.722ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_732.svg">" means
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_144"> is true; therefore <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_87"> is true<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_40" id="FNanchor_40">[40]</a>." The first of these does
not necessarily involve the truth either of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_145"> or of <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_88">, while
the second involves the truth of both.</p>

<p>(4) <i>Assertion of a propositional function</i>. Besides the assertion
of definite propositions, we need what we shall call "assertion of a
propositional function." The general notion of asserting <i>any</i>
propositional function is not used until <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>, but we use at once the
notion of asserting various special elementary propositional functions.
Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_71"> be a propositional function whose argument is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_297">;
then we may assert <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_72"> without assigning a value to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_298">.<span class="pagenum" id="Page_97">[Pg 97]</span>
This is done, for example, when the law of identity is asserted in
the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_22"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_23">." Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_24"> is left undetermined, because,
however <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_25"> may be determined, the result will be true. Thus when
we assert <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_73">, leaving <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_299"> undetermined, we are asserting an
ambiguous value of our function. This is only legitimate if, however
the ambiguity may be determined, the result will be true. Thus take, as
an illustration, the primitive proposition <a href="#_1_2" class="pginternal">*1·2</a> below, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash \colon p \lor p.\supset.p,\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/733.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.986ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_733.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> "'<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_146"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_147">' implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_148">." Here p may be <i>any</i>
elementary proposition: by leaving <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_149"> undetermined, we obtain
an assertion which can be applied to any particular elementary
proposition. Such assertions are like the particular enunciations in
Euclid: when it is said "let <img alt="" data-tex="\(ABC\)" src="images/734.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 5.133ex; height: 1.67ex;" id="img_images_734.svg"> be an isosceles triangle; then the
angles at the base will be equal," what is said applies to <i>any</i>
isosceles triangle; it is stated concerning <i>one</i> triangle, but
not concerning a definite one. All the assertions in the present
work, with a very few exceptions, assert propositional functions, not
definite propositions.</p>

<p>As a matter of fact, no constant elementary proposition will occur in
the present work, or can occur in any work which employs only logical
ideas. The ideas and propositions of logic are all <i>general</i>: an
assertion (for example) which is true of Socrates but not of Plato,
will not belong to logic<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_41" id="FNanchor_41">[41]</a>, and if an assertion which is true of
both is to occur in logic, it must not be made concerning either, but
concerning a variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_300">. In order to obtain, in logic, a definite
proposition instead of a propositional function, it is necessary to
take some propositional function and assert that it is true always or
sometimes, <i>i.e.</i> with all possible values of the variable or with
some possible value. Thus, giving the name "individual" to whatever
there is that is neither a proposition nor a function, the proposition
"every individual is identical with itself" or the proposition "there
are individuals" will be a proposition belonging to logic. But these
propositions are not elementary.</p>

<p>(5) <i>Negation</i>. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_150"> is any proposition, the proposition
"not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_151">," or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_152"> is false," will be represented by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim{p}\)" src="images/735.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.527ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_735.svg">."
For the present, <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_153"> must be an <i>elementary</i> proposition.</p>

<p>(6) <i>Disjunction</i>. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_154"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_89"> are any propositions,
the proposition "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_155"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_90">," <i>i.e.</i> "either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_156"> is true
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_91"> is true," where the alternatives are to be not mutually
exclusive, will be represented by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}p \lor q.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/736.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.962ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_736.svg"></span>
This is called the <i>disjunction</i> or the <i>logical sum</i> of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_157"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_92">. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim{p \lor q}\)" src="images/737.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.082ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_737.svg">" will mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_158"> is false or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_93"> is true"; <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim{(p \lor q)}\)" src="images/738.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.842ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_738.svg"> will mean "it is false that either
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_159"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_94"> is true," which is equivalent to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_160"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_95"> are
both false";<span class="pagenum" id="Page_98">[Pg 98]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim{(\sim{p} \lor \sim{q}}\)" src="images/739.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.362ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_739.svg">) will mean "it is false
that either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_161"> is false or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_96"> is false," which is equivalent to
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_162"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_97"> are both true"; and so on. For the present, <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_163"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_98"> must be elementary propositions.</p>

<p>The above are all the primitive ideas required in the theory of
deduction. Other primitive ideas will be introduced in <a href="#SECTION_B_a" class="pginternal">Section B</a>.</p>

<p><i>Definition of Implication</i>. When a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_99"> follows
from a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_164">, so that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_165"> is true, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_100"> must also be
true, we say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_166"> <i>implies</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_101">. The idea of implication,
in the form in which we require it, can be defined. The meaning to be
given to implication in what follows may at first sight appear somewhat
artificial; but although there are other legitimate meanings, the one
here adopted is very much more convenient for our purposes than any of
its rivals. The essential property that we require of implication is
this: "What is implied by a true proposition is true." It is in virtue
of this property that implication yields proofs. But this property by
no means determines whether anything, and if so what, is implied by a
false proposition. What it does determine is that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_167"> implies
<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_102">, then it cannot be the case that <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_168"> is true and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_103"> is
false, <i>i.e.</i> it must be the case that either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_169"> is false or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_104"> is true. The most convenient interpretation of implication is to
say, conversely, that if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_170"> is false or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_105"> is true, then
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_171"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_106">" is to be true. Hence "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_172"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_107">" is to
be defined to mean: "Either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_173"> is false or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_108"> is true." Hence we
put:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_01">*1·01</a></b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\supset q.=.\sim {p} \lor q \qquad \text{Df}.\)" src="images/740.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 23.625ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_740.svg"></p>

<p>Here the letters "Df" stand for "definition." They and the sign of
equality together are to be regarded as forming one symbol, standing
for "is defined to mean<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_42" id="FNanchor_42">[42]</a>." Whatever comes to the left of the sign
of equality is defined to mean the same as what comes to the right of
it. Definition is not among the primitive ideas, because definitions
are concerned solely with the symbolism, not with what is symbolised;
they are introduced for practical convenience, and are theoretically
unnecessary.</p>

<p>In virtue of the above definition, when "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \supset q\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.196ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_8">" holds,
then either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_174"> is false or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_109"> is true; hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_175"> is true,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_110"> must be true. Thus the above definition preserves the essential
characteristic of implication; it gives, in fact, the most general
meaning compatible with the preservation of this characteristic.</p>


<p class="nindc space-above2">
<span class="allsmcap">PRIMITIVE PROPOSITIONS.</span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_1">*1·1</a>.</b> Anything implied by a true elementary proposition is true.
Pp<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_43" id="FNanchor_43">[43]</a>.</p>

<p>The above principle will be extended in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a> to propositions which
are not elementary. It is not the same as "<i>if</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_176"> is true,
then <i>if</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_177"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_111">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_112"> is<span class="pagenum" id="Page_99">[Pg 99]</span> true." This is a true
proposition, but it holds equally when <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_178"> is not true and when <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_179">
does not imply <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_113">. It does not, like the principle we are concerned
with, enable us to assert <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_114"> simply, without any hypothesis. We
cannot express the principle symbolically, partly because any symbolism
in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_180"> is variable only gives the <i>hypothesis</i> that <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_181">
is true, not the fact that it is true<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_44" id="FNanchor_44">[44]</a>.</p>

<p>The above principle is used whenever we have to deduce a
<i>proposition</i> from a <i>proposition</i>. But the immense majority
of the assertions in the present work are assertions of propositional
functions, <i>i.e.</i> they contain an undetermined variable. Since the
assertion of a propositional function is a different primitive idea
from the assertion of a proposition, we require a primitive proposition
different from <a href="#_1_1" class="pginternal">*1·1</a>, though allied to it, to enable us to deduce the
assertion of a propositional function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_14">" from the assertions
of the two propositional functions "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_74">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset\psi x\)" src="images/741.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_741.svg">."
This primitive proposition is as follows:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_11">*1·11</a></b>. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_75"> can be asserted, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_301"> is a real
variable, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_173.svg_2"> can be asserted, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_302"> is
a real variable, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_15"> can be asserted, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_303"> is a real
variable. Pp.</p>

<p>This principle is also to be assumed for functions of several variables.</p>

<p>Part of the importance of the above primitive proposition is due to the
fact that it expresses in the symbolism a result following from the
theory of types, which requires symbolic recognition. Suppose we have
the two assertions of <i>propositional functions</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi x\)" src="images/742.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.031ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_742.svg">"
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.815ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_743.svg">"; then the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_304">" in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_76">
is not absolutely anything, but anything for which as argument
the function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_77">" is significant; similarly in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_173.svg_3">"
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_305"> is anything for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_173.svg_4">"
is significant. Apart from some axiom, we do not know that
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_306">'s for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_173.svg_5">" is significant are
the same as those for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_78">" is significant. The primitive
proposition <a href="#_1_11" class="pginternal">*1·11</a>, by securing that, as the result of the assertions of
the <i>propositional functions</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_79">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_173.svg_6">"
the propositional function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_16"> can also be asserted,
secures partial symbolic recognition, in the form most useful in
actual deductions, of an important principle which follows from the
theory of types, namely that, if there is any one argument a for which
both "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_12">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg">" are significant, then the range of
arguments for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_80">" is significant is the same as the
range of arguments for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_17">" is significant. It is obvious
that, if the propositional function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.427ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_173.svg_7">" can be
asserted, there must be arguments a for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a \supset \psi a\)" src="images/745.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.232ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_745.svg">"
is significant, and for which, therefore, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_13">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg_1">"
must be significant. Hence, by our principle, the values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_307">
for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_81">" is significant are the same as those for which
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_18">" is significant, <i>i.e.</i> the type of possible arguments
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_42"> (cf. <a href="#Page_15" class="pginternal">p. 15</a>) is the same as that of possible
arguments for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi \hat{x}\)" src="images/223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_223.svg_3">. The<span class="pagenum" id="Page_100">[Pg 100]</span> primitive proposition <a href="#_1_11" class="pginternal">*1·11</a>, since
it states a practically important consequence of this fact, is called
the "axiom of identification of type."</p>

<p>Another consequence of the principle that, if there is an argument
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_74"> for which both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg_2"> are significant, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_82"> is significant whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_19"> is significant, and
vice versa, will be given in the "axiom of identification of real
variables," introduced in *<a href="#_1_72" class="pginternal">*1·72</a>. These two propositions, <a href="#_1_11" class="pginternal">*1·11</a>
and <a href="#_1_72" class="pginternal">*1·72</a>, give what is symbolically essential to the conduct of
demonstrations in accordance with the theory of types.</p>

<p>The above proposition <a href="#_1_11" class="pginternal">*1·11</a> is used in every inference from one
asserted propositional function to another. We will illustrate the use
of this proposition by setting forth at length the way in which it is
first used, in the proof of <a href="#_2_06" class="pginternal">*2·06</a>. That proposition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash \colon\ldotp p\supset q.\supset \colon q\supset r.\supset .p\supset r.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/746.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 30.285ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_746.svg"></span>
We have already proved, in <a href="#_2_05" class="pginternal">*2·05</a>, the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp q\supset r.\supset \colon p\supset q.\supset.p\supset r. \]" src="images/747.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 27.017ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_747.svg"></span>
It is obvious that <a href="#_2_06" class="pginternal">*2·06</a> results from <a href="#_2_05" class="pginternal">*2·05</a> by means of <a href="#_2_04" class="pginternal">*2·04</a>, which is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\ldotp p.\supset.q\supset r \colon \supset \colon q.\supset.p\supset r. \]" src="images/748.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 27.772ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_748.svg"></span>
For if, in this proposition, we replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_182"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(q \supset r\)" src="images/749.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.078ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_749.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_115">
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(p \supset q\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.196ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_9">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_19"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(p \supset r\)" src="images/750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.175ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_750.svg">, we obtain, as an
instance of <a href="#_2_04" class="pginternal">*2·04</a>, the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash \colon\colon q \supset r.\supset \colon p\supset q.\supset.p\supset r\colon\ldotp\supset\colon\ldotp p\supset q.\supset \colon q\supset r.\supset.p\supset r \qquad \text{(1)}, \]" src="images/751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.212ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_751.svg"></span>
and here the hypothesis is asserted by <a href="#_2_05" class="pginternal">*2·05</a>. Thus our primitive
proposition *1·11 enables us to assert the conclusion.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_2">*1·2</a></b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p \lor p.\supset.p \quad \text{Pp}.\)" src="images/752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 17.779ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_752.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition states: "If either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_183"> is true or <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_184"> is true,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_185"> is true." It is called the "principle of tautology," and
will be quoted by the abbreviated title of "Taut." It is convenient,
for purposes of reference, to give names to a few of the more important
propositions; in general, propositions will be referred to by their
numbers.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_3">*1·3</a></b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon q.\supset .p \lor q \qquad \text{Pp}.\)" src="images/753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 19.847ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_753.svg"></p>

<p>This principle states: "If <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_116"> is true, then '<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_186"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_117">'
is true." Thus <i>e.g.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_118"> is "to-day is Wednesday" and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_187"> is "to-day is Tuesday," the principle states: "If to-day is
Wednesday, then to-day is either Tuesday or Wednesday." It is called
the "principle of addition," because it states that if a proposition
is true, any alternative may be added without making it false. The
principle will be referred to as "Add."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*1·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p \lor q.\supset.p \lor p \qquad \text{Pp}.\)" src="images/754.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 23.597ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_754.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_101">[Pg 101]</span></p>

<p>This principle states that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_188"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_119">" implies "<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_120"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_189">."
It states the permutative law for logical addition of propositions, and
will be called the "principle of permutation." It will be referred to
as "Perm."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>1·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p \lor (q \lor r).\supset.q \lor (p\lor r) \qquad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/755.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.461ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_755.svg">.</p>

<p>This principle states: "If either <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_190"> is true, or '<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_121"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_20">' is
true, then either <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_122"> is true, or '<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_191"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_21">' is true." It is a
form of the associative law for logical addition, and will be called
the "associative principle." It will be referred to as "Assoc." The
proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ p \lor (q\lor r).\supset.(p\lor q) \lor r, \]" src="images/756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.378ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_756.svg"></span>
which would be the natural form for the associative law, has less
deductive power, and is therefore not taken as a primitive proposition.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_6">*1·6</a></b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp q\supset r.\supset\colon p \lor q.\supset.p \lor r \qquad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/757.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 32.707ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_757.svg">.</p>

<p>This principle states: "If <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_123"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_22">, then '<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_192"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_124">' implies '<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_193"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_23">.'" In other words, in an implication,
an alternative may be added to both premiss and conclusion without
impairing the truth of the implication. The principle will be called
the "principle of summation," and will be referred to as "Sum."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_7">*1·7</a></b>. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_194"> is an elementary proposition, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim{p}\)" src="images/735.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.527ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_735.svg_1"> is an
elementary proposition. Pp.</p>


<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_71">*1·71</a>.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_195"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_125"> are elementary propositions, <img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor q\)" src="images/758.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.693ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_758.svg"> is an elementary proposition. Pp.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_1_72">*1·72</a>.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi p\)" src="images/759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.486ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_759.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi p\)" src="images/760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.611ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_760.svg"> are elementary propositional
functions which take elementary propositions as arguments, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi p \lor \psi p\)" src="images/761.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.612ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_761.svg"> is an elementary propositional function. Pp.</p>

<p>This axiom is to apply also to functions of two or more variables. It
is called the "axiom of identification of real variables." It will
be observed that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_38"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_8"> are functions which take
arguments of different types, there is no such function as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\lor \psi x\)" src="images/762.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.924ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_762.svg">,"
because <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_39"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_9"> cannot significantly have
the same argument. A more general form of the above axiom will be given
in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>.</p>

<p>The use of the above axioms will generally be tacit. It is only through
them and the axioms of *9 that the theory of types explained in the
Introduction becomes relevant, and any view of logic which justifies
these axioms justifies such subsequent reasoning as employs the theory
of types.</p>

<p>This completes the list of primitive propositions required for the
theory of deduction as applied to elementary propositions.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_102">[Pg 102]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_2">*2. IMMEDIATE CONSEQUENCES OF THE PRIMITIVE PROPOSITIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *2.</p>

<p>The proofs of the earlier of the propositions of this number consist
simply in noticing that they are instances of the general rules given
in <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>. In such cases, these rules are not premisses, since they
assert any instance of themselves, not something other than their
instances. Hence when a general rule is adduced in early proofs, it
will be adduced in brackets<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_45" id="FNanchor_45">[45]</a>, with indications, when required, as
to the changes of letters from those given in the rule to those in
the case considered. Thus "Taut <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dfrac{\sim{p}}{p}\)" src="images/763.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.991ex; width: 4.522ex; height: 4.52ex;" id="img_images_763.svg">" will mean
what "Taut" becomes when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim{p}\)" src="images/735.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.527ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_735.svg_2"> is written in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_196">. If
"Taut <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dfrac{\sim{p}}{p}\)" src="images/763.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.991ex; width: 4.522ex; height: 4.52ex;" id="img_images_763.svg_1">" is enclosed in square brackets before
an asserted proposition, that means that, in accordance with "Taut,"
we are asserting what "Taut" becomes when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim{p}\)" src="images/735.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.527ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_735.svg_3"> is written in
place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_197">. The recognition that a certain proposition is an
instance of some general proposition previously proved or assumed is
essential to the process of deduction from general rules, but cannot
itself be erected into a general rule, since the application required
is particular, and no general rule can <i>explicitly</i> include a
particular application.</p>

<p>Again, when two different sets of symbols express the same proposition
in virtue of a definition, say <a href="#_1_01" class="pginternal">*1·01</a>, and one of these, which we will
call (1), has been asserted, the assertion of the other is made by
writing "[(1).(*1·01)]" before it, meaning that, in virtue of *1·01,
the new set of symbols asserts the same proposition as was asserted in
(1). A reference to a definition is distinguished from a reference to a
previous proposition by being enclosed in round brackets.</p>

<p>The propositions in this number are all, or nearly all, actually needed
in deducing mathematics from our primitive propositions. Although
certain abbreviating processes will be gradually introduced, proofs
will be given very fully, because the importance of the present subject
lies, not in the propositions themselves, but (1) in the fact that
they follow from the primitive propositions, (2) in the fact that
the subject is the easiest, simplest, and most elementary example of
the symbolic method of dealing with the principles of mathematics
generally. Later portions—the theories of classes, relations, cardinal
numbers, series, ordinal numbers, geometry, etc.—all employ the same
method, but with an increasing complexity in the entities and functions
considered.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_103">[Pg 103]</span></p>

<p>The most important propositions proved in the present number are the
following:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_2_02">*2·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon q.\supset.p\supset q\)" src="images/764.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 12.397ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_764.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_126"> implies that <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_198"> implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_127">, <i>i.e.</i> a true
proposition is implied by any proposition. This proposition is called
the "principle of simplification" (referred to as "Simp"), because,
as will appear later, it enables us to pass from the joint assertion
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_128"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_199"> to the assertion of <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_129"> simply. When the special
meaning which we have given to implication is remembered, it will be
seen that this proposition is obvious.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p\supset \sim{q}.\supset.q\supset \sim{p}\)" src="images/765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.073ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_765.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon \sim{p}\supset q.\supset.\sim{q}\supset p\)" src="images/766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 21.33ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_766.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p\supset q.\supset.\sim{q}\supset\sim{p}\)" src="images/767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.701ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_767.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\sim{q}\supset\sim{p}.\supset.p\supset q\)" src="images/768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.701ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_768.svg"></p>

<p>These four analogous propositions constitute the "principle of
transposition," referred to as "Transp." They lead to the rule that in
an implication the two sides may be interchanged by turning negative
into positive and positive into negative. They are thus analogous
to the algebraical rule that the two sides of an equation may be
interchanged by changing the signs.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp p.\supset.q\supset r:\supset:q.\supset.p\supset r\)" src="images/769.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 27.646ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_769.svg"></p>

<p>This is called the "commutative principle" and referred to as "Comm."
It states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_24"> follows from <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_130"> provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_200"> is true,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_25"> follows from <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_201"> provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_131"> is true.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·05.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp q\supset r.\supset \colon p\supset q.\supset.p\supset r\)" src="images/770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 26.388ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_770.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·06.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp p\supset q.\supset \colon q\supset r.\supset.p\supset r\)" src="images/771.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 26.388ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_771.svg"></p>

<p>These two propositions are the source of the syllogism in Barbara (as
will be shown later) and are therefore called the "principle of the
syllogism" (referred to as "Syll"). The first states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_26">
follows from <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_132">, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_133"> follows from <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_202">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_27"> follows
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_203">. The second states the same thing with the premisses
interchanged.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·08.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.p\supset p\)" src="images/772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.681ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_772.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> any proposition implies itself. This is called the
"principle of identity" and referred to as "Id." It is not the same as
the "law of identity" ("<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_308"> is identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_309">"), but the law of
identity is inferred from it (cf. <a href="#_13_15" class="pginternal">*13·15</a>).</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\sim{p}.\supset.p\supset q\)" src="images/773.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 14.883ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_773.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> a false proposition implies any proposition.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_104">[Pg 104]</span></p>

<p>The later propositions of the present number are mostly subsumed
under propositions in <a href="#_3" class="pginternal">*3</a> or <a href="#_4" class="pginternal">*4</a>, which give the same results in more
compendious forms. We now proceed to formal deductions.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p \supset \sim{p} . \supset . \sim{p}\)" src="images/774.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 16.741ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_774.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_204"> implies its own falsehood, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_205"> is false. It is called the "principle of the<i> reductio ad
absurdum</i>," and will be referred to as "Abs."<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_46" id="FNanchor_46">[46]</a> The proof is as
follows (where "<i>Dem.</i>" is short for demonstration"):</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \left[\text{Taut}\, \frac{\sim{p}}{p}\right] &amp;\vdash \colon \sim{p} \lor \sim{p} . \supset . \sim{p} \qquad \text{(1)}\\ [\text{(1).(*1·01)}] &amp;\vdash \colon p \supset \sim{p} . \supset . \sim{p} \end{array} \]" src="images/775.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.053ex; width: 40.249ex; height: 7.238ex;" id="img_images_775.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon q . \supset . p \supset q\)" src="images/776.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 12.397ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_776.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \left[\text{Add}\, \frac{\sim{p}}{p}\right] &amp;\vdash \colon q . \supset . \sim{p} \lor q \qquad \text{(1)}\\ [\text{(1).(*1·01)}] &amp;\vdash \colon q . \supset . p \supset q \end{array} \]" src="images/777.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.053ex; width: 35.654ex; height: 7.238ex;" id="img_images_777.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*2·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon p \supset \sim{q} . \supset . q \supset \sim{p}\)" src="images/778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.073ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_778.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \left[\text{Perm}\, \frac{\sim{p}, \sim{q}}{p, q}\right] &amp;\vdash \colon \sim{p} \lor \sim{q} . \supset . \sim{q} \lor \sim{p} \qquad \text{(1)}\\ [\text{(1).(*1·01)}] &amp;\vdash \colon p \supset \sim{q} . \supset . q \supset \sim{p} \end{array} \]" src="images/779.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.053ex; width: 47.327ex; height: 7.238ex;" id="img_images_779.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_2_04">*2·04</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp p . \supset . q \supset r \colon \supset \colon q . \supset . p \supset r\)" src="images/780.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 27.144ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_780.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \left[\text{Assoc}\, \frac{\sim{p}, \sim{q}}{p, q}\right] &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp \sim{p} \lor (\sim{q} \lor r) . \supset . \sim{q} \lor (\sim{p} \lor r) \qquad \text{(1)}\\ [\text{(1).(*1·01)}] &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp p . \supset . q \supset r \colon \supset \colon q . \supset . p \supset r \end{array} \]" src="images/781.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.053ex; width: 59.976ex; height: 7.238ex;" id="img_images_781.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_2_05">*2·05</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp q \supset r . \supset \colon p \supset q . \supset . p \supset r\)" src="images/782.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 26.388ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_782.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \left[\text{Sum} \frac{\sim{p}}{p}\right] &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp q \supset r . \supset \colon \sim{p} \lor q . \supset . \sim{p} \lor r \qquad \text{(1)}\\ [\text{(1).(*1·01)}] &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp q \supset r . \supset \colon p \supset q . \supset . p \supset r \end{array} \]" src="images/783.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.053ex; width: 51.532ex; height: 7.238ex;" id="img_images_783.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
