<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_132">[Pg 132]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_B_a">SECTION B.<br>
THEORY OF APPARENT VARIABLES.</h2>
</div>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_9">*9. EXTENSION OF THE THEORY OF DEDUCTION FROM LOWER TO
HIGHER TYPES OF PROPOSITIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *9.</p>

<p>In the present number, we introduce two new primitive ideas, which may
be expressed as "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_53"> is always<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_50" id="FNanchor_50">[50]</a> true" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_54"> is
sometimes<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_51" id="FNanchor_51">[51]</a> true," or, more correctly, as "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_55"> always" and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_56"> sometimes." When we assert "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_57"> always," we are
asserting all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_34">, where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_35">" means
the function itself, as opposed to an ambiguous value of the function
(cf. <a href="#Page_15" class="pginternal">pp. 15</a>, <a href="#Page_42" class="pginternal">42</a>); we are not asserting that <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_58"> is true for
all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_311">, because, in accordance with the theory of types,
there are values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_312"> for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_59">" is meaningless; for
example, the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_36"> itself must be such a value. We
shall denote "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_60"> always" by the notation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x) . {\phi}x, \]" src="images/1127.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.332ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1127.svg"></span>
where the "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x)\)" src="images/91.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_91.svg_2">" will be followed by a sufficiently large number of
dots to cover the function of which "all values" are concerned. The
form in which such propositions most frequently occur is the "formal
implication," <i>i.e.</i> such a proposition as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x): {\phi}x .\supset. {\psi}x\text{,} \]" src="images/1128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.751ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1128.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_61"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}x\)" src="images/245.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_245.svg_4">." This is the form
in which we express the universal affirmative "all objects having the
property <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_41"> have the property <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_11">."</p>

<p>We shall denote "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_62"> sometimes" by the notation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists x). {\phi}x\text{.} \]" src="images/1129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.59ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1129.svg"></span>
Here "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists\)" src="images/317.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.258ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_317.svg_2">" stands for "there exists," and the whole symbol may
be read "there exists an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_313"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_63">."</p>

<p>In a proposition of either of the two forms <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_542.svg_1">, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/1130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1130.svg">,
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_314"> is called an <i>apparent variable</i>.
A proposition which contains no apparent variables is called
"elementary," and a function, all whose values are<span class="pagenum" id="Page_133">[Pg 133]</span> elementary
propositions, is called an elementary function. For reasons explained
in <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a> of the Introduction, it would seem that negation and
disjunction and their derivatives must have a different meaning when
applied to elementary propositions from that which they have when
applied to such propositions as <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).\phi x\)" src="images/1131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1131.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/1132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1132.svg">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_43"> is an elementary function, we will in this
number call <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).\phi x\)" src="images/1131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1131.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/1132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1132.svg_1"> "first-order
propositions." Then in virtue of the fact that disjunction and
negation do not have the same meanings as applied to elementary or to
first-order propositions, it follows that, in asserting the primitive
propositions of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>, we must either confine them, in their application,
to propositions of a single type, or we must regard them as the
simultaneous assertion of a number of different primitive propositions,
corresponding to the different meanings of "disjunction" and
"negation." Likewise in regard to the primitive ideas of disjunction
and negation, we must either, in the primitive propositions of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>,
confine them to disjunctions and negations of elementary propositions,
or we must regard them as really each multiple, so that in regard
to each type of propositions we shall need a new primitive idea of
negation and a new primitive idea of disjunction. In the present
number, we shall show how, when the primitive ideas of negation
and disjunction are restricted to elementary propositions, and the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_252">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_172">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_42"> of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a> are therefore necessarily elementary
propositions, it is possible to obtain definitions of the negation and
disjunction of first-order propositions, and proofs of the analogues,
for first-order propositions, of the primitive propositions <a href="#_1_2" class="pginternal">*1·2</a>—<a href="#_1_6" class="pginternal">·6</a>.
(<a href="#_1_1" class="pginternal">*1·1</a> and <a href="#_1_11" class="pginternal">*1·11</a> have to be assumed afresh for first-order propositions,
and the analogues of *1·7·71·72 require a fresh treatment.) It follows
that the analogues of the propositions of <a href="#_2" class="pginternal">*2</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a> follow by merely
repeating previous proofs. It follows also that the theory of deduction
can be extended from first-order propositions to such as contain two
apparent variables, by merely repeating the process which extends
the theory of deduction from elementary to first-order propositions.
Thus by merely repeating the process set forth in the present
number, propositions of any order can be reached. Hence negation and
disjunction may be treated in practice as if there were no difference
in these ideas as applied to different types; that is to say, when
"<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}p\)" src="images/58.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.898ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_58.svg_7">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor q\)" src="images/59.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.693ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_59.svg_8">" occurs, it is unnecessary in practice
to know what is the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_253"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_173">, since the properties
of negation and disjunction assumed in <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a> (which are alone used in
proving other properties) can be asserted, without formal change, of
propositions of any order or, in the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor q\)" src="images/59.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.693ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_59.svg_9">, of any two
orders. The limitation, in practice, to the treatment of negation or
disjunction as single ideas, the same in all types, would only arise
if we ever wished to assume that there is some one function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_254">
whose value is always <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}p\)" src="images/58.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.898ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_58.svg_8">, whatever may be the order of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_255">,
or that there is some one function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_256"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_174"> whose value is
always <img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor q\)" src="images/59.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.693ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_59.svg_10">, whatever may be the orders of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_257"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_175">.
Such an assumption is not involved so long as <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_258"> (and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_176">) remain
<i>real</i> variables,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_134">[Pg 134]</span> since, in that case, there is no need to give
the same meaning to negation and disjunction for different values
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_259"> (and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_177">), when these different values are of different
types. But if <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_260"> (or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_178">) is going to be turned into an apparent
variable, then, since our two primitive ideas <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).\phi x\)" src="images/1131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1131.svg_2"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/1132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1132.svg_2"> both demand some definite function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_42">,
and restrict the apparent variable to possible arguments for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_43">,
it follows that negation and disjunction must, wherever they occur in
the expression in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_261"> (or <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_179">) is an apparent variable, be
restricted to the kind of negation or disjunction appropriate to a
given type or pair of types. Thus, to take an instance, if we assert
the law of excluded middle in the form
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash.p \lor {\sim}p\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/1133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 11.83ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1133.svg"></span>
there is no need to place any restriction upon <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_262">: we may give
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_263"> a value of any order, and then give to the negation and
disjunction involved those meanings which are appropriate to that
order. But if we assert
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash.(p).p \lor {\sim}p\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/1134.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.734ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1134.svg"></span>
it is necessary, if our symbol is to be significant, that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor{\sim}p\)" src="images/1135.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.551ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_1135.svg">"
should be the value, for the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_264">, of a function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi p\)" src="images/759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.486ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_759.svg_1">; and this is only possible if the negation and disjunction
involved have meanings fixed in advance, and if, therefore, <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_265"> is
limited to one type. Thus the assertion of the law of excluded middle
in the form involving a real variable is more general than in the form
involving an apparent variable. Similar remarks apply generally where
the variable is the argument to a typically ambiguous function.</p>

<p>In what follows the single letters p and q will represent
<i>elementary</i> propositions, and so will "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_85">," "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_22">,"
etc. We shall show how, assuming the primitive ideas and propositions
of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a> as applied to elementary propositions, we can define and prove
analogous ideas and propositions as applied to propositions of the
forms <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).\phi x\)" src="images/1131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1131.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/1132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1132.svg_3">. By mere repetition of
the analogous process, it will then follow that analogous ideas and
propositions can be defined and proved for propositions of any order;
whence, further, it follows that, in all that concerns disjunction
and negation, so long as propositions do not appear as apparent
variables, we may wholly ignore the distinction between different
types of propositions and between different meanings of negation and
disjunction. Since we never have occasion, in practice, to consider
propositions as apparent variables, it follows that the hierarchy of
propositions (as opposed to the hierarchy of functions) will never be
relevant in practice after the present number.</p>

<p>The purpose and interest of the present number are purely
philosophical, namely to show how, by means of certain primitive
propositions, we can deduce the theory of deduction for propositions
containing apparent variables from the theory of deduction for
elementary propositions. From the purely technical point of view,
the distinction between elementary and other propositions may be
ignored, so long as propositions do not appear as apparent variables;
we may then regard the primitive propositions of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a> as applying<span class="pagenum" id="Page_135">[Pg 135]</span> to
propositions of any type, and proceed as in <a href="#_10" class="pginternal">*10</a>, where the purely
technical development is resumed.</p>

<p>It should be observed that although, in the present number, we prove
that the analogues of the primitive propositions of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>, if they hold
for propositions containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_35"> apparent variables, also hold for
such as contain <img alt="" data-tex="\(n+1\)" src="images/1136.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.254ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_1136.svg">, yet we must not suppose that mathematical
induction may be used to infer that the analogues of the primitive
propositions of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a> hold for propositions containing any number of
apparent variables. Mathematical induction is a method of proof which
is not yet applicable, and is (as will appear) incapable of being used
freely until the theory of propositions containing apparent variables
has been established. What we are enabled to do, by means of the
propositions in the present number, is to prove our desired result for
any assigned number of apparent variables—say ten—by ten applications
of the same proof. Thus we can prove, concerning any assigned
proposition, that it obeys the analogues of the primitive propositions
of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>, but we can only do this by proceeding step by step, not by any
such compendious method as mathematical induction would afford. The
fact that higher types can only be reached step by step is essential,
since to proceed otherwise we should need an apparent variable which
would wander from type to type, which would contradict the principle
upon which types are built up.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p><i>Definition of Negation.</i> We have first to define the negations of
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) \ldotp \phi x\)" src="images/1137.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1137.svg"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) \ldotp \phi x\)" src="images/1138.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1138.svg">. We define
the negation of <img alt="" data-tex="\((x)\ldotp \phi x\)" src="images/1139.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1139.svg"> as <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x)\ldotp \sim \phi x\)" src="images/1140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.349ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1140.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> "it is not the case that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_86"> is always true"
is to mean "it is the case that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{not-}\phi x\)" src="images/1141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.665ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1141.svg"> is sometimes
true." Similarly the negation of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) \ldotp \phi x\)" src="images/1138.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1138.svg_1"> is to be
defined as <img alt="" data-tex="\((x)\ldotp \sim \phi x\)" src="images/1142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.092ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1142.svg">. Thus we put</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim \{(x)\ldotp \phi x\}\ldotp =\ldotp (\exists x)\ldotp \sim \phi x \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.159ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1143.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim \{(\exists x)\ldotp  \phi x\}\ldotp =\ldotp (x)\ldotp \sim \phi x \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.159ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1144.svg"></p>

<p>To avoid brackets, we shall write <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim (x)\ldotp \phi x\)" src="images/1145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.092ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1145.svg"> in place of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim \{(x)\ldotp \phi x\}\)" src="images/1146.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.354ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1146.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim (\exists x)\ldotp \phi x\)" src="images/1147.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.349ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1147.svg"> in
place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim \{(\exists x)\ldotp \phi x\}\)" src="images/1148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.612ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1148.svg">. Thus:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·011.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim (x)\ldotp  \phi x\ldotp =\ldotp \sim \{(x)\ldotp \phi x\} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1149.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.901ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1149.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·021.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sim (\exists x)\ldotp \phi x\ldotp =\ldotp \sim \{(\exists x)\ldotp \phi x\} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1150.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.417ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1150.svg"></p>

<p><i>Definition of Disjunction.</i> To define disjunction when one or
both of the propositions concerned is of the first order, we have to
distinguish six cases, as follows:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_03">*9·03</a>.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x)\ldotp \phi x\ldotp  \lor  \ldotp p\colon=\ldotp (x)\ldotp \phi x \lor  p \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1151.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.293ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1151.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\ldotp  \lor  \ldotp (x)\ldotp \phi x\colon=\ldotp (x)\ldotp p \lor  \phi x \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1152.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.173ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1152.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_05">*9·05</a>.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x)\ldotp \phi x\ldotp  \lor  \ldotp p\colon=\ldotp (\exists x)\ldotp \phi x \lor  p \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1153.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.809ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1153.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·06.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\ldotp  \lor  \ldotp (\exists x)\ldotp \phi x\colon=\ldotp (\exists x)\ldotp p \lor  \phi x \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1154.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.689ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1154.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·07.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x)\ldotp \phi x\ldotp  \lor  \ldotp (\exists y)\ldotp \psi y \colon=\colon(x)\colon(\exists y)\ldotp \phi x \lor  \psi y \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1155.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.445ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1155.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·08.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists y)\ldotp  \psi y\ldotp  \lor  \ldotp (x)\ldotp  \phi x\colon=\colon(x)\colon(\exists y)\ldotp  \psi y \lor  \phi x \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1156.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.445ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1156.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_136">[Pg 136]</span></p>

<p>(The definitions *9·07·08 are to apply also when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_44"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_12">
are not both elementary functions.)</p>

<p>In virtue of these definitions, the true scope of an apparent
variable is always the whole of the asserted proposition in which
it occurs, even when, typographically, its scope appears to be only
part of the asserted proposition. Thus when (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/1130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1130.svg_1">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_542.svg_2"> <i>appears</i> as <i>part</i> of an asserted
proposition, it does not really occur, since the scope of the apparent
variable really extends to the whole asserted proposition. It will be
shown, however, that, so far as the theory of deduction is concerned,
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/1130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1130.svg_2"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/1157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1157.svg"> behave like propositions
not containing apparent variables.</p>

<p>The definitions of implication, the logical product, and equivalence
are to be transferred unchanged to (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/1157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1157.svg_1"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/1158.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1158.svg">.</p>

<p>The above definitions can be repeated for successive types, and thus
reach propositions of any type.</p>

<p><i>Primitive Propositions.</i> The primitive propositions required
are six in number, and may be divided into three sets of two. We have
first two propositions which effect the passage from elementary to
first-order propositions, namely</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_1">*9·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \phi x .\supset. (\exists z).\phi z \quad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/1159.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.592ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1159.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_11">*9·11</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \phi x \lor \phi y .\supset. (\exists z) . \phi z \quad \text{Pp}\)" src="images/1160.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.564ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1160.svg"></p>

<p>Of these, the first states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_87"> is true, then there is a
value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_24"> which is true; <i>i.e.</i> if we can find an
instance of a function which is true, then the function is "sometimes
true." (When we speak of a function as "sometimes" true, we do not
mean to assert that there is <i>more</i> than one argument for which
it is true, but only that there is <i>at least</i> one.) Practically,
the above primitive proposition gives the only method of proving
"existence-theorems": in order to prove such theorems, it is necessary
(and sufficient) to find some instance in which an object possesses
the property in question. If we were to assume what may be called
"existence-axioms," <i>i.e.</i> axioms stating (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists z).\phi z\)" src="images/1161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.597ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1161.svg">
for some particular <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_45">, these axioms would give other methods
of proving existence. Instances of such axioms are the multiplicative
axiom (<a href="#_88" class="pginternal">*88</a>) and the axiom of infinity (defined in *120·03). But we have
not assumed any such axioms in the present work.</p>

<p>The second of the above primitive propositions is only used once,
in proving (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists z).\phi z .\lor. (\exists z).\phi z :\supset.(\exists z). \phi z\)" src="images/1162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.095ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1162.svg">,
which is the analogue of <a href="#_1_2" class="pginternal">*1·2</a> (namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor p .\supset. p)\)" src="images/1163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.581ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1163.svg">
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_266"> is replaced by (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists z).\phi z\)" src="images/1161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.597ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1161.svg_1">. The
effect of this primitive proposition is to emphasize the ambiguity of
the <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_15"> required in order to secure (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists z).\phi z\)" src="images/1161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.597ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1161.svg_2">. We have,
of course, in virtue of <a href="#_9_1" class="pginternal">*9·1</a>,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi x .\supset. (\exists z).\phi z ~ \text{and} ~ \phi y .\supset. (\exists z).\phi z. \]" src="images/1164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.005ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1164.svg"></span>
But if we try to infer from these that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x \lor \phi y .\supset.(\exists z).\phi z\)" src="images/1165.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.863ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1165.svg">,
we must use the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_137">[Pg 137]</span> proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(q \supset p.r \supset p .\supset. q \lor r \supset p\)" src="images/1166.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 23.88ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_1166.svg">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_267"> is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists z).\phi z\)" src="images/1161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.597ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1161.svg_3">. Now it will be found, on
referring to <a href="#_4_77" class="pginternal">*4·77</a> and the propositions used in its proof, that this
proposition depends upon <a href="#_1_2" class="pginternal">*1·2</a>, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(p \lor p .\supset. p\)" src="images/1167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.701ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_1167.svg">.
Hence it cannot be used by us to prove (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x .\lor. (\exists x).\phi x :\supset. (\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/1168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.547ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1168.svg">, and thus we are
compelled to assume the primitive proposition <a href="#_9_11" class="pginternal">*9·11</a>.</p>

<p>We have next two propositions concerned with <i>inference</i> to
or from propositions containing apparent variables, as opposed to
implication. First, we have, for the new meaning of implication
resulting from the above definitions of negation and disjunction, the
analogue of <a href="#_1_1" class="pginternal">*1·1</a>, namely</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{What is implied by a true premiss is true.} \quad \text{Pp}\text{.}\)" src="images/1169.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 45.86ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_1169.svg"></p>

<p>That is to say, given "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .p\)" src="images/1170.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.526ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1170.svg">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. p \supset q\)" src="images/1171.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.584ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1171.svg">,"
we may proceed to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. q\)" src="images/1172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.429ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_1172.svg">," even when the propositions <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_268">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_180"> are not elementary. Also, as in <a href="#_1_11" class="pginternal">*1·11</a>, we may proceed
from "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \phi x\)" src="images/1173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.031ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1173.svg">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \phi x \supset \psi x\)" src="images/1174.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.815ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1174.svg">"
to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\psi x\)" src="images/1175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1175.svg">" where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_315"> is a real variable, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_46">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_13"> are not necessarily elementary functions. It is in this
latter form that the axiom is usually needed. It is to be assumed for
functions of several variables as well as for functions of one variable.</p>

<p>We have next the primitive proposition which permits the passage
from a real to an apparent variable, namely "when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_10"> may be
asserted, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_96"> may be any possible argument, then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_3">
may be asserted." In other words, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_11"> is true however
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_97"> may be chosen among possible arguments, then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_4"> is
true, <i>i.e.</i> all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_47"> are true. That is to say,
if we can assert a wholly ambiguous value <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_12">, that must be
because all values are true. We may express this primitive proposition
by the words: "What is true in <i>any</i> case, however the case may
be selected, is true in <i>all</i> cases." We cannot symbolise this
proposition, because if we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\vdash:\phi y .\supset. (x).\phi x \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/1176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.463ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1176.svg"></span>
that means: "However <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_98"> may be chosen, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_13"> implies (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_5">,"
which is in general false. What we mean is: "If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_14"> is
true however <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_99"> may be chosen, then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_6"> is true." But we
have not supplied a symbol for the mere <i>hypothesis</i> of what is
<i>asserted</i> in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi y\)" src="images/1177.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.845ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1177.svg">," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_100"> is a real variable,
and it is not worth while to supply such a symbol, because it would be
very rarely required. If, for the moment, we use the symbol <img alt="" data-tex="\([\phi y]\)" src="images/1178.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.715ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1178.svg">
to express this hypothesis, then our primitive proposition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash:[\phi y] .\supset. (x).\phi x \quad \text{Pp}\text{.} \]" src="images/1179.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.52ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1179.svg"></span>
In practice, this primitive proposition is only used for
<i>inference</i>, not for implication; that is to say, when we actually
have an assertion containing a real variable, it enables us to turn
this real variable into an apparent variable by placing it in brackets
immediately after the assertion-sign, followed by enough dots to reach
to the end of the assertion. This process will be called "turning
a real variable into an apparent variable." Thus we may assert our
primitive proposition, for technical use, in the form:</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_138">[Pg 138]</span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_13">*9·13</a>.</b> In any assertion containing a real variable, this real
variable may be turned into an apparent variable of which all possible
values are asserted to satisfy the function in question. Pp.</p>

<p>We have next two primitive propositions concerned with types. These
require some preliminary explanations.</p>

<p><i>Primitive Idea: Individual.</i> We say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_316"> is "individual" if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_317"> is neither a proposition nor a function (cf. <a href="#Page_53" class="pginternal">pp. 53</a>, <a href="#Page_54" class="pginternal">54</a>).</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_131">*9·131</a>.</b> <i>Definition of "being of the same type."</i> The
following is a step-by-step definition, the definition for higher types
presupposing that for lower types. We say that <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg"> "are of
the same type" if (1) both are individuals, (2) both are elementary
functions taking arguments of the same type, (3) <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_1"> is a function
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg_1"> is its negation, (4) <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_2"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_44"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_2">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg_2"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x} \lor \psi \hat{x}\)" src="images/1182.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.924ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1182.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_45">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi \hat{x}\)" src="images/223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_223.svg_4"> are elementary functions, (5) <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_3">
is <img alt="" data-tex="\((y). \phi (\hat{x},y)\)" src="images/1183.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.392ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1183.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg_3"> is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(z). \psi (\hat{x},z)\)" src="images/1184.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.523ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1184.svg">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (\hat{x}, \hat{y})\)" src="images/1185.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1185.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi (\hat{x}, \hat{y})\)" src="images/1186.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.642ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1186.svg"> are
of the same type, (6) both are elementary propositions, (7) <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_4"> is
a proposition and <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg_4"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}u\)" src="images/1187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1187.svg">, or (8) <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_5"> is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_7">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg_5"> is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).\psi y\)" src="images/1188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.576ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1188.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_46"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi \hat{x}\)" src="images/223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_223.svg_5">
are of the same type.</p>

<p>Our primitive propositions are:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_14">*9·14</a>.</b> If "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_88">" is significant, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_318"> is of the
same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_75">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_15">" is significant, and vice versa. Pp.
(Cf. note on *10·121, <a href="#Page_146" class="pginternal">p. 146</a>.)</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_15">*9·15</a>.</b> If, for some <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_76">, there is a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_16">,
then there is a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_47">, and vice versa. Pp.</p>

<p>It will be seen that, in virtue of the definitions,</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp;(x).\phi x .\supset. p &amp;~\text{means}~ {\sim}(x).\phi x .\lor. p, ~\textit{i.e.}~ (\exists x).{\sim}\phi x .\lor. p,\\ &amp; &amp;\textit{i.e.}~ (\exists x).{\sim}\phi x \lor p, ~\textit{i.e.}~ (\exists x).\phi x \supset p\\ &amp;(\exists x).\phi x .\supset. p &amp;~\text{means}~ {\sim}(\exists x).\phi x .\lor. p, ~\textit{i.e.}~ (x).{\sim}\phi x .\lor. p,\\ &amp; &amp;\textit{i.e.}~ (x).{\sim}\phi x \lor p, ~\textit{i.e.}~ (x).\phi x\supset p\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/1189.svg" style="vertical-align: -4.977ex; width: 58.189ex; height: 11.086ex;" id="img_images_1189.svg"></span>
In order to prove that (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_8"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_610.svg_1"> obey
the same rules of deduction as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_89">, we have to prove that
propositions of the forms (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_9"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_610.svg_2">
may replace one or more of the propositions <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_269">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_181">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_43"> in
<a href="#_1_2" class="pginternal">*1·2</a>—<a href="#_1_6" class="pginternal">·6</a>. When this has been proved, the previous proofs of subsequent
propositions in <a href="#_2" class="pginternal">*2</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a> become applicable. These proofs are given below.
Certain other propositions, required in the proofs, are also proved.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_2">*9·2</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(x). \phi x .\supset. \phi y\)" src="images/1190.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.572ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1190.svg"></p>

<p>The above proposition states the principle of deduction from the
general to the particular, <i>i.e.</i> "what holds in all cases, holds
in any one case."</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp;\vdash.\text{*2·1.} \supset \vdash. {\sim}\phi y \lor \phi y&amp; \quad &amp;(1)\\ &amp;\vdash.\text{*9·1.} \supset \vdash: {\sim} \phi y \lor \phi y &amp; .\supset.(\exists x). {\sim}\phi x \lor \phi y \quad &amp;(2)\\ &amp;\vdash.\text{(1).(2).*1·11.} \supset &amp;\vdash.(\exists x). {\sim}\phi x \lor \phi y \quad &amp;(3)\\ &amp;\text{[(3).(*9·05)]} &amp;\vdash:(\exists x).{\sim}\phi x .\lor. \phi y \quad &amp;(4)\\ &amp;\text{[(4).(*9·01.*1·01)]} &amp;\vdash:(x). \phi x .\supset.\phi y \quad &amp;\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/1191.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.448ex; width: 50.532ex; height: 14.027ex;" id="img_images_1191.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_139">[Pg 139]</span></p>

<p>In the second line of the above proof, "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\phi y \lor \phi y\)" src="images/1192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.189ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1192.svg">"
is taken as the value, for the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_101">, of the function
"<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\phi x \lor \phi y\)" src="images/1193.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.374ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1193.svg">," where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_319"> is the argument. A similar
method of using <a href="#_9_1" class="pginternal">*9·1</a> is employed in most of the following proofs.</p>

<p><a href="#_1_11" class="pginternal">*1·11</a> is used, as in the third line of the above proof, in almost all
steps except such as are mere applications of definitions. Hence it
will not be further referred to, unless in cases where its employment
is obscure or specially important.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_21">*9·21</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  (x) . \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  : (x) . \phi x . \supset  . (x) . \psi x\)" src="images/1194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.207ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1194.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_90"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_23">, then "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_91">
always" implies "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_24"> always." The use of this proposition is
constant throughout the remainder of this work.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin {array}{l} \vdash . \text{*2·08}. &amp;\supset  \vdash : \phi z \supset  \psi z . \supset  . \phi z \supset  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash . \text{(1) . *9·1}.    &amp;\supset  \vdash : (\exists y) : \phi z \supset  \psi z . \supset  . \phi y \supset  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .\text{(2). *9·1}.     &amp;\supset  \vdash \colon\ldotp  (\exists x) \colon\ldotp  (\exists y) : \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  . \phi y \supset  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash . \text{(3). *9·13}.    &amp;\supset  \vdash \colon\colon  (z) \colon\colon  (\exists x) \colon\ldotp  (\exists y) : \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  . \phi y \supset  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ [\text{(4).(*9·06)}]      &amp;\vdash \colon\colon  (z) \colon\colon  (\exists x) \colon\ldotp  \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  : (\exists y) . \phi y \supset  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ [\text{(5).(*1·01.*9·08)}] &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp  (\exists x) . {\sim}(\phi x \supset  \psi x) : \lor  : (z) : (\exists y) . {\sim}\phi y \lor  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(6)}\\ [\text{(6).(*9·08)}]       &amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp  (\exists x) . {\sim}(\phi x \supset  \psi x) : \lor  : (\exists y) . {\sim}\phi y . \lor  . (z) . \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(7)}\\ [\text{(7).(*1·01)}]      &amp; \vdash \colon\ldotp  (x) . \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  : (y) . \phi y . \supset  . (z) . \psi z \end{array} \]" src="images/1195.svg" style="vertical-align: -11.652ex; width: 74.571ex; height: 24.434ex;" id="img_images_1195.svg"></span></p>

<p>This is the proposition to be proved, since "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(y) . \phi y\)" src="images/1196.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.452ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1196.svg">" is the
same proposition as "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_14">," and "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(z) . \psi z\)" src="images/1197.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.463ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1197.svg">" is the
same proposition as "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \psi x\)" src="images/1198.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.947ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1198.svg">."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_22">*9·22</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  (x) . \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  : (\exists x) . \phi x . \supset  . (\exists x) . \psi x\)" src="images/1199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.723ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1199.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_92"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_25">, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_93">
is sometimes true, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_26">. This proposition, like <a href="#_9_21" class="pginternal">*9·21</a>, is
constantly used in the sequel.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin {array}{l} \vdash . \text{*2·08}.&amp;\supset  \vdash : \phi y \supset  \psi y . \supset  . \phi y \supset  \psi y   &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .\text{(1) . *9·1}.   &amp; \supset  \vdash : (\exists z) : \phi y \supset  \psi y . \supset  . \phi y \supset  \psi z   &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash . \text{(2) . *9·1}.     &amp;\supset  \vdash \colon\ldotp  (\exists x) \colon\ldotp  (\exists z) : \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  . \phi y \supset  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .\text{(3) . *9·13}.   &amp; \supset  \vdash \colon\colon  (y) \colon\colon  (\exists x) \colon\ldotp  (\exists z) : \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  . \phi y \supset  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ [\text{(4).(*9·06)}]    &amp;\vdash \colon\colon  (y) \colon\colon  (\exists x) \colon\ldotp  \phi x \supset \psi x . \supset  : (\exists z) . \phi y \supset  \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ [\text{(5).(*1·01.*9·08)}]    &amp; \vdash \colon\colon  (\exists x) . {\sim}(\phi x \supset  \psi x) : \lor  : (y) : (\exists z) . \phi y \supset  \psi z   &amp;\qquad \text{(6)}\\ [\text{(6).(*1·01.*9·07)}]     &amp;\vdash \colon\colon  (\exists x) . {\sim}(\phi x \supset  \psi x) : \lor  : (y) . {\sim}\phi y . \lor  . (\exists z) . \psi z  &amp;\qquad \text{(7)}\\ [\text{(7).(*1·01.*9·01·02)}]   &amp; \vdash \colon\ldotp  (x) . \phi x \supset  \psi x . \supset  : (\exists y) . \phi y . \supset  . (\exists z) . \psi z \end{array} \]" src="images/1200.svg" style="vertical-align: -11.652ex; width: 77.462ex; height: 24.434ex;" id="img_images_1200.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_140">[Pg 140]</span></p>

<p>This is the proposition to be proved, because (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists y).\phi y\)" src="images/1201.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.71ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1201.svg"> is
the same proposition as (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_610.svg_3">, and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists z).\psi z\)" src="images/1202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.721ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1202.svg">
is the same proposition as (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\psi x\)" src="images/1203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.205ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1203.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(x).\phi x.\supset .(x).\phi x \quad[\text{Id.*9·13·21}]\)" src="images/1204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.087ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1204.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists x).\phi x.\supset .(\exists x).\phi x \quad[\text{Id.*9·13·22}]\)" src="images/1205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.603ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1205.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_9_25">*9·25</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).p\lor \phi x.\supset :p.\lor .(x).\phi x \quad[\text{*9·23.(*9·04)}]\)" src="images/1206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.353ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1206.svg"></p>

<p>We are now in a position to prove the analogues of <a href="#_1_2" class="pginternal">*1·2</a>—<a href="#_1_6" class="pginternal">·6</a>, replacing
one of the letters <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_270">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_182">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_44"> in those propositions by
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_10"> or (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_610.svg_4">. The proofs are given below.</p>

<p class="nind">

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·61.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_37"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_3"> are elementary
functions of the same type, there is a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x} \lor \psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/1239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.924ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1239.svg">.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p>By *9·14·15, there is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_77"> for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg_3">," and therefore
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_17">," are significant, and therefore so is "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\lor \psi a\)" src="images/1240.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.73ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1240.svg">,"
by the primitive idea of disjunction. Hence the result by <a href="#_9_15" class="pginternal">*9·15</a>.</p>

<p>The same proof holds for functions of any number of variables.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·62.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1241.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1241.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{z}\)" src="images/459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_459.svg_2"> are
elementary functions, and the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_320">-argument to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_48"> is of the same
type as the argument to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_14">, there are functions
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (y).\phi(\hat{x},y). \lor .\psi\hat{x}, (\exists y).\phi(\hat{x},y). \lor .\psi\hat{x}. \]" src="images/1242.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.253ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1242.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p>By <a href="#_9_15" class="pginternal">*9·15</a>, there are propositions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,b)\)" src="images/1243.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.379ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1243.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg_4">, where
by hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_321"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_78"> are of the same type. Hence by <a href="#_9_14" class="pginternal">*9·14</a>
there is a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(a,b)\)" src="images/1244.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.282ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1244.svg">, and therefore, by the primitive
idea of disjunction, there is a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(a,b)\lor \psi a\)" src="images/1245.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.466ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1245.svg">,
and therefore, by *9·15 and <a href="#_9_03" class="pginternal">*9·03</a>, there is a proposition
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).\phi(a,y).\lor .\psi a\)" src="images/1246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.606ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1246.svg">. Similarly there is a proposition
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists y).\phi(a,y).\lor .\psi a\)" src="images/1247.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.863ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1247.svg">. Hence the result, by *9·15.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*9·63.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1241.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1241.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1248.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.762ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1248.svg">
are elementary functions of the same type, there are functions
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).\phi(\hat{x},y).\lor .(z).\psi(\hat{x},z)\)" src="images/1249.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.437ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1249.svg">, etc. [Proof as above]</p>

<p>We have now completed the proof that, in the primitive propositions
of *1, any one of the propositions that occur may be replaced by
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_11"> or (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_610.svg_5">. It follows that, by merely
repeating the proofs, we can show that any other of the propositions
that occur in these propositions can be simultaneously replaced by
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\psi x\)" src="images/1250.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.947ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1250.svg"> or (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\psi x\)" src="images/1203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.205ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1203.svg_1">. Thus all the primitive
propositions of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>, and therefore all the propositions of <a href="#_2" class="pginternal">*2</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a>, hold
equally when some or all of the propositions concerned are of one of
the forms (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_12">, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_610.svg_6">, which was to be
proved.</p>

<p>It follows, by mere repetition of the proofs, that the propositions
of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a> hold when <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_271">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_183">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_45"> are replaced by propositions
containing any number of apparent variables.</p>

times." A similar remark applies to "sometimes."</p>

</div>
