<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_143">[Pg 143]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_10">*10. THEORY OF PROPOSITIONS CONTAINING ONE APPARENT
VARIABLE.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *10.</p>

<p>The chief purpose of the propositions of this number is to extend
to formal implications (<i>i.e.</i> to propositions of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\((x).{\phi}x \supset {\psi}x\)" src="images/1251.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.487ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1251.svg">) as many as possible of the
propositions proved previously for material implications, <i>i.e.</i>
for propositions of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(p \supset q\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.196ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_11">. Thus <i>e.g.</i> we have
proved in <a href="#_3_33" class="pginternal">*3·33</a> that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ p \supset q . q \supset r .\supset. p \supset r\text{.} \]" src="images/1252.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.857ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_1252.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} \text{Put}\quad &amp;p &amp;=~ &amp;\text{Socrates is a Greek}\text{,}\\ &amp;q &amp;=~ &amp;\text{Socrates is a man}\text{,}\\ &amp;r &amp;=~ &amp;\text{Socrates is a mortal}\text{.}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/1253.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 34.895ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_1253.svg"></span>
Then we have "if 'Socrates is a Greek' implies 'Socrates is a man,'
and 'Socrates is a man' implies 'Socrates is a mortal,' it follows
that 'Socrates is a Greek' implies 'Socrates is a mortal.'" But this
does not of itself prove that if all Greeks are men, and all men are
mortals, then all Greeks are mortals.</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} \text{Putting} \quad &amp;{\phi}x &amp;.=.~ &amp;x~ \text{is a Greek}\text{,}\\ &amp;{\psi}x &amp;.=.~ &amp;x~ \text{is a man}\text{,}\\ &amp;{\chi}x &amp;.=.~ &amp;x~ \text{is a mortal}\text{,}\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/1254.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 34.284ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_1254.svg"></span>
we have to prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x).{\phi}x \supset {\psi}x : (x).{\psi}x \supset {\chi}x :\supset: (x).{\phi}x \supset {\chi}x\text{.} \]" src="images/1255.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.262ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1255.svg"></span>
It is such propositions that have to be proved in the present
number. It will be seen that formal implication <img alt="" data-tex="\(((x).{\phi}x \supset {\psi}x\)" src="images/1256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.367ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1256.svg">)
is a relation of two functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_38">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_4">. Many of the formal properties of this relation
are analogous to properties of the relation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p \supset q\)" src="images/71.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.196ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_71.svg_12">" which
expresses material implication; it is such analogues that are to be
proved in this number.</p>

<p>We shall assume in this number, what has been proved in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>, that
the propositions of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a> can be applied to such propositions as
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/1157.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1157.svg_2"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . {\phi}x\)" src="images/1257.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1257.svg">. Instead of the method
adopted in *9, it is possible to take negation and disjunction as
new primitive ideas, as applied to propositions containing apparent
variables, and to assume that, with the new meanings of negation and
disjunction, the primitive propositions of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a> still hold. If this<span class="pagenum" id="Page_144">[Pg 144]</span>
method is adopted, we need not take <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/1132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1132.svg_4"> as a
primitive idea, but may put</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_01">*10·01</a>.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x.=.{\sim}(x).{\sim} \phi x\quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1258.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.759ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1258.svg"></p>

<p>In order to make it clear how this alternative method can be developed,
we shall, in the present number, assume nothing of what has been proved
in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a> except certain propositions which, in the alternative method,
will be primitive propositions, and (what in part characterizes the
alternative method) the applicability to propositions containing
apparent variables of analogues of the primitive ideas and propositions
of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>, and therefore of their consequences as set forth in <a href="#_2" class="pginternal">*2</a>—<a href="#_5" class="pginternal">*5</a>.</p>

<p>The two following definitions merely serve to introduce a notation
which is often more convenient than the notation <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).\phi x\supset\psi x\)" src="images/1259.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.487ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1259.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).\phi x\equiv\psi x\)" src="images/1260.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.487ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1260.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\supset_{x}\psi x.=.(x).\phi x\supset\psi x\,\quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1261.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.85ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1261.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\equiv_{x}\psi x.=.(x).\phi x\equiv \psi x\,\quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1262.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.85ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1262.svg"></p>

<p>The first of these notations is due to Peano, who, however, has no
notation for (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_13"> except in the special case of a formal
implication.</p>

<p>The following propositions (*10·1·11·12·121·122) have already been
given in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>. <a href="#_10_1" class="pginternal">*10·1</a> is *9·2*10·11 is <a href="#_9_13" class="pginternal">*9·13</a>, <a href="#_10_12" class="pginternal">*10·12</a> is <a href="#_9_25" class="pginternal">*9·25</a>, <a href="#_10_121" class="pginternal">*10·121</a>
is <a href="#_9_14" class="pginternal">*9·14</a>, and <a href="#_10_122" class="pginternal">*10·122</a> is <a href="#_9_15" class="pginternal">*9·15</a>. These five propositions must all be
taken as primitive propositions in the alternative method; on the other
hand, <a href="#_9_1" class="pginternal">*9·1</a> and <a href="#_9_11" class="pginternal">*9·11</a> are not required as primitive propositions in the
alternative method.</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number are very much used throughout
the rest of the work. The propositions most used are the following:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_1">*10·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(x).\phi x.\supset.\phi y\)" src="images/1263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.572ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1263.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> what is true in all cases is true in any one case.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·11.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_15"> is true whatever possible argument
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_102"> may be, then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_14"> is true. In other words, whenever
the propositional function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_16"> can be asserted, so can the
proposition (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_15">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).p\supset\phi x.\equiv:p.\supset.(x).\phi x\)" src="images/1264.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.889ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1264.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x:(x).\psi x:\equiv.(x).\phi x.\psi x\)" src="images/1265.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.31ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1265.svg"></p>

<p>The conditions of significance in this proposition demand that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_49">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_15"> should take arguments of the same type.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp (x).\phi x\supset p.\equiv \colon(\exists x).\phi x.\supset.p\)" src="images/1266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.896ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1266.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_94"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_272">, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_95"> is
ever true, <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_273"> is true.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\phi y.\supset.(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/1267.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.83ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1267.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_145">[Pg 145]</span></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_17"> is true, then there is an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_322"> for
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_96"> is true. This is the sole method of proving
existence-theorems.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·27.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (z).\phi z\supset\psi z.\supset:(z).\phi z.\supset.(z).\psi z\)" src="images/1268.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.513ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1268.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi z\)" src="images/1269.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1269.svg"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi z\)" src="images/1270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1270.svg">, then "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi z\)" src="images/1269.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1269.svg_1">
always" implies "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi z\)" src="images/1270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1270.svg_1"> always." The three following propositions,
which are equally useful, are analogous to <a href="#_10_27" class="pginternal">*10·27</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·271.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (z).\phi z\equiv\psi z.\supset:(z).\phi z.\equiv.(z).\psi z\)" src="images/1271.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.513ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1271.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·28.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x\supset\psi x.\supset:(\exists x).\phi x.\supset.(\exists x).\psi x\)" src="images/1272.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.723ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1272.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·281.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x\equiv\psi x.\supset:(\exists x).\phi x.\equiv.(\exists x).\psi x\)" src="images/1273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.723ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1273.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists x).p.\phi x.\equiv:p:(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/1274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.508ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1274.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists x).\phi x.\lor .(\exists x).\psi x:\equiv.(\exists x).\phi x \lor \psi x\)" src="images/1275.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.228ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1275.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists x).\phi x.\psi x.\supset:(\exists x).\phi x:(\exists x).\psi x\)" src="images/1276.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.084ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1276.svg"></p>

<p>It should be noticed that whereas <a href="#_10_42" class="pginternal">*10·42</a> expresses an equivalence,
<a href="#_10_5" class="pginternal">*10·5</a> only expresses an implication. This is the source of many
subsequent differences between formulae concerning addition and
formulae concerning multiplication.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp {\sim}\{(\exists x).\phi x.\psi x\}.\equiv:\phi x.\supset_{x}.{\sim}\psi x\)" src="images/1277.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.219ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1277.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is analogous to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash:{\sim}(p.q).\equiv.p\supset{\sim}q \]" src="images/1278.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.073ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1278.svg"></span>
which results from <a href="#_4_63" class="pginternal">*4·63</a> by transposition.</p>

<p>Of the remaining propositions of this number, some are employed fairly
often, while others are lemmas which are used only once or twice,
sometimes at a much later stage.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*10·01.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x.=.{\sim}(x).{\sim}\phi x \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1279.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.759ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1279.svg"></p>

<p>This definition is only to be used when we discard the method of *9 in
favour of the alternative method already explained. In either case we
have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash:(\exists x).\phi x.\equiv.{\sim}(x).{\sim}\phi x. \]" src="images/1280.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.225ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1280.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\supset_{x}\psi x.=.(x).\phi x\supset\psi x \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1281.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.472ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1281.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\equiv_{x}\psi x.=.(x).\phi x\equiv\psi x \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1282.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.472ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1282.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(x).\phi x.\supset \phi y \quad[\text{*9·2}]\)" src="images/1283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.737ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1283.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_11">*10·11</a>.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_18"> is true whatever possible argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_103">
may be, then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x\)" src="images/426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_426.svg_16"> is true. [<a href="#_9_13" class="pginternal">*9·13</a>]</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_146">[Pg 146]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is, in a sense, the converse of <a href="#_10_1" class="pginternal">*10·1</a>. *10·1 may be
stated: "What is true of all is true of any," while <a href="#_10_11" class="pginternal">*10·11</a> may be
stated: "What is true of any, however chosen, is true of all."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_12">*10·12</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).p\lor\phi x.\supset:p.\lor.(x).\phi x \quad[\text{*9·25}]\)" src="images/1284.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.81ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1284.svg"></p>

<p>According to the definitions in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>, this proposition is a mere
example of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(q\supset q\)" src="images/1285.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.099ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_1285.svg">," since by definition the two sides of the
implication are different symbols for the same proposition. According
to the alternative method, on the contrary, <a href="#_10_12" class="pginternal">*10·12</a> is a substantial
proposition.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_121">*10·121</a>.</b> If "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_97">" is significant, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_79"> is of the
same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_323">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_18">" is significant, and vice versa. [<a href="#_9_14" class="pginternal">*9·14</a>]</p>

<p>It follows from this proposition that two arguments to the same
function must be of the same type; for if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_324"> and a are arguments
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_39">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_98">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_19">" are significant,
and therefore <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_325"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_80"> are of the same type. Thus the above
primitive proposition embodies the outcome of our discussion of the
vicious-circle paradoxes in <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a> of the Introduction.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_122">*10·122</a>.</b> If, for some <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_81">, there is a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_20">,
then there is a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_40">, and vice versa. [<a href="#_9_15" class="pginternal">*9·15</a>]</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_13">*10·13</a>.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_41"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_5"> take arguments of
the same type, and we have "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi x\)" src="images/742.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.031ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_742.svg_1">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\psi x\)" src="images/1175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1175.svg_1">,"
we shall have "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi x.\psi x\)" src="images/1286.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.804ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1286.svg">."</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p>By repeated use of 9·61·62·63·131 (3), there is a function
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\phi\hat{x}\lor{\sim}\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/1287.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.444ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1287.svg">. Hence by <a href="#_2_11" class="pginternal">*2·11</a> and <a href="#_3_01" class="pginternal">*3·01</a>,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash:{\sim}\phi x\lor{\sim}\psi x.\lor.\phi x.\psi x &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*2·32.(*1·01)}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x.\supset:\psi x.\supset.\phi x.\psi x &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).*9·12}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1288.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 54.066ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1288.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_14">*10·14</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x:(x).\psi x:\supset.\phi y.\psi y\)" src="images/1289.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.879ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1289.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is true whenever it is significant, but it is not
always significant when its hypothesis is significant. For the thesis
demands that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_50"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_16"> should take arguments of the same
type, while the hypothesis does not demand this. Hence, if it is to
be applied when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_51"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_17"> are given, or when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_18"> is
given as a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_52"> or vice versa, we must not argue from
the hypothesis to the thesis unless, in the supposed case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_53"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_19"> take arguments of the same type.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·1}. &amp;\supset\vdash:(x).\phi x.\supset.\phi y &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*10·1}. &amp;\supset\vdash:(x).\psi x.\supset.\psi y &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).*10·13}.&amp;\supset\vdash:(x).\phi x.\supset.\phi y:(x).\psi x.\supset.\psi y:\\ [\text{*3·47}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x:(x).\psi x:\supset.\phi y.\psi y\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1290.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 69.9ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_1290.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_147">[Pg 147]</span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_2">*10·2</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).p\lor \phi x.\equiv:p.\lor .(x)\phi x\)" src="images/1291.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.129ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1291.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·1.*1·6}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp p.\lor .(x).\phi x:\supset.p\lor \phi y\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·11}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (y)\colon\ldotp p.\lor .(x).\phi x:\supset.p\lor \phi y\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·12}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp p.\lor .(x).\phi x:\supset.(y).p\lor \phi y &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*10·12}. &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (y).p\lor \phi y.\supset:p.\lor .(x).\phi x &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2)}. &amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}. \end{array} \]" src="images/1292.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 57.93ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_1292.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_21">*10·21</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).p\supset\phi x.\equiv:p.\supset.(x).\phi x \quad\left[\text{*10·2}\, \frac{{\sim}p}{p}\right]\)" src="images/1293.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.469ex; width: 43.241ex; height: 4.07ex;" id="img_images_1293.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is much more used than <a href="#_10_2" class="pginternal">*10·2</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\psi x.\equiv:(x).\phi x:(x).\psi x\)" src="images/1294.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.31ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1294.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·1}. &amp;\supset\vdash:(x).\phi x.\psi x.\supset.\phi y.\psi y. &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ [\text{*3·26}] &amp;\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\supset.\phi y:\\ [\text{*10·11}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (y):(x).\phi x.\psi x.\supset.\phi y\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·21}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\psi x.\supset.(y).\phi y &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*3·27}. &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\psi x.\supset.\psi z\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·11}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (z):(x).\phi x.\psi x.\supset.\psi z\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·21}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\psi x.\supset.(z).\psi z &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(3).Comp}. &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\psi x.\supset:(y).\phi y:(z).\psi z &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{*10·14·11}. &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (y)\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x:(x).\psi x:\supset.\phi y.\psi y\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·21}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x:(x).\psi x:\supset.(y).\phi y.\psi y &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash.\text{(4).(5)}. &amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1295.svg" style="vertical-align: -16.403ex; width: 65.061ex; height: 33.937ex;" id="img_images_1295.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition is true whenever it is significant; but, as was
pointed out in connexion with <a href="#_10_14" class="pginternal">*10·14</a>, it is not always significant when
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).\phi x:(x).\psi x\)" src="images/1296.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.536ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1296.svg">" is significant.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_10_221">*10·221</a>.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_99"> contains a constituent <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi(x, y, z, ...)\)" src="images/917.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.667ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_917.svg_1">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_27"> contains a constituent <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi(x, u, v, \ldots)\)" src="images/916.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.532ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_916.svg_1">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_3"> is an elementary function and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y, z, \ldots u, v, \ldots\)" src="images/1297.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 14.256ex; height: 1.466ex;" id="img_images_1297.svg">
are either constants or apparent variables,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_42"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_6"> take arguments of the
same type. This can be proved in each particular case, though not
generally, provided that, in obtaining <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_54"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_20"> from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_5"> is only submitted to negations, disjunctions and
generalizations. The process may be illustrated by an example. Suppose
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_100"> is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).\chi(x,y).\supset.\theta x\)" src="images/1298.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.707ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1298.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_28">
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(fx.\supset.(y).\chi(x,y)\)" src="images/1299.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.771ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1299.svg">. By the definitions of <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_101">
is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists y).{\sim}\chi(x,y)\lor \theta x\)" src="images/1300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.468ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1300.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_29">
is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).{\sim}fx\lor \chi(x,y)\)" src="images/1301.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.393ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1301.svg">. Hence since the primitive ideas
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).Fx\)" src="images/1302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.169ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1302.svg"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).Fx\)" src="images/1303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.427ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1303.svg"> only apply to functions, there
are functions <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\chi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\lor \theta\hat{x}\)" src="images/1304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.215ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1304.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}f\hat{x}\lor \chi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.398ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1305.svg">. Hence there is a
proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\chi(a,b)\lor \theta a\)" src="images/1306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.883ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1306.svg">. Hence, since "<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\lor q\)" src="images/1098.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.693ex; height: 1.792ex;" id="img_images_1098.svg_1">"
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}p\)" src="images/58.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.898ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_58.svg_9">" are only significant<span class="pagenum" id="Page_148">[Pg 148]</span> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_274"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_184">
are propositions, there is a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi(a, b)\)" src="images/1307.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.35ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1307.svg">. Similarly,
for some <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg_6">, there are propositions <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}fu \lor \chi(u,v)\)" src="images/1308.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.387ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1308.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi(u, v)\)" src="images/1309.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.574ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1309.svg">. Hence by <a href="#_9_14" class="pginternal">*9·14</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_82">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg_7">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_21"> are respectively of the same type, and (again by *9·14) there
is a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}fa\lor \chi(a, b)\)" src="images/1310.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.066ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1310.svg">. Hence (<a href="#_9_15" class="pginternal">*9·15</a>) there are
functions <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\chi(a, \hat{y}) \lor \theta a\)" src="images/1311.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.021ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1311.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}fa \lor \chi(a, \hat{y})\)" src="images/1312.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.204ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1312.svg">,
therefore there are propositions
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists y).{\sim}\chi(a, y) \lor  \theta a, (y).{\sim}fa \lor  \chi(a, y), \]" src="images/1313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.867ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1313.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> there are propositions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_21">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg_5">, which was to
be proved. This process can be applied similarly in any other instance.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_23">*10·23</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x\supset p.\equiv:(\exists x).\phi x.\supset.p\)" src="images/1314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.147ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1314.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*4·2.(*9·03)}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).{\sim}\phi x \lor  p.&amp;\equiv:(x).{\sim}\phi x. \lor  .p:\\ [\text{(*9·02)}] &amp;\equiv.(\exists x).\phi x.\supset.p &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(*1·01)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1315.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 62.198ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1315.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the above proof, we employ the definitions of <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>. In the alternative
method, in which (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi x\)" src="images/610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_610.svg_7"> is defined in accordance with
<a href="#_10_01" class="pginternal">*10·01</a>, the proof proceeds as follows.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x\supset p.\equiv:(\exists x).\phi x.\supset.p\)" src="images/1314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.147ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1314.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_149">[Pg 149]</span></p>

<p>Whenever we have an asserted proposition of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\supset\phi x\)" src="images/1317.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.798ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1317.svg">,
we can pass by *10·11·21 to an asserted proposition
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p.\supset.(x).\phi x\)" src="images/1318.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.613ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1318.svg">. This passage is constantly required, as in
the last line but one of the above proof. It will be indicated merely
by the reference "*10·11·21," and the two steps which it requires will
not be separately put down.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (z).\phi z\supset\psi z:\phi x:\supset.\psi x \quad[\text{*10·1. Imp}]\)" src="images/1327.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.302ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1327.svg"></p>

<p>This is one form of the syllogism in Barbara. <i>E.g.</i> put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi z.=.z\)" src="images/1328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.225ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1328.svg">
is a man, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi z.=.z\)" src="images/1329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.349ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1329.svg"> is mortal, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_326"> = Socrates. Then the
proposition becomes:</p>

<p>"If all men are mortal, and Socrates is a man, then Socrates is mortal."</p>

<p>Another form of the syllogism in Barbara is given in <a href="#_10_3" class="pginternal">*10·3</a>. The two
forms, formerly wrongly identified, were first distinguished by Peano
and Frege.</p>

method, the proof is as follows.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*3·26}. &amp;\supset\vdash:p.\phi x.\supset.p:\\ [\text{*10·11}] &amp;\supset\vdash:(x):p.\phi x.\supset.p:\\ [\text{*10·23}] &amp;\supset\vdash:(\exists x).p.\phi x.\supset.p &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*3·27}. &amp;\supset\vdash:p.\phi x.\supset.\phi x:\\ [\text{*10·11}] &amp;\supset\vdash:(x):p.\phi x.\supset.\phi x:\\ [\text{*10·28}] &amp;\supset\vdash:(\exists x).p.\phi x.\supset.(\exists x).\phi x &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*3·2}. &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp p.\supset:\phi x.\supset.p.\phi x.\\ [\text{*10·11·21}] \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp p.&amp;\supset:(x):\phi x.\supset.p.\phi x:\\ [\text{*10·28}] &amp;\supset:(\exists x).\phi x.\supset.(\exists x).p.\phi x &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).(3).Imp}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1355.svg" style="vertical-align: -14.819ex; width: 65.059ex; height: 30.769ex;" id="img_images_1355.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·36.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists x).\phi x\lor p.\equiv:(\exists x).\phi x.\lor .p\)" src="images/1356.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.651ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1356.svg"></p>

proof is as follows.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*4·64} &amp;\supset\vdash:\phi x\lor p.\equiv.{\sim}\phi x\supset p:\\ [\text{*10·11}]     &amp;\supset\vdash:(x):\phi x\lor p.\equiv.{\sim}\phi x\supset p:\\ [\text{*10·281}]    \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists x).\phi x\lor p.&amp;\equiv:(\exists x).{\sim}\phi x\supset p:\\ [\text{*10·34}]  &amp;\equiv:(x).{\sim}\phi x.\supset.p:\\ [\text{*4·6.(*10·01)}]  &amp;\equiv:(\exists x).\phi x.\lor .p\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1357.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 58.185ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_1357.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition is only required in order to lead to the
following:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·37.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists x).p\supset\phi x.\equiv:p.\supset.(\exists x).\phi x \quad\left[\text{*10·36}\, \frac{{\sim}p}{p}\right]\)" src="images/1358.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.469ex; width: 46.888ex; height: 4.07ex;" id="img_images_1358.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_39">*10·39</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x\supset_{x}\chi x:\psi x\supset_{x}\theta x:\supset:\phi x.\psi x.\supset_{x}.\chi x.\theta x\)" src="images/1359.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 45.633ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1359.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·22}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset:(x):\phi x\supset\chi x.\psi x\supset\theta x:\\ [\text{*3·47.*10·27}]  &amp;\supset:(x):\phi x.\psi x.\supset.\chi x.\theta x\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1360.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 51.434ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_1360.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is only true when the conclusion is significant; the
significance of the hypothesis does not insure that of the conclusion.
On the conditions of significance, see the remarks on <a href="#_10_4" class="pginternal">*10·4</a>, below.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_4">*10·4</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x\equiv_{x}\chi x.\psi x\equiv_{x}\theta x.\supset:\phi x.\psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x.\theta x\)" src="images/1361.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 44.501ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1361.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·22}. &amp; \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset:\phi x\supset_{x}\chi x.\psi x\supset_{x}\theta x:\\ [\text{*10·39}]  &amp;\supset:\phi x.\psi x.\supset_{x}.\chi x.\theta x &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \text{Similarly}  &amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset:\chi x.\theta x.\supset_{x}.\phi x.\psi x &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).Comp}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset:\phi x.\psi x.\supset_{x}.\chi x.\theta x:\chi x.\theta x.\supset_{x}.\phi x.\psi x:\\ [\text{*10·22}]  &amp;\qquad\qquad\supset:\phi x.\psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x.\theta x\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1362.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 77.907ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_1362.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_154">[Pg 154]</span></p>

<p>In <a href="#_10_4" class="pginternal">*10·4</a> and many later propositions, as in <a href="#_10_39" class="pginternal">*10·39</a>, the conclusion may
be not significant when the hypothesis is true. Hence, in order that it
may be legitimate to use *10·4 in <i>inference</i>, <i>i.e.</i> to pass
from the <i>assertion</i> of the hypothesis to the <i>assertion</i> of
the conclusion, the functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_55">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_21">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_6">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_2">
must be such as to have overlapping ranges of significance. In virtue
of <a href="#_10_221" class="pginternal">*10·221</a>, this is secured if they are of the forms <img alt="" data-tex="\(F\{x, \chi(x, \hat{y}, \hat{z}, ...)\}\)" src="images/1363.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.925ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1363.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{x, \chi (x, \hat{y}, \hat{z},\ldots)\}\)" src="images/1364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.108ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1364.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(G\{x, \chi (x, \hat{y}, \hat{z}, \ldots)\}\)" src="images/1365.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.642ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1365.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(g\{x, \chi (x, \hat{y}, \hat{z}, \ldots)\}\)" src="images/1366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.943ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1366.svg">.
It is also secured if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_56"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_22"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_57"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_3">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_23"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_4"> are of such forms,
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_58"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_9"> must have overlapping ranges of significance
if the hypothesis is to be significant, and so must <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_24"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_5">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_10_41">*10·41</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\lor .(x).\psi x:\supset.(x).\phi x\lor \psi x\)" src="images/1367.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.454ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1367.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·1}. &amp;\supset\vdash:(x).\phi x.\supset.\phi y.\\ [\text{*2·2}] &amp;\qquad\qquad\quad\supset.\phi y\lor \psi y &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*10·1}. &amp;\supset\vdash:(x).\psi x.\supset.\psi y.\\ [\text{*1·3}] &amp;\qquad\qquad\quad\supset.\phi y\lor \psi y &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).*10·13}. &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\supset.\phi y\lor \psi y:(x).\psi x.\supset.\phi y\lor \psi y\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*3·44}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\lor .(x).\psi x:\supset.\phi y\lor \psi y\\ [\text{*10·11·21}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (x).\phi x.\lor .(x).\psi x:\supset.(y).\phi y\lor \psi y\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1368.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.068ex; width: 76.919ex; height: 21.267ex;" id="img_images_1368.svg"></span></p>

<p>Observe that in the above proof the uses of <a href="#_2_2" class="pginternal">*2·2</a> and <a href="#_1_3" class="pginternal">*1·3</a> are only
legitimate if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_19"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi y\)" src="images/208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.581ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_208.svg_1"> have overlapping ranges
of significance, for otherwise, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_104"> is such that there is a
proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_20">, it is such that there is no proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi y\)" src="images/208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.581ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_208.svg_2">,
and conversely.</p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·413}\, \frac{\psi,\,\phi,\,\theta,\,\chi}{\phi,\,\psi,\,\chi,\,\theta}.\text{*10·32}. &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset:\psi x\supset\phi x.\equiv_{x}.\theta     x\supset\chi x &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*10·413.(1).*10·4}. &amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1375.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.685ex; width: 70.771ex; height: 6.501ex;" id="img_images_1375.svg"></span></p>

<p>The propositions *10·413·414 are chiefly used in cases where either
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_10"> is replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_59"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_6"> is replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_25">,
in which case half the hypothesis becomes superfluous, being true by
<a href="#_4_2" class="pginternal">*4·2</a>.</p>

<p>This proposition is very frequently used. It should be contrasted with
<a href="#_10_5" class="pginternal">*10·5</a>, in which we have only an implication, not an equivalence.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .\text{*3·26 . *10·11}. &amp;\supset \vdash : (x) : \phi x . \psi x . \supset . \phi x:\\ [\text{*10·28}]    &amp; \supset \vdash : (\exists x) . \phi x . \psi x . \supset . (\exists x) . \phi x  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .\text{*3·27 . *10·11}. &amp;\supset \colon\ldotp  (x) : \phi x . \psi x . \supset . \psi x :\\ [\text{*10·28}]    &amp; \supset \vdash : (\exists x) . \phi x . \psi x . \supset . (\exists x) . \psi x  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .\text{(1).(2).Comp}. &amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp  \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1381.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 56.149ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_1381.svg"></span></p>

<p>The converse of the above proposition is false. The fact that
this proposition states an implication, while <a href="#_10_42" class="pginternal">*10·42</a> states an
equivalence, is the source of many subsequent differences between
formulae concerning logical addition and formulae concerning logical
multiplication.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*10·542.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \phi y.\supset_{y}.p\supset\psi y:\equiv:p.\supset.\phi y\supset_{y}\psi y \quad\left[\text{*10·541}\, \frac{{\sim}p}{p}\right]\)" src="images/1390.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.469ex; width: 51.159ex; height: 4.07ex;" id="img_images_1390.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_157">[Pg 157]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_11">*11. THEORY OF TWO APPARENT VARIABLES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *11.</p>

<p>In this number, the propositions proved for one variable in *10 are to
be extended to two variables, with the addition of a few propositions
having no analogues for one variable, such as *11·2·21·23·24 and
*11·53·55·6·7. "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_8">" stands for a proposition containing
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_327"> and containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_105">; when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_328"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_106"> are unassigned,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_9"> is a propositional function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_329"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_107">. The
definition <a href="#_11_01" class="pginternal">*11·01</a> shows that "the truth of all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_10">"
does not need to be taken as a new primitive idea, but is definable
in terms of "the truth of all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_30">." The reason is
that, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_330"> is assigned, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_11"> becomes a function of one
variable, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_108">, whence it follows that, for every possible
value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_331">, "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.512ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1397.svg">" embodies merely the primitive idea
introduced in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>. But "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.512ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1397.svg_1">" is again only a function of
one variable, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_332">, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_109"> has here become an apparent
variable. Hence the definition *11·01 below is legitimate. We put:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_11_01">*11·01</a>.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y).\phi(x,y).=:(x):(y).\phi(x,y) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.851ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1398.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·02.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y,z).\phi(x,y,z).=:(x):(y,z).\phi(x,y,z) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.084ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1399.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·03.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x,y).\phi(x,y).=:(\exists x):(\exists y).\phi(x,y) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.625ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1400.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·04.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x,y,z).\phi(x,y,z).=:(\exists x):(\exists y,z).\phi(x,y,z) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.857ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1401.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·05.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y) .\supset_{x,y}. \psi(x,y) :=: (x,y):\phi(x,y) .\supset. \psi(x,y) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1402.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 52.207ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1402.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·06.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y) .\equiv_{x,y}. \psi(x,y) :=: (x,y):\phi(x,y) .\equiv. \psi(x,y) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1403.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 52.207ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1403.svg"></p>

<p>All the above definitions are supposed extended to any number of
variables that may occur.</p>

<p>The propositions of this section can all be extended to any finite
number of variables; as the analogy is exact, it is not necessary to
carry the process beyond two variables in our proofs.</p>

<p>In addition to the definition <a href="#_11_01" class="pginternal">*11·01</a>, we need the primitive proposition
that "whatever possible argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_333"> may be, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_12"> is true
whatever possible argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_110"> may be" implies the corresponding
statement with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_334"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_111"> interchanged. Either may be taken as the
meaning of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_13"> is true whatever possible arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_335"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_112"> may be."</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_158">[Pg 158]</span></p>

<p>The propositions of the present number are somewhat less used than
those of <a href="#_10" class="pginternal">*10</a>, but some of them are used frequently. Such are the
following:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(x,y)\ldotp\phi (x,y)\ldotp \supset .\phi (z,w)\)" src="images/1404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.891ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1404.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_11_11">*11·11</a>.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\( \phi (z,w) \)" src="images/1405.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.787ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1405.svg"> is true whatever possible arguments
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_16"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_11"> may be, then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y)\ldotp\phi (x,y)\)" src="images/1406.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.812ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1406.svg"> is true.</p>

<p>These two propositions are the analogues of *10·1·11.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :(x,y)\ldotp\phi (x,y)\ldotp\equiv \ldotp(y,x)\ldotp\phi (x,y)\)" src="images/1407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.797ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1407.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> to say that "for all possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_336">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_14">
is true for all possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_113">" is equivalent to
saying "for all possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_114">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (x,y)\)" src="images/1408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1408.svg"> is true for
all possible values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_337">."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon \ldotp p \ldotp\supset \ldotp (x,y)\ldotp\phi (x,y):\equiv :(x,y):p\ldotp\supset \ldotp\phi (x,y)\)" src="images/1409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.754ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1409.svg"></p>

<p>This is the analogue of <a href="#_10_21" class="pginternal">*10·21</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon \ldotp (x,y):\phi (x,y).\supset \ldotp\psi (x,y):\supset:(x,y)\ldotp\phi (x,y)\ldotp\supset\ldotp (x,y)\ldotp\psi (x,y)\)" src="images/1410.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.937ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1410.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (x,y)\)" src="images/1408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1408.svg_1"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi (x,y)\)" src="images/1411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.642ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1411.svg">, then
'<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (x,y)\)" src="images/1408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1408.svg_2"> always' implies '<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi(x,y)\)" src="images/1412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.642ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1412.svg"> always.'" This is the
analogue of <a href="#_10_21" class="pginternal">*10·21</a>. *11·33·34·341 are respectively the analogues of
*10·271·28·281, and are also much used.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon \ldotp (x,y)\colon \phi (x,y)\ldotp\supset\ldotp p\colon\equiv\colon (\exists x,y)\ldotp \phi(x,y)\ldotp\supset\ldotp p\)" src="images/1413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.63ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1413.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi (x,y)\)" src="images/1408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1408.svg_3"> always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_275">, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_15">
is ever true, <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_276"> is true. This is the analogue of <a href="#_10_23" class="pginternal">*10·23</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·45.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp (\exists x,y)\colon p\ldotp \phi (x,y)\colon \equiv\colon p\colon (\exists x,y)\ldotp \phi (x,y)\)" src="images/1414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.355ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1414.svg"></p>

<p>This is the analogue of <a href="#_10_35" class="pginternal">*10·35</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·54.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists x,y)\ldotp\phi x\ldotp\psi y\ldotp \equiv\colon (\exists x)\ldotp\phi x\colon (\exists y).\psi y\)" src="images/1415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.511ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1415.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is useful because it analyses a proposition containing
two apparent variables into two propositions which each contain only
one. "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\ldotp\psi y\)" src="images/1416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.23ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1416.svg">" is a function of two variables, but is
compounded of two functions of one variable each. Such a function
is like a conic which is two straight lines: it may be called an
"analysable" function.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists x,y)\ldotp \phi x\ldotp \psi (x,y)\ldotp \equiv\colon (\exists x)\colon \phi x\colon (\exists y).\psi (x,y)\)" src="images/1417.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.631ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1417.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> to say "there are values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_338"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_115"> for which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\ldotp \psi (x,y)\)" src="images/1418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.29ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1418.svg"> is true" is equivalent to saying "there is
a value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_339"> for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_102"> is true and for which there is a
value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_116"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi (x,y)\)" src="images/1411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.642ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1411.svg_1"> is true."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·6.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\colon (\exists x)\colon\ldotp (\exists y)\ldotp \phi (x,y)\ldotp \psi y\colon\chi x\colon\ldotp\equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists y)\colon\ldotp (\exists x)\ldotp \phi (x,y)\ldotp \chi x\colon \psi y\)" src="images/1419.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.735ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1419.svg"></p>

<p>This gives a transformation which is useful in many proofs.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·62.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\colon\phi x\ldotp \psi (x,y)\ldotp \supset_{x,y}\ldotp \chi (x,y)\colon\equiv\colon\ldotp\phi x\ldotp\supset_{x}\colon\psi (x,y)\ldotp \supset_{y}.\chi(x,y)\)" src="images/1420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 56.641ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1420.svg"></p>

<p>This transformation also is often useful.</p>

<b>*11·04.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x,y,z).\phi(x,y,z).=:(\exists x):(\exists y,z).\phi(x,y,z) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.857ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1424.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·05.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y).\supset_{x,y}.\psi(x,y):=:(x,y):\phi(x,y).\supset.\psi(x,y) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 52.207ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1425.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·06.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi(x,y):=:(x,y):\phi(x,y).\equiv.\psi(x,y) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 52.207ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1426.svg"></p>

<p>with similar definitions for any number of variables.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_11_07">*11·07</a>.</b> "Whatever possible argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_340"> may be, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_16"> is true
whatever possible argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_117"> may be" implies the corresponding
statement with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_341"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_118"> interchanged. Pp.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(x,y).\phi(x,y).\supset.\phi(z,w)\)" src="images/1427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.891ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1427.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·1}.\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset.(y).\phi(z,y).\\ [\text{*10·1}] \supset.\phi(z,w):&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1428.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 33.658ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_1428.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·11.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_17"> is true whatever possible arguments
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_17"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_12"> may be, then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.812ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1429.svg"> is true.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p>By <a href="#_10_11" class="pginternal">*10·11</a>, the hypothesis implies that (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).\phi(z,y)\)" src="images/1430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.27ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1430.svg"> is true
whatever possible argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_18"> may be; and this, by *10·11, implies
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.812ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1429.svg_1">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp(x,y).p\lor\phi(x,y).\supset:p.\lor.(x,y).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.114ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1431.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{10·12}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp(y).p\lor\phi(x,y). &amp;\supset:p.\lor.(y).\phi(x,y)\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*10·11·27}]\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp(x,y).p\lor\phi(x,y).&amp;\supset:(x):p.\lor.(y).\phi(x,y):\\ [\text{*10·12}] &amp;\supset:p.\lor.(x,y).\phi(x,y)\colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1432.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 66.8ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_1432.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is only used for proving <a href="#_11_2" class="pginternal">*11·2</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_11_13">*11·13</a>.</b> If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1241.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1241.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.642ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1433.svg">
take their first and second arguments respectively of the same type,
and we have "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.906ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1434.svg">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\psi(x,y)\)" src="images/1435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.03ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1435.svg">," we shall
have "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\phi(x,y).\psi(x,y)\)" src="images/1436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.554ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1436.svg">." [Proof as in <a href="#_10_13" class="pginternal">*10·13</a>]</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_11_14">*11·14</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp(x,y).\phi(x,y):(x,y).\psi(x,y):\supset:\phi(z,w).\psi(z,w)\)" src="images/1437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.768ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1437.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·14}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset:(y).\phi(z,y):(y).\psi(z,y)\\ [\text{*10·14}] &amp;\supset:\phi(z,w).\psi(z,w)\colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1438.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 49.379ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_1438.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_160">[Pg 160]</span></p>

<p>This proposition, like <a href="#_10_14" class="pginternal">*10·14</a>, is not always significant when its
hypothesis is true. <a href="#_11_13" class="pginternal">*11·13</a>, on the contrary, is always significant
when its hypothesis is true. For this reason, *11·13 may always be
safely used in <i>inference</i>, whereas <a href="#_11_14" class="pginternal">*11·14</a> can only be used
in <i>inference</i> (<i>i.e.</i> for the actual assertion of the
conclusion when the hypothesis is asserted) if it is known that the
conclusion is significant.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_11_2">*11·2</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(x,y).\phi(x,y).\equiv.(y,x).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.797ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1439.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{11·1}. \supset\vdash:(x,y).\phi(x,y).&amp;\supset.\phi(z,w) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*11·07·11}. \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp(w,z):(x,y).\phi(x,y).&amp;\supset.\phi(z,w) &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).*11·12}. \frac{{\sim}\{(x,y).\phi(x,y)\}}{p} .\supset\\ &amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp(x,y).\phi(x,y).\supset.(w,z).\phi(z,w) &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \text{Similarly} &amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp(w,z).\phi(z,w).\supset.(x,y).\phi(x,y) &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(3).(4)}. \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1440.svg" style="vertical-align: -9.083ex; width: 86.922ex; height: 19.297ex;" id="img_images_1440.svg"></span></p>

<p>Note that "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(w,z).\phi(z,w)\)" src="images/1441.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.351ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1441.svg">" is the same proposition as
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\(y,x).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.812ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1442.svg">"; a proposition is not a function of any apparent
variable which occurs in it.</p>
