<p class="nind">
<b>*11·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:{\sim}\{(\exists x,y).\phi(x,y)\}.\equiv.(x,y).{\sim}\phi(x,y) \quad[\text{*11·22.Transp}]\)" src="images/1451.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.331ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1451.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_161">[Pg 161]</span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*11·26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp(\exists x):(y).\phi(x,y):\supset:(y):(\exists x).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.85ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1452.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*10·1·28}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp(\exists x):(y).\phi(x,y):\supset:(\exists x).\phi(x,y) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*10·11·21}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1453.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 58.974ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_1453.svg"></span></p>

<p>Note that the converse of this proposition is false. <i>E.g.</i> let
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_18"> be the propositional function "if <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_119"> is a proper fraction,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_342"> is a proper fraction greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_120">." Then for all
values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_121"> we have (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1454.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.956ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1454.svg">, so that (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y):(\exists x).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.71ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1455.svg">
is satisfied. In fact "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(y):(\exists x).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.71ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1455.svg_1">"
expresses the proposition: "If <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_122"> is a proper fraction, then there
is always a proper fraction greater than <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_123">." But "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x):(y).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.71ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1456.svg">"
expresses the proposition: "There is a proper fraction which is greater
than any proper fraction," which is false.</p>

variables. The more important of these are proved in what follows.</p>

<p>The proofs of most of the following propositions are conducted exactly
as those of *11·3·31 are conducted: the analogous proposition in <a href="#_10" class="pginternal">*10</a> is
used<span class="pagenum" id="Page_162">[Pg 162]</span> twice, together with <a href="#_10_27" class="pginternal">*10·27</a> or <a href="#_10_271" class="pginternal">*10·271</a> or <a href="#_10_28" class="pginternal">*10·28</a> or <a href="#_10_281" class="pginternal">*10·281</a> as
the case may be. When proofs conform to this pattern we shall merely
give references to the propositions used.</p>

<p>In the last line of the above proof, use is made of the fact that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists x,y).\phi(x,y)\, \text{and}\, (\exists y,x).\phi(y,x) \]" src="images/1520.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.303ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1520.svg"></span>

<p>The first use of the following proposition occurs in the proof of
*234·12. Its utility lies in its enabling us to pass from a hypothesis
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi z.\chi w.\supset_{z,w}.\psi z.\theta w, \]" src="images/1521.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 19.578ex; height: 2.245ex;" id="img_images_1521.svg"></span>
containing two apparent variables, to the product of two hypotheses
each containing only one.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_168">[Pg 168]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_12">*12. THE HIERARCHY OF TYPES AND THE AXIOM OF REDUCIBILITY.</h2>
</div>


<p>The primitive idea "<img alt="" data-tex="\((x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_542.svg_3">" has been explained to mean
"<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_64"> is always true," <i>i.e.</i> "all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_65">
are true." But whatever function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_61"> may be, there will be
arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_343"> with which <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_66"> is meaningless, <i>i.e.</i> with
which as arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_62"> does not have any value. The arguments
with which <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_67"> has values form what we will call the "range of
significance" of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_68">. A "<i>type</i>" is defined as the range
of significance of some function. In virtue of <a href="#_9_14" class="pginternal">*9·14</a>, if <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_69">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}y\)" src="images/526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_526.svg_2">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}x\)" src="images/245.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_245.svg_5"> are significant, <i>i.e.</i> either true
or false, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}y\)" src="images/456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.581ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_456.svg_2">. From this it follows that two types
which have a common member coincide, and that two different types
are mutually exclusive. Any proposition of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_542.svg_4">,
<i>i.e.</i> any proposition containing an apparent variable, determines
some type as the range of the apparent variable, the type being fixed
by the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_63">.</p>

<p>The division of objects into types is necessitated by the
vicious-circle fallacies which otherwise arise<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_52" id="FNanchor_52">[52]</a>. These fallacies
show that there must be no totalities which, if legitimate, would
contain members defined in terms of themselves. Hence any expression
containing an apparent variable must not be in the range of that
variable, <i>i.e.</i> must belong to a different type. Thus the
apparent variables contained or presupposed in an expression are what
determines its type. This is the guiding principle in what follows.</p>

<p>As explained in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>, propositions containing variables are generated
from propositional functions which do not contain these apparent
variables, by the process of asserting all or some values of such
functions. Suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}a\)" src="images/145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_145.svg_2"> is a proposition containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_83">;
we will give the name of <i>generalization</i> to the process which
turns <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}a\)" src="images/145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_145.svg_3"> into <img alt="" data-tex="\((x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.703ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_542.svg_5"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\((\exists x).{\phi}x\)" src="images/1524.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.961ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1524.svg">,
and we will give the name of <i>generalized propositions</i> to all
such as contain apparent variables. It is plain that propositions
containing apparent variables presuppose others not containing
apparent variables, from which they can be derived by generalization.
Propositions which contain no apparent variables we call <i>elementary
propositions</i><a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_53" id="FNanchor_53">[53]</a>, and the terms of such propositions, other than
functions, we call <i>individuals</i>. Then individuals form the first
type.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_169">[Pg 169]</span></p>

<p>It is unnecessary, in practice, to know what objects belong to the
lowest type, or even whether the lowest type of variable occurring
in a given context is that of individuals or some other. For in
practice only the <i>relative</i> types of variables are relevant;
thus the lowest type occurring in a given context may be called that
of individuals, so far as that context is concerned. It follows that
the above account of individuals is not essential to the truth of what
follows; all that is essential is the way in which other types are
generated from individuals, however the type of individuals may be
constituted.</p>

<p>By applying the process of generalization to individuals occurring in
elementary propositions, we obtain new propositions. The legitimacy of
this process requires only that no individuals should be propositions.
That this is so, is to be secured by the meaning we give to the word
<i>individual</i>. We may explain an individual as something which
exists on its own account; it is then obviously not a proposition,
since propositions, as explained in Chapter II of the Introduction (<a href="#Page_46" class="pginternal">p. 46</a>),
are incomplete symbols, having no meaning except in use. Hence in
applying the process of generalization to individuals we run no risk of
incurring reflexive fallacies. We will give the name of <i>first-order
propositions</i> to such as contain one or more apparent variables
whose possible values are individuals, but contain no other apparent
variables. First-order propositions are not all of the same type,
since, as was explained in <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>, two propositions which do not contain
the same number of apparent variables cannot be of the same type. But
owing to the systematic ambiguity of negation and disjunction, their
differences of type may usually be ignored in practice. No reflexive
fallacies will result, since no first-order proposition involves any
totality except that of individuals.</p>

<p>Let us denote by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{x}\)" src="images/1525.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1525.svg">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.146ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1526.svg">"
or etc. an elementary function whose argument or arguments are
individual. We will call such a function a <i>predicative function of
an individual</i>. Such functions, together with those derived from
them by generalization, will be called <i>first-order functions</i>. In
practice we may without risk of reflexive fallacies treat first-order
functions as a type, since the only totality they involve is that of
individuals, and, by means of the systematic ambiguity of negation
and disjunction, any function of a first-order function which will
concern us will be significant whatever first-order function is taken
as argument, provided the right meanings are given to the negations and
disjunctions involved.</p>

<p>For the sake of clearness, we will repeat in somewhat different terms
our account of what is meant by a first-order function. Let us give
the name of <i>matrix</i> to any function, of however many variables,
which does not involve any apparent variables. Then any possible
function other than a matrix is derived from a matrix by means of
generalization, <i>i.e.</i> by considering the proposition which
asserts that the function in question is true with all<span class="pagenum" id="Page_170">[Pg 170]</span> possible values
or with some value of one of the arguments, the other argument or
arguments remaining undetermined. Thus <i>e.g.</i> from the function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_19"> we shall be able to derive the four functions
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x).\phi(x,y),\quad (\exists x).\phi(x,y),\quad (y).\phi(x,y),\quad (\exists y).\phi(x,y), \]" src="images/1527.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.89ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1527.svg"></span>
of which the two first are functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_124">, while the two last are
functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_344">. (All <i>propositions</i>, with the exception of
such as are values of matrices, are also derived from matrices by the
above process of generalization. In order to obtain a proposition from
a matrix containing <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_36"> variables, without assigning values to any of
the variables, it is necessary to turn all the variables into apparent
variables. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/256.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_256.svg_20"> is a matrix, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y).\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.812ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1429.svg_2"> is
a proposition.) We will give the name <i>first-order matrices</i> to
such as have only individuals for their arguments, and we will give the
name of <i>first-order functions</i> (of any number of variables) to
such as either are first-order matrices or are derived from first-order
matrices by generalization applied to some (not all) of the arguments
to such matrices. First-order <i>propositions</i> will be such as
result from applying generalization to <i>all</i> the arguments to a
first-order matrix.</p>

<p>As we have already stated, the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg">" is used
for any elementary function of one variable. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!x\)" src="images/1529.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1529.svg">"
represents any value of any elementary function of one variable. It
will be seen that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!x\)" src="images/1529.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1529.svg_1">" is a function of two variables, namely
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_345">. Since it contains no apparent variable, it
is a matrix, but since it contains a variable (namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z})\)" src="images/1530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.91ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1530.svg">
which is not an individual, it is not a first-order matrix. The same
applies to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!a\)" src="images/1531.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.174ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1531.svg">, where a is some definite constant. We can build
up a number of new matrices, such as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{split} {\sim} \phi!a,\quad {\sim} \phi!x,\quad \phi!x\lor \phi!y,\quad \phi!x\lor \psi!x,\quad \phi!x\lor\psi!y,\\ \phi!x.\supset.\psi!x,\quad \phi!x.\psi!x,\quad \phi!x\lor\psi!y\lor\chi!z,\quad\text{ and so on.} \end{split} \]" src="images/1532.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 52.912ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1532.svg"></span>
All these are matrices which involve first-order functions among their
arguments. Such matrices we will call <i>second-order matrices</i>.
From these matrices, by applying generalization to their arguments,
whether to such as are functions or to such (if any) as are
individuals, we obtain new functions and propositions. Such functions
(together with second-order matrices) will be called <i>second-order
functions</i>, and such propositions will be called <i>second-order
propositions</i>. Thus we are led to the following definitions:</p>

<p>A <i>second-order matrix</i> is one which has at least one first-order
matrix among its arguments, but has no arguments other than first-order
matrices and individuals.</p>

<p>A <i>second-order function</i> is one which either is a second-order
matrix or results from one by applying generalization to some (not all)
of the arguments to a second-order matrix.</p>

<p>A <i>second-order proposition</i> is one which results from a
second-order matrix by applying generalization to all its arguments.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_171">[Pg 171]</span></p>

<p>In addition to the above illustrations of second-order matrices, we may
give the following examples of second-order functions:</p>

<p>(1) Functions in which the argument is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}: (x).\phi!x\)" src="images/1533.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.247ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1533.svg">,
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x).\phi!x\)" src="images/1534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.71ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1534.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!a.\supset.\phi!b\)" src="images/1535.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.894ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1535.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_84"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_22"> are constants, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!x.\supset_{x}.g!x\)" src="images/1536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.149ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1536.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(g!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.76ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1537.svg"> is
a constant function, and so on.</p>

<p>(2) Functions in which the arguments are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_2"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_611.svg_2">:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi!x.\supset_{x}.\psi!x,\quad \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi!x,\quad (\exists x).\phi x.\psi x,\quad \phi!a.\supset.\psi!b, \]" src="images/1538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 55.272ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1538.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_85"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_23"> are constants, and so on.</p>

<p>(3) Functions in which the argument is an individual
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x: (\phi).\phi!x\)" src="images/1539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.566ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1539.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists \phi).\phi!x\)" src="images/1540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.764ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1540.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!x.\supset_{\phi}.\phi!a\)" src="images/1541.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 11.359ex; height: 2.287ex;" id="img_images_1541.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_86"> is constant, and so on.</p>

<p>(4) Functions in which the arguments are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x:\phi!x\)" src="images/1542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.451ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1542.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!x.\supset.\phi!a\)" src="images/1543.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.218ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1543.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_87"> is constant,
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists \psi):\phi!x.\equiv.\psi!x\)" src="images/1544.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.936ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1544.svg"> and so on.</p>

<p>Examples of second-order functions might, of course, be multiplied
indefinitely, but the above seem sufficient for purposes of
illustration.</p>

<p>A second-order matrix of one variable will be called a <i>predicative
second-order function of one variable</i> or a <i>predicative function
of a first-order matrix</i>. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!a\)" src="images/1531.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.174ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1531.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\phi!a\)" src="images/1545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.934ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1545.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!a\supset\phi!b\)" src="images/1546.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.139ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1546.svg"> are predicative functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_4">.
Similarly a function of several variables of which at least one
is a first-order matrix, while the rest are either individuals or
first-order matrices, will be called <i>predicative</i> if it is a
matrix.</p>

<p>It will be seen, however, that a second-order function may have only
individuals for its arguments; instances were given just now under
the heading (3). Such functions we shall not call predicative, since
predicative functions of individuals have already been defined as
being such as are of the first order. Thus the order of a function is
not determined by the order of its argument or arguments; indeed, the
function may be of any order superior to the order or orders of its
arguments.</p>

<p>A variable matrix whose argument is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_5"> will be denoted
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(f!\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1547.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.903ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1547.svg">, and generally, a matrix whose arguments are
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_6">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_611.svg_3">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_346">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_125">, ... (where there
is at least one function among the arguments) will be denoted by
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f!(\phi!\hat{z}, \psi!\hat{z}, ... x, y, ...). \]" src="images/1548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.909ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1548.svg"></span>
Such a matrix is not of the first or second order, since it contains
the new variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_11"> whose values are second-order matrices.
We proceed to construct new matrices as we did with the matrix
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{x}\)" src="images/1525.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1525.svg_1">; these constitute <i>third-order matrices</i>. These
together with the functions derived from them by generalization are
called <i>third-order functions</i>, and the propositions derived
from third-order matrices by generalization are called <i>third-order
propositions</i>.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_172">[Pg 172]</span></p>

<p>In this way we can proceed indefinitely to matrices, functions and
propositions of higher and higher orders. We introduce the following
definition:</p>

<p>A function is said to be <i>predicative</i> when it is a matrix. It
will be observed that, in a hierarchy in which all the variables are
individuals or matrices, a matrix is the same thing as an elementary
function (cf. <a href="#Page_132" class="pginternal">pp. 132</a>, <a href="#Page_133" class="pginternal">133</a>).</p>

<p>"Matrix" or "predicative function" is a primitive idea.</p>

<p>The fact that a function is predicative is indicated, as above, by a
note of exclamation after the functional letter.</p>

<p>The variables occurring in the present work, from this point onwards,
will all be either individuals or matrices of some order in the above
hierarchy. Propositions, which have occurred hitherto as variables,
will no longer do so except in a few isolated cases of which no
subsequent use is made. In practice, for the reasons explained on <a href="#Page_169" class="pginternal">p. 169</a>,
a function of a matrix may be regarded as capable of any argument
which is a function of the same order and takes arguments of the same
type.</p>

<p>In practice, we never need to know the absolute types of our variables,
but only their <i>relative</i> types. That is to say, if we prove
any proposition on the assumption that one of our variables is an
individual, and another is a function of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_37">, the proof will
still hold if, in place of an individual, we take a function of order
<img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_7">, and in place of our function of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_38"> we take a function
of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n + m\)" src="images/1549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.11ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_1549.svg">, with corresponding changes for any other variables
that may be involved. This results from the assumption that our
primitive propositions are to apply to variables of any order.</p>

<p>We shall use small Latin letters (other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_277">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_185">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_46">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(s)\)" src="images/1550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 1.941ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1550.svg"> for variables of the lowest type concerned in any context. For
functions, we shall use the letters <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_64">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_27">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_11">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_7">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_12">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(g\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.079ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(F\)" src="images/45.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.695ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_45.svg_3"> (except that, at a later stage, <img alt="" data-tex="\(F\)" src="images/45.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.695ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_45.svg_4">
will be defined as a constant relation, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_8"> will be defined
as the order-type of the continuum).</p>

<p>We shall explain later a different hierarchy, that of classes and
relations, which is derived from the functional hierarchy explained
above, but is more convenient in practice.</p>

<p>When any predicative function, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_7">, occurs as
apparent variable, it would be strictly more correct to indicate the
fact by placing "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z})\)" src="images/1530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.91ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1530.svg_1">" before what follows, as thus:
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}).f(\phi!\hat{z})\)" src="images/1551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.949ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1551.svg">." But for the sake of brevity we
write simply "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi)\)" src="images/1552.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 2.229ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1552.svg">" instead of "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z})\\)" src="images/1553.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.475ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1553.svg">." Since what
follows the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_65"> in brackets must always contain <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_66"> with
arguments supplied, no confusion can result from this practice.</p>

<p>It should be observed that, in virtue of the manner in which our
hierarchy of functions was generated, non-predicative functions always
result from such as are predicative by means of generalization. Hence
it is unnecessary to introduce a special notation for non-predicative
functions of a given order<span class="pagenum" id="Page_173">[Pg 173]</span> and taking arguments of a given order.
For example, second-order functions of an individual <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_347"> are always
derived by generalization from a matrix
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f!(\phi!\hat{z},\, \psi!\hat{z},\, \ldots x,\, y,\, z,\, ...), \]" src="images/1554.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.867ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1554.svg"></span>
where the functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_13">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_67">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_28">, ... are predicative. It
is possible, therefore, without loss of generality, to use no apparent
variables except such as are predicative.</p>

<p>We require, however, a means of symbolising a function whose order is
not assigned. We shall use "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_103">" or "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\chi!\hat{z})\)" src="images/1555.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.102ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1555.svg">" or
etc. to express a function (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_68"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_14">) whose order, relatively
to its argument, is not given. Such a function cannot be made into an
apparent variable, unless we suppose its order previously fixed. As the
only purpose of the notation is to avoid the necessity of fixing the
order, such a function will not be used as an apparent variable; the
only functions which will be so used will be predicative functions,
because, as we have just seen, this restriction involves no loss of
generality.</p>

<p>We have now to state and explain the <i>axiom of reducibility</i>.</p>

<p>It is important to observe that, since there are various types of
propositions and functions, and since generalization can only be
applied within some one type (or, by means of systematic ambiguity,
within some well-defined and completed set of types), all phrases
referring to "all propositions" or "all functions," or to "some
(undetermined) proposition" or "some (undetermined) function," are
<i>prima facie</i> meaningless, though in certain cases they are
capable of an unobjectionable interpretation. Contradictions arise from
the use of such phrases in cases where no innocent meaning can be found.</p>

<p>If mathematics is to be possible, it is absolutely necessary (as
explained in the Introduction, <a href="#CHAPTER_II" class="pginternal">Chapter II</a>) that we should have some
method of making statements which will usually be equivalent to what
we have in mind when we (inaccurately) speak of "all properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_348">." (A "property of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_349">" may be defined as a propositional
function satisfied by <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_350">.) Hence we must find, if possible, some
method of reducing the order of a propositional function without
affecting the truth or falsehood of its values. This seems to be what
common-sense effects by the admission of <i>classes</i>. Given any
propositional function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_31"> of whatever order, this is assumed
to be equivalent, for all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_351">, to a statement of the form
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_352"> belongs to the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_73">." Now assuming that there is
such an entity as the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_74">, this statement is of the first
order, since it involves no allusion to a variable function. Indeed
its only practical advantage over the original statement <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_32">
is that it is of the first order. There is no advantage in assuming
that there really are such things as classes, and the contradiction
about the classes which are not members of themselves shows that, if
there are classes, they must be something radically different from
individuals. It would seem that the sole purpose which classes serve,
and one main reason which makes them linguistically convenient, is<span class="pagenum" id="Page_174">[Pg 174]</span>
that they provide a method of reducing the order of a propositional
function. We shall, therefore, not assume anything of what may seem to
be involved in the common-sense admission of classes, except this, that
every propositional function is equivalent, for all its values, to some
predicative function of the same argument or arguments.</p>

<p>This assumption with regard to functions is to be made whatever may be
the type of their arguments. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(fu\)" src="images/1556.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.538ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1556.svg"> be a function, of any order,
of an argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_8">, which may itself be either an individual or a
function of any order. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_15"> is a matrix, we write the function in
the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(f!u\)" src="images/1557.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.167ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1557.svg">; in such a case we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_16"> a <i>predicative</i>
function. Thus a predicative function of an individual is a first-order
function; and for higher types of arguments, predicative functions take
the place that first-order functions take in respect of individuals. We
assume, then, that every function of one variable is equivalent, for
all its values, to some predicative function of the same argument. This
assumption seems to be the essence of the usual assumption of classes;
at any rate, it retains as much of classes as we have any use for,
and little enough to avoid the contradictions which a less grudging
admission of classes is apt to entail. We will call this assumption the
<i>axiom of classes</i>, or the <i>axiom of reducibility</i>.</p>

<p>We shall assume similarly that every function of two variables is
equivalent, for all its values, to a predicative function of those
variables, <i>i.e.</i> to a matrix. This assumption is what seems to
be meant by saying that any statement about two variables defines
a relation between them. We will call this assumption the <i>axiom
of relations</i> or (like the previous axiom) the <i>axiom of
reducibility</i>.</p>

<p>In dealing with relations between more than two terms, similar
assumptions would be needed for three, four, ... variables. But these
assumptions are not indispensable for our purpose, and are therefore
not made in this work.</p>

<p>Stated in symbols, the two forms of the axiom of reducibility are as
follows:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_12_1">*12·1</a></b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists f):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.f!x\quad\text{Pp}\)" src="images/1558.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.534ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1558.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_12_11">*12·11</a></b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists f):\phi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.f!(x,y)\quad\text{Pp}\)" src="images/1559.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 33.512ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1559.svg"></p>

<p>We call two functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_43">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_7"> formally
equivalent when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x\)" src="images/1560.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.285ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1560.svg">, and similarly we call
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1241.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.517ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1241.svg_4"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.642ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1433.svg_2"> formally
equivalent when
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \phi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi(x,y). \]" src="images/1561.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 19.892ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1561.svg"></span>
Thus the above axioms state that any function of one or two variables
is formally equivalent to some <i>predicative</i> function of one or
two variables, as the case may be.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_175">[Pg 175]</span></p>

<p>Of the above two axioms, the first is chiefly needed in the theory of
classes (<a href="#_20" class="pginternal">*20</a>), and the second in the theory of relations (<a href="#_21" class="pginternal">*21</a>). But the
first is also essential to the theory of identity, if identity is to be
defined (as we have done, in <a href="#_13_01" class="pginternal">*13·01</a>); its use in the theory of identity
is embodied in the proof of <a href="#_13_101" class="pginternal">*13·101</a>, below.</p>

<p>We may sum up what has been said in the present number as follows:</p>

<p>(1) A function of the first order is one which involves no variables
except individuals, whether as apparent variables or as arguments.</p>

<p>(2) A function of the (<img alt="" data-tex="\(n + 1)\)" src="images/1562.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.134ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1562.svg">th order is one which has at least one
argument or apparent variable of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_39">, and contains no argument
or apparent variable which is not either an individual or a first-order
function or a second-order function or ... or a function of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_40">.</p>

<p>(3) A predicative function is one which contains no apparent variables,
<i>i.e.</i> is a matrix. It is possible, without loss of generality, to
use no variables except matrices and individuals, so long as variable
<i>propositions</i> are not required.</p>

<p>(4) Any function of one argument or of two is formally equivalent to a
predicative function of the same argument or arguments.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_176">[Pg 176]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_13">*13. IDENTITY.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *13.</p>

<p>The propositional function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_353"> is identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_126">" will
be written "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x = y\)" src="images/418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_418.svg_1">." We shall find that this use of the sign
of equality covers all the common uses of equality that occur in
mathematics. The definition is as follows:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_13_01">*13·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x = y .=: (\phi):{\phi}!x.\supset. {\phi}!y \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1563.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.251ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1563.svg"></p>

<p>This definition states that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_354"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_127"> are to be called identical
when every predicative function satisfied by <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_355"> is also satisfied by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_128">. We cannot state that <i>every</i> function satisfied by <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_356"> is
to be satisfied by <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_129">, because <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_357"> satisfies functions of various
orders, and these cannot all be covered by one apparent variable.
But in virtue of the axiom of reducibility it follows that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x = y\)" src="images/418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_418.svg_2">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_358"> satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}x\)" src="images/245.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_245.svg_6">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_29"> is any function,
predicative or non-predicative, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_130"> also satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}y\)" src="images/456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.581ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_456.svg_3">
(cf. <a href="#_13_101" class="pginternal">*13·101</a>, below). Hence in effect the definition is as powerful as
it would be if it could be extended to cover <i>all</i> functions of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_359">.</p>

<p>Note that the second sign of equality in the above definition is
combined with "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Df}\)" src="images/1564.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.421ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_1564.svg">," and thus is not really the same symbol
as the sign of equality which is defined. Thus the definition is not
circular, although at first sight it appears so.</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number are constantly referred to. Most
of them are self-evident, and the proofs offer no difficulty. The most
important of the propositions of this number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_13_101">*13·101</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : x = y .\supset. {\psi}x \supset {\psi}y\)" src="images/1565.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 20.197ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1565.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_360"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_131"> are identical, any property of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_361"> is
a property of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_132">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_13_12">*13·12</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : x = y .\supset. {\psi}x \equiv {\psi}y\)" src="images/1566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 20.197ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1566.svg"></p>

<p>This includes <a href="#_13_101" class="pginternal">*13·101</a> together with the fact that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_362"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_133">
are identical any property of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_134"> is a property of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_363">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·15·16·17</b>, which state that identity is reflexive, symmetrical and transitive.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·191.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp y = x .\supset_{y}. {\phi}y :\equiv. {\phi}x\)" src="images/1567.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 22.681ex; height: 2.237ex;" id="img_images_1567.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_177">[Pg 177]</span></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> to state that everything that is identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_364"> has a
certain property is equivalent to stating that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_365"> has that property.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·195.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists y).y=x.\phi y.\equiv.\phi x\)" src="images/1568.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.07ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1568.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> to state that something identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_366"> has a certain
property is equivalent to saying that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_367"> has that property.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists z,w).z=x.w=y.\phi(z,w).\equiv.\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1569.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.539ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1569.svg"></p>

<p>This is the analogue of <a href="#_13_195" class="pginternal">*13·195</a> for two variables.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y.=:(\phi):\phi!x.\supset.\phi!y \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.251ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1570.svg"></p>

<p>The following definitions embody abbreviations which are often
convenient.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y.=.{\sim}(x=y) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1571.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.815ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1571.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y=z.=.x=y.y=z \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1572.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 29.548ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1572.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp x=y.\equiv:\phi!x.\supset_{\phi}.\phi!y \quad[\text{*4·2.(*13·01).(*10·02)}]\)" src="images/1573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 49ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1573.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x=y.\supset.\psi x\supset\psi y\)" src="images/1574.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 20.197ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1574.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\vdash.\text{*12·1}.\quad\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp(\exists \phi)\colon\ldotp\psi x.\equiv.\phi!x:\psi y.\equiv.\phi!y &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ &amp;\vdash.\text{*13·1}.\quad\supset\vdash\colon\colon\text{Hp}.\supset\colon\ldotp \phi!x.\supset_{\phi}.\phi!y\colon\ldotp\\ &amp;[\text{*4·84·85.*10·27}] \quad\supset\colon\ldotp\psi x.\equiv.\phi!x:\psi y.\equiv.\phi!y:\supset_{\phi}:\psi x.\supset.\psi y\colon\ldotp\\ &amp;[\text{*10·23}] \quad\supset\colon\ldotp(\exists \phi):\psi x.\equiv.\phi!x:\psi y.\equiv.\phi!y:\supset:\psi x.\supset.\psi y &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ &amp;\vdash.\text{(1).(2)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1575.svg" style="vertical-align: -7.002ex; width: 72.13ex; height: 15.136ex;" id="img_images_1575.svg"></span></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y\)" src="images/722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_722.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_135"> satisfies any
function, whether predicative or non-predicative, which is satisfied
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_368">. It will be observed that the proof uses the axiom of
reducibility (<a href="#_12_1" class="pginternal">*12·1</a>). But for this axiom, two terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_369"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_136">
might agree in respect of all predicative functions, but not in respect
of all non-predicative functions. We should thus be led to identities
of different degrees, according to the degree of the functions in
respect of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_370"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_137"> agreed. Strict identity would, in this
case, have to be taken as a primitive idea, and <a href="#_13_101" class="pginternal">*13·101</a> would have to
be a primitive proposition, as would also *13·15·16·17.</p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .\text{*13·1}. \supset\vdash \colon\colon \text{Hp} . &amp;\supset \colon\ldotp \phi ! x . \supset_\phi . \phi ! y : \phi ! y . \supset_\phi . \phi ! z \colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*10·3}] &amp;\supset \colon\ldotp \phi ! x . \supset_\phi . \phi ! z \colon\colon \supset \vdash . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1585.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.251ex; width: 49.142ex; height: 5.633ex;" id="img_images_1585.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the above use of <a href="#_10_3" class="pginternal">*10·3</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! x\)" src="images/485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_485.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! y\)" src="images/1586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.086ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1586.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi ! z\)" src="images/1587.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_1587.svg">
are regarded as three different functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_69">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_70">
replaces the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_371"> of *10·3.</p>

<p>The above three propositions show that identity is reflexive (<a href="#_13_15" class="pginternal">*13·15</a>),
symmetrical (<a href="#_13_16" class="pginternal">*13·16</a>), and transitive (<a href="#_13_17" class="pginternal">*13·17</a>). These are the three
marks of relations having the formal properties which we associate
commonly with the sign of equality.</p>
