<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*11·62}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\colon z=x.w=y.\supset_{z,w}.\phi(z,w):&amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp z=x.\supset_{z}:w=y.\supset_{w}.\phi(z,w)\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*13·191}] &amp; \equiv\colon\ldotp w=y.\supset_{w}.\phi(x,w)\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*13·191}]  &amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp\phi(x,y)\colon\colon\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1606.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.359ex; width: 65.473ex; height: 11.849ex;" id="img_images_1606.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is the analogue, for two variables, of <a href="#_13_191" class="pginternal">*13·191</a>.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_180">[Pg 180]</span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*13·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists z,w).z=x.w=y.\phi(z,w).\equiv.\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1569.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.539ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1569.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*11·55}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp(\exists z,w).z=x.&amp;w=y.\phi(z,w).\\ &amp;\equiv:(\exists z):z=x:(\exists w).w=y.\phi(z,w):\\ [\text{*13·195}]  &amp;\equiv:(\exists w).w=y.\phi(x,w):\\ [\text{*13·195}]  &amp;\equiv:\phi(x,y)\colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array}\\ \]" src="images/1607.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 67.453ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_1607.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is the analogue, for two variables, of <a href="#_13_195" class="pginternal">*13·195</a>. It is
frequently used, especially in the theory of couples (<a href="#_54" class="pginternal">*54</a>, <a href="#_55" class="pginternal">*55</a>, <a href="#_56" class="pginternal">*56</a>).</p>

<p>The following proposition is useful in the theory of types. Its purpose
is to show that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_88"> is any argument for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_22">" is
significant, <i>i.e.</i> for which we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a\)" src="images/1608.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.365ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1608.svg">,
then "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_104">" is significant when, and only when, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_372"> is either
identical with a or not identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_89">. It follows (as will be
proved in <a href="#_20_81" class="pginternal">*20·81</a>) that, if "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_23">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg_6">" are both
significant, the class of values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_373"> for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_105">" is
significant is the same as the class of those for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi x\)" src="images/176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_176.svg_33">"
is significant, <i>i.e.</i> two types which have a common member are
identical.</p>

<p>In the following proof, the chief point to observe is the use of
<a href="#_10_221" class="pginternal">*10·221</a>. There are two variables, <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_90"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_374">, to be identified.
In the first use, we depend upon the fact that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_24"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x=a\)" src="images/1609.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_1609.svg">
both occur in both (4) and (5): the occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_25"> in both
justifies the identification of the two <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_91">'s, and when these
have been identified, the occurrence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x=a\)" src="images/1609.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_1609.svg_1"> in both justifies
the identification of the two <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_375">'s. (Unless the <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_92">'s had been
already identified, this would not be legitimate, because "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x=a\)" src="images/1609.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_1609.svg_2">" is
typically ambiguous if neither <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_376"> nor <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_93"> is of given type.) The
second use of *10·221 is justified by the fact that both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_26"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_106"> occur in both (2) and (6).</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_13_3">*13·3</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\colon\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset\colon\ldotp\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x.\equiv:x=a.\lor.x\neq a\)" src="images/1610.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 45.659ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_1610.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*2·11}. &amp; \supset\vdash.\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).Simp}.  &amp;\supset\vdash:\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset.\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*2·11}.  &amp;\supset\vdash:x=a.\lor.x\neq a  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(3).Simp}. &amp; \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset:x=a.\lor.x\neq a  &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{*13·101.Comm}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset:x=a.\supset.\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x  &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash.\text{(4).(5).*10·13·221}.&amp;\supset\\ \vdash\colon\colon\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.&amp;\supset:x=a.\lor.x\neq a\colon\ldotp\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset:x=a.\supset.\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x  &amp;\qquad \text{(6)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(6).*10·13·221}.&amp;\supset\\ \vdash\colon\colon\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.&amp;\supset.\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x\colon\ldotp\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset:x=a.\lor.x\neq a\colon\ldotp\\ &amp;\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset:x=a.\supset.\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x  &amp;\qquad \text{(7)}\\ \vdash.\text{(7).Simp}.&amp;\supset\\ \vdash\colon\colon\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.&amp;\supset.\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x\colon\ldotp\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset:x=a.\lor.x\neq a  &amp;\qquad \text{(8)}\\ \vdash.\text{(8).*5·35}.  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon\phi a\lor{\sim}\phi a.\supset\colon\ldotp\phi x\lor{\sim}\phi x.\equiv:x=a.\lor.x\neq a\colon\colon\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1611.svg" style="vertical-align: -19.57ex; width: 90.703ex; height: 40.271ex;" id="img_images_1611.svg"></span></p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_181">[Pg 181]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_14">*14. DESCRIPTIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *14.</p>

<p>A <i>description</i> is a phrase of the form "the term which etc.,"
or, more explicitly, "the term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_377"> which satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_44">,"
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_45">, is some function satisfied by one and only
one argument. For reasons explained in the Introduction (<a href="#CHAPTER_III" class="pginternal">Chapter III</a>),
we do not define "the <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_378"> which satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_46">,"
but we define any proposition in which this phrase occurs. Thus when
we say: "The term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_379"> which satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_47"> satisfies
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_8">," we shall mean: "There is a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_24"> such that
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_70"> is true when, and only when, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_380"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_25">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\psi}b\)" src="images/1612.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.443ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1612.svg"> is true." That is, writing "<img alt="" data-tex="\((℩x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/1613.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.814ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1613.svg">" for "the
term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_381"> which satisfies <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x\)" src="images/140.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_140.svg_71">," <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi(℩x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/1614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.287ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1614.svg"> is to
mean
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists b): {\phi}x .\equiv_{x}. x = b: {\psi}b\text{.} \]" src="images/1615.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.632ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1615.svg"></span>
This, however, is not yet quite adequate as a definition, for when
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/561.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_561.svg_4"> occurs in a proposition which is part of a
larger proposition, there is doubt whether the smaller or the larger
proposition is to be taken as the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi(℩x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/1614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.287ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1614.svg_1">." Take, for
example, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi({℩}x)({\phi}x) .\supset. p\)" src="images/1616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.198ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1616.svg">. This may be either
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp;(\exists b):\phi x .\equiv_{x}. x = b :\psi b :\supset. p \\ \text{or} \quad &amp;(\exists b) \colon\ldotp \phi x .\equiv_{x}. x = b: \psi b .\supset.p. \\ \end{align} \]" src="images/1617.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 32.949ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1617.svg"></span>
If "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists b): {\phi}x .\equiv_{x}. x = b\)" src="images/1618.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.794ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1618.svg">" is false, the first of these must be true, while the
second must be false. Thus it is very necessary to distinguish them.</p>

<p>The proposition which is to be treated as the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi({℩}x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/1619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.287ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1619.svg">"
will be called the <i>scope</i> of (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/561.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_561.svg_5">. Thus
in the first of the above two propositions, the scope of
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/561.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_561.svg_6"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi({℩}x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/1619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.287ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1619.svg_1">, while in the second
it is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi({℩}x)({\phi}x) .\supset. p\)" src="images/1616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.198ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1616.svg_1">. In order to avoid
ambiguities as to scope, we shall indicate the scope by writing
"<img alt="" data-tex="\([({℩}x)({\phi}x)]\)" src="images/97.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.072ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_97.svg_1">" at the beginning of the scope, followed by
enough dots to extend to the end of the scope. Thus of the above two
propositions the first is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ [({℩} x)(\phi x)].\psi({℩} x)(\phi x) .\supset. p \]" src="images/1620.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.276ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1620.svg"></span>
while the second is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ [({℩} x)(\phi x)]:\psi({℩} x)(\phi x) .\supset. p. \]" src="images/1621.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.785ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1621.svg"></span>
Thus we arrive at the following definition:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_14_01">*14·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\([({℩} x)(\phi x)].\psi({℩} x)(\phi x).=:(\exists b):\phi x .\equiv_{x}. x = b:\psi b \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1622.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.076ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1622.svg"></p>

<p>It will be found in practice that the scope usually required is
the smallest proposition enclosed in dots or brackets in which
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)({\phi}x)\)" src="images/561.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_561.svg_7">" occurs. Hence<span class="pagenum" id="Page_182">[Pg 182]</span> when this scope is to be given
to (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_34">, we shall usually omit explicit mention of the
scope. Thus <i>e.g</i>. we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} a\neq (℩x)(\phi x)\ldotp &amp;=:~ (\exists b):\phi x\ldotp \equiv_{x}\ldotp x=b:a\neq b,\\ \sim \{a=(℩x)(\phi x)\}\ldotp &amp;=\ldotp \sim\{(\exists b):\phi x\ldotp \equiv_{x}\ldotp x=b:a=b\}. \end{aligned} \]" src="images/1623.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 52.728ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1623.svg"></span>
Of these the first necessarily implies (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists b):\phi x\ldotp\equiv_{x}\ldotp x=b\)" src="images/1624.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.794ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1624.svg">,
while the second does not. We put</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_14_02">*14·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\ldotp =:(\exists b):\phi x\ldotp \equiv_{x}\ldotp x=b\quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.365ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1625.svg"></p>

<p>This defines: "The <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_382"> satisfying <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_48"> exists," which
holds when, and only when, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \hat{x}\)" src="images/188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_188.svg_49"> is satisfied by one value
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_383"> and by no other value.</p>

<p>When two or more descriptions occur in the same proposition, there is
need of avoiding ambiguity as to which has the larger scope. For this
purpose, we put</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_14_03">*14·03</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}[({℩}x)(\phi x),\,&amp;({℩}x)(\psi x)]\ldotp f\{({℩}x)(\phi x),({℩}x)(\psi x)\}\ldotp =:\\ &amp;[({℩}x)(\phi x)]:[({℩}x)(\psi x)]\ldotp f\{({℩}x)(\phi x),({℩}x)(\psi x)\}\quad\text{Df}\end{align}\]" src="images/1626.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 60.561ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1626.svg"></span></p>

<p>It will be shown <a href="#_14_113" class="pginternal">*14·113</a> that the truth-value of a proposition
containing two descriptions is unaffected by the question which has
the larger scope. Hence we shall in general adopt the convention that
the description occurring first typographically is to have the larger
scope, unless the contrary is expressly indicated. Thus <i>e.g</i>.
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (℩x)(\phi x)=(℩x)(\psi x) \]" src="images/1627.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.77ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1627.svg"></span>
will mean
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists b):\phi x\ldotp \equiv_{x}\ldotp x=b:b=(℩x)(\psi x), \]" src="images/1628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.115ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1628.svg"></span>
<i>i.e</i>.
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists b)\colon\ldotp \phi x\ldotp \equiv_{x}\ldotp x=b\colon\ldotp (\exists c):\psi x\ldotp \equiv_{x}\ldotp x=c:b=c. \]" src="images/1629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.111ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1629.svg"></span>
By this convention we are able almost always to avoid explicit
indication of the order of elimination of two or more descriptions. If,
however, we require a larger scope for the later description, we put</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·04</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}[({℩}x)(\psi x)]\ldotp &amp;f\{({℩}x)(\phi x),\,({℩}x)(\psi x)\}\ldotp =\ldotp\\ &amp;[({℩}x)(\psi x),\,({℩}x)(\phi x)]\ldotp f\{({℩}x)(\phi x),\,({℩}x)(\psi x)\}\quad\text{Df}\end{align}\]" src="images/1630.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 59.554ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1630.svg"></span></p>

<p>Whenever we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x),~({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.37ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1631.svg"> behaves,
formally, like an ordinary argument to any function in which it may
occur. This fact is embodied in the following proposition:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·18</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\ldotp \supset :(x)\ldotp \psi x\ldotp \supset \ldotp \psi ({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1632.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.289ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1632.svg"></p>

<p>That is to say, when (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_35"> exists, it has any property
which belongs to everything. This does not hold when (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_36">
does not exist; for example, the present King of France does not have
the property of being either bald or not bald.</p>

<p>If (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_37"> has any property whatever, it must exist. This
fact is stated in the proposition:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·21</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\psi (℩x)(\phi x)\ldotp \supset \ldotp \text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1633.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.684ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1633.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is obvious, since "E<img alt="" data-tex="\(!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1634.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.443ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1634.svg">" is, by
the definitions, part<span class="pagenum" id="Page_183">[Pg 183]</span> of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1635.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.287ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1635.svg">." When, in ordinary
language or in philosophy, something is said to "exist," it is always
something <i>described</i>, <i>i.e.</i> it is not something immediately
presented, like a taste or a patch of colour, but something like
"matter" or "mind" or "Homer" (meaning "the author of the Homeric
poems"), which is known by description as "the so-and-so," and is thus
of the form (<img alt="" data-tex="\(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_580.svg_1">. Thus in all such cases, the existence of
the (grammatical) subject (<img alt="" data-tex="\(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_580.svg_2"> can be analytically inferred
from any true proposition having this grammatical subject. It would
seem that the word "existence" cannot be significantly applied to
subjects immediately given; <i>i.e.</i> not only does our definition
give no meaning to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!x\)" src="images/1636.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.464ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_1636.svg">," but there is no reason, in
philosophy, to suppose that a meaning of existence could be found which
would be applicable to immediately given subjects.</p>

<p>Besides the above, the following are among the more useful propositions
of the present number.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·202.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\equiv:({℩}x)(\phi x)=b:\equiv:\phi x.\equiv_{x}.b=x:\equiv:b=({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 67.423ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1637.svg"></p>

<p>From the first equivalence in the above, it follows that</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·204.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x).\equiv.(\exists b).({℩}x)(\phi x)=b\)" src="images/1638.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.193ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1638.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_38"> exists when there is something which
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_39"> is.</p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·205.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\psi({℩}x)(\phi x).\equiv.(\exists b).b=({℩}x)(\phi x).\psi b\)" src="images/1639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.946ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1639.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_40"> has the property <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_30"> when there
is something which is (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_41"> and which has the property
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_31">.</p>

<p>We have to prove that such symbols as "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_42">" obey the
same rules with regard to identity as symbols which directly represent
objects. To this, however, there is one partial exception, for instead
of having
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ ({℩}x)(\phi x)=(℩x)(\phi x), \]" src="images/1640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.275ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1640.svg"></span>
we only have</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·28.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x).\equiv.({℩}x)(\phi x)=({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.042ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1641.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_43">" only satisfies the reflexive property
of identity if (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_44"> exists.</p>

<p>The symmetrical property of identity holds for such symbols as
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_45">, without the need of assuming existence, <i>i.e.</i>
we have</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:a=({℩}x)(\phi x).\equiv.({℩}x)(\phi x)=a\)" src="images/1642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.469ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1642.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·131.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:({℩}x)(\phi x)=({℩}x)(\psi x).\equiv.({℩}x)(\psi x)=({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.953ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1643.svg"></p>

<p>Similarly the transitive property of identity holds without the need of
assuming existence. This is proved in *14·14·142·144.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_184">[Pg 184]</span></p>

<p class="nind">

is explicitly indicated, the above proposition is the same as the
following:</p>

<p class="nind">

after the statement of <a href="#_14_03" class="pginternal">*14·03</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_14_113">*14·113</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash:[({℩}x)(\psi x)].f\{({℩}x)(\phi x),({℩}x)(\psi x)\}.\equiv.f\{({℩}x)(\phi x),\,({℩}x)(\psi x)\}\\ &amp;[\text{*14·111·112}]\end{align}\]" src="images/1654.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 63.154ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1654.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition shows that when two descriptions occur in the same
proposition, the truth-value of the proposition is unaffected by the
question which has the larger scope.</p>

<p class="nind">

<p class="nind">

<p>This proposition is not an <i>immediate</i> consequence of <a href="#_13_16" class="pginternal">*13·16</a>,
because "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a=({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.028ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1666.svg">" is not a value of the function
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y\)" src="images/722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_722.svg_2">." Similar remarks apply to the following propositions.</p>

<p>In the above proposition, in accordance with our convention, the
descriptive expression (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_46"> is eliminated before
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\psi x)\)" src="images/589.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_589.svg_4">, because it occurs first in "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)=({℩}x)(\psi x)\)" src="images/1669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.89ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1669.svg">";
but in "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\psi x)=({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1670.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.89ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1670.svg">,"
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\psi x)\)" src="images/589.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_589.svg_5"> is to be first eliminated. The order of elimination
makes no difference to the truth-value, as was proved in <a href="#_14_113" class="pginternal">*14·113</a>.</p>

<p>It should be observed that we do <i>not</i> have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ ({℩}x)(\phi x) = b . \equiv : \psi ! ({℩}x)(\phi x) . \supset_{\psi} . \psi ! b \]" src="images/1685.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 35.816ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1685.svg"></span>
for, if <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\text{E} ! ({℩}x)(\phi x), \psi ! ({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1686.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.667ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1686.svg"> is
always false, and therefore
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \psi ! ({℩}x)(\phi x) . \supset_{\psi} . \psi ! b \]" src="images/1687.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 18.99ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1687.svg"></span>
holds for all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_26">. But we do have</p>

<p>The above proposition shows that, provided (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_47"> exists,
it has (speaking formally) all the logical properties of symbols which
directly represent objects. Hence when (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_48"> exists,
the fact that it is an incomplete symbol becomes irrelevant to the
truth-values of logical propositions in which it occurs.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_14_21">*14·21</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\psi({℩}x)(\phi x).\supset.\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1703.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.684ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1703.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*14·1}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp \psi\{({℩}x)(\phi x)\}.&amp;\supset:(\exists b):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\psi b:\\ [\text{*10·5}]      &amp;\supset:(\exists b):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\\ [\text{*14·11}] &amp;\supset:\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1704.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 46.114ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_1704.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition shows that if any true statement can be made about
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_49">, then (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_50"> must exist. Its use
throughout the remainder of the work will be very frequent.</p>

<p>When (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_51"> does not exist, there are still true
propositions in which "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_52">" occurs, but it has, in such
propositions, a <i>secondary</i> occurrence, in the sense explained in
<a href="#CHAPTER_III" class="pginternal">Chapter III</a> of the Introduction, <i>i.e.</i> the asserted proposition
concerned is not of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1705.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.287ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1705.svg">, but of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\psi({℩}x)(\phi x)\}\)" src="images/1706.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.794ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1706.svg">, in other words, the proposition which is
the scope of (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_53"> is only part of the whole asserted
proposition.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x).\equiv.\phi({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1707.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.559ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1707.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*14·122}.  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\supset.\phi b &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*4·71}. &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\equiv:\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\phi b\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·11·281}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists b):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\equiv:(\exists b):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\phi b\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*14·11·101}]  &amp;\supset\vdash:\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x).\equiv.\phi({℩}x)(\phi x):\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1708.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 76.25ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_1708.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_191">[Pg 191]</span></p>

<p>As an instance of the above proposition, we may take the following:
"The proposition 'the author of Waverley existed' is equivalent to
'the man who wrote Waverley wrote Waverley.'" Thus such a proposition
as "the man who wrote Waverley wrote Waverley" does not embody a
logically necessary truth, since it would be false if Waverley had not
been written, or had been written by two men in collaboration. For
example, "the man who squared the circle squared the circle" is a false
proposition.</p>

<p>Note that in the second line of the above proof <a href="#_10_5" class="pginternal">*10·5</a>, not only <a href="#_3_26" class="pginternal">*3·26</a>,
is required. For the scope of the descriptive symbol (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x.\psi x)\)" src="images/1711.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.707ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1711.svg">
is the whole product <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi \{({℩}x)(\phi x.\psi x)\}\psi\{({℩}x)(\phi x.\psi x)\}\)" src="images/1712.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.521ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1712.svg">,
so that, applying <a href="#_14_1" class="pginternal">*14·1</a>, the proposition on the right in the first line
becomes
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists b):\phi x.\psi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\phi b.\psi b \]" src="images/1713.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.101ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1713.svg"></span>
which, by <a href="#_10_5" class="pginternal">*10·5</a> and <a href="#_3_26" class="pginternal">*3·26</a>, implies
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} (\exists b):&amp;\phi x.\psi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\phi b,\\ \textit{i.e.} &amp;\phi\{({℩}x)(\phi x.\psi x)\}. \end{array} \]" src="images/1714.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 28.915ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_1714.svg"></span></p>

<b>*14·272.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:\supset:\chi(℩x)(\phi x).\equiv.\chi({℩}x)(\psi x)\)" src="images/1728.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.312ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1728.svg"></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*4·86}.  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \phi x\equiv\psi x.\supset\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv.x=b:\equiv:\psi x.\equiv.x=b\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·11·414}]&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.  \supset\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\equiv:\psi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{Fact}] &amp;\supset\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\chi b:\equiv:\psi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\chi b\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·11·21}]  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.\supset\colon\ldotp (b)\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\chi b:\equiv:\psi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\chi b\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·281}]    &amp;\supset\colon\ldotp (\exists b)\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\chi b:\equiv\\ &amp;:(\exists b):\psi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\chi b\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*14·101}]   &amp;\supset\colon\ldotp \chi({℩}x)(\phi x).\equiv.\chi({℩}x)(\psi x)\colon\colon \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1729.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.068ex; width: 71.637ex; height: 21.267ex;" id="img_images_1729.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above two propositions show that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_315.svg_6"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.231ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1730.svg"> are "extensional" properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_48">,
<i>i.e.</i> their truth-value is unchanged by the substitution, for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_49">, of any formally equivalent function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_9">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_14_28">*14·28</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x).\equiv.(℩x)(\phi x)=({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1731.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.042ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1731.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*13·15.*4·73}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\equiv:\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:b=b  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*10·11·281}.&amp;\supset\\ &amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists b):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\equiv:(\exists b):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:b=b  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).*14·1·11}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1732.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 80.648ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_1732.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition states that (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_55"> is identical with
itself whenever it exists, but not otherwise. Thus for example the
proposition "the present King of France is the present King of France"
is false.</p>

<p>The purpose of the following propositions is to show that, when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_315.svg_7">, the scope of (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_56"> does not
matter to the truth-value of any proposition in which (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_57">
occurs. This proposition cannot be proved generally, but it can
be proved in each particular case. The following propositions show the
method, which proceeds always by means of <a href="#_14_242" class="pginternal">*14·242</a>, <a href="#_10_23" class="pginternal">*10·23</a> and <a href="#_14_11" class="pginternal">*14·11</a>.
The proposition can be proved generally when (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_58">
occurs in the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.231ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1730.svg_1">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.231ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1730.svg_2">
occurs in what we may call a "truth-function," <i>i.e.</i> a function
whose truth or falsehood depends only upon the truth or falsehood of
its argument or arguments. This covers all the cases with which we are
ever concerned. That is to say, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1730.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.231ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1730.svg_3"> occurs in
any of the ways which can be generated by the processes of <a href="#_1" class="pginternal">*1</a>—<a href="#_11" class="pginternal">*11</a>,
then, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_315.svg_8">, the truth-value of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{[({℩}x)(\phi x)].\chi({℩}x)(\phi x)\}\)" src="images/1733.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.816ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1733.svg"> is the same as that of
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ [({℩}x)(\phi x)].f\{\chi({℩}x)(\phi x)\}. \]" src="images/1734.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.445ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1734.svg"></span>
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_194">[Pg 194]</span>This is proved in the following proposition. In this proposition,
however, the use of propositions as apparent variables involves an
apparatus not required elsewhere, and we have therefore not used this
proposition in subsequent proofs.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_14_3">*14·3</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp p\equiv q.\supset_{p,q}.f(p)\equiv f(q):\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x):\supset:\\ &amp;f\{[({℩}x)(\phi x)].\chi({℩}x)(\phi x)\}.\equiv.[({℩}x)(\phi x)].f\{\chi(℩x)(\phi x)\}\end{align}\]" src="images/1735.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.078ex; width: 53.404ex; height: 5.288ex;" id="img_images_1735.svg"></span></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*14·242}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\supset:[(℩x)(\phi x)].\chi(℩x)(\phi x).\equiv.\chi b &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1)}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp p\equiv q.\supset_{p,q}.f(p)\equiv f(q):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\supset:\\ \qquad\qquad f\{[(℩x)(\phi x)].\chi(℩x)(\phi x)\}.\equiv.f(\chi b) &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*14·242}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp \phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\supset:[(℩x)(\phi x)].f\{\chi(℩x)(\phi x)\}.\equiv.f(\chi b) &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(3)}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp p\equiv q.\supset_{p,q}.f(p)\equiv f(q):\phi x.\equiv_{x}.x=b:\supset:\\ \qquad\qquad f\{[(℩x)(\phi x)].\chi(℩x)(\phi x)\}.\equiv.[(℩x)(\phi x)].f\{\chi(℩x)(\phi x)\} &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(4).*10·23.*14·11}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1736.svg" style="vertical-align: -14.903ex; width: 72.133ex; height: 30.937ex;" id="img_images_1736.svg"></span></p>

They are, however, independently proved, because <a href="#_14_3" class="pginternal">*14·3</a> introduces

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_14_31">*14·31</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash\colon\colon \text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x).\supset\colon\ldotp [(℩x)(\phi x)].&amp;p\lor \chi(℩x)(\phi x).\\ &amp;\equiv:p.\lor.[(℩x)(\phi x)].\chi(℩x)(\phi x)\end{align}\]" src="images/1737.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 59.473ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_1737.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*14·32.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x).\equiv:[(℩x)(\phi x)].{\sim}&amp;\chi(℩x)(\phi x).\\ &amp;\equiv.{\sim}\{[(℩x)(\phi x)].\chi(℩x)(\phi x)\}\\ \quad[\text{*14·242.*4·11.*10·23.*14·11}]\end{align}\]" src="images/1739.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.507ex; width: 59.967ex; height: 8.145ex;" id="img_images_1739.svg"></span></p>

<p>The equivalence asserted here fails when <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}\text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/1740.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.744ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1740.svg">.
Thus, for example, let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi y\)" src="images/194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.457ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_194.svg_21"> be "<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_138"> is King of France."
Then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_580.svg_3"> = the King of France. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi y\)" src="images/1741.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_1741.svg"> be "<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_139">
is bald." Then <img alt="" data-tex="\([(℩x)(\phi x)].{\sim}\chi(℩x)(\phi x).=.\)" src="images/1742.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.465ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1742.svg"> the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_195">[Pg 195]</span>
King of France exists and is not bald; but <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}{[(℩x)(\phi x)].\chi(℩x)(\phi x)}.=.\)" src="images/1743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.465ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1743.svg">
it is false that the King of France exists and is bald. Of these the
first is false, the second true. Either might be meant by "the King of
France is not bald," which is ambiguous; but it would be more natural
to take the first (false) interpretation as the meaning of the words.
If the King of France existed, the two would be equivalent; thus as
applied to the King of England, both are true or both false.</p>

<p>It should be observed that the proposition in which (<img alt="" data-tex="\(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_580.svg_4">

and is the reason why we get an equivalence without the hypothesis
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_324.svg_5">. The proposition in which (<img alt="" data-tex="\(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_580.svg_6">
has the larger scope always implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_324.svg_6">, in

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_196">[Pg 196]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_C_a">SECTION C.<br>
CLASSES AND RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>

<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_20">*20. GENERAL THEORY OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *20.</p>

<p>The following theory of classes, although it provides a notation to
represent them, avoids the assumption that there are such things
as classes. This it does by merely defining propositions in whose
expression the symbols representing classes occur, just as, in <a href="#_14" class="pginternal">*14</a>, we
defined propositions containing descriptions.</p>

<p>The characteristics of a class are that it consists of all the terms
satisfying some propositional function, so that every propositional
function determines a class, and two functions which are formally
equivalent (<i>i.e.</i> such that whenever either is true, the other
is true also) determine the same class, while conversely two functions
which determine the same class are formally equivalent. When two
functions are formally equivalent, we shall say that they have the
same <i>extension</i>. The incomplete symbols which take the place of
classes serve the purpose of technically providing something identical
in the case of two functions having the same extension; without
something to represent classes, we cannot, for example, count the
combinations that can be formed out of a given set of objects.</p>

<p>Propositions in which a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_71"> occurs may depend, for their
truth-value, upon the particular function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_72">, or they may depend
only upon the <i>extension</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_73">. In the former case, we
will call the proposition concerned an <i>intensional</i> function
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_74">; in the latter case, an <i>extensional</i> function of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_75">. Thus, for example, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . {\phi}x\)" src="images/457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_457.svg_1"> or (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x). {\phi}x\)" src="images/458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.081ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_458.svg_1">
is an extensional function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_76">, because, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_77"> is
formally equivalent to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_32">, <i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x .\equiv_{x}. {\psi}x\)" src="images/1750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.285ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1750.svg">,
we have (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).{\phi}x .\equiv. (x) . {\psi}x\)" src="images/1751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.422ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1751.svg">
and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x) . {\phi}x .\equiv. (\exists x) . {\psi}x\)" src="images/1752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.938ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1752.svg">. But on
the other hand "I believe (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . {\phi}x\)" src="images/457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_457.svg_2">" is an <i>intensional</i>
function, because, even if <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}x .\equiv_{x}. {\psi}x\)" src="images/1750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.285ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1750.svg_1">, it by no
means follows that I believe (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . {\psi}x\)" src="images/1753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.947ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1753.svg"> provided I believe
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . {\phi}x\)" src="images/457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_457.svg_3">. The mark of an extensional function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_17"> of a
function <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!\hat{z}\)" src="images/496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_496.svg_5"> is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\phi}!x .\equiv_{x}. {\psi}!x :\supset_{\phi,\psi}:f({\phi}!\hat{z}) .\equiv. f({\psi}!\hat{z})\text{.} \]" src="images/1754.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 35.039ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1754.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_197">[Pg 197]</span>
(We write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_8">" when we wish to speak of the function
itself as opposed to its argument.) The functions of functions with
which mathematics is specially concerned are all extensional.</p>

<p>When a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_9"> is extensional, it may be regarded
as being about the class determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_10">, since its
truth-value remains unchanged so long as the class is unchanged.
Hence we require, for the theory of classes, a method of obtaining an
extensional function from any given function of a function. This is
effected by the following definition:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_01">*20·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}.=:(\exists \phi):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:f\{\phi!\hat{z}\}\quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1755.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.139ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1755.svg"></p>

<p>Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}\)" src="images/1756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.844ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1756.svg"> is in reality a function of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_11">, which is defined whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\phi!\hat{z}\}\)" src="images/1757.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.536ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1757.svg">
is significant for predicative functions <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/1528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.029ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1528.svg_12">. But it
is convenient to regard <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}\)" src="images/1756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.844ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1756.svg_1"> as though it had
an argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z\)" src="images/629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.457ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_629.svg_2">), which we will call "the class
determined by the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_611.svg_4">." It will be proved
shortly that <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}\)" src="images/1756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.844ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1756.svg_2"> is always an <i>extensional</i>
function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_611.svg_5">, and that, applying the definition of
identity (<a href="#_13_01" class="pginternal">*13·01</a>) to the fictitious objects <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z\)" src="images/614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.333ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_614.svg_11">) and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z\)" src="images/629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.457ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_629.svg_3">), we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{z}(\phi z)=\hat{z}(\psi z).\equiv:(x):\phi x.\equiv.\psi x. \]" src="images/1758.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.341ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1758.svg"></span>
This last is the distinguishing characteristic of classes, and
justifies us in treating <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z\)" src="images/629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.457ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_629.svg_4">) as the class determined by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_611.svg_6">.</p>

<p>With regard to the scope of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z\)" src="images/629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.457ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_629.svg_5">), and to the order
of elimination of two such expressions, we shall adopt the same
conventions as were explained in <a href="#_14" class="pginternal">*14</a> for (<img alt="" data-tex="\(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_580.svg_7">. The
condition corresponding to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \exists!(℩x)(\psi x)\,\, \text{is}\,\, (\exists \phi):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x, \]" src="images/1759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.652ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1759.svg"></span>
which is always satisfied because of <a href="#_12_1" class="pginternal">*12·1</a>.</p>

<p>Following Peano, we shall use the notation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x\in\hat{z}(\psi z) \]" src="images/1760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.397ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1760.svg"></span>
to express "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_384"> is a member of the class determined by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi!\hat{z}\)" src="images/611.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_611.svg_7">." We therefore introduce the following definition:</p>


<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_02">*20·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in(\phi!\hat{z}).=.\phi!x \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1761.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.577ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1761.svg"></p>

<p>In this form, the definition is never used; it is introduced for the
sake of the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash\colon\ldotp x\in\hat{z}(\psi z).\equiv:(\exists \phi):\psi y.\equiv_{y}.\phi!y:\phi!x \]" src="images/1762.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 38.636ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1762.svg"></span>
which results from <a href="#_20_02" class="pginternal">*20·02</a> and <a href="#_20_01" class="pginternal">*20·01</a>, and leads to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash\colon x\in\hat{z}(\psi z).\equiv.\psi x \]" src="images/1763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.325ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1763.svg"></span>
by the help of <a href="#_12_1" class="pginternal">*12·1</a>.</p>

<p>We shall use small Greek letters (other than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\epsilon\)" src="images/48.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.919ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_48.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_2">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\pi\)" src="images/1764.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.29ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_1764.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_78">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_33">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_12">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_9">) to represent
classes, <i>i.e.</i> to stand for symbols of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_13">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}!(\phi z)\)" src="images/1765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.842ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1765.svg">. When a small Greek letter occurs as
apparent variable, it is to be understood to stand for a<span class="pagenum" id="Page_198">[Pg 198]</span> symbol of
the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi!z)\)" src="images/1766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.842ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1766.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_79"> is properly the apparent
variable concerned. The use of single letters in place of such symbols
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi!z)\)" src="images/1766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.842ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1766.svg_1"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}!(\phi!z)\)" src="images/1767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.471ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1767.svg"> is practically almost
indispensable, since otherwise the notation rapidly becomes intolerably
cumbrous. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\alpha\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg">" will mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_385"> is a member of the
class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_75">," and may be used wherever no special defining
function of the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_76"> is in question.</p>

<p>The following definition defines what is meant by a class.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_03">*20·03</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}=\hat{\alpha}\{(\exists\phi).\alpha=\hat{z}!(\phi!z)\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1769.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.873ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1769.svg"></p>

<p>Note that the expression
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\alpha}\{(\exists\phi).\alpha=\hat{z}!(\phi!z)\}\)" src="images/1770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.019ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1770.svg">" has
no meaning in isolation: we have merely defined (in <a href="#_20_01" class="pginternal">*20·01</a>)
certain uses of such expressions. What the above definition
decides is that the symbol "Cls" may replace the symbol
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\alpha}\{(\exists\phi).\alpha=\hat{z}!(\phi!z)\}\)" src="images/1770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.019ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1770.svg_1">," wherever
the latter occurs, and that the meaning of the combination of symbols
concerned is to be unchanged thereby. Thus "Cls," also, has no meaning
in isolation, but merely in certain uses.</p>

<p>The above definition, like many future definitions, is ambiguous as
to type. The Latin letter <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_19">, according to our conventions, is to
represent the lowest type concerned; thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_80"> is of the type
next above this. It is convenient to speak of a class as being of the
same type as its defining function; thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_77"> is of the type
next above that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_20">, and "Cls" is of the type next above that of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_78">. Thus the type of "Cls" is fixed relatively to the lowest
type concerned; but if, in two different contexts, different types are
the lowest concerned, the meaning of "Cls" will be different in these
two contexts. The meaning of "Cls" only becomes definite when the
lowest type concerned is specified.</p>

<p>Equality between classes is defined by applying <a href="#_13_01" class="pginternal">*13·01</a>, symbolically
unchanged, to their defining functions, and then using <a href="#_20_01" class="pginternal">*20·01</a>.</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number may be divided into three sets.
First, we have those that deal with the fundamental properties of
classes; these end with <a href="#_20_43" class="pginternal">*20·43</a>. Then we have a set of propositions
dealing with both classes and descriptions; these extend from <a href="#_20_5" class="pginternal">*20·5</a>
to <a href="#_20_59" class="pginternal">*20·59</a> (with the exception of *20·53·54). Lastly, we have a set of
propositions designed to prove that classes of classes have all the
same formal properties as classes of individuals.</p>

<p>In the first set, the principal propositions are the following.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x:\equiv.\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z)\)" src="images/1771.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.405ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1771.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> two classes are identical when, and only when, their
defining functions are formally equivalent. This is the principal
property of classes.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z).\equiv:x\in\hat{z}(\psi z).\equiv_{x}.x\in\hat{z}(\chi z)\)" src="images/1772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.666ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1772.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_199">[Pg 199]</span></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> two classes are identical when, and only when, they have
the same members.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha=\beta.\equiv:x\in \alpha.\equiv_{x}.x\in \beta\)" src="images/1773.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 28.887ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1773.svg"></p>

<p>This is the same proposition as <a href="#_20_31" class="pginternal">*20·31</a>, merely employing Greek letters
in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z)\)" src="images/631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.337ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_631.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\chi z)\)" src="images/671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.281ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_671.svg_1">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·18.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \hat{z}(\phi z)=\hat{z}(\psi z).\supset:f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}.\equiv.f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}\)" src="images/1774.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.321ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1774.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if two classes are identical, any property of either
belongs also to the other. This is the analogue of <a href="#_13_12" class="pginternal">*13·12</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·2·21·22</b>, which prove that identity between classes is
reflexive, symmetrical and transitive.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x\in \hat{z}(\psi z).\equiv.\psi x\)" src="images/1775.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.576ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1775.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> a term belongs to a class when, and only when, it satisfies
the defining function of the class.</p>

<p>In the second set of propositions (<a href="#_20_3" class="pginternal">*20·3</a>—<a href="#_20_59" class="pginternal">·59</a>), we show that, under
suitable circumstances, expressions such as (<img alt="" data-tex="\(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_580.svg_8"> may be
substituted for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_386"> in <a href="#_20_3" class="pginternal">*20·3</a> and various other propositions of
the first set, and we prove a few properties of such expressions as
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\(℩ \alpha)(f \alpha)\)" src="images/1776.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.138ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1776.svg">," <i>i.e.</i> "the class which satisfies
the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_18">." Here it is to be remembered that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_79">"
stands for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_14">," and that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f \alpha\)" src="images/1777.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.692ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1777.svg">" therefore
stands for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_14">." This is, in reality, a function
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_25">, namely the extensional function associated with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(f(\psi!\hat{z})\)" src="images/1778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.158ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1778.svg"> by means of <a href="#_20_01" class="pginternal">*20·01</a>. Thus an expression containing a
variable class is always an abbreviation for an expression containing a
variable function.</p>

<p>In the third set of propositions, we prove that variable classes
satisfy all the primitive propositions assumed for variable individuals
or functions, whence it follows, by merely repeating the proofs of the
first set of propositions (<a href="#_20_1" class="pginternal">*20·1</a>—<a href="#_20_43" class="pginternal">·43</a>), that classes of classes have
all the formal properties of classes of individuals or functions. We
shall never have occasion explicitly to consider classes of functions,
but classes of classes will occur constantly—for example, every
cardinal number will be defined as a class of classes. Classes of
relations, which will also frequently occur, will be considered in <a href="#_21" class="pginternal">*21</a>.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind">
