<p>The three following definitions serve merely for purposes of
abbreviation.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x,\,y\in \alpha.=.x\in \alpha.y\in \alpha \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1782.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 28.293ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1782.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·05.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x,\,y,\,z\in \alpha.=.x,\,y\in \alpha.z\in \alpha \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1783.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 33.164ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1783.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·06.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x{\sim}\in \alpha.=.{\sim}(x\in \alpha) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.752ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1784.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_200">[Pg 200]</span></p>

<p>The following definitions merely extend to symbols representing classes
the definitions which have already been given for other symbols, with
the smallest possible modifications.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_07">*20·07</a>.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha).f\alpha.=.(\phi).f\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1785.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.945ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1785.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·071.</b> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists \alpha).f\alpha.=.(\exists \phi).f\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1786.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.461ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1786.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·072.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\([(℩\alpha)(\phi\alpha)].f(℩\alpha)(\phi\alpha).=:(\exists \gamma):\phi\alpha.\equiv_{\alpha}.\alpha=\gamma:f\gamma \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1787.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.425ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1787.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·08.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{\alpha}(\psi\alpha)\}.=:(\exists \phi):\psi\alpha.\equiv_{\alpha}.\phi!\alpha:f(\phi!\hat{\alpha}) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1788.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.241ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1788.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·081.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\in \psi!\hat{\alpha}.=.\psi!\alpha \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1789.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 19.769ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_1789.svg"></p>

<p>The propositions which follow give the most general properties of
classes.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_1">*20·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}.\equiv:(\exists \phi):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:f\{\phi!\hat{z}\} \quad[\text{*4·2.(*20·01)}]\)" src="images/1790.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.067ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1790.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x:\supset:f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}.\equiv.f\{\hat{z}(\chi z)\}\)" src="images/1791.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.425ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1791.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*4·86}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.\supset\colon\ldotp \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:\equiv_{\phi}:\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*4·36}]  &amp; \supset\colon\ldotp \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:f\{\phi!\hat{z}\}:\equiv_{\phi}:\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x:f{\phi!\hat{z}}\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*10·281}]  &amp; \supset\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:f\{\phi!\hat{z}\}:\\ &amp;\equiv:(\exists \phi):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x:f\{\phi!\hat{z}\}\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*20·1}]   &amp;\supset\colon\ldotp f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}.\equiv.f\{\hat{z}(\chi z)\}\colon\colon \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1792.svg" style="vertical-align: -7.274ex; width: 58.112ex; height: 15.679ex;" id="img_images_1792.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proves that every proposition about a class expresses an
extensional property of the determining function of the class,
and therefore does not depend for its truth or falsehood upon the
particular function selected for determining the class, but only upon
the extension of the determining function.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·111.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp f(\phi!\hat{z}).\equiv_{\phi}.g(\phi!\hat{z}):\supset:f\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\}.\equiv_{\phi}.g\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\}\)" src="images/1793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 47.931ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1793.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{Fact}.  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.\supset\colon\ldotp \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi!x:f(\psi!\hat{z}):\equiv:\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi!x:g(\psi!\hat{z})\colon\colon\\ [\text{*10·11·21}] &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.\supset\colon\ldotp \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi!x:f(\psi!\hat{z}):\equiv_{\psi}:\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi!x:g(\psi!\hat{z})\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*10·281}] &amp;\supset\colon\ldotp (\exists \psi):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi!x:f(\psi!\hat{z}):\equiv:(\exists \psi):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi!x:g(\psi!\hat{z})\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*20·1}]  &amp; \supset\colon\ldotp f\{\hat{z}(\phi!x)\}.\equiv.g\{\hat{z}(\phi!x)\} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*10·11·21}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1794.svg" style="vertical-align: -7.223ex; width: 89.1ex; height: 15.577ex;" id="img_images_1794.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_112">*20·112</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists g)\colon\ldotp f\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\}.\equiv_{\phi}.g!\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\}\)" src="images/1795.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 33.578ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1795.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\vdash.\text{*12·1}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists g):f(\phi!\hat{z}).\equiv_{\phi}.g!(\phi!\hat{z}) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ &amp;\vdash.\text{(1).*20·111}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1796.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.268ex; width: 49.072ex; height: 5.667ex;" id="img_images_1796.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus the axiom of reducibility still holds for classes as arguments.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_201">[Pg 201]</span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists \phi):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:f\{\hat{z}(\psi z)\}.\equiv.f\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\} \quad[\text{*20·11.*12·1}]\)" src="images/1797.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.244ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1797.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_13">*20·13</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x:\supset.\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z)\)" src="images/1798.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.405ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1798.svg"></p>

<p>The meaning of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z)\)" src="images/1799.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.635ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1799.svg">" is obtained by a
double application of <a href="#_20_01" class="pginternal">*20·01</a> to <a href="#_13_01" class="pginternal">*13·01</a>, remembering the convention that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi z)\)" src="images/631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.337ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_631.svg_3"> is to have a larger scope than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\chi z)\)" src="images/671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.281ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_671.svg_2">
because it occurs first.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*20·1}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z).\equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi):\psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\phi!\hat{z}=\hat{z}(\chi z)\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*20·1}]   &amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi,\theta)\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\chi x.\equiv_{x}.\theta!x:\phi!\hat{z}=\theta!\hat{z} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*12·1.*10·321}.&amp;\supset\\ &amp;\vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.\supset\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi):\psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\chi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*13·195}]&amp;\supset\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi,\theta)\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\chi x.\equiv_{x}.\theta!x:\phi!\hat{z}=\theta!\hat{z} &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2)}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1800.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.688ex; width: 83.739ex; height: 18.507ex;" id="img_images_1800.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z).\supset:\psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x\)" src="images/1801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.405ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1801.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*20·1}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z).\equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi):\psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\phi!\hat{z}=\hat{z}(\chi z)\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*20·1}]  &amp; \equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi,\theta)\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\chi x.\equiv_{x}.\theta!x:\phi!\hat{z}=\theta!\hat{z}\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*13·195}]  &amp; \equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi)\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\chi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·322}] &amp;\supset\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x\colon\colon \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1802.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.452ex; width: 66.518ex; height: 12.036ex;" id="img_images_1802.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is the converse of <a href="#_20_13" class="pginternal">*20·13</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x:\equiv.\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z) \quad[\text{*20·13·14}]\)" src="images/1803.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.102ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1803.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition states that two functions determine the same class
when, and only when, they are formally equivalent, <i>i.e.</i> are
satisfied by the same set of values. This is the essential property of
classes, and gives the justification of the definition <a href="#_20_01" class="pginternal">*20·01</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_151">*20·151</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.(\exists \phi).\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\phi!z)\)" src="images/1804.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.957ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1804.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*20·15}.   &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\supset.\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\phi!z)\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·11·28}]  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi):\psi x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\supset.(\exists \phi).\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\phi!z) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*12·1}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1805.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.869ex; width: 69.545ex; height: 8.869ex;" id="img_images_1805.svg"></span></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition, all classes can be obtained from
predicative functions. This fact is especially important when classes
are used as apparent variables. For in that case, according to the
definitions *20·07·071, the apparent variable really involved is a
predicative function. In virtue of <a href="#_20_151" class="pginternal">*20·151</a>, this places no limitation
upon the classes concerned, except the limitation which inevitably
results from the nature of their membership.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_202">[Pg 202]</span></p>

<p>A class, therefore, unlike a function, has its order completely
determined by the order of its possible members, <i>i.e.</i> of the
arguments which render its defining function significant.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*20·18.*10·11·21}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z).\supset:\\ &amp;\qquad(f):f!\hat{z}(\psi z).\supset.f!\hat{z}(\chi z) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*20·18·15}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:\theta!x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x:f!\hat{z}(\psi z).\supset.f!\hat{z}(\chi z):\supset:\\ &amp;\qquad f!\hat{z}(\phi!z).\supset.f!\hat{z}(\theta!z)   &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).*10·11·27·33}.&amp;\supset\\ &amp;\vdash\colon\colon \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:\theta!x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x\colon\ldotp (f):f!\hat{z}(\psi z).\supset.f!\hat{z}(\chi z)\colon\ldotp \supset\colon\ldotp (f):f!\hat{z}(\phi!z).\supset.f!\hat{z}(\theta!z)\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*20·112.*10·1}]  &amp;\supset\colon\ldotp \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\phi!x:\supset:\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\theta!x\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*4·2}]    &amp; \supset\colon\ldotp \phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\theta!x\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*10·301·32.Hp}]  &amp;\supset\colon\ldotp \psi x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*20·15}] &amp; \supset\colon\ldotp \hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z) &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(3).*10·11·23·35}.&amp;\supset\\ &amp;\vdash\colon\colon (\exists \phi,\theta):\phi!x.\equiv_{x}.\psi x:\theta!x.\equiv_{x}.\chi x\colon\ldotp (f):f!\hat{z}(\psi z).\supset.f!\hat{z}(\chi z)\colon\ldotp \\ &amp;\supset.\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z) &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(4).*12·1}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp (f):f!\hat{z}(\psi z).\supset.f!\hat{z}(\chi z):\supset.\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z) &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(5)}.  &amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1810.svg" style="vertical-align: -23.348ex; width: 114.076ex; height: 47.828ex;" id="img_images_1810.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_203">[Pg 203]</span></p>

<p>The above propositions are not <i>immediate</i> consequences of
*13·15·16·17, for a reason analogous to that explained in the note
to <a href="#_14_13" class="pginternal">*14·13</a>, namely because <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{z}(\phi z)\}\)" src="images/604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.719ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_604.svg_15"> is not a value of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(fx\)" src="images/570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.538ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_570.svg_1">, and therefore in particular "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)=\hat{z}(\psi z)\)" src="images/1816.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.567ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1816.svg">"
is not a value of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y\)" src="images/722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_722.svg_3">."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\hat{z}(\phi z)=\hat{z}(\psi z).\hat{z}(\phi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z).\supset.\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z) \quad[\text{*20·21·22}]\)" src="images/1817.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.827ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1817.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\phi z).\hat{z}(\chi z)=\hat{z}(\phi z).\supset.\hat{z}(\psi z)=\hat{z}(\chi z) \quad[\text{*20·21·22}]\)" src="images/1818.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.827ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1818.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">

<p>The following propositions deal with cases in which both classes and
descriptions occur. In such cases, we shall, in the absence of any
indication to the contrary, adopt the convention that the descriptions
are to have a larger scope than the classes, in applying the
definitions <a href="#_14_01" class="pginternal">*14·01</a> and <a href="#_20_01" class="pginternal">*20·01</a>.</p>

<p>In the following propositions, we shall prove that classes have all
the formal properties of individuals, and have the same relations to
classes of classes as individuals have to classes of individuals.
It is only necessary to prove the analogues of our primitive
propositions, and of our definitions in cases where their analogues
are not themselves definitions. We shall take the propositions
*10·1·11·12·121·122, rather than those of <a href="#_9" class="pginternal">*9</a>, and we shall prove the
analogue of <a href="#_10_01" class="pginternal">*10·01</a>. As was pointed out in <a href="#_10" class="pginternal">*10</a>, we shall thus have
proved everything upon which subsequent proofs depend. The analogues
of *20·01·02 and of <a href="#_14_01" class="pginternal">*14·01</a> remain definitions, but those of <a href="#_10_01" class="pginternal">*10·01</a>
and <a href="#_13_01" class="pginternal">*13·01</a> become propositions to be proved. <a href="#_9_131" class="pginternal">*9·131</a> must be extended
by the definition: Two classes are "of the same type" when they
have predicative defining functions of the same type. In addition
to these, we have to prove the analogues of *10·1·11·12·121·122,
<a href="#_11_07" class="pginternal">*11·07</a> and *12·1·11. When these have been proved, the analogues of
other propositions follow by merely repeating previous proofs. These
analogues will, therefore, be quoted by the numbers of the original
propositions whose analogues they are.</p>

<p class="nind">

<b>*20·64.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (\alpha).f\alpha:(\alpha).g\alpha:\supset .f\beta.g\beta\)" src="images/1867.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.842ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1867.svg"></p>

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin {array}{l} \vdash.\text{*4·2.(*20·07)}.&amp;\supset \\ \vdash\colon\ldotp (\alpha).f\alpha:(\alpha).g\alpha:&amp;\equiv :(\phi).f\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\}:(\phi).g\{\hat{z}(\phi!z)\}:\\ [\text{*10·14}]   &amp;\supset :f\{\hat{z}(\psi!z)\}.g\{\hat{z}(\psi!z)\}\colon\ldotp \supset \vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1868.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.869ex; width: 56.23ex; height: 8.869ex;" id="img_images_1868.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_208">[Pg 208]</span></p>

<p>Observe that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_26">" is merely an abbreviation for any symbol of
the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\psi!z)\)" src="images/653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.966ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_653.svg_2">. This is why nothing further is required
in the above proof.</p>

<p>The above proposition is the analogue of <a href="#_10_14" class="pginternal">*10·14</a>. Like that proposition,
it requires, for the significance of the conclusion, that <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\)" src="images/53.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.244ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_53.svg_19"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(g\)" src="images/54.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.079ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_54.svg_3"> should be functions which take arguments of the same type. This
is not required for the significance of the hypothesis. Hence, though
the above proposition is true whenever it is significant, it is not
true whenever its hypothesis is significant.</p>

<p>*20·701·702·703 give the analogues, for classes, of <a href="#_12_11" class="pginternal">*12·11</a>.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*20·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha=\beta.\equiv :g!\alpha.\supset_{g}.g!\beta \quad[\text{*20·19}]\)" src="images/1874.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 33.837ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1874.svg"></p>

<p>This is the analogue of <a href="#_13_01" class="pginternal">*13·01</a>.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_209">[Pg 209]</span></p>

<p>This completes the proof that all propositions hitherto given apply to
classes as well as to individuals. Precisely similar reasoning extends
this result to classes of classes, classes of classes of classes, etc.</p>

<p>From the above propositions it appears that, although expressions such
as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_16"> have no meaning in isolation, yet those of their
formal properties with which we have been hitherto concerned are the
same as the corresponding properties of symbols which have a meaning
in isolation. Hence nothing in the apparatus hitherto introduced
requires us to determine whether a given symbol stands for a class or
not, unless the symbol occurs in a way in which only a class can occur
significantly. This is an important result, which enables us to give
much greater generality to our propositions than would otherwise be
possible.</p>

<p>The two following propositions (*20·8·81) are consequences of <a href="#_13_3" class="pginternal">*13·3</a>.
The "type" of any object <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_389"> will be defined in <a href="#_63" class="pginternal">*63</a> as the class of
terms either identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_390"> or not identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_391">. We may
define the "type of the arguments to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_26">" as the class of
arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_392"> for which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_107">" is significant, <i>i.e.</i> the
class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim} \phi x)\)" src="images/1875.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.614ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1875.svg">. Then the first of the
following propositions shows that if "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_27">" is significant, the
type of the arguments to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_27"> is the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_94">; the
second proposition shows that, if "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_28">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg_7">" are
both significant, the type of the arguments to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_28"> is the
same as the type of the arguments to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{z}\)" src="images/459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.525ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_459.svg_3">, because each is
the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_95">. <a href="#_20_8" class="pginternal">*20·8</a> will be used in <a href="#_63_11" class="pginternal">*63·11</a>, which is a fundamental
proposition in the theory of relative types.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_8">*20·8</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\phi a \lor {\sim}\phi a.\supset.\hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim} \phi x)=\hat{x}(x=a.\lor.x \neq a)\)" src="images/1876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1876.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*13·3.*10·11·21}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.\supset\colon\ldotp \phi x \lor {\sim} \phi x.\equiv_{x}:x=a.\lor.x \neq a\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*20·15}]\supset\colon\ldotp \hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim} \phi x)=\hat{x}(x=a.\lor.x \neq a)\colon\colon \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1877.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.801ex; width: 56.144ex; height: 8.733ex;" id="img_images_1877.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_20_81">*20·81</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\phi a \lor {\sim} \phi a.\psi a \lor {\sim} \psi a.\supset.\hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim}\phi x)=\hat{x}(\psi x \lor {\sim} \psi x)\)" src="images/1878.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.892ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1878.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*20·8}.\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim} \phi x)=\hat{x}(x=a.\lor.x \neq a) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*20·8}.\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\hat{x}(\psi x \lor {\sim} \psi x)=\hat{x}(x=a.\lor.x \neq a) &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).*10·121·13.Comp}.\supset\\ \vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim} \phi x)=\hat{x}(x=a.\lor.x \neq a).\hat{x}(\psi x \lor {\sim} \psi x)=\hat{x}(x=a.\lor.x \neq a).\\ [\text{*20·24}]\supset.\hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim} \phi x)=\hat{x}(\psi x \lor {\sim} \psi x):\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/1879.svg" style="vertical-align: -7.172ex; width: 87.375ex; height: 15.475ex;" id="img_images_1879.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the third line of the above proof, the use of <a href="#_10_121" class="pginternal">*10·121</a> depends upon
the fact that the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_96">" in both (1) and (2) must be such as to render
the hypothesis significant, <i>i.e.</i> such as to render
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}\phi a \lor {\sim}\phi a.\psi a \lor {\sim} \psi a\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/1880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 22.248ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1880.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_210">[Pg 210]</span>
significant. Hence the "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_97">" in (1) and the "a" in (2) must be of the
same type, by <a href="#_10_121" class="pginternal">*10·121</a>, and hence by <a href="#_10_13" class="pginternal">*10·13</a> we can assert the product of
(1) and (2), identifying the two "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_98">'s."</p>

<p>Since a type is the range of significance of a function, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_108">
is a function which is always true, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_17"> must be
a type. For if a function is always true, the arguments for which it
is true are the same as the arguments for which it is significant;
hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.213ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_415.svg_18"> is the range of significance of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_109">,
if (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . \phi x\)" src="images/163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.823ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_163.svg_15"> holds. Thus any class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_88"> is a type
if (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x).x\in \alpha\)" src="images/1881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.688ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1881.svg">. It follows that, whatever function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_82">
may be, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim}\phi x)\)" src="images/1882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.614ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1882.svg"> is a type; and in
particular, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}(x=a.\lor.x \neq a)\)" src="images/1883.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.592ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1883.svg"> is a type. Since <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_99"> is
a member of this class, this class is the type to which a belongs. In
virtue of <a href="#_20_8" class="pginternal">*20·8</a>, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_29"> is significant, the type to which a
belongs is the class of arguments for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi x\)" src="images/128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_128.svg_110"> is significant,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}(\phi x \lor {\sim}\phi x)\)" src="images/1882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.614ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1882.svg_1">. And if there is any
argument a for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi a\)" src="images/420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_420.svg_30"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi a\)" src="images/744.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.67ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_744.svg_8"> are both significant,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{x}\)" src="images/29.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.643ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_29.svg_50"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\hat{x}\)" src="images/246.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.767ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_246.svg_10"> have the same range of
significance, in virtue of <a href="#_20_81" class="pginternal">*20·81</a>.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_211">[Pg 211]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_21">*21. GENERAL THEORY OF RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *21.</p>

<p>The definitions and propositions of this number are exactly analogous
to those of <a href="#_20" class="pginternal">*20</a>, from which they differ by being concerned with
functions of two variables instead of one. A <i>relation</i>, as we
shall use the word, will be understood in extension: it may be regarded
as the class of couples (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y)\)" src="images/1884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.289ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1884.svg"> for which some given function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi(x,y)\)" src="images/1412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.642ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1412.svg_1"> is true. Its relation to the function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi(\hat{x},\hat{y})\)" src="images/1433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.642ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1433.svg_3">
is just like that of the class to its determining function.
We put</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_21_01">*21·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)\} .=: (\exists \phi):{\phi}!(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi(x,y): f\{{\phi}!(\hat{u}, \hat{v})\} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 59.93ex; height: 2.502ex;" id="img_images_1885.svg"></p>

<p>Here "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x, y)\)" src="images/1886.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.044ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1886.svg">" has no meaning in isolation, but
only in certain of its uses. In <a href="#_21_01" class="pginternal">*21·01</a> the <i>alphabetical</i> order
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(u\)" src="images/1180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_1180.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(v\)" src="images/1181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.097ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_1181.svg_8"> corresponds to the <i>typographical</i> order of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_21"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}\)" src="images/143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_143.svg_1"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)\}\)" src="images/1887.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.551ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1887.svg">, so that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f\{\hat{y}\hat{x}\psi(x,y)\} .=: (\exists \phi):{\phi}!(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi(x,y):f\{{\phi}!(\hat{v}, \hat{u})\} \quad \text{Df} \]" src="images/1888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 59.93ex; height: 2.502ex;" id="img_images_1888.svg"></span>
This is important in relation to the substitution-convention below.</p>

<p>It will be shown that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y) = \hat{x}\hat{y}\chi(x,y) .\equiv:\psi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\chi(x,y)\text{,} \]" src="images/1889.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 45.033ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1889.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> that two relations, as above defined, are identical when,
and only when, they are satisfied by the same pairs of arguments.</p>

<p>For substitution in <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!(\hat{x}, \hat{y})\)" src="images/1890.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.146ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1890.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}!(\hat{y}, \hat{x})\)" src="images/1891.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.146ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1891.svg">, we adopt the convention that when a
function (as opposed to its values) is represented in a form involving
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_22"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}\)" src="images/143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_143.svg_2">, or any other two letters of the alphabet,
the value of this function for the arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_100"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_27"> is to be
found by substituting <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_101"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_23"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_28"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}\)" src="images/143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_143.svg_3">,
while the value for the arguments <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_29"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_102"> is to be found by
substituting <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_30"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\)" src="images/142.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.857ex;" id="img_images_142.svg_24"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_103"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}\)" src="images/143.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_143.svg_4">. That
is, the argument mentioned first is to be substituted for the letter
which comes first in the alphabet, and the argument mentioned second
for the later letter; thus the mode of substitution depends upon the
<i>alphabetical</i> order of the letters which have circumflexes and
the <i>typographical</i> order of the other letters.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_212">[Pg 212]</span></p>

<p>The above convention as to order is presupposed in the following
definition, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_104"> is the first argument mentioned and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_31"> the
second:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\{\phi!(\hat{x},\hat{y})\}b.=.\phi!(a,b) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1892.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.943ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1892.svg"></p>

<p>Hence, following the convention,</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ b\{\phi!(\hat{x},\hat{y})\}a.=.\phi!(b,a) \quad\text{Df}\\ a\{\phi!(\hat{y},\hat{x})\}b.=.\phi!(b,a) \quad\text{Df}\\ b\{\phi!(\hat{y},\hat{x})\}a.=.\phi!(a,b) \quad\text{Df} \]" src="images/1893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 80.828ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1893.svg"></span>
This definition is not used as it stands, but is introduced for the
sake of
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ a\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)\}b.\equiv:(\exists \phi):\phi!(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi(x,y):\phi!(a,b) \]" src="images/1894.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 52.439ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1894.svg"></span>
which results from *21·01·02. We shall use capital Latin
letters to represent variable expressions of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)\)" src="images/1895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.549ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1895.svg">, just as we used Greek letters for
variable expressions of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi!z)\)" src="images/1766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.842ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1766.svg_4">. If a capital
Latin letter, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_77">, is used as an apparent variable, it is
supposed that the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_78"> which occurs in the form "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(R)\)" src="images/1896.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 2.597ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1896.svg">" or
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists R)\)" src="images/1897.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.855ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1897.svg">" is to be replaced by "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi)\)" src="images/1552.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 2.229ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1552.svg_1">" or "(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists\phi)\)" src="images/1898.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.486ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1898.svg">,"
while the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_79"> which occurs later is to be replaced by
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)\)" src="images/1895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.549ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1895.svg_1">." In fact we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (R).fR.=.(\phi).f\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/1899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.7ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1899.svg"></span>
The use of single letters for such expressions as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi(x,y)\)" src="images/1900.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.92ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1900.svg"> is a practically indispensable convenience.</p>

<p>The following is the definition of the class of relations:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}=\hat{R}{(\exists \phi).R=\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/1901.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.372ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_1901.svg"></p>

<p>Similar remarks apply to it as to the definition of "Cls" (<a href="#_20_03" class="pginternal">*20·03</a>).</p>

<p>In virtue of the definitions *21·01·02 and the convention as to
capital Latin letters, the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xRy\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_266.svg_3">" will mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_393"> has the
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_80"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_140">." This notation is practically convenient, and
will, after the preliminaries, wholly replace the cumbrous notation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi(x,y)\}y\)" src="images/1902.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.585ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1902.svg">.</p>

<p>The proofs of the propositions of this number are usually omitted,
since they are exactly analogous to those of <a href="#_20" class="pginternal">*20</a>, merely substituting
<a href="#_12_11" class="pginternal">*12·11</a> for <a href="#_12_1" class="pginternal">*12·1</a>, and propositions in <a href="#_11" class="pginternal">*11</a> for propositions in <a href="#_10" class="pginternal">*10</a>.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number, like those of <a href="#_20" class="pginternal">*20</a>, fall into three
sections. Those of the second section are seldom referred to. Those
of the third section, extending to relations the formal properties
hitherto assumed or proved for individuals and functions, are not
explicitly referred to in the sequel, but are constantly relevant,
namely whenever a proposition which has been assumed or proved for
individuals and functions is applied to relations. The principal
propositions of the first section are the following.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp\psi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\chi(x,y):\equiv.\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y}\chi(x,y)\)" src="images/1903.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 47.798ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1903.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> two relations are identical when, and only when, their
defining functions are formally equivalent.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y}\chi(x,y).\equiv:x\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)\}y.\equiv_{x,y}.x\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\chi(x,y)\}y\)" src="images/1904.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 61.934ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1904.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_213">[Pg 213]</span></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> two relations are identical when, and only when, they hold
between the same pairs of terms. The same fact is expressed by the
following proposition:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b><a id="_21_43">*21·43</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp R=S.\equiv:xRy.\equiv_{x,y}.xSy\)" src="images/1905.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 27.697ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1905.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·2·21·22</b> show that identity of relations is reflexive,
symmetrical and transitive.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x{\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)}y.\equiv.\psi(x,y)\)" src="images/1906.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.501ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1906.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> two terms have a given relation when, and only when, they
satisfy its defining function.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·151.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.(\exists \phi).\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)\)" src="images/1907.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.372ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1907.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<i>I.e.</i> every relation can be defined by a predicative function.
Hence when, using <a href="#_21_07" class="pginternal">*21·07</a> or <a href="#_21_071" class="pginternal">*21·071</a>, we have a relation as apparent
variable, and are therefore confined to predicative defining functions,
there is no loss of generality.</p>

<p class="nind">

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f\{\hat{y}\hat{x}\psi(x,y)\}.=:(\exists \phi):\phi!(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi(x,y):f\{\phi!(\hat{v},\hat{u})\} \quad\text{Df} \]" src="images/1911.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 59.93ex; height: 2.502ex;" id="img_images_1911.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following definitions merely extend to relations, with as little
modification as possible, the definitions already given for other
symbols.</p>

<p>This proposition proves that every proposition about a relation
expresses an extensional property of the determining function.</p>

<p class="nind">

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·112</b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp(\exists g)\colon\ldotp f\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)\}.\equiv_{\phi}.g!\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)\} \quad[\text{*12·1.*21·111}]\)" src="images/1923.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 57.712ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1923.svg"></p>

<p>It is <a href="#_12_1" class="pginternal">*12·1</a>, not <a href="#_12_11" class="pginternal">*12·11</a>, which is required in this proposition, because
we are concerned with a function (<img alt="" data-tex="\(f)\)" src="images/1924.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 2.124ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1924.svg"> of <i>one</i> variable, namely
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_83">, although that one variable is itself a function of two
variables.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·12.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp (\exists \phi)\colon\ldotp \phi!(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\psi(x,y):f\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)\}.\equiv.f\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)\}\\ &amp;\quad[\text{*21·11.*12·11}]\end{align}\]" src="images/1925.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.155ex; width: 61.558ex; height: 5.441ex;" id="img_images_1925.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \psi(x,y).\equiv_{x,y}.\chi(x,y):\equiv.\hat{x}\hat{y}\psi(x,y)=\hat{x}\hat{y}\chi(x,y) \quad[\text{*21·13·14}]\)" src="images/1928.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 60.495ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_1928.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition states that two double functions determine the same
relation when, and only when, they are formally equivalent, <i>i.e.</i>
are satisfied by the same pairs of arguments. This is a fundamental
property of relations as defined above (<a href="#_21_01" class="pginternal">*21·01</a>).</p>

<b>*21·56.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{E}!(℩R)\{xRy.\equiv_{x,y}.\phi(x,y)\} \quad[\text{*21·55.*14·21}]\)" src="images/1953.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 45.116ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1953.svg"></p>

<b>*21·57.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash\colon\ldotp \hat{x}\hat{y}\phi(x,y)=(℩R)(fR).\supset:g\{\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi(x,y)\}.&amp;\equiv.g\{(℩R)(fR)\}\\ &amp;\quad[\text{*14·1.*21·54.*13·183}]\end{align}\]" src="images/1954.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.104ex; width: 65.436ex; height: 5.339ex;" id="img_images_1954.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·58.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi(x,y)=({℩}R)\{R=\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi(x,y)\} \quad[\text{*4·2.*10·11.*21·54.*14·1}]\)" src="images/1955.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.231ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1955.svg"></p>

<p>The following propositions are the analogues of <a href="#_20_6" class="pginternal">*20·6</a> ff., and have a
similar purpose.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·6.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists R).fR.\equiv.{\sim}\{(R).{\sim}fR\} \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·6}]\)" src="images/1956.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.006ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1956.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·61.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(R).fR.\supset.fS \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·61}]\)" src="images/1957.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.355ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1957.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·62.</b> When <img alt="" data-tex="\(fR\)" src="images/1958.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.962ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1958.svg"> is true, whatever possible argument of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}\phi!(x,y)\)" src="images/1895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.549ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1895.svg_2">
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_82"> may be, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(R).fR\)" src="images/1959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.565ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1959.svg"> is true. [Proof as in <a href="#_20_62" class="pginternal">*20·62</a>]</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·63.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (R).p\lor fR.\supset:p.\lor.(R).fR \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·63}]\)" src="images/1960.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 51.414ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1960.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·631.</b> If "<img alt="" data-tex="\(fR\)" src="images/1958.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.962ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1958.svg_1">" is significant, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_18"> is of the
same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_83">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(fS\)" src="images/1961.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.704ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1961.svg">" is significant, and vice versa.</p>

<p>[Proof as in <a href="#_20_631" class="pginternal">*20·631</a>]</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_216">[Pg 216]</span></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·632.</b> If, for some <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_84">, there is a proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(fR\)" src="images/1958.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.962ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_1958.svg_2">, then
there is a function <img alt="" data-tex="\(f\hat{R}\)" src="images/706.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.962ex; height: 2.842ex;" id="img_images_706.svg_1">, and vice versa.</p>

<p>[Proof as in <a href="#_20_632" class="pginternal">*20·632</a>]</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·633.</b> "Whatever possible relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_85"> may be, <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(R,S)\)" src="images/1962.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.187ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1962.svg">
is true whatever possible relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_19"> may be" implies "whatever
possible relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_20"> may be, <img alt="" data-tex="\(f(R,S)\)" src="images/1962.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.187ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1962.svg_1"> is true whatever possible
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_86"> may be."</p>

<p>[Proof as in <a href="#_20_633" class="pginternal">*20·633</a>]</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·64.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp (R).fR:(R).gR:\supset.fS.gS \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·64}]\)" src="images/1963.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 51.071ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1963.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·7.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists g):fR.\equiv_{R}.g!R \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·7}]\)" src="images/1964.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.847ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1964.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·701.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists g):f(R, x).\equiv_{R,x}.g!(R, x) \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·701}]\)" src="images/1965.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 51.59ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1965.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·702.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists g):f(x, R).\equiv_{R,x}.g!(R, x) \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·702}]\)" src="images/1966.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 51.59ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1966.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·703.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists g):f(R, S).\equiv_{R,S}.g!(R, S) \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·703}]\)" src="images/1967.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 52.037ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1967.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·704.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists g):f(R, \alpha).\equiv_{R,\alpha}.g!(R, \alpha) \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·703}]\)" src="images/1968.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 52.006ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1968.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·705.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:(\exists g):f(\alpha, R).\equiv_{\alpha,R}.g!(\alpha, R) \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·703}]\)" src="images/1969.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 52.006ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_1969.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*21·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp R=S.\equiv:g!R.\supset_{g}.g!S \quad[\text{Proof as in *20·71}]\)" src="images/1970.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 45.722ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_1970.svg"></p>

<p>From the above propositions it appears that relations, like classes,
have all the formal properties which they would have if they were
symbols having a meaning in isolation. Hence unless a symbol occurs
in a way in which only a relation can occur significantly, we do not
need to decide whether it stands for a relation or not. This result,
like the corresponding result for classes mentioned at the end of *20,
is important as giving greater generality to our propositions than
they would otherwise possess. The results obtained in <a href="#_20" class="pginternal">*20</a> and <a href="#_21" class="pginternal">*21</a> for
classes and relations whose members or terms are neither classes nor
relations can be extended, by mere repetition of the proofs, to classes
of classes, classes of relations, relations of classes, relations of
relations, and so on.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_217">[Pg 217]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_22">*22. CALCULUS OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *22.</p>

<p>In this number we reach what was historically the starting-point of
symbolic logic. The Greek letters used (except <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\)" src="images/55.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.348ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_55.svg_84">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\psi\)" src="images/56.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.473ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_56.svg_37">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\chi\)" src="images/57.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.462ex; width: 1.416ex; height: 1.462ex;" id="img_images_57.svg_13">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\theta\)" src="images/51.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.618ex;" id="img_images_51.svg_10">) are always to stand for expressions of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}({\phi}!x)\)" src="images/1971.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.326ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1971.svg">, or, where the Greek letters are not apparent
variables, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}({\phi}x)\)" src="images/235.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.697ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_235.svg_1">. The small Latin letters may either
be such as have a meaning in isolation, or may represent classes or
relations; this is possible in virtue of the notes at the ends of <a href="#_20" class="pginternal">*20</a>
and <a href="#_21" class="pginternal">*21</a>. We put:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset \beta .=: x \in \alpha .\supset_{x}. x \in \beta \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1972.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 30.176ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1972.svg"></p>

<p>This defines "the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_89"> is contained in the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_27">," or "all <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_90">'s are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_28">'s."</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta  = \hat{x}(x \in \alpha . x \in \beta) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1973.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.852ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1973.svg"></p>

<p>This defines the logical product or common part of two classes
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_91"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_29">.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \beta = \hat{x}(x \in \alpha .\lor. x \in \beta) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1974.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.368ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1974.svg"></p>

<p>This defines the logical sum of two classes; it is the class consisting
of all the members of one together with all the members of the other.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(-\alpha = \hat{x}(x {\sim}{\in} \alpha) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1975.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.974ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1975.svg"></p>

<p>This defines the negation of a class. It is read "not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_92">." It
does not contain every object <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_396"> concerning which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_3">"
is <i>not true</i>, but only those objects concerning which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_4">"
is <i>false</i>; <i>i.e.</i> it excludes those objects for
which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_5">" is meaningless. Thus it consists of all
objects, of the type next below <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_93">, which are not members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_94">; but it does not contain objects of any other type but this.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·05.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha - \beta = \alpha \cap -\beta \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/1976.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1976.svg"></p>

<p>This definition gives an abbreviation which is often convenient.</p>

<p>The postulates required for the algebra of logic have been enumerated
by Huntington<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_54" id="FNanchor_54">[54]</a>. In our notation, they are as follows.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_218">[Pg 218]</span></p>

<p>We assume a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(K\)" src="images/1977.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.011ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1977.svg">, with two rules of combination, namely
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\cup\)" src="images/1978.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_1978.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\cap\)" src="images/1979.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_1979.svg">; and we then require the following ten postulates:</p>

<p>I <i>a.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup b\)" src="images/1980.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.682ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1980.svg"> is in the class whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_105"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_32"> are
in the class.</p>

<p>I <i>b.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap b\)" src="images/1981.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.682ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1981.svg"> is in the class whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_106"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_33"> are
in the class.</p>

<p>II <i>a.</i> There is an element <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_5"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup \Lambda = a\)" src="images/1982.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.495ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_1982.svg">
for every element <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_107">.</p>

<p>II <i>b.</i> There is an element <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_3"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap\text{V} = a\)" src="images/1983.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.622ex; height: 1.731ex;" id="img_images_1983.svg">
for every element <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_108">.</p>

<p>III <i>a.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup b = b \cup a\)" src="images/1984.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 12.381ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_1984.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_109">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_34">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup b\)" src="images/1980.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.682ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1980.svg_1">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b \cup a\)" src="images/1985.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.682ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1985.svg"> are in the class.</p>

<p>III <i>b.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap b = b \cap a\)" src="images/1986.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 12.381ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_1986.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_110">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_35">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap b\)" src="images/1981.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.682ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1981.svg_1">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(b \cap a\)" src="images/1987.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.682ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1987.svg"> are in the class.</p>

<p>IV <i>a.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup (b \cap c) = (a \cup b) \cap (a \cup c)\)" src="images/1988.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.361ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1988.svg">
whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_111">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_36">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_18">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup b\)" src="images/1980.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.682ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1980.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup c\)" src="images/1989.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.691ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_1989.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(b \cap c\)" src="images/1990.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.465ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1990.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup (b \cap c)\)" src="images/1991.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.936ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1991.svg">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\((a \cup b) \cap (a \cup c)\)" src="images/1992.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.408ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1992.svg"> are in the
class.</p>

<p>IV <i>b.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap (b \cup c) = (a \cap b) \cup (a \cap c)\)" src="images/1993.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.361ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1993.svg">
whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_112">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_37">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_19">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap b\)" src="images/1981.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.682ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1981.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap c\)" src="images/1994.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.691ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_1994.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(b \cup c\)" src="images/1995.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.465ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_1995.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap (b \cup c)\)" src="images/1996.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.936ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1996.svg">, and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap b) \cup (a \cap c)\)" src="images/1997.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.528ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_1997.svg"> are in the
class.</p>

<p>V. If the elements <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_4"> in postulates II
<i>a</i> and II <i>b</i> exist and are unique, then for every element
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_113"> there is an element <img alt="" data-tex="\(-a\)" src="images/1998.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 2.957ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_1998.svg"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cup -a = \text{V}\)" src="images/1999.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 11.382ex; height: 1.731ex;" id="img_images_1999.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a \cap -a = \Lambda\)" src="images/2000.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 11.256ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_2000.svg">.</p>

<p>VI. There are at least two elements, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_397"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_142">, in the class,
such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \neq y\)" src="images/2001.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2001.svg">.</p>

<p>The form of the above postulates is such that they are mutually
independent, <i>i.e.</i> any nine of them are satisfied by
interpretations of the symbols which do not satisfy the remaining one.</p>

<p>For our purposes, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(K\)" src="images/1977.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.011ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_1977.svg_1">" must be replaced by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/2002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2002.svg">."
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_5"> will be the null-class and the universal
class, which are defined in <a href="#_24" class="pginternal">*24</a>. Then the above ten postulates are
proved below, as follows:</p>

<p>I <i>a</i>. in *22·37, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \alpha \cup \beta \in \text{Cls}\)" src="images/2003.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 13.551ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2003.svg">"</p>

<p>I <i>b</i>. in *22·36, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \alpha \cap \beta \in \text{Cls}\)" src="images/2004.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 13.551ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2004.svg">"</p>

<p>II <i>a</i>. in *24·24, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \alpha \cup \Lambda = \alpha\)" src="images/2005.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 12.386ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_2005.svg">"</p>

<p>II <i>b</i>. in *24·26, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . a \cap \text{V} = \alpha\)" src="images/2006.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 12.262ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_2006.svg">"</p>

<p>III <i>a</i>. in *22·57, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . a \cup \beta = \beta \cup \alpha\)" src="images/2007.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.641ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2007.svg">"</p>

<p>III <i>b</i>. in *22·51, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \alpha \cap \beta = \beta \cap \alpha\)" src="images/2008.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.892ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2008.svg">"</p>

<p>IV <i>a</i>. in *22·69, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . (\alpha \cup \beta) \cap (\alpha \cup \gamma) = \alpha \cup (\beta \cap \gamma)\)" src="images/2009.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.621ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2009.svg">"</p>

<p>IV <i>b</i>. in *22·68, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . (\alpha \cap \beta) \cup (\alpha \cap \gamma) = \alpha \cap (\beta \cup \gamma)\)" src="images/2010.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.621ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2010.svg">"</p>

<p>V. in *24·21·22, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \alpha \cap -\alpha = \Lambda\)" src="images/2011.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 14.146ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_2011.svg">" and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \alpha \cup -\alpha = \text{V}\)" src="images/2012.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 14.273ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_2012.svg">"</p>

<p>VI. in *24·1, namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \Lambda \neq \text{V}\)" src="images/2013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 8.672ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2013.svg">"</p>

<p>Hence, assuming Huntington's analysis of the postulates for the formal
algebra of logic, the propositions proved in what follows suffice
to establish that this algebra holds for classes. The corresponding
propositions of <a href="#_23" class="pginternal">*23</a> and <a href="#_25" class="pginternal">*25</a> prove that it holds for relations,
substituting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}\)" src="images/2014.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 3.299ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_2014.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x228d}\)" src="images/2015.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2015.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\cap}\)" src="images/2016.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 2.138ex;" id="img_images_2016.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\text{V}}\)" src="images/311.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 2.33ex;" id="img_images_311.svg_2"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/2002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2002.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\cup\)" src="images/1978.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_1978.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\cap\)" src="images/1979.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_1979.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_8">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_6">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_219">[Pg 219]</span></p>

<p>The principal propositions of the present number are the following:</p>

<p>(1) Those embodying the formal rules:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \alpha \cap \beta = \beta \cap \alpha\)" src="images/2017.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.892ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2017.svg"></p>

<p>These embody the commutative law.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. (\alpha \cap \beta) \cap \gamma = \alpha \cap (\beta \cap \gamma)\)" src="images/2019.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.898ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2019.svg"></p>

<p>These embody the associative law.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \alpha \cap \alpha = \alpha\)" src="images/2021.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 12.264ex; height: 1.756ex;" id="img_images_2021.svg"></p>
