<p>These embody the law of tautology.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·68.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. (\alpha \cap \beta) \cup (\alpha \cap \gamma) = \alpha \cap (\beta \cup \gamma)\)" src="images/2023.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.621ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2023.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·69.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. (\alpha \cup \beta) \cap (\alpha \cup \gamma) = \alpha \cup (\beta \cap \gamma)\)" src="images/2024.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.621ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2024.svg"></p>

<p>These embody the distributive law. It will be seen that the second
results from the first by everywhere interchanging the signs of
addition and multiplication.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·8.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. -(-\alpha) = \alpha\)" src="images/2025.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.582ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2025.svg"></p>

<p>This is the principle of double negation.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·81.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \alpha \subset \beta .\equiv. -\beta \subset -\alpha\)" src="images/2026.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 21.424ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2026.svg"></p>

<p>This is the principle of transposition.</p>

<p>(2) Other useful propositions:</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·44.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \alpha \subset \beta . \beta \subset \gamma .\supset. \alpha \subset \gamma\)" src="images/2027.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 24.383ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2027.svg"></p>

<p>These embody the two forms of the syllogism in Barbara.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·62.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \alpha \subset \beta .\equiv. \alpha \cup \beta = \beta\)" src="images/2029.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 21.698ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2029.svg"></p>

into an equation.</p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_95"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_30">" is identical with "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_96"> or
the part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_31"> which is excluded from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_97">."</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*22·35.*5·19}.&amp;\supset\vdash:{\sim}\{x\in -\alpha.\equiv.x\in \alpha\}:\\ [\text{*10·11}] &amp;\supset\vdash:(x):{\sim}\{x\in -\alpha.\equiv.x\in \alpha\}:\\ [\text{*10·251}]  &amp;\supset\vdash:{\sim}\{(x):x\in -\alpha.\equiv.x\in \alpha\}:\\ [\text{*20·43.Transp}]&amp;\supset\vdash:{\sim}(-\alpha=\alpha):\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/2045.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 48.662ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_2045.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is used in proving that the null-class is not
identical with the class containing everything (<a href="#_24_1" class="pginternal">*24·1</a>), which is used
to show that at least two classes exist. Our axioms do not suffice
to prove that more than one <i>individual</i> exists, but they
prove the existence of at least two <i>classes</i> and at least two
<i>relations</i>.</p>

<p class="nind">

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*22·33}. \supset\vdash:x\in \hat{z}(\phi z)\cap \hat{z}(\psi z).&amp;\equiv.x\in \hat{z}(\phi z).x\in \hat{z}(\psi z).\\ [\text{*20·3}] &amp;\equiv.\phi x.\psi x &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*20·33}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/2050.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.801ex; width: 66.845ex; height: 8.733ex;" id="img_images_2050.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind">

<p>Thus logical multiplication of classes obeys the commutative and
associative laws. References to *22·33·34·35 and to <a href="#_20_43" class="pginternal">*20·43</a> will in
future often be omitted.</p>

is false. We have only
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha\subset\beta.\lor.\alpha\subset\gamma:\supset.\alpha\subset\beta\cup\gamma \]" src="images/2082.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 28.473ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2082.svg"></span></p>

<p>The proof proceeds as in <a href="#_22_62" class="pginternal">*22·62</a>. The proposition <a href="#_22_621" class="pginternal">*22·621</a> is one of the
most useful propositions in the present number.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_22_63">*22·63</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha\cup(\alpha\cap\beta)=\alpha  \quad[\text{*4·44}]\)" src="images/2089.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.745ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2089.svg"></p>

<p>The process of obtaining <a href="#_22_63" class="pginternal">*22·63</a> from <a href="#_4_44" class="pginternal">*4·44</a> is of the same kind as the
process employed in the proofs that have been written out in this
number.<span class="pagenum" id="Page_223">[Pg 223]</span> Hence only *4·44 is referred to. We shall similarly restrict
references for later propositions in this number. The process is always
roughly as follows: <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_279">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(q\)" src="images/32.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.041ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_32.svg_187">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_47"> are replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\alpha\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\beta\)" src="images/2090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.341ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2090.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\gamma\)" src="images/2091.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.289ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2091.svg">; then <a href="#_10_11" class="pginternal">*10·11</a> is applied, and such further
propositions of <a href="#_10" class="pginternal">*10</a> as may be required, together with *22·33·34·35.</p>

<p class="nind">
<b>*22·631.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\alpha\cap(\alpha\cup\beta)=\alpha \quad[\text{*22·58·621}]\)" src="images/2092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.647ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2092.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">

<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*22·47·51}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\alpha\subset\gamma.\supset.\alpha\cap\beta\subset\gamma:\beta\subset\gamma.\supset.\alpha\cap\beta\subset\gamma &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*4·77}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/2096.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 68.162ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_2096.svg"></span></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_226">[Pg 226]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_23">*23. CALCULUS OF RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *23.</p>

<p>The definitions and propositions of this number are to be exact
analogues of those of <a href="#_22" class="pginternal">*22</a>. Properties of relations which have no
analogues for classes will not be dealt with till Section D. Proofs
will be omitted in the present number, as they are precisely analogous
to those of analogous propositions in *22. In this number, as always
in future, capital Latin letters stand for expressions of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}{\phi}!(x, y)\)" src="images/2130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.549ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2130.svg">, or, where they are not being used as
apparent variables, for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}{\phi}(x, y)\)" src="images/2131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.92ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2131.svg">. The principal
propositions of this number are the analogues of those of *22.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_229">[Pg 229]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_24">*24. THE UNIVERSAL CLASS, THE NULL-CLASS, AND THE EXISTENCE
OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *24.</p>

<p>The universal class, denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_7">, is the class of all
objects of the type which, in the given context, is being denoted by
small Latin letters, <i>i.e.</i> of the lowest type concerned. Thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_8">, like "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/2002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2002.svg_2">," is ambiguous as to type. Its
definition is as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V} = \hat{x}(x = x) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/2211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.057ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2211.svg"></p>

<p>Any other property possessed by everything would do as well as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x = x\)" src="images/2212.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.605ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_2212.svg">,"
but this is the only such property which we have hitherto studied.</p>

<p>The null-class, denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_9">, is the class which has no
members. Like <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_9">, it is ambiguous as to type. We use the
same symbol, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_10">, for null-classes of various types; but these
null-classes differ. The type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_11"> is determined by that of
the terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_398"> concerning which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \Lambda\)" src="images/2213.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.63ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2213.svg">" is false: whatever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_399"> may be, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \Lambda\)" src="images/2213.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.63ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2213.svg_1">" will not represent a <i>true</i>
proposition, but unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_400"> is of the appropriate type, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \Lambda\)" src="images/2213.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.63ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2213.svg_2">"
will be meaningless, not false. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_12"> is of the
type next above that of an <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_401"> concerning which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \Lambda\)" src="images/2213.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.63ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2213.svg_3">"
is significant and false. The definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_13"> is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda = -\text{V} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/2214.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 12.728ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_2214.svg"></p>

<p>When a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_98"> is not null, so that it has one or more
members, it is said to <i>exist</i>. (This sense of "existence" must
not be confused with that defined in <a href="#_14_02" class="pginternal">*14·02</a>.) We write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\alpha\)" src="images/2215.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.335ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_2215.svg">"
for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_99"> exists." The definition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists! \alpha .=. (\exists x) . x \in \alpha \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/2216.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.617ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2216.svg"></p>

<p>In the present number, we shall deal first with the properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_10">, then with those of existence. In
comparing the algebra of symbolic logic with ordinary algebra,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_15"> takes the place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(0\)" src="images/979.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.557ex;" id="img_images_979.svg_8">, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_11"> combines the
properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_12"> and of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\infty\)" src="images/2217.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_2217.svg">.</p>

<p>Among the more important properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_16"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_12"> which are
proved in this number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_24_1">*24·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \Lambda \neq \text{V}\)" src="images/2013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 8.672ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2013.svg_1"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "nothing is not everything." This is useful as giving us
the existence of at least two classes. If the monistic philosophers
were right in maintaining that only one individual exists, there would
be only two classes,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_230">[Pg 230]</span> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_17"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_13">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_14"> being
(in that case) the class whose only member is the one individual. Our
primitive propositions do not require the existence of more than one
individual.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·102·103</b> show that any function which is always true
determines the universal class, and any function which is always false
determines the null-class.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·21·22</b> give forms of the laws of contradiction and excluded
middle, namely "nothing is both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_100"> and not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_101">"
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cap - \alpha = \Lambda)\)" src="images/2218.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.638ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2218.svg"> and "everything is either
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_102"> or not-<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_103">" (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cap - \alpha = \text{V})\)" src="images/2219.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.765ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2219.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·23·24·26·27</b> give the properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_15"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_18"> with respect to addition and multiplication, namely:
multiplication by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_16"> and addition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_19"> make
no change in a class (*24·26·24); addition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_17"> gives
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_18">, and multiplication by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_20"> gives <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_21">
(*24·27·23). It will be observed that the properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_22">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_19"> result from each other by interchanging addition and
multiplication.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_24_3">*24·3</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon \alpha\subset\beta.\equiv.\alpha - \beta = \Lambda\)" src="images/2220.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 21.988ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_2220.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_104"> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_32">" is equivalent to
"nothing is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_105"> but not <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_33">."</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·311.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon \alpha\subset - \beta.\equiv.\alpha\cap\beta = \Lambda\)" src="images/2221.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 23.497ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_2221.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "no <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_106"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_34">" is equivalent to "nothing is
both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_107"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_35">."</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·411.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\beta\subset\alpha.\supset\alpha = \beta\cup(\alpha - \beta)\)" src="images/2222.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.043ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2222.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\alpha - \beta\subset\gamma.\equiv.\alpha\subset\beta\cup\gamma\)" src="images/2223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 25.389ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_2223.svg"></p>

<p>As a rule, propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_20"> are much less used than
the correlative propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_23">.</p>

<p>The properties of the existence of classes result from those of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_24">, owing to the fact that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\alpha\)" src="images/2215.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.335ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_2215.svg_1"> is the
contradictory of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = \Lambda\)" src="images/2224.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.035ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_2224.svg">, as is proved in <a href="#_24_54" class="pginternal">*24·54</a>. Thus we
have, in virtue of <a href="#_24_3" class="pginternal">*24·3</a>,</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon{\sim}(\alpha\subset\beta).\equiv.\exists!\alpha - \beta\)" src="images/2225.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.808ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2225.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "not all <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_108">'s are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_36">'s" is equivalent
to "there are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_109">'s which are not <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_37">'s." This is the
familiar proposition of formal logic, that the contradictory of the
universal affirmative is the particular negative.</p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·56.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \exists!(\alpha\cup\beta).\equiv:\exists!\alpha.\lor.\exists!\beta\)" src="images/2226.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.332ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2226.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·561.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\exists!(\alpha\cap\beta).\supset.\exists!\alpha.\exists!\beta\)" src="images/2227.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.559ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2227.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if a sum exists, then one of the summands exists, and vice
versa; and if a product exists, both the factors exist (but not vice
versa).</p>

<p>The proofs of propositions in the present number offer no difficulty.</p>

<p>In the remainder of this number we shall be concerned with the
existence of classes. Many of the properties of the existence of
classes follow from the fact that to say a class exists is equivalent
to saying that the class is not equal to the null-class. This is proved
in <a href="#_24_54" class="pginternal">*24·54</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\exists!\alpha.\equiv.(\exists x).x \in \alpha \quad[\text{*4·2.(*24·03)}]\)" src="images/2325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.539ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2325.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24*51</b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon{\sim}\exists!\alpha.\equiv.\alpha=\Lambda\)" src="images/2326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 17.291ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_2326.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*24·5}.\supset\vdash\colon{\sim}\exists!\alpha.&amp;\equiv.{\sim}\{(\exists x).x  \in \alpha\}.\\ [\text{*10·252}] &amp;\equiv.(x).x{\sim}\in \alpha.\\ [\text{*24·15}] &amp;\equiv.\alpha=\Lambda\colon\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/2327.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 39.456ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_2327.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_24_52">*24·52</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\exists!\text{V} \quad [\text{*24·51·1.Transp}]\)" src="images/2328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.225ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2328.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition states that the class of all objects of the type in
question is not null, but has at least one member. The assumption
that there is something, which is equivalent to this proposition,
is implicit in the proposition <a href="#_10_1" class="pginternal">*10·1</a>, that what is true always is
true in any instance. This would not hold if there were no instances
of anything; hence it implies the existence of something. It will
be observed that the above proposition (<a href="#_24_52" class="pginternal">*24·52</a>) depends on <a href="#_24_1" class="pginternal">*24·1</a>,
which depends on <a href="#_23_351" class="pginternal">*23·351</a>, which depends on <a href="#_10_251" class="pginternal">*10·251</a>, which depends on
<a href="#_10_24" class="pginternal">*10·24</a>, which depends on *10·1 or on <a href="#_9_1" class="pginternal">*9·1</a>. The assumption that there
is something is involved in the use of the real variable, which would
otherwise be meaningless. This is made explicit in *9·1, and in the
proof of <a href="#_9_2" class="pginternal">*9·2</a>, which is the same proposition as *10·1.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·53.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.{\sim}\exists!\Lambda \quad[\text{*24·51.*20·2}]\)" src="images/2329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.194ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2329.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*24·63.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp\Lambda{\sim}\in\kappa.\equiv:\alpha\in\kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\exists!\alpha\)" src="images/2343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 28.653ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2343.svg"></p>


<p>In this proposition, the conditions of significance require that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_2"> should be a class of classes. The condition "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in\kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\exists!\alpha\)" src="images/2344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 13.836ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2344.svg">"
is one required as hypothesis in many propositions. In virtue of the
above proposition, this hypothesis may be replaced by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda{\sim}\in\kappa\)" src="images/2345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.399ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2345.svg">."</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*13·191}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp\Lambda{\sim}\in\kappa.&amp;\equiv\colon \alpha = \Lambda.\supset_{\alpha}.\alpha{\sim}\in\kappa\colon\\ [\text{Transp}]&amp;\equiv\colon\alpha\in\kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\alpha\neq\Lambda\colon\\ [\text{*24·54}]&amp;\equiv\colon\alpha\in\kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\exists!\alpha \colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/2346.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 53.836ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_2346.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is frequently used in later parts of the work. We
often have to deal with classes of existent classes, and the most
convenient form in which to state that all the members of a class of
classes exist is "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda{\sim}\in\kappa\)" src="images/2345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 7.399ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_2345.svg_1">."</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_241">[Pg 241]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_25">*25. THE UNIVERSAL RELATION, THE NULL RELATION, AND THE
EXISTENCE OF RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *25.</p>

<p>This number contains the analogues, for relations, of the definitions
and propositions of <a href="#_24" class="pginternal">*24</a>. Proofs will not be given, as they proceed
precisely as in *24.</p>

<p>The universal relation, denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\text{V}}\)" src="images/311.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 2.33ex;" id="img_images_311.svg_3">, is the relation
which holds between any two terms whatever of the appropriate types,
whatever these may be in the given context. The null relation,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_4">, is the relation which does not hold between any
pair of terms whatever, its type being fixed by the types of the terms
concerning which the denial that it holds is significant. A relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_87"> is said to <i>exist</i> when there is at least one pair of terms
between which it holds; "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_88"> exists" is written "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\exists}!R\)" src="images/2347.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.604ex; height: 2.353ex;" id="img_images_2347.svg">."</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are much less often referred to
than those of *24, but for the sake of uniformity we have given the
analogues of all propositions in *24, with the same numeration (except
for the integral part).</p>

<p>All the remarks made in *24 apply, <i>mutatis mutandis</i>, in the
present number.</p>

<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_244">[Pg 244]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_D_a">SECTION D.<br>
LOGIC OF RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p>In the present section we shall be concerned with such of the general
properties of relations as have no analogues in the theory of classes.
The notations introduced in this section will be used constantly
throughout the rest of the work, and the ideas expressed in the
definitions will be found to be of fundamental importance.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_245">[Pg 245]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_30">*30. DESCRIPTIVE FUNCTIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *30.</p>

<p>The functions hitherto considered, with the exception of a few
particular functions such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta\)" src="images/267.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_267.svg_2">, have been
propositional, <i>i.e.</i> have had propositions for their values.
But the ordinary functions of mathematics, such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x^{2}\)" src="images/2421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.912ex;" id="img_images_2421.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin x\)" src="images/147.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.449ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_147.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\log x\)" src="images/148.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 4.563ex; height: 2.036ex;" id="img_images_148.svg_1">, are not propositional. Functions of this kind always
mean "the term having such and such a relation to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_402">." For this
reason they may be called <i>descriptive</i> functions, because
they <i>describe</i> a certain term by means of its relation to
their argument. Thus "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)" src="images/2422.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.552ex; width: 5.44ex; height: 4.057ex;" id="img_images_2422.svg">" describes the number
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_13">; yet propositions in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)" src="images/2422.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.552ex; width: 5.44ex; height: 4.057ex;" id="img_images_2422.svg_1"> occurs are
not the same as they would be if <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_14"> were substituted for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)" src="images/2423.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.552ex; width: 5.44ex; height: 4.057ex;" id="img_images_2423.svg">. This appears <i>e.g.</i> from the proposition
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\)" src="images/2424.svg" style="vertical-align: -1.552ex; width: 9.589ex; height: 4.057ex;" id="img_images_2424.svg">," which conveys valuable information,
whereas "<img alt="" data-tex="\(1 = 1\)" src="images/2425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.28ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_2425.svg">" is trivial. Descriptive functions, like
descriptions in general, have no meaning by themselves, but only as
constituents of propositions<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_55" id="FNanchor_55">[55]</a>.</p>

<p>The general definition of a descriptive function is:</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_30_01">*30·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy=({℩}x)(xRy) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/2426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.175ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2426.svg"></p>

<p>That is, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_8">" is to mean "the term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_403"> which has the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_89"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_143">." If there are several terms or none having the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_90"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_144">, all propositions about <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_9">, <i>i.e.</i> all
propositions of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(Rʻy)\)" src="images/2427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.292ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2427.svg">," will be false. The apostrophe
in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_10">" may be read "of." Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_91"> is the relation of father
to son, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_11">" means "the father of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_145">." If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_92"> is the relation
of son to father, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_12">" means "the son of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_146">"; in this case, all
propositions of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi(Rʻy)\)" src="images/2427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.292ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2427.svg_1">" will be false unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_147"> has
one son and no more.</p>

<p>All the functions that occur in ordinary mathematics are instances
of the above definition; all are obtained in the above manner from
some relation. Thus in our notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_13">" takes the place of what
would commonly be "<img alt="" data-tex="\(fy\)" src="images/330.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.353ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_330.svg_3">," this latter notation being reserved for
<i>propositional</i> functions. We should write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin ʻy\)" src="images/329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.621ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_329.svg_2">" in place
of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin y\)" src="images/328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.264ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_328.svg_1">," using "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin\)" src="images/2428.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.778ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_2428.svg">" to express the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_404"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_148"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x = \sin y\)" src="images/2429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.575ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_2429.svg">.</p>

<p>A definition such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy = (℩x)(xRy)\)" src="images/2430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.492ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2430.svg">, where the meaning given to
the term defined is a description, must be understood to mean that the
term defined (in this case <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_14">) and the description assigned as
its meaning (in<span class="pagenum" id="Page_246">[Pg 246]</span> this case (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩} x)(xRy))\)" src="images/2431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.292ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2431.svg"> are to be interchangeable
in use: the definition is, in a sense, more purely symbolic than other
definitions, since the description assigned as the meaning has itself
no meaning except in use. It would perhaps be more formally correct to
write
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ f(Rʻy) .=. f\{({℩} x)(xRy)\} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/2432.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.071ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2432.svg"></span></p>

<p>But even this definition would not be quite complete, because it
omits mention of the <i>scope</i> of the two descriptions <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_15"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\((℩x)(xRy)\)" src="images/2433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.292ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2433.svg">. Thus the complete form would be
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ [Rʻy].f(Rʻy) .=. [({℩}x)(xRy)] . f\{({℩}x)(xRy)\} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/2434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.074ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2434.svg"></span>
But it is unnecessary to adopt this form of definition, provided it
is understood that the definition <a href="#_30_01" class="pginternal">*30·01</a> means that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_16">" may
be written for "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(xRy)\)" src="images/2435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.412ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2435.svg">" <i>everywhere</i>, <i>i.e.</i> in
indications of scope as well as elsewhere. The use of the definition
occurs always in accordance with the proposition:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash: [Rʻy].f(Rʻy) .\equiv. [({℩}x)(xRy)] . f({℩}x)(xRy)\text{,} \]" src="images/2436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.768ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2436.svg"></span>
which is <a href="#_30_1" class="pginternal">*30·1</a>, below.</p>

<p>It is to be observed that *30·01 does not necessarily involve
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Rʻy = ({℩}x)(xRy)\text{.} \]" src="images/2437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.121ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2437.svg"></span>
For this, by the definition, is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ ({℩}x)(xRy) = ({℩}x)(xRy)\text{,} \]" src="images/2438.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.23ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2438.svg"></span>
which, by <a href="#_14_28" class="pginternal">*14·28</a>, only holds when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(xRy)\)" src="images/2439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.462ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2439.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>
when there is one term, and no more, which has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_93"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_149">.</p>

<p>All the conventions as to scope explained in <a href="#_14" class="pginternal">*14</a> are to be transferred
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻx\)" src="images/2440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2440.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>, in the absence of any contrary indication, the
scope of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻx\)" src="images/2440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2440.svg_1"> is to be the smallest proposition, enclosed in dots or
other brackets, in which the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻx\)" src="images/2440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2440.svg_2"> in question occurs.</p>

<p>We put</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_30_02">*30·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(RʻSʻy = Rʻ(Sʻy) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/2441.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.461ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2441.svg"></p>

<p>This definition serves merely for the avoidance of brackets. It is to
be interpreted as meaning
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ [RʻSʻy].f(RʻSʻy) .=. [Rʻ(Sʻy)].f\{Rʻ(Sʻy)\} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/2442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 51.644ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2442.svg"></span>
In future, we shall often define a new expression as having a
descriptive phrase for its meaning; in such a case, the definition is
always to be interpreted as above. That is, any proposition in which
the new expression occurs is to be the proposition which is obtained
by substituting the old expression for the new one wherever the latter
occurs.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_247">[Pg 247]</span></p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ(Sʻy)\)" src="images/2443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.76ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2443.svg">, in the above, is to be interpreted by first treating
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2444.svg"> as if it were not a descriptive symbol, and applying <a href="#_30_01" class="pginternal">*30·01</a> and
<a href="#_14_01" class="pginternal">*14·01</a> or <a href="#_14_02" class="pginternal">*14·02</a> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ(Sʻy)\)" src="images/2443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.76ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2443.svg_1">,
and by then applying *30·01 and *14·01 or *14·02 to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2444.svg_1">.</p>

<p>The majority of the propositions of the present number are immediate
consequences of the corresponding propositions in *14. Thus <a href="#_14_31" class="pginternal">*14·31</a>—<a href="#_14_34" class="pginternal">·34</a>
and <a href="#_14_113" class="pginternal">*14·113</a> lead immediately to <a href="#_30_12" class="pginternal">*30·12</a>—<a href="#_30_16" class="pginternal">·16</a>, which show that, either
always or when <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_17"> exists, the "scope" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_18"> or of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_19"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2444.svg_2"> makes no difference to the truth-values of such propositions as
we are concerned with. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*30·18.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp\exists!Rʻy:(z).\phi z:\supset.\phi(Rʻy)\)" src="images/2445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.885ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2445.svg"></p>

<p>so that what holds of everything holds of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_20">, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_21">
exists. This results immediately from <a href="#_14_18" class="pginternal">*14·18</a>, and shows that, provided
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_22"> exists, the fact that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_23">" is an incomplete symbol does
not prevent its being substituted as a value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_21"> whenever we have
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(z).\phi z\)" src="images/2446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.339ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2446.svg">, or an assertion of the propositional function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi z\)" src="images/2447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2447.svg">.</p>

<p>One of the most used propositions of this number is:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*30·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp x=Rʻy.\equiv:zRy.\equiv_{z}.z=x\)" src="images/2448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 29.858ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2448.svg"></p>

<p>which results immediately from <a href="#_14_202" class="pginternal">*14·202</a>. The following analogous
proposition results from the above by means of <a href="#_14_122" class="pginternal">*14·122</a>:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*30·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp x=Rʻy.\equiv:xRy:zRy.\supset_{z}.z=x\)" src="images/2449.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 35.863ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2449.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x=Rʻy\)" src="images/2450.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.494ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2450.svg">" involves, in addition to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xRy\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_266.svg_4">," the
statement that whatever has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_94"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_150"> is identical
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_405">.</p>

<p>A proposition constantly referred to is:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*30·37.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists!Rʻy.y=z.\supset.Rʻy=Rʻz\)" src="images/2451.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 29.993ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2451.svg"></p>

<p>In the hypothesis, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!Rʻy\)" src="images/2452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.07ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2452.svg"> might be replaced by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!Rʻz\)" src="images/2453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.014ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2453.svg">, but one or other of them is essential. For, by <a href="#_14_21" class="pginternal">*14·21</a>,
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy=Rʻz\)" src="images/2454.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.327ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2454.svg">" implies <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!Rʻy\)" src="images/2452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.07ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2452.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!Rʻz\)" src="images/2453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.014ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2453.svg_1"> (these are
equivalent when <img alt="" data-tex="\(y=z\)" src="images/2455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.178ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_2455.svg">), and therefore cannot be true when <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_24"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻz\)" src="images/2456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.127ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2456.svg"> do not exist.</p>

<p>The use of *30·37 is chiefly in cases where <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_151"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_22"> or both are
replaced by descriptive functions. Suppose, for example, that <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_23"> is
replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻw\)" src="images/2457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.437ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2457.svg">. By <a href="#_30_18" class="pginternal">*30·18</a>, we may substitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻw\)" src="images/2457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.437ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2457.svg_1"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_24"> if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻw\)" src="images/2457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.437ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2457.svg_2"> exists. By <a href="#_14_21" class="pginternal">*14·21</a>, both sides of the implication in <a href="#_30_37" class="pginternal">*30·37</a> will
become false if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻw\)" src="images/2457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.437ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2457.svg_3"> does not exist, and therefore the implication
will still hold. Hence whether <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻw\)" src="images/2457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.437ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2457.svg_4"> exists or not, we may substitute
it for <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_25"> and obtain
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash:\exists!Rʻy.y=Sʻw.\supset.Rʻy=RʻSʻw. \]" src="images/2458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 37.391ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2458.svg"></span>
In like manner, if we replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_152"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Tʻv\)" src="images/2459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.048ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2459.svg">, we obtain
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash:\exists x!RʻTʻv.Tʻv=Sʻw.\supset.RʻTʻv=RʻSʻw. \]" src="images/2460.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 47.502ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2460.svg"></span></p>

<p>A very important proposition is:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*30·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp\exists!Rʻy.\supset:a=Rʻy.\equiv.aRy\)" src="images/2461.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 29.68ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2461.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition states that, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_25"> exists, to say that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_114"> is <i>the</i> term which has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_95"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_153"> is
equivalent to saying that a has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_96"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_154">. Thus for
example "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_115"> is the occupier of the house <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_155">" is equivalent to
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_116"> occupies the house <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_156">," "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_117"> is the writer of Waverley" is
equivalent to<span class="pagenum" id="Page_248">[Pg 248]</span> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_118"> wrote Waverley," "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_119"> is the father of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_157">"
is equivalent to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_120"> begot <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_158">." But we cannot argue from "John
Smith inhabits London" to "John Smith is <i>the</i> inhabitant of
London."</p>

<p>We shall introduce in this and subsequent sections many constant
relations for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!Rʻy\)" src="images/2452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.07ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2452.svg_2"> is always true. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_97"> is such
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!Rʻy\)" src="images/2452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.07ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2452.svg_3"> is always true, we have, in virtue of <a href="#_30_4" class="pginternal">*30·4</a>,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ a=Rʻy.\equiv.aRy \]" src="images/2462.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 16.192ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2462.svg"></span>
for every possible value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_159">. The following proposition is useful
in cases where both <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_98"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_21"> are such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_26"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2444.svg_3">
always exist:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*30·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp(y).Rʻy=Sʻy.\equiv:(y).\exists!Rʻy:R=S\)" src="images/2463.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.443ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2463.svg"></p>

<p>Thus if we know that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_27"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2444.svg_4"> are always identical, we know
not only that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_99"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_22"> are identical, but also that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_28"> (and
therefore <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2444.svg_5">) always exists.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*30·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy=({℩}x)(xRy)   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.175ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2464.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*30·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(RʻSʻy=Rʻ(Sʻy)   \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.461ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2465.svg"></p>

<p>In interpreting <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ(Sʻy)\)" src="images/2443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.76ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2443.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2444.svg_6"> is to be treated as an ordinary
symbol until <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ(Sʻy)\)" src="images/2443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.76ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2443.svg_3"> has been eliminated by <a href="#_30_01" class="pginternal">*30·01</a> and <a href="#_14_01" class="pginternal">*14·01</a> or
<a href="#_14_02" class="pginternal">*14·02</a>, and then the above definitions are to be applied to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Sʻy\)" src="images/2444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.925ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2444.svg_7">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_30_1">*30·1</a>.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:[Rʻy].f(Rʻy).\equiv.[({℩}x)(xRy)].f({℩}x)(xRy) \quad[\text{*4·2.(*30·01)}]\)" src="images/2466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.356ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2466.svg"></p>

<p>In proving *30·2, we have to use the definition <a href="#_30_01" class="pginternal">*30·01</a>, not <a href="#_30_1" class="pginternal">*30·1</a>,

<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.984ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_315.svg_10">, which leads to an expression containing
the meaningless constituent <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!b\)" src="images/2479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.14ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_2479.svg">. But by the definition
*30·01, every typographical occurrence of the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_29">" means

"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.353ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_332.svg_1">" means "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!({℩}x)(xRy)\)" src="images/2439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 12.462ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2439.svg_1">."</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_251">[Pg 251]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_31">*31. CONVERSES OF RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *31.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_100"> is a relation, the relation which <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_160"> has to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_406"> when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x R y\)" src="images/2506.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2506.svg"> is called the <i>converse</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_101">. Thus <i>greater</i>
is the converse of <i>less</i>, <i>before</i> of <i>after</i>,
<i>husband</i> of <i>wife</i>. The converse of identity is identity,
and the converse of diversity is diversity. The converse of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_102"> is
written <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}\)" src="images/335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_335.svg_1"> (read "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_103">-converse"). When <img alt="" data-tex="\(R = \breve{R}\)" src="images/337.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.451ex; height: 2.6ex;" id="img_images_337.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_104"> is called a <i>symmetrical</i> relation, otherwise it is called
<i>not-symmetrical</i>. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_105"> is incompatible with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}\)" src="images/335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_335.svg_2">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_106"> is called <i>asymmetrical</i>. Thus "cousin" is symmetrical,
"brother" is not-symmetrical (because when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_407"> is the brother of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_161">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_162"> may be either the brother or the sister of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x)\)" src="images/434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 2.174ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_434.svg_1">, and
"husband" is asymmetrical.</p>

<p>The relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}\)" src="images/335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_335.svg_3"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_107"> is called "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}\)" src="images/2507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.086ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2507.svg">." It
will be shown that every relation has one, and only one, converse;
hence, applying the notation of <a href="#_30" class="pginternal">*30</a>, that one is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}ʻR\)" src="images/334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.161ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_334.svg_2">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R} = \text{Cnv}ʻR\)" src="images/2508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.895ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_2508.svg">. We have thus two notations for the
converse of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_108">; the second is more convenient for the converse of a
relation not denoted by a single letter.</p>

<p>The more important propositions of the present number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*31·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \text{E}! \text{Cnv}ʻP\)" src="images/2509.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.701ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2509.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> any relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_8"> has a converse. Hence the relation
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}\)" src="images/2507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.086ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2507.svg_1">" verifies the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\((y).\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/2510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.228ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2510.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> we have <img alt="" data-tex="\((P).\text{E}!\text{Cnv}ʻP\)" src="images/2511.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.778ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2511.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*31·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : P = Q .\equiv. \breve{P} = \breve{Q}\)" src="images/2512.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 19.424ex; height: 2.9ex;" id="img_images_2512.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> two relations are identical when, and only when, their
converses are identical.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*31·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \text{Cnv}ʻ\text{Cnv}ʻP = P\)" src="images/2513.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.691ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2513.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> any relation is the converse of its converse.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_252">[Pg 252]</span></p>

relation require only the propositions which embody the definitions of
