<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_278">[Pg 278]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_35">*35. RELATIONS WITH LIMITED DOMAINS AND CONVERSE DOMAINS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *35.</p>

<p>In this section, we have to consider the relation derived from a given
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_152"> by limiting either its domain or its converse domain
to members of some assigned class. A relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_153"> with its domain
limited to members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_111"> is written "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/2869.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2869.svg">";
with its converse domain limited to members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_38">, it
is written "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/2870.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2870.svg">"; with both limitations, it
is written "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonleft R \upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/2871.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.846ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2871.svg">." Thus
<i>e.g.</i> "brother" and "sister" express the same relation (that of a
common parentage), with the domain limited in the first case to males,
in the second to females. "The relation of white employers to coloured
employees" is a relation limited both as to its domain and as to its
converse domain. We put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonright R =\hat{x}\hat{y}(x \in \alpha . xRy) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/2872.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.863ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2872.svg"></p>

<p>with similar definitions for <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/2873.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2873.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonleft R \upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/2874.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.846ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2874.svg">.</p>

<p>A particularly important case is the case in which the same limitation
is imposed on the domain and on the converse domain, <i>i.e.</i>
where we have a relation of the form "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonleft R\upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/2875.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.014ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2875.svg">."
In this case, the limitation to members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_112"> may be more briefly stated as being imposed on
the <i>field</i>. For this case, it is convenient to adopt "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\unicode{x294f} \alpha\)" src="images/2876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2876.svg">"
as an alternative notation. This case will be considered in <a href="#_36" class="pginternal">*36</a>.</p>

<p>It is convenient to consider in the present connection the relation
between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_426"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_189"> which is constituted by x being a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_113"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_190"> being a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_39">. This relation will be
denoted by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \uparrow \beta\)" src="images/2877.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.117ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2877.svg">." Thus we put</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_35_04">*35·04</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \uparrow \beta = \hat{x}\hat{y}(x \in \alpha . y \in \beta) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/2878.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.649ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2878.svg"></p>

<p>The chief importance of relations with limited <i>fields</i> arises
in the theory of series. Given a series generated by a relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_154">, let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_114"> be a class consisting of part of this series.
Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_115"> is the field of the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonleft R \upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/2879.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.014ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2879.svg">
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_279">[Pg 279]</span>or <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \unicode{x294f} \alpha\)" src="images/2880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2880.svg">, and it is this relation which is the
generating relation of the series of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_116"> in the same
order which they have as parts of the original series. Thus parts of a
series, considered not merely as classes but as series, are dealt with
by means of serial relations with limited fields.</p>

<p>Relations with limited <i>domains</i> are not nearly so much used
as relations with limited <i>converse domains</i>. Relations with
limited converse domains play a great part in arithmetic, especially
in establishing the formal laws. What is wanted in such cases is a
one-one relation correlating two classes or two series. That is,
we want a relation such that not only does <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_43"> exist whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/2881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.307ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_2881.svg">, but also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻx\)" src="images/2882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_2882.svg"> exists whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2883.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2883.svg">. The kind of relation which is most frequently found
to effect such a correlation is some such relation as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_3">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\)" src="images/2637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2637.svg_4"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(C\)" src="images/42.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.719ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_42.svg_6">, or some other constant relation for
which we always have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.353ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_332.svg_3">, with its converse domain so
limited that, subject to the limitation, only one value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_191">
gives any given value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_44">. Thus for example let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg">
be a class of relations no two of which have the same domain; then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda\)" src="images/2885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.248ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2885.svg"> will give a one-one correlation
of these relations with their domains: if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_155">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in \lambda\)" src="images/2886.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.544ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_2886.svg">, we
shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{D}ʻR=\text{D}ʻS.\supset.R=S. \]" src="images/2887.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.96ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2887.svg"></span>
We shall also have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR=(\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda)ʻR\)" src="images/2888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.903ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2888.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻS=(\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda)ʻS\)" src="images/2889.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.387ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2889.svg">. Moreover the
converse domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda\)" src="images/2885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.248ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2885.svg_1"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_1">,
and the domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda\)" src="images/2885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.248ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2885.svg_2"> is the class
of domains of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_2">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright\lambda\)" src="images/2890.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.248ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2890.svg">
gives a one-one correlation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_3"> with the domains
of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_4">. It is chiefly in such ways that relations
with limited converse domains are useful.</p>

<p>For purposes of reference, a great many propositions are given in the
present number, but the propositions that will be used frequently are
comparatively few. Among these are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\alpha\upharpoonleft R\upharpoonright \beta=(\alpha\upharpoonleft R)\upharpoonright \beta=\alpha\upharpoonleft (R\upharpoonright \beta)\)" src="images/2891.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.482ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2891.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.(R\upharpoonright \alpha)\upharpoonright \beta=R\upharpoonright (\alpha\cap \beta)\)" src="images/2892.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.933ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2892.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·354.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.(R\upharpoonright \alpha)\mid S=R\mid \alpha\upharpoonleft S\)" src="images/2893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.587ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2893.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> in a relative product it makes no difference whether we
limit the converse domain of the first factor, or the domain of the
second.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·412.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.R\upharpoonright (\beta\cup \beta') = R\upharpoonright \beta\unicode{x228d}R\upharpoonright \beta'\)" src="images/2894.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.168ex; height: 2.283ex;" id="img_images_2894.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·452.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset\beta.\supset.R\upharpoonright \beta=R\)" src="images/2895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.074ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2895.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·48.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{ᗡ}ʻP\subset\alpha.\supset.P\mid (\alpha\upharpoonleft R)=P\mid R\)" src="images/2896.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.321ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2896.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cnv}ʻ(R\upharpoonright \beta)=\beta\upharpoonleft \breve{R}\)" src="images/2897.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.005ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_2897.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·61.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{D}ʻ(\alpha\upharpoonleft R)=\alpha\cap \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/2898.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.383ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2898.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·64.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{ᗡ}ʻ(R\upharpoonright \beta)=\beta\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/2899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.306ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2899.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·65.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\beta\subset\text{ᗡ}ʻR.\supset.\text{ᗡ}ʻ(R\upharpoonright \beta)=\beta\)" src="images/2900.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.113ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2900.svg"></p>

<p>The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\subset\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/2901.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.73ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2901.svg"> is fulfilled in the great
majority of cases in which we have occasion to use <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\upharpoonright\beta\)" src="images/2902.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2902.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·66.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset\beta.\equiv.R\upharpoonright \beta=R\)" src="images/2903.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.074ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2903.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·7.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\phi\{(R\upharpoonright \beta)ʻy\}.\equiv.y\in \beta.\phi(Rʻy)\)" src="images/2904.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.9ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2904.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_280">[Pg 280]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is used very frequently, owing to the fact that limitation
of the converse domain is chiefly applied to such relations as give rise to
descriptive functions (<i>e.g.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\)" src="images/2637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2637.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(C\)" src="images/42.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.719ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_42.svg_7">).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp y\in \beta.\supset_{y}.Rʻy=Sʻy:\supset.R\upharpoonright \beta=S\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/2905.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 41.598ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_2905.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is useful for a reason similar to that which makes
*35·7 useful.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·82.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\alpha\uparrow \beta=\alpha\upharpoonleft \dot{\text{V}}\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/2906.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 19.348ex; height: 2.719ex;" id="img_images_2906.svg"></p>

<p>Owing to this proposition, the properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\uparrow\beta\)" src="images/2907.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.117ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2907.svg">
can be deduced from the already proved properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft R\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/2908.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.846ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2908.svg">, by putting <img alt="" data-tex="\(R =\dot{\text{V}}\)" src="images/2909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 6.431ex; height: 2.466ex;" id="img_images_2909.svg">.</p>

<p>The relation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\uparrow \beta\)" src="images/2910.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.117ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2910.svg">" is what may be called an
"analysable" relation, <i>i.e.</i> it holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_427"> and y when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \alpha\)" src="images/2911.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_2911.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in \beta\)" src="images/2912.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_2912.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_428"> has a
property independent of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_192">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_193"> has a property independent of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_429">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·85.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !\beta.\supset.\text{D}ʻ(\alpha\uparrow \beta)=\alpha\)" src="images/2913.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.007ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2913.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·86.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !\alpha.\supset.\text{ᗡ}ʻ(\alpha\uparrow \beta)=\beta\)" src="images/2914.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.636ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2914.svg"></p>

<p>If either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_117"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_40"> is null, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\uparrow\beta\)" src="images/2907.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.117ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2907.svg_1">
(<a href="#_35_88" class="pginternal">*35·88</a>).</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*35·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft R=\hat{x}\hat{y}(x\in \alpha.xRy) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2915.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.863ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2915.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\upharpoonright \beta=\hat{x}\hat{y}(xRy.y\in \beta) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2916.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.342ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2916.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft R\upharpoonright \beta=\hat{x}\hat{y}(x\in \alpha.xRy.y\in \beta)\quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2917.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.505ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2917.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\uparrow \beta=\hat{x}\hat{y}(x\in \alpha.y\in \beta) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2918.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.649ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_2918.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·05.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻx\uparrow \beta=(Rʻx)\uparrow \beta \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/2919.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.535ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2919.svg"></p>

<p>The last definition serves merely for the avoidance of brackets.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·1.</b>   <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x(\alpha\upharpoonleft R)y.\equiv.x\in \alpha.xRy \quad[\text{*21·3.(*35·01)}]\)" src="images/2920.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.923ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2920.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x(R\upharpoonright \beta)y.\equiv.xRy.y\in \beta\)" src="images/2921.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.054ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2921.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·102.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x(\alpha\upharpoonleft R\upharpoonright \beta)y.\equiv.x\in \alpha.xRy.y\in \beta\)" src="images/2922.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.216ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2922.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*35·103.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x(\alpha\uparrow \beta)y.\equiv.x\in \alpha.y\in \beta\)" src="images/2923.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.361ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_2923.svg"></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_36">*36. RELATIONS WITH LIMITED FIELDS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *36.</p>

<p>In this number we are concerned with the special case in which the
same limitation is imposed upon the domain and the converse domain
of a relation. In this case, the same result is achieved by imposing
the limitation on the field. It is convenient to be able to regard
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonleft P \upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/3049.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 8.996ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3049.svg"> as a descriptive
function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_118"> or of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_12">, which we secure by the notation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x294f} \alpha\)" src="images/3050.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3050.svg">, whence, as will be explained in <a href="#_38" class="pginternal">*38</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x294f} ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3051.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3051.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x294f} \alphaʻP\)" src="images/3052.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3052.svg"> will both
mean <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x294f} \alpha\)" src="images/3050.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3050.svg_1">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_13"> is a serial relation, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \subset CʻP\)" src="images/3053.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.241ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3053.svg">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x294f} \alpha\)" src="images/3050.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3050.svg_2">" will stand for
"the terms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_119"> arranged in the order determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_14">,"
or, as we may call it briefly, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_120"> in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_15">-order."
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x294f} \alpha\)" src="images/3054.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3054.svg"> is defined as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*36·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x294f} \alpha = \alpha \upharpoonleft P \upharpoonright \alpha \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3055.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.201ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3055.svg"></p>

<p>We thus have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*36·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: x (P \unicode{x294f} \alpha) y .\equiv. x,y \in \alpha . x P y\)" src="images/3056.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.81ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3056.svg"></p>

demand that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_16"> should have some at least of the characteristics

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_37">*37. PLURAL DESCRIPTIVE FUNCTIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *37.</p>

<p>In this number, we introduce what may be regarded as the plural of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_45">. "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_46">" was defined to mean "the term which has the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_156"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_194">." We now introduce the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg">" to mean
"the terms which have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_157"> to members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_41">."
Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_42"> is the class of great men, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_158"> is the relation
of wife to husband, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_1"> will mean "wives of great men." If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_43"> is the class of fractions of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(1-\tfrac{1}{2}^{n}\)" src="images/3089.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.781ex; width: 6.84ex; height: 2.827ex;" id="img_images_3089.svg">
for integral values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_41">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_159"> is the relation "less than,"
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_2"> will be the class of fractions each of which is less than
some member of this class of fractions, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_3"> will
be the class of proper fractions. Generally, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_4"> is the class
of those referents which have relata that are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_44">.</p>

<p>We require also a notation for the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_5"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_45">. This relation we will call <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in}\)" src="images/3090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 1.949ex;" id="img_images_3090.svg">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in}\)" src="images/3090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 1.949ex;" id="img_images_3090.svg_1"> is
the relation which holds between two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_121"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_46">
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_122"> consists of all terms which have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_160"> to
some member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_47">.</p>

<p>A specially important case arises when <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_47"> always exists if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in \beta\)" src="images/2912.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_2912.svg_1">. In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_6"> is the class of all terms of
the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_48"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \beta\)" src="images/3091.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3091.svg">. We will denote the hypothesis
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_49"> always exists if <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \beta\)" src="images/3091.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3091.svg_1"> by the notation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}‼Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.611ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3092.svg">, meaning "the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_161">'s of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_48">'s exist."</p>

<p>The definitions are as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta = \hat{x}\{(\exists y) . y \in \beta . x R y\} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3093.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.383ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3093.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in} = \hat{\alpha}\hat{\beta}(\alpha = Rʻʻ\beta) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3094.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.339ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_3094.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_37_03">*37·03</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}_{\in} = \text{Cnv}ʻ(R_{\in}) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3095.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.848ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_3095.svg"></p>

<p>This definition serves merely for the avoidance of brackets.
Without it, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}_{\in}\)" src="images/3096.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 2.817ex;" id="img_images_3096.svg">" would be ambiguous as between
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R})_{\in}\)" src="images/3097.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.852ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_3097.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}ʻ(R_{\in})\)" src="images/3098.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.176ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3098.svg">, which are not
equal. In all cases in which a suffix occurs, we shall adopt the same
convention, <i>i.e.</i> we shall always put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \breve{R}_{\text{suffix}} = \text{Cnv}ʻ(R_{\text{suffix}}). \]" src="images/3099.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.236ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_3099.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_294">[Pg 294]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻʻ\kappa = R_{\in}ʻʻ\kappa \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3100.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.783ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3100.svg"></p>

<p>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.093ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3101.svg"> consists of all classes which have the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in}\)" src="images/3090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 1.949ex;" id="img_images_3090.svg_2"> to some member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_3">. <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.093ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3101.svg_1"> is only
significant when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_4"> is a class of classes relatively to members
of the converse domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_162">; in this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.093ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3101.svg_2"> is a
class of classes relatively to members of the domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_163">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_37_05">*37·05</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!!Rʻʻ\beta .=: y \in \beta .\supset_{y}. \text{E}!Rʻy \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3102.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 33.47ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3102.svg"></p>

<p>Here the symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!!Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3103.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.511ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3103.svg">" must be treated as a whole,
<i>i.e.</i> we must not regard it as making an assertion about
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_7">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta = \alpha\)" src="images/3104.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.178ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3104.svg">, we must not suppose that we
shall be able to put "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!!\alpha\)" src="images/3105.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.247ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_3105.svg">," which would be nonsense,
just as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!x\)" src="images/1636.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.464ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_1636.svg_1">" is nonsense even when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x = Rʻy\)" src="images/3106.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.494ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3106.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.353ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_332.svg_4">.</p>

<p>The notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg_3">, introduced in the present number, is
extremely useful, and embodies a very important idea. Its use is
somewhat different according to the kind of relation concerned.
Consider first the kind of relation which leads to a descriptive
function, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_5">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_5"> is a class of relations,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3107.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.762ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3107.svg"> is the class of the domains of these relations.
In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3107.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.762ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3107.svg_1"> is a class each of whose members
is of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_9">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \lambda\)" src="images/3108.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.802ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_3108.svg">. Again, let
us denote by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\times n\)" src="images/3109.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.118ex; height: 1.136ex;" id="img_images_3109.svg">" the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_8"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(m \times n\)" src="images/3110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 6.11ex; height: 1.136ex;" id="img_images_3110.svg">;
then if we denote by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(NC\)" src="images/3111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 3.729ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_3111.svg">" the class of cardinal numbers, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\times nʻʻNC\)" src="images/3112.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.561ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3112.svg">
will denote all numbers that result from multiplying a cardinal
number by <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_42">, <i>i.e.</i> all multiples of <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_43">. Thus <i>e.g.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\times 2ʻʻNC\)" src="images/3113.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.335ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3113.svg"> will be the class of even numbers. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_164"> is a
correlation between two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_123"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_49">, <i>i.e.</i> a
relation such that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \beta\)" src="images/3091.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3091.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_50"> exists and is a member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_124">, while conversely, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_6">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻx\)" src="images/2882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_2882.svg_1">
exists and is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_50">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.178ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3114.svg">, and
we may regard <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_165"> as a transformation applied to each member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_51"> and giving rise to a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_125">. It is by means of
such transformations that two classes are shown to be <i>similar</i>,
<i>i.e.</i> to have the same (cardinal) number of terms.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_295">[Pg 295]</span></p>

<p>In the case of serial relations, the utility of the notation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_8"> is somewhat different. Suppose, for example, that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_166"> is
the relation of less to greater among real numbers. Then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_52">
is any class of real numbers, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_9"> will be the segment of
real numbers determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_53">, <i>i.e.</i> the class of real
numbers which are less than the limit or maximum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_54">. In any
series, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_55"> is a class contained in the series and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_167"> is
the generating relation of the series, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_10"> is the segment
determined by <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_56">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_57"> has either a limit or a maximum,
say <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_430">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_11"> will be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/3115.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3115.svg">. But if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_58"> has neither a limit nor a maximum, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_12"> will be what
we may call an "irrational" segment of the series. We shall see at a
later stage that the real numbers may be identified with the segments
of the series of rationals, <i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_168"> is the relation of
less to greater among rationals, the real numbers will be all classes
such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_13">, for different values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_59">. The real
numbers which correspond to rationals will be those resulting from a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_60"> which has a limit or maximum; the irrationals will be those
resulting from a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_61"> which has no limit or maximum.</p>

<p>The present number may be divided into various sections, as follows:
(1) First, we have various elementary properties of the terms defined
at the beginning of the number; this section ends with <a href="#_37_29" class="pginternal">*37·29</a>. (2) We
have next a set of propositions dealing with relative products, and
with such symbols as <img alt="" data-tex="\(PʻʻQʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3116.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.147ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3116.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(PʻʻQʻʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.579ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3117.svg">, and so on.
The central proposition here is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.(P\mid Q)ʻʻ\gamma=PʻʻQʻʻ\gamma\)" src="images/3118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.631ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3118.svg"></p>

<p>By the definition, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Qʻʻʻ\kappa=Q_{\in}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3119.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.245ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3119.svg">. Thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(PʻʻQʻʻʻ\kappa=(P\mid Q_{\in})ʻʻ\kappa.\)" src="images/3120.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.633ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3120.svg"> This connects propositions
concerning such symbols as <img alt="" data-tex="\(PʻʻQʻʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.579ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3117.svg_1"> with propositions
concerning relative products. This second section consists of
the propositions from <a href="#_37_3" class="pginternal">*37·3</a> to <a href="#_37_39" class="pginternal">*37·39</a>. (3) We have next a set of
propositions on relations with limited domains and converse domains.
The chief of these are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·401.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{D}ʻ(R\upharpoonright \beta)=Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3121.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.162ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3121.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·412.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.(R\upharpoonright \alpha)ʻʻ\beta=Rʻʻ(\alpha\cap \beta)\)" src="images/3122.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.962ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3122.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{D}ʻ(R\unicode{x0294f}\alpha)=\alpha\cap Rʻʻ\alpha.\text{ᗡ}ʻ(R\unicode{x0294f}\alpha)=\alpha\cap \breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3123.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.48ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_3123.svg"></p>

<p>These propositions on relations with limited domains and converse
domains, together with certain others naturally connected with
them, extend from <a href="#_37_4" class="pginternal">*37·4</a> to <a href="#_37_52" class="pginternal">*37·52</a>. (4) We next have a number of
very important propositions on the consequences of the hypothesis
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}‼Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.611ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3092.svg_1">, <i>i.e.</i> the hypothesis that, for any
argument which is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_62">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_169"> gives rise to a
descriptive function <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_51">. The chief proposition in this section is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·6.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{E}‼Rʻʻ\beta.\supset.Rʻʻ\beta=\hat{x}\{(\exists y).y\in \beta.x=Rʻy\}\)" src="images/3124.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.098ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3124.svg"></p>

<p>Propositions with the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}‼Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.611ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3092.svg_2"> are applied to
the cases of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_349.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}\)" src="images/350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.451ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_350.svg_9">, in which
the hypothesis is verified. This section extends from <a href="#_37_6" class="pginternal">*37·6</a> to <a href="#_37_791" class="pginternal">*37·791</a>.
(5) Finally, we have three propositions on the relative product of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\uparrow \beta\)" src="images/2910.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.117ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2910.svg_2"> with other relations. These propositions are
useful in relation-arithmetic (Part IV).</p>

Etonian, his father must be rich." In virtue of the above proposition,
these two statements are equivalent.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha\subset \beta.\supset.Pʻʻ\alpha\subset Pʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.731ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3173.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*22·1}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset:y\in \alpha.\supset_{y}.y\in \beta:\\ [\text{*10·31}] &amp;\supset:y\in \alpha.xPy.\supset_{y}.y\in \beta.xPy:\\ [\text{*10·28}] &amp;\supset:(\exists y).y\in \alpha.xPy.\supset.(\exists y).y\in \beta.xPy:\\ [\text{*37·1}]  &amp;\supset:x\in \alpha Pʻʻ\alpha.\supset.x\in Pʻʻ\beta\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3174.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.418ex; width: 58.555ex; height: 11.968ex;" id="img_images_3174.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition (*37·2) is one of the forms of asyllogistic
inference due to Leibniz's teacher Jungius. The instance given by
Jungius is: "Circulus est figura; ergo qui circulum describit, is
figuram describit<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_56" id="FNanchor_56">[56]</a>." Here the class of circles is our <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_127">,
the class of figures is our <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_64">, and the relation of describing
is our <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_17">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·201.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\unicode{x2abd}Q.\supset.Pʻʻ\alpha\subset Qʻʻ\alpha  \quad[\text{Similar proof}]\)" src="images/3175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.323ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3175.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·212.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.(P\dot{\cap}Q)ʻʻ(\alpha\cap \beta)\subset Pʻʻ\alpha\cap Pʻʻ\beta\cap Qʻʻ\alpha\cap Qʻʻ\beta  \quad[\text{*37·21·211}]\)" src="images/3180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 66.548ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_3180.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.Pʻʻ(\alpha\cup \beta)=Pʻʻ\alpha\cup Pʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.894ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3181.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_299">[Pg 299]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is very frequently used. The fact that here we have
identity, while in *37·21 we only have inclusion, is due to the
fact that <a href="#_10_42" class="pginternal">*10·42</a> states an equivalence, while <a href="#_10_5" class="pginternal">*10·5</a> only states an
implication.</p>

<p>The type of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/2002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2002.svg_3">" here is that type whose members are of
the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_11">. In the proof, use is made of the
convention that a Greek letter always stands for an expression of the
form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z}(\phi!z)\)" src="images/1766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.842ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_1766.svg_5">.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*37·101}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\alpha R_{\in}\hat{z}(\phi!z).\equiv.\alpha=Rʻʻ\hat{z}(\phi!z):\\ [\text{*10·11·281}] &amp;\supset\vdash:(\exists \alpha).\alpha R_{\in}\hat{z}(\phi!z).\equiv.(\exists \alpha).\alpha=Rʻʻ\hat{z}(\phi!z):\\ [\text{*33·131}] &amp;\supset\vdash:\hat{z}(\phi!z)\in \text{ᗡ}ʻR_{\in}.\equiv.(\exists \alpha).\alpha=Rʻʻ\hat{z}(\phi!z) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*20·2.(*37·01)}. &amp;\supset\vdash:\hat{x}{(\exists y).y\in \hat{z}(\phi!z).xRy}=Rʻʻ\hat{z}(\phi!z):\\ [\text{*10·11·24}] &amp;\supset\vdash:(\phi):(\exists \alpha).\alpha=Rʻʻ\hat{z}(\phi!z) &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).*2·02}. &amp;\supset\vdash:\hat{z}(\phi!z)\in \text{Cls}.\supset.\hat{z}(\phi!z)\in \text{ᗡ}ʻR_{\in} &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{*20·41.*2·02}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\hat{z}(\phi!z)\in \text{ᗡ}ʻR_{\in}.\supset.\hat{z}(\phi!z)\in \text{Cls} &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(3).(4)}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3187.svg" style="vertical-align: -12.127ex; width: 74.161ex; height: 25.385ex;" id="img_images_3187.svg"></span></p>

<p>As appears in the above proof, it is necessary, when a proposition
containing "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/2002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2002.svg_4">" is to be proved, to abandon the notation
with Greek letters, and revert to the explicit functional notation.</p>

<p>The following propositions, down to <a href="#_37_7" class="pginternal">*37·7</a> exclusive, are concerned
with the special properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_14"> which result from the

<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}‼Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.611ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3092.svg_4"> is important, because it has many consequences
and is satisfied in many cases with which we wish to deal.</p>

<p>This proposition is very important, and is used constantly.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_307">[Pg 307]</span></p>

<p>The above is the type of inference concerning which Jevons says<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_57" id="FNanchor_57">[57]</a>:
"I remember the late Prof. De Morgan remarking that all Aristotle's
logic could not prove that 'Because a horse is an animal, the head of a
horse is the head of an animal.'" It must be confessed that this was a
merit in Aristotle's logic, since the proposed inference is fallacious
without the added premiss "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!\)" src="images/3272.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.17ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_3272.svg"> the head of the horse in
question." <i>E.g.</i> it does not hold for an oyster or a hydra. But
with the addition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.353ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_332.svg_5">, the above proposition gives an
important and common type of asyllogistic inference.</p>

<p>This proposition is very frequently used.</p>

<p>A specially important case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_15"> is

case will be further studied later (in <a href="#_70" class="pginternal">*70</a>); for the present, we
shall only give a few preliminary propositions about it. It will be
observed that the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}‼\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3288.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.611ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3288.svg"> or

*32·12·121. Hence the following applications of <a href="#_37_6" class="pginternal">*37·6</a> ff.:</p>

<p>Observe that the <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_27">'s which occur in this proposition will not
be all of the same type. <i>E.g.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_171"> relates individuals to
individuals, the first <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_28"> will be the class of no individuals,
while the second and third will be the class of no classes. Thus
the ambiguity which attaches to the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_29"> must be
differently determined for different occurrences of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_30"> in
this proposition. In general, when this is the case with our ambiguous
symbols, we shall adopt a notation which indicates the fact. But when
the ambiguous symbol is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_31">, it seems hardly worth while.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*37·79.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{V}= \hat{\alpha}\{\exists y).\alpha=\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\}    \quad[\text{*37·601.*32·12}]\)" src="images/3321.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.996ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_3321.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_37_791">*37·791</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \overleftarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{V}= \hat{\beta}\{(\exists x).\beta=\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\}     \quad[\text{*37·601.*32·121}]\)" src="images/3322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.511ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_3322.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_311">[Pg 311]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_38">*38. RELATIONS AND CLASSES DERIVED FROM A DOUBLE
DESCRIPTIVE FUNCTION.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *38.</p>

<p>A double descriptive function is a non-propositional function of two
arguments, such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta\)" src="images/267.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_267.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \beta\)" src="images/270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_270.svg_2">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \dot{\cap} S\)" src="images/357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.686ex; height: 2.138ex;" id="img_images_357.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \unicode{x228d} S\)" src="images/3327.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.534ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3327.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/3328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3328.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/2873.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_2873.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \unicode{x294f}\alpha\)" src="images/3329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3329.svg">. The
propositions of the present number apply to all such functions,
assuming the notation to be (as in the above instances) a functional
sign placed between the two arguments. In order to deal with all
analogous cases at once, we shall in this number adopt the notation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x \unicode{x2640} y\text{,} \]" src="images/3330.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.389ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3330.svg"></span>
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x2640}\)" src="images/3331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3331.svg">" stands for any such sign as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\cap\)" src="images/1979.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_1979.svg_2">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\cup\)" src="images/1978.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_1978.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\cap}\)" src="images/2016.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 2.138ex;" id="img_images_2016.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x228d}\)" src="images/2015.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2015.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid\)" src="images/3332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 0.629ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3332.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\upharpoonleft\)" src="images/3333.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 0.943ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3333.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\upharpoonright\)" src="images/3334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 0.943ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3334.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x294f}\)" src="images/3335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3335.svg">, or any
functional sign to be hereafter defined and satisfying the condition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x, y) . \text{E}!(x \unicode{x2640} y)\text{.} \]" src="images/3336.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.494ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3336.svg"></span>
The derived relations and classes with which we shall be concerned
may be illustrated by taking the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta\)" src="images/267.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_267.svg_4">. The
relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta\)" src="images/267.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_267.svg_5"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_65"> will be written <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cap\)" src="images/3337.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.957ex; height: 1.403ex;" id="img_images_3337.svg">,
and the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta\)" src="images/267.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_267.svg_6"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_128"> will be
written <img alt="" data-tex="\(\cap \beta\)" src="images/3338.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.79ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3338.svg">. Thus we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash . \alpha \cap \beta = \alpha \cap ʻ\beta = \cap \betaʻ\alpha\text{.} \]" src="images/3339.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.49ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3339.svg"></span>
The utility of this notation is chiefly due to the possibility of such
notations as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3340.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.981ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3340.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\cap \beta ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3341.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.808ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3341.svg">. For
example, take such a phrase as "the foreign members of English Clubs."
Then if we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_129"> = foreigners, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_5"> = English Clubs, we
have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \cap ʻʻ\kappa = \text{the classes of foreign members of the various English Clubs.} \]" src="images/3342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 68.769ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_3342.svg"></span>
Or again, let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_130"> be a conic, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_6"> a pencil of lines;
then
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \cap ʻʻ\kappa = \text{the various pairs of points in which members of \(\kappa\) meet \(\alpha\).} \]" src="images/3343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 66.613ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3343.svg"></span>
In this case, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap \beta = \beta \cap \alpha\)" src="images/3344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 13.503ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3344.svg">, we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap = \cap \alpha\)" src="images/3345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 8.931ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_3345.svg">. But when the function concerned is not
commutative, this does not hold. Thus for example we do not have <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid = \mid R\)" src="images/3346.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 7.709ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3346.svg">.</p>

<p>The notations of this number will be frequently applied hereafter to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_3">. In accordance with what was said above, we write <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid\)" src="images/3347.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.975ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3347.svg">
for the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_4"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_27">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid S\)" src="images/3348.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.717ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3348.svg"> for the
relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_5"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_172">. Hence we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \mid ʻS = \mid SʻR = R \mid S\text{.} \]" src="images/3349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 23.308ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3349.svg"></span>
Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid Sʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 6.751ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3350.svg"> will be the class of relations obtained by
taking members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_6"><span class="pagenum" id="Page_312">[Pg 312]</span> and relatively multiplying them by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_28">. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \)" src="images/3351.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_3351.svg"> were the class of relations first cousin,
second cousin, etc., and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_29"> were the relation of parent to child,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid Sʻʻ\lambda \)" src="images/3352.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 6.751ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3352.svg"> would be the class of relations first cousin once
removed, second cousin once removed, etc., taken in the sense which
goes from the older to the younger generation.</p>

<p>It is often convenient to be able to exhibit <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid Sʻʻ\lambda \)" src="images/3352.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 6.751ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3352.svg_1"> and
kindred expressions as descriptive functions of the first argument
instead of the second. For this purpose we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \lambda \mid_{,,}S=\mid Sʻʻ\lambda \]" src="images/3353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 14.881ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3353.svg"></span>
with similar notations for other descriptive double functions. We then
have, just as in the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_6">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \lambda \mid_{,,}ʻS=\mid_{,,}Sʻ\lambda =\lambda \mid_{,,}S. \]" src="images/3354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 25.345ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3354.svg"></span>
This enables us to form the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda \mid_{,,}ʻʻ\mu \)" src="images/3355.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.361ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3355.svg">. This class is chiefly useful because the members of its members
(<i>i.e</i>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda \mid_{,,}ʻʻ\mu \)" src="images/3356.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 10.78ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3356.svg">, as we shall define it
in <a href="#_40" class="pginternal">*40</a>) constitute the class of all products <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_7"> that can be
formed of a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_7"> and a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg">.</p>

<p>Thus we are led to three general definitions for descriptive double
functions, namely (if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\unicode{x2640} y\)" src="images/3358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.76ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3358.svg"> be any such function)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;x\unicode{x2640} \text{ is the relation of }x\unicode{x2640} y\text{ to }&amp;y\text{ for any }&amp;y,\\ &amp;\unicode{x2640} y &amp;x \quad \quad \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,&amp;x,\\ &amp;\alpha \unicode{x2640}_{,,} y\text{ is the class of values of }&amp;x\unicode{x2640} y\text{ when }&amp;x\text{ is an }\alpha . \end{aligned} \]" src="images/3359.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.645ex; width: 51.464ex; height: 8.422ex;" id="img_images_3359.svg"></span>
Since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \unicode{x2640}_{,,}y\)" src="images/3360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.843ex; width: 4.991ex; height: 2.54ex;" id="img_images_3360.svg"> is again a descriptive double
function, the first two of the above definitions can be applied to it.
The third definition, for typographical reasons, cannot be applied
conveniently, though theoretically it is of course applicable. The
relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\unicode{x2640}\)" src="images/3361.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 2.652ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3361.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x2640} y\)" src="images/3362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.466ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3362.svg"> represent the
general idea contained in some of the uses in mathematics of the term
'operation,' <i>e.g</i>. +1 is the operation of adding 1.</p>

<p>The uses of the notations introduced in the present number occur
chiefly in arithmetic (Parts III and IV). Few propositions can be given
at this stage, since most of the important uses of the notation here
introduced depend upon the substitution of some special function for
the general function "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x2640}\)" src="images/3331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3331.svg_1">" here used. In the present
number, the propositions given are all immediate consequences of the
definitions.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*38·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\unicode{x2640} =\hat{u}\hat{y}(u=x\unicode{x2640} y)\quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3363.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.586ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3363.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*38·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\unicode{x2640} y=\hat{u}\hat{x}(u=x\unicode{x2640} y)\quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3364.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.586ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3364.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*38·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \unicode{x2640}_{,,}y=\unicode{x2640} yʻʻ\alpha\quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3365.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.843ex; width: 19.321ex; height: 2.54ex;" id="img_images_3365.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*38·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :u(x\unicode{x2640} )y\ldotp \equiv \ldotp u=x\unicode{x2640} y\quad [\text{(*38·01)}]\)" src="images/3366.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.863ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3366.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_313">[Pg 313]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*38·101.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:u(\unicode{x2640}y)x.\equiv.u=x\unicode{x2640}y   \quad[\text{(*38·02)}]\)" src="images/3367.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.863ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3367.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*38·11.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.x\unicode{x2640}ʻy=\unicode{x2640}yʻx=x\unicode{x2640}y  \quad[\text{*38·1·101.*30·3}]\)" src="images/3368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.898ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3368.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*38·12.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{E}!x\unicode{x2640}ʻy.\text{E}!\unicode{x2640}yʻx  \quad[\text{*38·11.*14·21}]\)" src="images/3369.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.689ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3369.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*38·13.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:u\in x\unicode{x2640}ʻʻ\alpha.\equiv.(\exists y).y\in \alpha.u=x\unicode{x2640}y  \quad[\text{*38·1.*37·1}]\)" src="images/3370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 51.276ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3370.svg"></p>
