<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_314">[Pg 314]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="NOTE_TO_SECTION_D">NOTE TO SECTION D.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>General Observations on Relations.</i> The notion of "relation"
is so general that it is important to realize the different sorts of
relations to which the notations defined in the preceding section may
be applied. It often happens that a proposition which holds for any
relation is only important for relations of certain kinds; hence it is
desirable that the reader should have in mind some of the principal
kinds of relations. Of the various uses to which different sorts of
relations may be put, there are three which are specially important,
namely (1) to give rise to descriptive functions, (2) to establish
correlations between different classes, (3) to generate series. Let us
consider these in succession.</p>

<p>(1) In order that a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_173"> may give rise to a descriptive
function, it must be such that the referent is unique when the
relatum is given. Thus, for example, the relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}\)" src="images/2507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.086ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2507.svg_3">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_349.svg_10">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}\)" src="images/350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.451ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_350.svg_10">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_6">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\)" src="images/2637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2637.svg_6">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(C\)" src="images/42.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.719ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_42.svg_8">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\in}\)" src="images/3090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 1.949ex;" id="img_images_3090.svg_3">, defined above, all give rise to
descriptive functions. In general, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_174"> gives rise to a descriptive
function, there will be a certain class, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_12">, to
which the argument of the function must belong in order that the
function may have a value for that argument. For example, taking
the sine as an illustration, and writing "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\sin}ʻy\)" src="images/3380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3380.svg">" instead of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin y\)" src="images/328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.264ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_328.svg_2">," <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_195"> must be a number in order that <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sin}ʻy\)" src="images/3380.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.244ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3380.svg_1"> may
exist. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\sin}\)" src="images/3381.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.778ex; height: 2.407ex;" id="img_images_3381.svg"> is the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_196"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_431"> when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x = {\sin}ʻy\)" src="images/3382.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.556ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3382.svg">. If we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha =\)" src="images/3383.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 3.837ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_3383.svg"> numbers between <img alt="" data-tex="\(-\pi/2\)" src="images/3384.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.312ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3384.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\pi/2\)" src="images/3385.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.552ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3385.svg">, both included, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin \upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/3386.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.427ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3386.svg"> will
be the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_432"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_197"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x = {\sin}ʻy\)" src="images/3382.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.556ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3382.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(-\pi/2\le y \le \pi/2\)" src="images/3387.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.007ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3387.svg">.
The converse of this relation, which is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonleft \breve{\sin}\)" src="images/3388.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.427ex; height: 2.821ex;" id="img_images_3388.svg">,
will also give rise to a descriptive function; thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\alpha \upharpoonleft \breve{\sin})ʻx =\)" src="images/3389.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.227ex; height: 2.948ex;" id="img_images_3389.svg"> that
value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin^{-1}x\)" src="images/2559.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 6.682ex; height: 1.986ex;" id="img_images_2559.svg_1"> which lies between <img alt="" data-tex="\(-\pi/2\)" src="images/3384.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.312ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3384.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\pi/2\)" src="images/3385.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.552ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3385.svg_1">.
This illustrates a case which arises very frequently, namely, that
a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_175"> does not, as it stands, give rise to a descriptive
function, but does do so when its domain or converse domain is suitably
limited. Thus for example the relation "parent" does not give rise to
a descriptive function, but does do so when its domain is limited to
males or limited to females. The relation "square root," similarly,
gives rise to a descriptive function when its domain is limited
to positive numbers, or limited to negative numbers. The relation
"wife" gives rise to a descriptive function when its converse domain
is limited to Christian men, but not when Mohammedans are included.
The domain<span class="pagenum" id="Page_315">[Pg 315]</span> of a relation which gives rise to a descriptive function
without limiting its domain or converse domain consists of all
possible values of the function; the converse domain consists of all
possible arguments to the function. Again, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_176"> gives rise to a
descriptive function, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.102ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_344.svg_7"> will be the class of
those arguments for which the value of the function is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_433">. Thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{\sin}ʻx\)" src="images/2558.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.807ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_2558.svg_1"> consists of all numbers whose sine is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_434">,
<i>i.e.</i> all values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin^{-1}x\)" src="images/2559.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 6.682ex; height: 1.986ex;" id="img_images_2559.svg_2">. Again, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sinʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.318ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3390.svg"> will
be the sines of the various members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_131">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_132"> is a
class of numbers, then, by the notation of *38, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2\timesʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3391.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.06ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3391.svg">
will be the doubles of those numbers, <img alt="" data-tex="\(3\timesʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3392.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.06ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3392.svg"> the trebles
of them, and so on. To take another illustration, let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_133"> be a
pencil of lines, and let <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻx\)" src="images/2440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2440.svg_3"> be the intersection of a line <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_435">
with a given transversal. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg_4"> will be the intersections
of lines belonging to the pencil with the transversal.</p>

<p>(2) Relations which establish a correlation between two classes are
really a particular case of relations giving rise to descriptive
functions, namely the case in which the converse relation also
gives rise to a descriptive function. In this case, the relation is
"one-one," <i>i.e.</i> given the referent, the relatum is determinate,
and vice versa. A relation which is to be conceived as a correlation
will generally be denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_30"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_9">. In such cases, we are
as a rule less interested in the particular terms <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_436"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_198">
for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(xRy\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_266.svg_9">, than in classes of such terms. We generally, in
such cases, have some class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_66"> contained in the converse
domain of our relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_31">, and we have a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_134"> such
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha=Sʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.92ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3393.svg">. In this case, the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_32"> correlates
the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_135"> and the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_67">. We shall
have also <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta=\breve{S}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.92ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_3394.svg">, so that, for such a relation,
the correlation is reciprocal. Such relations are fundamental in
arithmetic, since they are used in defining what is meant by saying
that two classes (or series) have the same cardinal (or ordinal) number
of terms.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_316">[Pg 316]</span></p>

<p>(3) Relations which give rise to series will in general be denoted
by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_18"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_2">, and in propositions whose chief importance
lies in their application to series we shall also, as a rule,
denote a variable relation by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_19"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_3">. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_20"> is used,
it may be read as "precedes." Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{P}\)" src="images/2514.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 2.414ex;" id="img_images_2514.svg_1"> may be read
"follows," <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/3395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3395.svg"> may be read "predecessors of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_437">," <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{P}ʻx\)" src="images/3396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.287ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3396.svg"> may be read "followers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_438">."
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/3397.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.785ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3397.svg"> will be all members of the series generated by <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_21">
except the last (if any), <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/3398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.414ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3398.svg"> will be all members of the
series except the first (if any), <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg"> will be all the members of
the series. <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_396.svg_2"> will consist of all terms preceding some
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_136">. Suppose, for example, that our series is the
series of real numbers, and that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_137"> is the class of members of
an ascending series <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{1}\)" src="images/3400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3400.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{2}\)" src="images/3401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3401.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{3}\)" src="images/3402.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.375ex;" id="img_images_3402.svg">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu}\)" src="images/3403.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3403.svg">, ...
Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_396.svg_3"> will be the segment of the real numbers defined
by this series, <i>i.e.</i> it will be all the predecessors of the
limit of the series. (In the event of the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{1}\)" src="images/3400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3400.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{2}\)" src="images/3401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3401.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{3}\)" src="images/3402.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.375ex;" id="img_images_3402.svg_1">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(x_{\nu}\)" src="images/3403.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 2.33ex; height: 1.339ex;" id="img_images_3403.svg_1">, ... growing without limit, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Pʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/396.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.862ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_396.svg_4">
will be the whole series of real numbers.)</p>

<p>It very often happens that a relation has more or less of a serial
character, without having all the characteristics necessary for
generating series. Take, for example, the relation of son to father.
It is obvious that by means of this relation series can be generated
which start from any man and end with Adam. But these series are not
the field of the relation in question; moreover this relation is not
<i>transitive</i>, <i>i.e.</i> a son of a son of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_439"> is not a son of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_440">. If, however, we substitute for "son" the relation "descendant
in the direct male line" (which can be defined in terms of "son" by
the method explained in <a href="#_90" class="pginternal">*90</a> and <a href="#_91" class="pginternal">*91</a>), and if we limit the converse
domain of this relation to ancestors of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_441"> in the direct male line,
we obtain a new relation which <i>is</i> serial, and has for its
field <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_442"> and all his ancestors in the direct male line. Again, one
relation may generate a number of series, as for example the relation
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_443"> is east of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_199">." If <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_444"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_200"> are points on the earth's
surface, and in the eastern hemisphere, this relation generates one
series for every parallel of latitude. By confining the field of the
relation further to one parallel of latitude, we obtain a relation
which generates a series. (The reason for confining <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_445"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_201">
to one hemisphere is to insure that the relation shall be transitive,
since otherwise we might have <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_446"> east of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_202"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_203"> east of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_32">, but <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_447"> west of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_33">.)</p>

<p>A relation may have the characteristics of all the three kinds of
relations, provided we include in the third kind all those which
lead to series by some such limitations as those just described. For
example, the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(+1\)" src="images/3404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 2.891ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_3404.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> (in virtue of the notation of
<a href="#_38" class="pginternal">*38</a>) the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x+1\)" src="images/3405.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.191ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_3405.svg"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_448">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_449"> is supposed to be
a finite cardinal integer, has the characteristics of all three kinds
of relations. In the first place, it leads to the descriptive function
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(+1)ʻx\)" src="images/3406.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.423ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3406.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x+1\)" src="images/3405.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.191ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_3405.svg_1">. In the second place, it correlates
with any class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_138"> of numbers the class obtained by adding
1 to each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_139">, <i>i.e.</i> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(+1)ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3407.svg">. This
correlation may be used to prove that the number of finite integers is
infinite (in one of the two senses of the word "infinite"); for if we
take as our class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_140"> all the natural numbers including 0, the
class (<img alt="" data-tex="\(+1)ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3407.svg_1"> consists of all the natural numbers except 0, so
that the natural numbers can be correlated with a proper part<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_58" id="FNanchor_58">[58]</a> of
themselves. Again the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(+1\)" src="images/3404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 2.891ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_3404.svg_1"> may be used, like that of father
to son, to generate a series, namely the usual series of the natural
numbers in order of magnitude, in which each has to its immediate
predecessor the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(+1\)" src="images/3404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 2.891ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_3404.svg_2">. Thus this relation partakes of the
characteristics of all three kinds of relations.</p>


<div class="footnotes"><h3>FOOTNOTES:</h3>

<div class="footnote">

<p class="nind"><a class="label pginternal" href="#FNanchor_58" id="Footnote_58">[58]</a>
<i>I.e.</i> a part not the whole. On this definition of
infinity, see *124.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_317">[Pg 317]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_E_a">SECTION E.<br>
PRODUCTS AND SUMS OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>

<p><i>Summary of Section E.</i></p>


<p>In the present section, we make an extension of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cap\beta\)" src="images/3408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3408.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cup\beta\)" src="images/3409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3409.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\dot{\cap} S\)" src="images/3410.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.686ex; height: 2.138ex;" id="img_images_3410.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\unicode{x228d}S\)" src="images/3411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.534ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3411.svg">. Given
a class of classes, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_7">, the product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_8"> (which
is denoted by <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg"> is the common part of all the members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_9">, <i>i.e.</i> the class consisting of those terms which
belong to every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_10">. The definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ pʻ\kappa =\hat{x}(\alpha \in \kappa .\supset_\alpha .x\in \alpha ) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.191ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3413.svg"></span>
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_11"> has only two members, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_141"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_68">
say, <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa = \alpha\cap\beta\)" src="images/3414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.059ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3414.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_12"> has three
members, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_142">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_69">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_3">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa =\alpha\cap\beta\cap\gamma\)" src="images/3415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 15.802ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_3415.svg">;
and so on. But this process can only
be continued to a finite number of terms, whereas the definition of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_1"> does not require that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_13"> should be finite. This
notion is chiefly important in connection with the lower limits of
series. For example, let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_8"> be the class of rational numbers
whose square is greater than 2, and let "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xMy\)" src="images/3416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.781ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3416.svg">" mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \lt y\)" src="images/3417.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_3417.svg">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_450"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_204"> are rationals." Then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\lambda\)" src="images/3418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.379ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_3418.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{M}ʻx\)" src="images/3419.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.355ex; height: 3.966ex;" id="img_images_3419.svg"> will be the class of rationals less than
x. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{M}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.738ex; height: 3.966ex;" id="img_images_3420.svg"> will be the class of such
classes as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{M}ʻʻx\)" src="images/3421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.713ex; height: 3.966ex;" id="img_images_3421.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\lambda\)" src="images/3418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.379ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_3418.svg_1">. Thus
the product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{M}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.738ex; height: 3.966ex;" id="img_images_3420.svg_1">, which we call
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{M}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.233ex; height: 3.966ex;" id="img_images_3422.svg">, will be the class of rationals
which are less than every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_9">, <i>i.e.</i> the
class of rationals whose squares are less than 2. Each member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{M}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.738ex; height: 3.966ex;" id="img_images_3420.svg_2"> is a segment of the series of
rationals, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{M}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.233ex; height: 3.966ex;" id="img_images_3422.svg_1"> is the lower limit of
these segments. It is thus that we prove the existence of lower limits
of series of segments.</p>

<p>Similarly the <i>sum</i> of a class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_14"> is defined as
the class consisting of all terms belonging to <i>some</i> member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_15">; <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ sʻ\kappa =\hat{x}\{(\exists \alpha ).\alpha \in \kappa .x\in \alpha\} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/3423.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.111ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3423.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_451"> belongs to the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_16"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_452"> belongs
to some <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_17">. This notion plays the same part for upper limits
of series of segments as <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_2"> plays for lower limits. It has,
however, many more other uses than <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_3">, and is altogether
a more important conception. Thus in cardinal arithmetic, if no two
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_18"> have any term in common, the arithmetical sum of
the numbers of members possessed by the various members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_19">
is the number of members possessed by <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_318">[Pg 318]</span></p>

<p>The product of a class of relations (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_10"> say) is the relation
which holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_453"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_205"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_454"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_206"> have every
relation of the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_11">. The definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \dot{p}ʻ\lambda = \hat{x}\hat{y} (R\in\lambda . \supset_{R} . xRy) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3425.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.403ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3425.svg"></span>
The properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3426.svg"> are analogous to those of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_4">, but its uses are fewer.</p>

<p>The sum of a class of relations (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_12"> say) is the relation which
holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_455"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_207"> whenever there is a relation of the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_13"> which holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_456"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_208">. The definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \dot{s}ʻ\lambda =\hat{x}\hat{y} \{(\exists R) . R\in\lambda . xRy\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3427.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.401ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3427.svg"></span>
This conception, though less important than <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_1">, is more
important than <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3426.svg_1">. The summation of series and ordinal
numbers depends upon it, though the connection is less immediate than
that of the summation of cardinal numbers with <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_2">.</p>

<p>Instead of defining <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3426.svg_2">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3428.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3428.svg">, it would be formally more correct to define <img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_280">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/40.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_40.svg_6">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}\)" src="images/3429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 2.174ex;" id="img_images_3429.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}\)" src="images/3430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.758ex;" id="img_images_3430.svg">, which are the relations giving rise
to the above descriptive functions. Thus we should have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ p = \hat{\beta}\hat{\kappa}\{\beta=\hat{x}(\alpha \in \kappa . \supset_{\alpha} . x \in \alpha)\} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/3431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.674ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_3431.svg"></span>
whence we should proceed to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\vdash : \beta p\kappa . \equiv .\beta = \hat{x}(\alpha\in\kappa . \supset_{\alpha} . x\in\alpha),\\ &amp;\vdash . pʻ\kappa = \hat{x}(\alpha\in\kappa . \supset_{\alpha} . x\in\alpha)\\ \text{and}\qquad   &amp;\vdash . \text{E}!pʻ\kappa. \end{array} \]" src="images/3432.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.869ex; width: 44.558ex; height: 8.869ex;" id="img_images_3432.svg"></span></p>

<p>But in cases where the relation, as opposed to the descriptive
function, is very seldom required, it is simpler and easier to give
the definition of the descriptive function in the first instance. In
such cases, the relation is always tacitly assumed to be also defined;
<i>i.e.</i> when we give a definition of the form
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ Rʻx = Sʻx \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/3433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.809ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3433.svg"></span>
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_33"> is some previously defined relation, we always assume that
this definition is to be regarded as derived from
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R = \hat{u}\hat{x} (u = Sʻx) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/3434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.817ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3434.svg"></span></p>

<p>In addition to products and sums, we deal, in the present section,
with certain properties of the relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid\)" src="images/3435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.975ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3435.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid S\)" src="images/3348.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.717ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3348.svg_1">,
the meanings of which result from the notation introduced in <a href="#_38" class="pginternal">*38</a>.
Such relations are very useful in arithmetic. The reason for dealing
with them in the present section is that a large proportion of the
propositions to be proved involve sums of classes of classes or
relations.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_319">[Pg 319]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_40">*40. PRODUCTS AND SUMS OF CLASSES OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *40.</p>


<p>In this number, we introduce the two notations (explained above)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;pʻ\kappa = \hat{x} (\alpha\in\kappa . \supset_{\alpha} . x\in\alpha) \quad\text{Df}\\ &amp;sʻ\kappa = \hat{x} \{(\exists\alpha) . \alpha\in\kappa . x\in \alpha\} \quad\text{Df} \end{aligned} \]" src="images/3436.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.172ex; width: 32.482ex; height: 5.475ex;" id="img_images_3436.svg"></span>
Both these notions will be found increasingly useful as we proceed,
but <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_4"> remains more useful than <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_6"> throughout. It
is required for the significance of <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_7"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_5"> that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_20"> should be a class of classes.</p>

<p>In the present number, the most useful propositions are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \alpha \in \kappa . \supset . pʻ\kappa \subset \alpha\)" src="images/3437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.193ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3437.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> the product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_21"> is contained in every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_22">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \alpha \in \kappa . \supset . \alpha \subset sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3438.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.116ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3438.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_23"> is contained in the sum of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_24">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \beta \subset pʻ\kappa . \equiv : \gamma \in \kappa . \supset_{\gamma} . \beta \subset \gamma\)" src="images/3439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 31.167ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3439.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_70"> is contained in the product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_25"> if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_71"> is contained in every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_26">, and vice versa.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·151.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp sʻ\kappa \subset \beta . \equiv : \gamma \in \kappa . \supset_{\gamma} . \gamma \subset \beta\)" src="images/3440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 31.09ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_3440.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_27"> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_72"> if every
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_28"> is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_73">, and vice versa.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \kappa = \Lambda . \supset . pʻ\kappa = \text{V}\)" src="images/3441.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.815ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3441.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> the product of the null-class of classes is the universal
class. This may seem paradoxical at first sight, but it is really not
so. The fewer members <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_29"> has, the larger, speaking generally,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_8"> becomes. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_30"> has no members, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_31"> has
no members to which a given term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_457"> does not belong, and therefore
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_458"> belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_9">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \exists ! \kappa . \supset . pʻ\kappa \subset sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.14ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3442.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_32"> is null, its product is contained in its
sum.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·38.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . Rʻʻsʻ\kappa = sʻRʻʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 23.071ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3443.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is very often used in arithmetic. What it states
is as follows: Given a class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_33">, take its sum,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_6">, and then consider all the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_320">[Pg 320]</span> terms that have the
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_177"> to some member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_7">; this gives the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.154ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3444.svg">; next, take each separate member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_34">, say
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_143">, and form the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg_5">, consisting of all terms
having the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_178"> to some member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_144">. The class of
all such classes as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg_6">, for various <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_145">'s which are
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_35">, is <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.093ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3101.svg_3">; the sum of this class, by the
above proposition, is the same as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.154ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3444.svg_1">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{E} ‼ Rʻʻ\beta . \supset . sʻRʻʻ\beta = \hat{x} \{(\exists y) . y\in\beta . x\in Rʻy\}\)" src="images/3445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.02ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3445.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition requires, for significance, that <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_52"> should always
be a class. The proposition states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_53"> always exists when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in\beta\)" src="images/3446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3446.svg">, then the sum of all classes which have the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_179"> to some member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_74"> consists of all members of such
classes as <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_54">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in\beta\)" src="images/3446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3446.svg_1">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . sʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta = Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.249ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3447.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition results from *40·4 by substituting
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_349.svg_11"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_180"> in that proposition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . pʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta = \hat{x} \{y\in\beta . \supset_{y} . xRy\}\)" src="images/3448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 31.189ex; height: 3.857ex;" id="img_images_3448.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of <a href="#_40_5" class="pginternal">*40·5</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3449.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.208ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3449.svg"> is
correlative to <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_16">. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_181"> is a serial relation,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3449.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.208ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3449.svg_1"> consists of terms preceding the whole
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_75">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_17"> consists of terms preceding part of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_76">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_77"> has a lower limit, it will be the upper limit
or maximum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3449.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.208ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3449.svg_2">; if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_78"> has an upper
limit, it will be the upper limit of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_18">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·61.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \exists ! \beta . \supset . pʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta \subset Rʻʻ\beta . pʻ\overleftarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta \subset \breve{R}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3450.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 45.195ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3450.svg"></p>

<p>In this proposition the hypothesis is essential, since, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta =\Lambda\)" src="images/3451.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.868ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3451.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\beta = \text{V}\)" src="images/3452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.922ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3452.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta = \Lambda\)" src="images/3453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.3ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3453.svg">.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_40_01">*40·01</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa = \hat{x} (\alpha\in\kappa . \supset_{\alpha} . x\in\alpha) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3454.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.562ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3454.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_40_02">*40·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa = \hat{x} {(\exists\alpha) . \alpha\in\kappa . x\in\alpha} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.219ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3455.svg"></p>

<p>In the above proposition, the two <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_32">'s are of different types,
since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_36"> is of the type next above that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_8">. Thus
it would be more correct to write
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash\colon\kappa=\Lambda\cap\text{Cls}.\supset.sʻ\kappa=\Lambda\cap\text{V}. \]" src="images/3484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.869ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3484.svg"></span></p>

<p>But in the case of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_33"> it is not very important to keep the
types distinct.</p>

<p>Observe that the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\kappa\)" src="images/3489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.19ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_3489.svg"> is essential to this

<p>The above propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3562.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3562.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3563.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.127ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3563.svg"> of course have analogues for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3564.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.113ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3564.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3565.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.05ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3565.svg">.

properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_22"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_3566.svg">. <a href="#_37_264" class="pginternal">*37·264</a> is the analogue of <a href="#_40_67" class="pginternal">*40·67</a>. The above propositions concerning
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3562.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.19ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3562.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\overleftarrow{P}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3563.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.127ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3563.svg_1"> will
be used in the theory of series, but until we reach that stage they
will seldom be referred to.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_40_7">*40·7</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . sʻ \alpha \unicode{x2640}_{,,} ʻʻ \beta = \hat{z} \{( \exists x, y ). x \in \alpha . y \in \beta . z = x \, \unicode{x2640} y\}\)" src="images/3567.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.843ex; width: 47.332ex; height: 2.675ex;" id="img_images_3567.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .\text{*40·11 .*38·3} \supset\\ \vdash . sʻ \alpha \unicode{x2640} ʻʻ \beta = \hat{z} \{( \exists \gamma, y ). y \in \beta . \gamma = \unicode{x2640}yʻʻ \alpha . z \in \gamma\} \\ [\text{*38·131}] \quad = \hat{z} \{( \exists \gamma, x, y). y \in \beta . \gamma = \unicode{x2640} yʻʻ \alpha . x \in \alpha . z = x \unicode{x2640} y \}\\ [\text{*13·19}] \qquad = \hat{z} \{( \exists x, y). x \in \alpha . y \in \beta . z = x  \unicode{x2640}  y \} \supset \vdash . \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3568.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.52ex; width: 59.321ex; height: 12.172ex;" id="img_images_3568.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_330">[Pg 330]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is of considerable importance, since it gives
a compact form for the class of all values of the function
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\unicode{x2640}y\)" src="images/3569.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.76ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3569.svg"> obtained by taking <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_459"> in the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_146">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_209"> in the class<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_84">. Thus, for example, suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_147">
is the class of numbers which are multiples of 3, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_85"> is
the class of numbers which are multiples of 5, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \times y\)" src="images/3570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.168ex; height: 1.575ex;" id="img_images_3570.svg">
represents the arithmetical product of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_460"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_210">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha\times ʻʻ \beta\)" src="images/3571.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.628ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3571.svg">
will be the class of products of multiples of 3 and
multiples of 5, <i>i.e.</i> the class of multiples of 15. Again suppose
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_148"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_86"> are both classes of relations; then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha\mid_{,,} ʻʻ \beta\)" src="images/3572.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 10.825ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_3572.svg"> will be all relative products
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_8"> obtained by choosing <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_187"> in the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_149">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_34"> in the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_87">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*40·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . sʻ\unicode{x2640}_{,,}yʻʻ\kappa = (sʻ\kappa)\unicode{x2640}_{,,}y =  \unicode{x2640}ʻʻ sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.843ex; width: 35.222ex; height: 2.54ex;" id="img_images_3573.svg"></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} &amp;\vdash .\text{*40·38 .*38·31}. &amp;\supset \vdash . sʻ\unicode{x2640}_{,,}yʻʻ\kappa &amp;= \unicode{x2640} yʻʻ sʻ\kappa \\ &amp;[\text{*38·2}]  &amp;&amp;= (sʻ\kappa)\unicode{x2640}_{,,}y . \supset \vdash . \text{Prop} \end{aligned} \]" src="images/3574.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.313ex; width: 58.706ex; height: 5.758ex;" id="img_images_3574.svg"></span></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_331">[Pg 331]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_41">*41. THE PRODUCT AND SUM OF A CLASS OF RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *41.</p>

<p>The propositions to be given in this number, down to <a href="#_41_3" class="pginternal">*41·3</a> exclusive, are
the analogues of those of <a href="#_40" class="pginternal">*40</a>, excluding those from <a href="#_40_3" class="pginternal">*40·3</a> onwards, which
have no analogues. Proofs will not be given, in this number, when they are
exactly analogous to those of propositions with the same decimal part in *40.
The smaller importance of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3426.svg_3"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3428.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3428.svg_1">, as compared with <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3581.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3582.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3582.svg">, is
illustrated by the smaller number of propositions in <a href="#_41" class="pginternal">*41</a> as compared
with *40.</p>

<p>Our definitions are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*41·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}ʻ\lambda = \hat{x}\hat{y}\{R \in \lambda .\supset_{R}. xRy\} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.276ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3583.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*41·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻ\lambda = \hat{x}\hat{y}\{(\exists R) . R \in \lambda . xRy\} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3584.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.772ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3584.svg"></p>

<p>Of the propositions preceding *41·3, which are analogues of propositions
in *40, the only two that are frequently used are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*41·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : R \in \lambda .\supset. R \unicode{x2abd} \dot{s}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3585.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.026ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3585.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*41·151.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \dot{s}ʻ\lambda \unicode{x2abd} S .\equiv: R \in \lambda.\supset_{R} . R \unicode{x2abd} S\)" src="images/3586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.483ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3586.svg"></p>

<p>Of the remaining propositions of this number, which have no analogues
in *40, the most important are *41·43·44·45, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{D}ʻ\dot{s}ʻ\lambda = sʻ\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda, \text{ᗡ}ʻ\dot{s}ʻ\lambda = sʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\lambda, Cʻ\dot{s}ʻ\lambda = sʻCʻʻ\lambda. \]" src="images/3587.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 55.946ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3587.svg"></span>
These propositions are constantly required in the theory of selections
(Part II, Section D) and in relation-arithmetic. Most of the other
propositions of this number are used only once or not at all.</p>
