<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_336">[Pg 336]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_42">*42. MISCELLANEOUS PROPOSITIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *42.</p>

<p>The present number contains various propositions concerning products
and sums of classes. They are concerned chiefly with classes of classes
of classes, or with relations of relations of relations. These are
required respectively in cardinal and in ordinal arithmetic. Thus
<a href="#_42_1" class="pginternal">*42·1</a> is used in *112 and *113, which are concerned with cardinal
addition and multiplication, while *42·12·2 are used in *160 and
*162, which are concerned with ordinal addition. <a href="#_42_22" class="pginternal">*42·22</a>, though not
explicitly referred to, is useful in facilitating the comprehension
of propositions on series of series of series, or rather on relations
between relations between relations, which are required in connection
with the associative law of multiplication in relation-arithmetic.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_42_1">*42·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . sʻsʻʻ\kappa = sʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.043ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3644.svg"></p>

<p>Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_37"> must, for significance, be a class of classes
of classes. The proposition states that if we take each member,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_150">, of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_38">, and form <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.867ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3645.svg">, and then form the
sum of all the classes so obtained, the result is the same as if we
form the sum of the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_39">. This is the associative law for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/40.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_40.svg_7">, and is (as will appear later) the source of the associative law
of addition in cardinal arithmetic. The way in which this proposition
comes to be the associative law for <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/40.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_40.svg_8"> may be seen as follows:
Suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_40"> consists of two classes, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_151"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_88">;
suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_152"> in turn consists of the two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/3646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_3646.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.124ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_1">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_89"> of the two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi'\)" src="images/3647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.619ex; height: 2.181ex;" id="img_images_3647.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta'\)" src="images/3648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.752ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_3648.svg">. Then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha = \xi \cup \eta . sʻ\beta = \xi' \cup \eta'\)" src="images/3649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 25.121ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_3649.svg">. (This will
be proved later.) Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.079ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3650.svg"> has two members, one of which is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi \cup \eta\)" src="images/3651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.63ex; height: 2.081ex;" id="img_images_3651.svg">, while the other is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi' \cup \eta'\)" src="images/3652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.885ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_3652.svg">. Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ sʻsʻʻ\kappa = (\xi \cup \eta) \cup (\xi' \cup \eta'). \]" src="images/3653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.694ex; height: 2.396ex;" id="img_images_3653.svg"></span>
But <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_9"> has four members, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/3646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_3646.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.124ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi'\)" src="images/3647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.619ex; height: 2.181ex;" id="img_images_3647.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta'\)" src="images/3648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.752ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_3648.svg_1">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻsʻ\kappa = \xi \cup \eta \cup \xi' \cup \eta'\)" src="images/3654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 22.187ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_3654.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind">Thus our proposition leads to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\xi \cup \eta) \cup (\xi' \cup \eta') = \xi \cup \eta \cup \xi' \cup \eta'\text{,} \]" src="images/3655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.226ex; height: 2.396ex;" id="img_images_3655.svg"></span>
which is obviously a case of the associative law.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_337">[Pg 337]</span></p>

<p>Our proposition states the associative law generally, including the
case where the number of brackets, or of summands in any bracket, is
infinite. The proof is as follows.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*40·4}.\supset\vdash\colon\colon x\in sʻsʻʻ\kappa.&amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \alpha).\alpha\in \kappa.x\in sʻ\alpha\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*40·11}] &amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \alpha):\alpha\in \kappa:(\exists \xi).\xi\in \alpha.x\in \xi\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*11·6}] &amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \xi)\colon\ldotp (\exists \alpha).\alpha\in \kappa.\xi\in \alpha:x\in \xi\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*40·11}] &amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp (\exists \xi).\xi\in sʻ\kappa.x\in \xi\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*40·11}] &amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp x\in sʻsʻ\kappa\colon\colon \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3656.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 63.717ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_3656.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*42·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.pʻpʻʻ\kappa=pʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.274ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3657.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*40·41}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp x\in pʻpʻʻ\kappa.&amp;\equiv:\beta\in \kappa.\supset_{\beta}.x\in pʻ\beta:\\ [\text{*40·1.*11·62}] &amp;\equiv:\beta\in \kappa.\gamma\in \beta.\supset_{\beta,\gamma}.x\in \gamma:\\ [\text{*11·2.*10·23}] &amp;\equiv:(\exists \beta).\beta\in \kappa.\gamma\in \beta.\supset_{\gamma}.x\in \gamma:\\ [\text{*40·11}] &amp;\equiv:\gamma\in sʻ\kappa.\supset_{\gamma}.x\in \gamma:\\ [\text{*40·1}] &amp;\equiv:x\in pʻsʻ\kappa\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3658.svg" style="vertical-align: -7.121ex; width: 60.765ex; height: 15.374ex;" id="img_images_3658.svg"></span></p>

<p>This is the associative law for products. Supposing again, for
illustration, that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_41"> consists of the two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_153">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_90">, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_154"> consists of the two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/3646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_3646.svg_2">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta\)" src="images/50.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.124ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_50.svg_3"> and \beta of the two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi'\)" src="images/3647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.619ex; height: 2.181ex;" id="img_images_3647.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\eta'\)" src="images/3648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.752ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_3648.svg_2">, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3659.svg"> consists of the two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\cap \eta\)" src="images/3660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.63ex; height: 2.081ex;" id="img_images_3660.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi'\cap \eta'\)" src="images/3661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.885ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_3661.svg">, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻpʻʻ\kappa=(\xi\cap \eta)\cap (\xi'\cap \eta')\)" src="images/3662.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.219ex; height: 2.283ex;" id="img_images_3662.svg">, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻsʻ\kappa=\xi\cap \eta\cap \xi'\cap \eta'\)" src="images/3663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 22.264ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_3663.svg">. Thus
our proposition becomes
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\xi\cap \eta)\cap (\xi'\cap \eta') = \xi\cap \eta\cap \xi'\cap \eta'. \]" src="images/3664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.226ex; height: 2.396ex;" id="img_images_3664.svg"></span></p>

<p>A descriptive function <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3665.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.378ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3665.svg"> whose arguments are classes or
classes of classes may be said to obey the associative law provided
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ RʻRʻʻ\kappa=Rʻsʻ\kappa. \]" src="images/3666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.252ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3666.svg"></span></p>

<p>This equation may be interpreted as follows: Given a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_155">,
divide it into any number of subordinate classes, so that no member is
left out, though one member may belong to two or more classes. Let the
classes into which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_156"> is divided make up the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_42">,
so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_43"> is a class of classes, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa=\alpha\)" src="images/3667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.187ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3667.svg">. Then
the above equation asserts that if we first form the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R's\)" src="images/3668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.406ex; height: 1.765ex;" id="img_images_3668.svg"> of the
various sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_157">, and then the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_188"> of the resulting
class, the result is the same as if we formed the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_189"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_158">
directly.</p>

<p>In some cases—for example, that of arithmetical addition of
cardinals—the above equation holds only when no two members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_44"> have a common term, <i>i.e.</i> when the parts into which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_159"> is divided are mutually exclusive.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_338">[Pg 338]</span></p>

<p>For a descriptive function whose arguments are relations of relations,
we shall find another form for the associative law; this form plays in
ordinal arithmetic a part analogous to that played by the above form in
cardinal arithmetic.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*42·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{s}ʻ\dot{s}ʻʻ\lambda=\dot{s}ʻsʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.075ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3669.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*41·11}. \supset\vdash:x(\dot{s}ʻ\dot{s}ʻʻ\lambda)y.&amp;\equiv.(\exists \mu).\mu\in \lambda.x(\dot{s}ʻ\mu)y.\\ [\text{*41·11}] &amp;\equiv.(\exists \mu,P).\mu\in \lambda.P\in \mu.xPy.\\ [\text{*40·11}] &amp;\equiv.(\exists P).P\in sʻ\lambda.xPy.\\ [\text{*41·11}] &amp;\equiv.x(\dot{s}ʻsʻ\lambda)y:\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3670.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.355ex; width: 57.528ex; height: 11.842ex;" id="img_images_3670.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*42·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{p}ʻ\dot{p}ʻʻ\lambda=\dot{p}ʻsʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.306ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3671.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*41·1}. \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp x(\dot{p}ʻ\dot{p}ʻʻ\lambda)y.&amp;\equiv:\mu\in \lambda.\supset_{\mu}.x(\dot{p}ʻ\mu)y:\\ [\text{*41·1}] &amp;\equiv:\mu\in \lambda.R\in \mu.\supset_{\mu,R}.xRy:\\ [\text{*11·2.*10·23}] &amp;\equiv:(\exists \mu).\mu\in \lambda.R\in \mu.\supset_{R}.xRy:\\ [\text{*40·11}] &amp;\equiv:R\in sʻ\lambda.\supset_{R}.xRy:\\ [\text{*41·1}] &amp;\equiv:x(\dot{p}ʻsʻ\lambda)y\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3672.svg" style="vertical-align: -7.058ex; width: 59.685ex; height: 15.248ex;" id="img_images_3672.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*42·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.Cʻ\dot{s}ʻCʻP=sʻCʻʻCʻP=FʻʻCʻP=\overrightarrow{F}^{2}ʻP\)" src="images/3673.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 48.39ex; height: 3.636ex;" id="img_images_3673.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition assumes that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_22"> is a relation between relations.
For example, suppose we have a series of series, whose generating
relations are ordered by the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_23">. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg_1"> is the
class of these generating relations; <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/3674.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.195ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3674.svg"> is the relation
"one or other of the generating relations which compose <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg_2">,"
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Cʻ\dot{s}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/3675.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.271ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3675.svg"> is the class of all the terms occurring in any
of the series. <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/3676.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.21ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3676.svg"> is the fields of the various series, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻCʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/3677.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.629ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3677.svg"> is again all the terms occurring in any of the series.
<img alt="" data-tex="\(FʻʻCʻP\)" src="images/3678.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.186ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3678.svg"> is all the terms belonging to fields of series which are
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg_3">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{F}^{2}ʻP\)" src="images/3679.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.864ex; height: 3.636ex;" id="img_images_3679.svg"> is all members of
fields of members of the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_24">; each of these again is all the
terms occurring in any of the series. The proof is as follows:</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*41·45}.\supset\vdash.Cʻ\dot{s}ʻCʻP&amp;=sʻCʻʻCʻP &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*40·56}.\supset\vdash.sʻCʻʻCʻP&amp;=FʻʻCʻP &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*33·5}.\supset\vdash.FʻʻCʻP&amp;=Fʻʻ\overrightarrow{F}ʻP\\ [\text{*37·38}]  &amp; =\overrightarrow{F}^{2}ʻP &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).(3)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3680.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.406ex; width: 51.416ex; height: 17.943ex;" id="img_images_3680.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_339">[Pg 339]</span></p>

<p>The following propositions apply to a relation of relations of
relations. These propositions are useful for proving associative laws
in ordinal arithmetic, since these laws deal with series of series of
series, and series of series of series are most simply constituted by
supposing the generating relations of the constituent series to be
ordered by relations which are themselves ordered by a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_25">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*42·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.sʻCʻʻʻCʻʻCʻP=CʻʻsʻCʻʻCʻP=CʻʻCʻ\dot{s}ʻCʻP=CʻʻFʻʻCʻP=Cʻʻ\overrightarrow{F}^{2}ʻP\)" src="images/3681.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 86.565ex; height: 3.636ex;" id="img_images_3681.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*40·38}.&amp;\supset\vdash.sʻCʻʻʻCʻʻCʻP=CʻʻsʻCʻʻCʻP &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*42·2}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3682.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 64.283ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_3682.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_42_22">*42·22</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash.sʻsʻCʻʻʻCʻʻCʻP&amp;=sʻCʻʻsʻCʻʻCʻP=sʻCʻʻCʻ\dot{s}ʻCʻP\\ &amp;=Cʻ\dot{s}ʻCʻ\dot{s}ʻCʻP=sʻCʻʻFʻʻCʻP\\ &amp;=FʻʻFʻʻCʻP=Fʻʻ\overrightarrow{F}^{2}ʻP=\overrightarrow{F}^{3}ʻP\\ &amp;\quad[\text{*42·21.*41·45.*40·56.*42·2.*37·3}]\end{align}\]" src="images/3683.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.759ex; width: 63.868ex; height: 12.649ex;" id="img_images_3683.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_26">, in the above proposition, is a relation which generates a
series of series of series, the above gives various forms for the
class of ultimate terms of these series. Thus suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\in CʻP\)" src="images/3684.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.332ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3684.svg">;
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_4"> is a relation between generating relations of series. If
now <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in CʻQ\)" src="images/3685.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.35ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3685.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_190"> is the generating relation of a series which
we may regard as composed of individuals. The class of individuals so
obtainable may be expressed in any of the above forms, as well as in
others which are not given above.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*42·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.sʻsʻʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\alpha=sʻRʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3686.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.779ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3686.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*42·1}.\supset\vdash.sʻsʻʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\alpha&amp;=sʻsʻ\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\alpha\\ [\text{*40·5}] &amp;=sʻRʻʻ\alpha.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3687.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.896ex; width: 47.693ex; height: 6.923ex;" id="img_images_3687.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*42·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.sʻsʻʻ\overleftarrow{R}ʻʻ\alpha=sʻ\breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha \quad[\text{Proof as in *42·3}]\)" src="images/3688.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.175ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_3688.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_340">[Pg 340]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_43">*43. THE RELATIONS OF A RELATIVE PRODUCT TO ITS FACTORS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *43.</p>

<p>The purpose of the present number is to give certain propositions on
the relation which holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_27"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_5"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P = Q \mid R\)" src="images/3689.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 10.109ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3689.svg">,
or whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P = R \mid Q\)" src="images/3690.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 10.109ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3690.svg">, or whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(P = R \mid Q \mid S\)" src="images/3691.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 13.454ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3691.svg">,
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_191"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_35"> are fixed. In virtue of the general definitions
of <a href="#_38" class="pginternal">*38</a>, these relations are respectively <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid R\)" src="images/3692.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.975ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3692.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid\)" src="images/3435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.975ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3435.svg_1">, and
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid) \mid (\mid S)\)" src="images/3693.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.217ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3693.svg">. Such relations are of great utility both
in cardinal and in ordinal arithmetic; they are also much used in the
theory of induction (Part II, Section E). In place of the notation
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid) \mid (\mid S)\)" src="images/3693.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.217ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3693.svg_1">, which is cumbrous, we adopt the more compact
notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \parallel S\)" src="images/3694.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.565ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3694.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_18"> is a class of relations,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3695.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 7.637ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3695.svg"> will be the class of relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid P\)" src="images/3696.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.302ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3696.svg"> where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \in \lambda\)" src="images/3697.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.784ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_3697.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid Rʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3698.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 7.009ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3698.svg"> will be the class of relations
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \mid R\)" src="images/3699.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.302ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3699.svg"> where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \in \lambda\)" src="images/3697.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.784ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_3697.svg_1">, and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \parallel S)ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3700.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.479ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3700.svg"> will
be the class of relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid P \mid S\)" src="images/3701.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 8.647ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3701.svg"> where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \in \lambda\)" src="images/3697.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.784ex; height: 1.661ex;" id="img_images_3697.svg_2">.
These classes of relations are often required in subsequent work.</p>

<p>In virtue of our definitions, we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*43·112.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . (R \parallel S)ʻQ = R \mid Q \mid S\)" src="images/3702.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.615ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3702.svg"></p>

<p>The propositions most used in the present number (except such as merely
embody definitions) are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*43·302.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . (P).P \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ(R \parallel S)\)" src="images/3703.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.358ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3703.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*43·411.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \breve{R}ʻʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\lambda = \text{ᗡ}ʻʻ \mid Rʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3704.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 28.296ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_3704.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*43·421.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \dot{s}ʻ \mid Rʻʻ\lambda = (\dot{s}ʻ\lambda) \mid R\)" src="images/3705.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.562ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_3705.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_343">[Pg 343]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="PART_II">PART II.<br>
<br>
PROLEGOMENA TO CARDINAL ARITHMETIC.</h2>
</div>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_345">[Pg 345]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SUMMARY_OF_PART_II">SUMMARY OF PART II.</h2>
</div>


<p>THE objects to be studied in this Part are not sharply distinguished
from those studied in Part I. The difference is one of degree, the
objects in this Part being of somewhat less general importance than
those of Part I, and being studied more on account of their bearing
on cardinal arithmetic than on their own account. Although cardinal
arithmetic is the goal which determines our course in Part II, all the
objects studied will be found to be also required in ordinal arithmetic
and the theory of series. As this Part advances, the approach to
cardinal arithmetic becomes gradually more marked, until at last
nothing is lacking except the definition of cardinal numbers, with
which Part III opens.</p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_A_b" class="pginternal">Section A</a> of this Part deals with unit classes and couples. A
<i>unit</i> class is the class of terms identical with a given term,
<i>i.e.</i> the class whose only member is the given term. (As
explained in the Introduction, Chapter III, <a href="#Page_80" class="pginternal">pp. 80</a> to <a href="#Page_83" class="pginternal">83</a>, the class
whose only member is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_461"> is not identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_462">.) We define
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_15"> as the class of all unit classes, leaving it to Part III to show
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_16">, so defined, is a cardinal number. In like manner, we define
a (cardinal or ordinal) couple, and then define <img alt="" data-tex="\(2\)" src="images/3751.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_3751.svg"> as the class of
all couples. The propositions on couples will not be much referred to
in the remainder of the present Part, since their use belongs chiefly
to arithmetic (Parts III and IV). On the other hand, the properties of
unit classes are constantly required in Sections C, D, E of this Part.</p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_B_b" class="pginternal">Section B</a> deals, first, with the class of sub-classes of a given class,
<i>i.e.</i> of classes contained in a given class. The sub-classes
of a given class are often important in arithmetic. Next we consider
the class of sub-relations of a given relation, <i>i.e.</i> relations
contained in a given relation. The propositions on this subject are
analogous to those on sub-classes, but less important. Next we consider
the question of "relative types," <i>i.e.</i> taking any object <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_463">,
and calling its type <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg">, we give a notation for expressing in
terms of <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_1"> the type of classes of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_464"> is a member, or
of relations in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_465"> may be either referent or relatum, and
so on. The notations introduced in this connection are very useful
in arithmetic, especially in connection with existence-theorems. But
the propositions of Section B are very seldom required in the later
sections of the present Part.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_346">[Pg 346]</span></p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_C_b" class="pginternal">Section C</a>, which deals with one-many, many-one and one-one relations,
is very important, and is constantly relevant in the sequel. A relation
is one-many when no term has more than one referent, many-one if no
term has more than one relatum, and one-one if it is both one-many and
many-one. In this section, we define the notion of <i>similarity</i>,
upon which all cardinal arithmetic is based: two classes are said to
be <i>similar</i> when there is a one-one relation whose domain is the
one and whose converse domain is the other. We prove the elementary
properties of similarity, including the Schröder-Bernstein theorem,
namely: If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_160"> is similar to part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_91">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_92"> is
similar to part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_161">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_162"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_93">.</p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_D_b" class="pginternal">Section D</a> deals with the notion of <i>selections</i>, upon which both
cardinal and ordinal multiplication are based. A selection from a set
of classes is a class consisting of one member from each class of the
set. Thus a selective relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_192"> may be defined as one which, for
a given class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_45">, makes <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3753.svg"> a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_163"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_164"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_46">. More exactly,
a selective relation for a class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_47"> is one which
is one-many, which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_48"> for its converse domain, and is
such that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x R \alpha\)" src="images/3754.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.459ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_3754.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_7">. Such a relation
may be called an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_1">-selector from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_49">. More generally,
we may define a <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_28">-selector from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_50"> as a relation which
is one-many, which has <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_51"> for its converse domain, and which
is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_29">. The theory of selectors is very important in
arithmetic. But until we come to cardinal multiplication in Part III,
Section B, the propositions of this fourth section will seldom be
relevant.</p>

<p><a href="#SECTION_E_b" class="pginternal">Section E</a> deals with mathematical induction, not in the special
form in which it applies to finite integers (this is considered in
Part III, Section C), but in a general form in which it applies to
all relations. The propositions of this section are of very great
importance, primarily in the theory of finite and infinite (Part III,
Section C, and Part V, Section E), but also in many other subjects,
and especially in the derivation of series from one-many, many-one or
one-one relations—for example, in ordering the "rational" points of
a projective space by means of successive constructions of harmonic
points. The ideas involved in this section are somewhat complicated,
and we must refer the reader to the section itself for an account of
them.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_347">[Pg 347]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_A_b">SECTION A.<br>
UNIT CLASSES AND COUPLES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of Section A.</i></p>

<p>In this section we begin (<a href="#_50" class="pginternal">*50</a>) by introducing a notation for the
<i>relation</i> of identity, as opposed to the <i>function</i>
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x=y\)" src="images/722.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_722.svg_4">"; that is, calling the relation of identity I, we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ I=\hat{x}\hat{y}(x=y) \quad\text{Df.} \]" src="images/3755.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.052ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3755.svg"></span>
The purpose of this definition is chiefly convenience of notation.
The definition enables us to speak of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{I}\)" src="images/3756.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.14ex; height: 3.19ex;" id="img_images_3756.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻI\)" src="images/3757.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.226ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3757.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\mid R\)" src="images/3758.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 4.743ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3758.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft I\)" src="images/3759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.789ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3759.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Iʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.303ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3760.svg">,
etc., which we could not otherwise do.</p>

<p>At the same time we introduce <i>diversity</i>, which is defined as the
negation of identity, and denoted by the letter <img alt="" data-tex="\(J\)" src="images/47.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.432ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_47.svg_1">. The properties
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\)" src="images/46.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.14ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_46.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(J\)" src="images/47.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.432ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_47.svg_2"> result immediately from <a href="#_13" class="pginternal">*13</a>, since
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ xIy.\equiv.x=y. \]" src="images/3761.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 13.364ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3761.svg"></span></p>

<p>We next introduce a very important notation, due to Peano, for the
class whose only member is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_466">. If we took a strictly and purely
extensional view of classes, we should naturally suppose this class to
be identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_467">. But in view of the theory of classes explained
in <a href="#_20" class="pginternal">*20</a>, it is plain that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_468"> can never be identical with a class of
which it is a member, even when it is the only member of that class.
Peano uses the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota x\)" src="images/3762.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.095ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_3762.svg">" for the class whose only member
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_469">; we shall alter this to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/3763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3763.svg">," following our general
notation for descriptive functions. Thus we are to have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \iota ʻx=\hat{y}(y=x)=\hat{y}(yIx)=\overrightarrow{I}ʻx. \]" src="images/3764.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.625ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_3764.svg"></span>
Hence we take as our definition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \iota =\overrightarrow{I} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/3765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 10.27ex; height: 3.629ex;" id="img_images_3765.svg"></span>
since this definition gives the desired value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/3763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3763.svg_1">. The
properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_3"> are many and important.</p>

<p>It is important to observe that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_412.svg_1">" means
"the only member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_165">." Thus it exists when, and only when,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_166"> has one member and no more, in which case <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_167">
is of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/3763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3763.svg_2">, if x is its only member. Thus
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_412.svg_2">" means the same as "(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(x\in\alpha)\)" src="images/3766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.8ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3766.svg">,"
and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/3767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.371ex; height: 2.434ex;" id="img_images_3767.svg">" means the same as
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_59">." What we call "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_412.svg_3">" is
denoted, in Peano's notation, by "<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}\alpha\)" src="images/3768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 2.805ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3768.svg">."</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_348">[Pg 348]</span></p>

<p>Classes of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\)" src="images/3763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3763.svg_3"> are called <i>unit classes</i>, and
the class of all such classes is called 1. This is the cardinal number
1, according to the definition of cardinal numbers which will be given
in *100. The properties of 1, so far as they do not depend upon other
cardinals, or upon the fact that 1 is a cardinal, will be studied in
<a href="#_52" class="pginternal">*52</a>.</p>

<p>After a number (<a href="#_53" class="pginternal">*53</a>) containing various propositions involving 1 or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_4">, we pass to the consideration of cardinal couples (<a href="#_54" class="pginternal">*54</a>) and
ordinal couples (<a href="#_55" class="pginternal">*55</a>). A cardinal couple is a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\cup \iota ʻy\)" src="images/3769.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3769.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/3770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3770.svg">. The class of such couples is defined as
2, and will be shown at a later stage (*101) to be a cardinal number.
An ordinal couple, which, unlike a cardinal couple, involves an order
as between its members, is defined as a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\uparrow\iota ʻy\)" src="images/3771.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.108ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3771.svg">
(cf. <a href="#_35_04" class="pginternal">*35·04</a>), where we may either add <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/3770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3770.svg_1"> or not.
The properties of ordinal couples are in part analogous to those of
unit classes, in part to those of cardinal couples. In *56, we define
the ordinal number 2 (which we denote by <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg">, to distinguish
it from the cardinal 2) as the class of all ordinal couples
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx\uparrow \iota ʻy\)" src="images/3773.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.108ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3773.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/3770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3770.svg_2">. It will be shown
at a later stage that this is an ordinal number according to our
definition of ordinal numbers (*153 and *251).</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_349">[Pg 349]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_50">*50. IDENTITY AND DIVERSITY AS RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of *50.</i></p>

<p>The purpose of the present number is primarily notational. For
notational reasons, we must be able to express identity and
diversity as relations, and not merely as propositional functions,
<i>i.e.</i> we require a notation for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}(x=y)\)" src="images/3774.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.583ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3774.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{x}\hat{y}(x\neq y)\)" src="images/3775.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.583ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3775.svg">. We therefore put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} I=\hat{x}\hat{y}(x=y) &amp; \text{Df,} \\ J=\dot{-}I &amp; \text{Df.} \\ \end{array} \]" src="images/3776.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.396ex; width: 19.052ex; height: 5.923ex;" id="img_images_3776.svg"></span></p>

<p>In spite of the fact that diversity is merely the negation of
identity, the kinds of propositions which employ diversity are quite
different from the kinds that employ identity. Identity as a relation
is required, to begin with, in the theory of unit classes, which is
our reason for treating of it at this stage. It is next required,
constantly, in the theory of mathematical induction (Part II, Section
E). It is required also in showing that cardinal and ordinal similarity
are reflexive. These are its principal uses.</p>

<p>Diversity, on the other hand, is required almost exclusively in the
theory of series (Part V), and the first number in that theory will
be devoted to diversity. Until that stage, diversity will seldom be
referred to, with one important exception, namely in proving the
associative law of multiplication in relation-arithmetic (*174).</p>

<p>The most important propositions on identity in the present number are
the following:</p>

<p><b>50·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .Iʻʻ\alpha=\alpha\)" src="images/3777.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.157ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3777.svg"></p>

<p><b>50·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.R\mid I=I\mid R=R\)" src="images/3778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 19.626ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3778.svg"></p>

<p><b>50·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\alpha\upharpoonleft I=I\upharpoonright\alpha=\alpha\upharpoonleft I\upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/3779.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 26.437ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3779.svg"></p>

<p><b>50·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cnv}ʻ(\alpha\upharpoonleft I)=\alpha\upharpoonleft I\)" src="images/3780.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.186ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3780.svg"></p>

<p><b>50·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{D}ʻ(\alpha\upharpoonleft I)=\text{ᗡ}ʻ (\alpha\upharpoonleft I)=Cʻ(\alpha\upharpoonleft I)=\alpha\)" src="images/3781.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.412ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3781.svg"></p>

<p>The most important propositions on diversity in the present number are
the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*50·23</b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \unicode{x2abd} J .\equiv. \breve{R} \unicode{x2abd} J\)" src="images/3784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.426ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_3784.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*50·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \unicode{x2abd} J .\equiv. (x){\sim}(x R x)\)" src="images/3785.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.799ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3785.svg"></p>

<p>It will be observed that all these propositions are concerned with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \unicode{x2abd} J\)" src="images/3789.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.507ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3789.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{2} \unicode{x2abd} J\)" src="images/3790.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_3790.svg">, both of which are
satisfied if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_193"> is a <i>serial</i> relation. The hypothesis
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{2}\unicode{x2abd} J\)" src="images/3791.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.494ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_3791.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \dot{\cap} \breve{R} = \dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/3792.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.531ex; height: 2.6ex;" id="img_images_3792.svg">
characterizes an <i>asymmetrical</i> relation, <i>i.e.</i> one which,
if it holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_470"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_211">, cannot hold between <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_212"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_471">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*50·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(I=\hat{x}\hat{y}(x=y) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.423ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3793.svg"></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*13·171.Transp}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp y\neq z.&amp;\supset :x\neq y.\lor.x\neq z\colon\ldotp \\ [\text{*50·11}]         &amp; \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp yJz.&amp;\supset :xJy.\lor.xJz: \\ [\text{*33·14}]                &amp;&amp; \supset:x\in\text{D}ʻJ &amp;\qquad \text{(1)} \\ \vdash.\text{(1).*11·11·35}. \supset\vdash:\dot{\exists}!J. &amp;\supset .x\in \text{D}ʻJ: \\ [\text{*10·11·21}]      &amp; \supset\vdash:\dot{\exists}!J.&amp;\supset .(x).x\in \text{D}ʻJ. \\ [\text{*24·14}]               &amp;&amp;\supset .\text{D}ʻJ=\text{V} &amp;\qquad \text{(2)} \\ \vdash.\text{(2).*50·21}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3818.svg" style="vertical-align: -10.676ex; width: 70.201ex; height: 22.484ex;" id="img_images_3818.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the above proposition (<a href="#_50_33" class="pginternal">*50·33</a>), the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\exists}!J\)" src="images/3819.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 3.319ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_3819.svg">
is equivalent to the hypothesis that more than one object exists of
the type in question. This can be proved for all except the lowest
type. For the lowest type, we can only prove the existence of at
least one object: this is proved in <a href="#_24_52" class="pginternal">*24·52</a>. For the next type, we can
prove the existence of at least two objects, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_35"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_24">; these are distinct, by<a href="#_24_1" class="pginternal">*24·1</a>. For a class of order <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_44">,
we can prove the existence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{n}\)" src="images/545.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.279ex; height: 1.528ex;" id="img_images_545.svg_2"> objects. But for the class of
individuals we cannot prove,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_352">[Pg 352]</span> from our primitive propositions, that
there is more than one object in the universe, and therefore we cannot
prove <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\exists}!J\)" src="images/3819.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 3.319ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_3819.svg_1">. We might, of course, have included among our
primitive propositions the assumption that more than one individual
exists, or some assumption from which this would follow, such as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\exists\phi,x,y).\phi!x.{\sim}\phi!y. \]" src="images/3820.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.54ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3820.svg"></span>
But very few of the propositions which we might wish to prove depend
upon this assumption, and we have therefore excluded it. It should be
observed that most philosophers, being monists, deny this assumption.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*50·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{\exists}!J\unicode{x0294f}\text{Cls}\)" src="images/3821.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.219ex; height: 2.758ex;" id="img_images_3821.svg"></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*20·41.*22·38.(*24·01·02)}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\Lambda,\text{V}\in\text{Cls}. \\ [\text{*24·1}]                     &amp;\supset\vdash.\Lambda\neq \text{V}.\Lambda,\text{V}\in\text{Cls}. \\ [\text{*36·13.*50·11}]             &amp;\supset\vdash.\Lambda\{J\,\unicode{x0294f}\,\text{Cls}\}\text{V}. \\ [\text{*10·24}]                    &amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \\ \end{array} \]" src="images/3822.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 52.305ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_3822.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*50·35.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{\exists}!J\unicode{x0294f}\text{Rel} \quad[\text{Proof as in *50·34}]\)" src="images/3823.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.158ex; height: 2.871ex;" id="img_images_3823.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*50·75.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.I\Vert R=\mid R \quad[\text{Proof as in *50·74}]\)" src="images/3871.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.534ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3871.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*50·76.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\mid =R\mid .\equiv.P=R\)" src="images/3872.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 21.165ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3872.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*34·27.*30·41}.&amp;\supset\vdash:P=R.\supset.P\mid =R\mid  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*50·73.*30·36}.&amp;\supset\vdash:P\mid =R\mid .\supset.P=R &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3873.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 53.638ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_3873.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*50·761.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\mid P=\mid R.\equiv.P=R \quad[\text{Proof as in *50·76}]\)" src="images/3874.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.331ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3874.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_356">[Pg 356]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_51">*51. UNIT CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *51.</p>

<p>In this number we introduce a new descriptive function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\)" src="images/401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_401.svg_2">,
meaning "the class of terms which are identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_472">," which is
the same thing as "the class whose only member is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_473">." We are thus
to have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \iotaʻx = \hat{y} (y = x)\text{.} \]" src="images/3875.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.387ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3875.svg"></span>
But <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{y}(y = x) = \overrightarrow{I}ʻx\)" src="images/3876.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.098ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_3876.svg">. Hence we secure what we
require by the following definition:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota = \overrightarrow{I} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3877.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.642ex; height: 3.376ex;" id="img_images_3877.svg"></p>

<p>As a matter of notation, it might be thought that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{I}\)" src="images/3756.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.14ex; height: 3.19ex;" id="img_images_3756.svg_1"> would do as well as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_5">, and that this
definition is superfluous. But we need also the converse of this
relation, and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}ʻ\overrightarrow{I}\)" src="images/3878.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.584ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3878.svg">" is not a sufficiently
convenient symbol.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are constantly used in what follows. It
should be observed that the class whose members are <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_474"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_213"> is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx \cup \iotaʻy\)" src="images/3879.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3879.svg">, the class whose members are <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_475">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_214">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_34"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota ʻx \cup \iotaʻy \cup \iotaʻz\)" src="images/3880.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 14.959ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3880.svg">, the class formed by
adding <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_476"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_168"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup \iotaʻx\)" src="images/404.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.415ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_404.svg_1">, and the class
formed by taking <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_477"> away from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_169"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha - \iotaʻx\)" src="images/405.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.666ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_405.svg_1">.
(If <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_478"> is not a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_170">, this is equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_171">.)</p>

<p>The distinction between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_479"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\)" src="images/401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_401.svg_3"> is one of the merits of
Peano's symbolic logic, as well as of Frege's. On the basis of our
theory of classes, the necessity for the distinction is of course
obvious. But apart from this, the following consideration makes the
necessity apparent. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_172"> be a class; then the class whose
only member is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_173"> has only one member, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_174">, while
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_175"> may have many members. Hence the class whose only member is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_176"> cannot be identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_177"><a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_59" id="FNanchor_59">[59]</a>.</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number which are most used are the
following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : y \in \iotaʻx .\equiv. y = x\)" src="images/3881.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 19.159ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3881.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . x \in \iotaʻx\)" src="images/3882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.901ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3882.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_51_2">*51·2</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : x \in \alpha .\equiv. \iotaʻx \subset \alpha\)" src="images/3883.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.838ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3883.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_357">[Pg 357]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is useful because it enables us to replace membership
of a class (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_8">) by inclusion in the class (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\subset \alpha\)" src="images/3884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.918ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3884.svg">).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·211.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon x{\sim}\in\alpha.\equiv.\iotaʻx\cap \alpha=\Lambda\)" src="images/3885.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.431ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3885.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·221.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon x\in\alpha.\equiv.(\alpha-\iotaʻx)\cup \iotaʻx=\alpha\)" src="images/3886.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.527ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3886.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·222.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon x{\sim}\in\alpha.\equiv.\alpha-\iotaʻx=\alpha\)" src="images/3887.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.56ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3887.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_51_23">*51·23</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\iotaʻx=\iotaʻy.\equiv.y\in\iotaʻx.\equiv.x\in\iotaʻy.\equiv.x=y\)" src="images/3888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 43.516ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3888.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\exists!\alpha.\alpha\subset\iotaʻx.\equiv.\alpha=\iotaʻx\)" src="images/3889.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.337ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3889.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> an existent class contained in a unit class must be
identical with the unit class. From this proposition it will follow
that 0 is the only cardinal which is less than 1.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\alpha=\iotaʻx.\equiv.x=\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha.\equiv.x\breve{\iota}\alpha\)" src="images/3890.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.311ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_3890.svg"></p>

<p>For classes, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_412.svg_4"> has the same uses that
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_60"> has for functions; "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_412.svg_5">" means
"the only member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_178">." We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·59.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\psi{\breve{\iota}ʻ\hat{z}(\phi z)}.\equiv.\psi(℩x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/3891.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.543ex; height: 2.434ex;" id="img_images_3891.svg"></p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*51·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota=\overrightarrow{I} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/3892.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 9.642ex; height: 3.376ex;" id="img_images_3892.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\alpha \iota x.\equiv.\alpha=\hat{y}(y=x)\)" src="images/3893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 22.457ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3893.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*4·2.(*51·01)}.\supset\vdash\colon\alpha\iota x.&amp;\equiv.\alpha\overrightarrow{I}x. \\ [\text{*32·1}]               &amp; \equiv.\alpha=\hat{y}(yIx). \\ [\text{*50·1}]               &amp;\equiv.\alpha=\hat{y}(y=x):\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \\ \end{array} \]" src="images/3894.svg" style="vertical-align: -4.615ex; width: 52.417ex; height: 10.362ex;" id="img_images_3894.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\iotaʻ x=\hat{y}(y=x) \quad[\text{*30·3.*51·1}]\)" src="images/3895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.604ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3895.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash._\text{E}!\iotaʻ x \quad[\text{*51·11.*14·21}]\)" src="images/3896.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.467ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3896.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\alpha=\iotaʻ x.\equiv.\alpha=\hat{y}(y=x) \quad [\text{*20·57·2.*51·11}]\)" src="images/3897.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.311ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3897.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·131.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\alpha\iota x.\equiv.\alpha=\iotaʻ x \quad[\text{*51·1·13}]\)" src="images/3898.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.187ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3898.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha=\iotaʻ x.\equiv\colon y\in\alpha.\equiv_{y}.y=x \quad[\text{*51·13.*20·33}]\)" src="images/3899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 47.29ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3899.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·141.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha=\iotaʻ x.\equiv:\exists!\alpha\colon y\in\alpha.\supset_{y}.y&amp;=x\colon\equiv\colon     x\in\alpha\colon y\in\alpha.\supset_{y}.y=x\\ &amp;\quad[\text{*51·14.*14·122}]\end{align}\]" src="images/3900.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.087ex; width: 60.935ex; height: 5.305ex;" id="img_images_3900.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:y\in\iotaʻ x.\equiv.y=x \quad[\text{*51·11.*20·33}]\)" src="images/3901.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.878ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3901.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.x\in\iotaʻ x \quad[\text{*51·15.*13·15}]\)" src="images/3902.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.62ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3902.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51.161.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\exists!\iotaʻ x \quad[\text{*51·16.*10·24}]\)" src="images/3903.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.447ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3903.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{ᗡ}ʻ\iota=\text{V}\)" src="images/3904.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.618ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3904.svg"></p>


<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*51·1.*20·2}.&amp; \supset\vdash.\{\hat{y}(y=x)\}\iota x. \\ [*10·24]     &amp; \supset\vdash.(\exists\alpha).\alpha\iota x. \\ [\text{*33·131}]    &amp; \supset\vdash.x\in\text{ᗡ}ʻ\iota. \\ [\text{*10·11}]     &amp; \supset\vdash.(x).x\in\text{ᗡ}ʻ\iota. \\ [\text{*24·14}]     &amp; \supset\vdash.\text{ᗡ}ʻ\iota=\text{V} \\ \end{array} \]" src="images/3905.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.968ex; width: 33.64ex; height: 15.068ex;" id="img_images_3905.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition is used in the theory of selections (<a href="#_83_71" class="pginternal">*83·71</a>).</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_358">[Pg 358]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x\in\alpha.\equiv.\iotaʻ x\supset \alpha\)" src="images/3906.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.838ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3906.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*13·191}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp x\in\alpha.&amp;\equiv:y=x.\supset_{y}.y\in\alpha: \\ [\text{*51·15}]  &amp; \equiv:y\in\iotaʻ x.\supset_{y}.y\in\alpha: \\ [\text{*22·1}] &amp; \equiv:\iotaʻ x\supset \alpha\colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \\ \end{array} \]" src="images/3907.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.835ex; width: 46.277ex; height: 8.801ex;" id="img_images_3907.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition shows how to replace membership of a class by
inclusion in a class; thus for example it gives:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} \text{Socrates is a man}\,.\equiv.\,&amp;\text{the class of terms identical with Socrates is included} \\ &amp;\text{in the class of men}. \end{align} \]" src="images/3908.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.036ex; width: 71.377ex; height: 5.204ex;" id="img_images_3908.svg"></span></p>

<p>Before Peano and Frege, the relation of membership (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_2">) was
regarded as merely a particular case of the relation of inclusion
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\subset\)" src="images/3909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_3909.svg">). For this reason, the traditional formal logic treated
such propositions as "Socrates is a man" as instances of the universal
affirmative <img alt="" data-tex="\(A\)" src="images/38.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_38.svg_27">, "All <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_36"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_30">," which is what we express by
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\subset\beta\)" src="images/3910.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3910.svg">." This involved a confusion of fundamentally
different kinds of propositions, which greatly hindered the development
and usefulness of symbolic logic. But by means of the above proposition
(<a href="#_51_2" class="pginternal">*51·2</a>), we can always obtain a proposition stating an inclusion
(namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\subset\alpha\)" src="images/3911.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.918ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3911.svg">") which is equivalent to a given
proposition stating membership of a class (namely "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\alpha\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg_2">").</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.x{\sim} \in\alpha -\iotaʻ x\)" src="images/3912.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.875ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3912.svg"></p>
