<p>The following propositions are concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}\)" src="images/3958.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.891ex;" id="img_images_3958.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> with the relation of the only member of a unit class to
that class. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_179"> is a unit class, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_412.svg_6"> is
its only member. (<img alt="" data-tex="\({℩}x)(\phi x)\)" src="images/416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.934ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_416.svg_61"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ\hat{z}(\phi z)\)" src="images/3767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.371ex; height: 2.434ex;" id="img_images_3767.svg_1">
are equal whenever either exists, and any proposition about the
one is equivalent to the same proposition about the other.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*51·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha=\iotaʻ x.\equiv.x=\breve{\iota}ʻ\alpha.\equiv.x\breve{\iota}\alpha\)" src="images/3959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.562ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_3959.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_363">[Pg 363]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_52">*52. THE CARDINAL NUMBER 1.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of *52.</i></p>

<p>In this number, we introduce the cardinal number 1, defined as the
class of all unit classes. The fact that 1 so defined is a cardinal
number is not relevant at present, and cannot of course be proved until
"cardinal number" has been defined. For the present, therefore, 1 is to
be regarded simply as the class of all unit classes, unit classes being
such classes as are of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\)" src="images/401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_401.svg_4"> for some <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_482">.</p>

<p>Like <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_36"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_25">, 1 is ambiguous as to type: it means
"all unit classes of the type in question." The symbol "<img alt="" data-tex="\(1(\alpha)\)" src="images/3973.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.339ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3973.svg">,"
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_180"> is a type, will mean "all unit classes whose sole
members belong to the type <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_181">" (cf. <a href="#_65" class="pginternal">*65</a>). Thus <i>e.g.</i>
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\in 1(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/3974.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.924ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3974.svg">)" will mean "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\xi\)" src="images/3646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 0.991ex; height: 2.057ex;" id="img_images_3646.svg_3"> is a class consisting
of one individual," if "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Indiv}\)" src="images/3975.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.156ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_3975.svg">" stands for the class of
individuals.</p>

<p>The properties of 1 to be proved in the present number are what we
may call <i>logical</i> as opposed to <i>arithmetical</i> properties,
<i>i.e.</i> they are not concerned with the arithmetical operations
(addition, etc.) which can be performed with 1, but with the relations
of 1 to unit classes. The arithmetical properties of 1 will be
considered later, in Part III.</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number which are most used are the
following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*52·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha\in\text{1}.\equiv:\exists!\alpha\colon x,y\in\alpha.\supset_{x,y}.x=y\)" src="images/3976.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 36.25ex; height: 2.287ex;" id="img_images_3976.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_182"> is a unit class if, and only if, it is not null,
and all its members are identical.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*52·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .\iotaʻ x\in\text{1}\)" src="images/3977.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3977.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_52_4">*52·4</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha\in\text{1}\cup \iotaʻ\Lambda.\equiv\colon x,y\in\alpha.\supset_{x,y}.x=y\)" src="images/3978.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 37.901ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3978.svg"></p>

<p>We shall define 0 as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/3979.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.729ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3979.svg">. Thus the above proposition
states that a class has one member or none when, and only when, all its
members are identical.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*52·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\exists!\alpha.\alpha{\sim}\in\text{1}.\equiv.({\exists}x,y).x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y\)" src="images/3980.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 39.088ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3980.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_364">[Pg 364]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is obtainable from *52·4 by transposition, <i>i.e.</i>
by negating each side of the equivalence.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*52·46</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp  \alpha ,\beta  \in  1\ldotp \supset : \alpha \subset \beta \ldotp  \equiv  \ldotp \alpha  = \beta  \ldotp  \equiv  \ldotp  \exists !(\alpha \cap \beta )\)" src="images/3981.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.976ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3981.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e</i>. two unit classes are identical when, and only when, one is
contained in the other, and when and only when they have a common part.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*52·01</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\alpha }\{(\exists x) \ldotp  \alpha  = \iota ʻx\}\quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/3982.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.629ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3982.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*52·1</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \alpha  \in  1 \ldotp  \equiv  \ldotp  (\exists x) \ldotp  \alpha  = \iota ʻx\qquad\qquad\quad   [*20·3.(*52·01)]\)" src="images/3983.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.402ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_3983.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*52·11</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp  \alpha  \in  1 \ldotp  \equiv  : (\exists x): y \in  \alpha  \ldotp  \equiv _{y} \ldotp  y = x\quad [*52·1.*51·14]\)" src="images/3984.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 53.052ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_3984.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*52·12</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \hat{z} (\phi z) \in  1 \ldotp  \equiv  \ldotp  \text{E}! ({℩} x) (\phi x)\)" src="images/3985.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.506ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_3985.svg"></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*52·11}.\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp  \hat{z}(\phi z) \in  1\ldotp  &amp;\equiv  :(\exists x):y \in  \hat{z}(\phi z)\ldotp  \equiv _{y}\ldotp y=x:\\ [\text{*20·3}] &amp;\equiv  : (\exists x):\qquad \phi y\ldotp  \equiv _{y}\ldotp y=x:\\ [\text{*14·11}] &amp;\equiv  : \text{E}! <p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*51·131}. &amp;\supset \vdash: \alpha  = \iota ʻx\ldotp  \equiv  \ldotp \alpha \iota x :\\ [\text{*10·11·281}]  &amp;\supset \vdash:(\exists x)\ldotp  \alpha   =  \iota ʻx\ldotp  \equiv  \ldotp  (\exists x)\ldotp  \alpha \iota x:\\ [\text{*52·1}]\supset \vdash :\alpha \in 1 \ldotp  &amp;\equiv  \ldotp  (\exists x) \ldotp  \alpha \iota x\\ [\text{*33·13}]&amp;\equiv  \ldotp  \alpha  \in  \text{D}ʻ\iota : \supset \vdash \ldotp  \text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/3988.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 51.203ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_3988.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*52·173</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \alpha  \in  1 \ldotp  \equiv  \ldotp   \breve{\iota }ʻ\alpha   \in  \alpha \quad[\text{*51·53.*52·5}]\)" src="images/3995.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.166ex; height: 2.434ex;" id="img_images_3995.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_366">[Pg 366]</span></p>

<p>This proposition is frequently useful. We shall define the number 0 as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/3979.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.729ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3979.svg_1">; thus the above proposition states that a class has
one member or none when, and only when, all its members are identical.
It will be seen that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y\in\alpha.\supset_{x,y}.x=y\)" src="images/4013.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 19.146ex; height: 1.986ex;" id="img_images_4013.svg"> does not imply
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists!\alpha\)" src="images/2215.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.335ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_2215.svg_2">, and therefore allows the possibility of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_183">
having no members.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_368">[Pg 368]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_53">*53. MISCELLANEOUS PROPOSITIONS INVOLVING UNIT CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *53.</p>


<p>The propositions to be given in this number are mostly such as would
have come more naturally at an earlier stage, but could not be given
sooner because they involved unit classes. It is to be observed that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\cup\iotaʻy\)" src="images/3926.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3926.svg_2"> is the class consisting of the members <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_483"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_217">, while <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\uparrow\iotaʻy\)" src="images/4038.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.108ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4038.svg"> is the relation which holds
only between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_484"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_218">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_184"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_94"> are classes,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\alpha\cup\iotaʻ\beta\)" src="images/4039.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.56ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4039.svg"> is a class of classes, its members
being <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_185"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_95">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_195"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_37"> are relations,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻR\uparrow\iotaʻS\)" src="images/4040.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.881ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4040.svg"> is a relation of relations; and so on.</p>

<p>The present number begins by connecting products and sums <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_10">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_10">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3426.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.814ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3426.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/3428.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.738ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_3428.svg_2">, in cases
where the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_52"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_19"> are specified, with
the products or sums <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cap\beta\)" src="images/3408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3408.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cup\beta\)" src="images/3409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.243ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_3409.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\dot{\cap}S\)" src="images/4041.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.686ex; height: 2.138ex;" id="img_images_4041.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\unicode{x228d} S\)" src="images/4042.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.534ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4042.svg">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.pʻ\iotaʻ\alpha=\alpha\)" src="images/4043.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.955ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4043.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_53_1">*53·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.pʻ(\iotaʻ\alpha\cup\iotaʻ\beta)=\alpha\cap\beta\)" src="images/4044.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.464ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4044.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.pʻ(\kappa\cup\iotaʻ\alpha) =pʻ\kappa\cap\alpha\)" src="images/4045.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.846ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4045.svg"></p>

<p>with similar propositions for <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/40.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_40.svg_9">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}\)" src="images/3429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 2.174ex;" id="img_images_3429.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}\)" src="images/3430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.758ex;" id="img_images_3430.svg_1">.</p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions on sums and products of classes of
unit classes. The most important of these is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.sʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha=\alpha\)" src="images/4046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.236ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4046.svg"></p>

<p>We have next a proposition showing that the sum of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_53"> is null
when, and only when, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_54"> is either null or has the null-class
for its only member, <i>i.e.</i></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp sʻ\kappa=\Lambda.\equiv:\kappa=\Lambda\cap\text{Cls}.\lor.\kappa=\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/4047.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 38.856ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4047.svg"></p>

<p>(Here we write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\cap\text{Cls}\)" src="images/4048.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 7.239ex; height: 1.67ex;" id="img_images_4048.svg">," to show that the
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_37">" in question is of the next type above that of the other
two <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_38">'s.)</p>

<p>We have next various propositions on the relations of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/3115.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3115.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻx\)" src="images/2440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2440.svg_4"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg_8"> in various
cases, first for a general relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_196">, and then for the particular
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/40.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_40.svg_10"> defined in <a href="#_40" class="pginternal">*40</a>. Three of these propositions are very
frequently used, namely:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{E}!Rʻx.\equiv.\overrightarrow{R}ʻ x\in\text{1}\)" src="images/4049.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.216ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4049.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·301.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.Rʻʻ\iotaʻx=\overrightarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/4050.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.659ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4050.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_369">[Pg 369]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{E}!Rʻ x.\supset.Rʻʻ\iotaʻ x=\iotaʻRʻ x=\overrightarrow{R}ʻ x\)" src="images/4051.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 37.765ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4051.svg"></p>

<p>The remaining propositions of this number are of less importance, and
are seldom referred to.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.pʻ\iotaʻ\alpha=\alpha\)" src="images/4043.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.955ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4043.svg_1"></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*40·1}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp x\in pʻ \iotaʻ \alpha.&amp;\equiv:\beta\in\iotaʻ \alpha.\supset_{\beta}.x\in\beta:\\ [\text{*51·15}]           &amp; \equiv:\beta=\alpha.\supset_{\beta}.x\in\beta:\\ [\text{*13·191}]          &amp; \equiv:x\in\alpha\colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4052.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.817ex; width: 48.89ex; height: 8.766ex;" id="img_images_4052.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{ll} \vdash.\text{*40·11} .\supset\vdash:x\in sʻ \iotaʻ \alpha.&amp;\equiv.(\exists \beta).\beta\in\iotaʻ \alpha.x\in\beta.\\ [\text{*51·15}]           &amp; \equiv.(\exists \beta=\alpha.x\in\beta.\\ [\text{*13·195}]          &amp; \equiv.x\in\alpha:\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4054.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 49.755ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_4054.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{s}ʻ\iotaʻR=R \iotaʻ \quad[\text{Proof as in *53·02}]\)" src="images/4056.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 36.369ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_4056.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .pʻ (\iotaʻ\alpha\cup\iotaʻ\beta)=\alpha\cap \beta\)" src="images/4057.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.464ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4057.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*40·18}.\supset\vdash.pʻ(\iotaʻ \alpha\cup \iotaʻ \beta)&amp;=pʻ \iotaʻ \alpha\cap pʻ \iotaʻ \beta \\ [\text{*53·01}]              &amp; =\alpha\cap \beta.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4058.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 47.509ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_4058.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition can be extended to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\alpha\cup\iotaʻ\beta\cup\iotaʻ\gamma\)" src="images/4059.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 15.461ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_4059.svg">, etc. It
shows the connection (for finite classes of classes) between
the product <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_11"> and the product of the members
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cap\beta\cap\gamma\cap \ldots\ldotp\)" src="images/4060.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 15.158ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_4060.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*40·171}.\supset\vdash.sʻ(\iotaʻ \alpha\cup \iotaʻ \beta)&amp;=sʻ \iotaʻ \alpha\cup sʻ \iotaʻ \beta \\ [\text{*53·02}]                &amp; =\alpha\cup\beta.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4062.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 48.563ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_4062.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{p}ʻ (\iotaʻ R\cup \iotaʻ S)=R\dot{\cap}S \quad[\text{*41·18.*53·03}]\)" src="images/4063.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.074ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_4063.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition shows the connection between the product <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_12">
for a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_55"> consisting of two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_197"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_38">, and
the product <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\dot{\cap}S\)" src="images/4041.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 4.686ex; height: 2.138ex;" id="img_images_4041.svg_1">. The proposition can be extended to the
product of any given finite class of relations.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{s}ʻ(\iotaʻ R\cup \iotaʻ S)=R\unicode{x228d} S \quad[\text{*41·171.*53·04}]\)" src="images/4064.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.977ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_4064.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.pʻ (\kappa\cup\iotaʻ\alpha)=pʻ\kappa\cap\alpha\)" src="images/4065.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.846ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4065.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*40·18}.\supset\vdash.pʻ (\kappa\cup \iotaʻ\alpha)&amp;=pʻ\kappa\cap pʻ \iotaʻ\alpha\\ [\text{*53·01}]              &amp;=pʻ\kappa\cap\alpha\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4066.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 42.574ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_4066.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.sʻ (\kappa\cup \iotaʻ \alpha)=sʻ \kappa\cup \alpha \quad[\text{Proof as in *53·14}]\)" src="images/4067.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.487ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4067.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{p}ʻ (\lambda\cup \iotaʻ R)=\dot{p}ʻ \lambda\dot{cap}R \quad[\text{Proof as in *53·14}]\)" src="images/4068.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.011ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_4068.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·17.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{s}ʻ (\lambda\cup \iotaʻ R)=\dot{s}ʻ \lambda\unicode{x228d} R \quad[\text{Proof as in *53·14}]\)" src="images/4069.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 44.9ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_4069.svg"></p>

<p>The above proposition and the next are both used in connection with
mathematical induction (<a href="#_91_55" class="pginternal">*91·55</a> and <a href="#_97_46" class="pginternal">*97·46</a> respectively).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*53·18.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.sʻ (\alpha-\iotaʻ\Lambda)=sʻ \alpha\)" src="images/4070.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 21.393ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4070.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_376">[Pg 376]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_54">*54. CARDINAL COUPLES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary</i> of *54.</p>

<p>Couples are of two kinds, namely (1) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\cup\iotaʻy\)" src="images/3926.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3926.svg_3">,
in which there is no order as between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_485"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_219">, and (2)
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\uparrow\iotaʻy\)" src="images/4038.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.108ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4038.svg_1">, in which there is an order. We may
distinguish these two kinds of couples as cardinal and ordinal
respectively, since (as will be shown hereafter) the class of all
couples of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\cup\iotaʻy\)" src="images/3926.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3926.svg_4"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/3770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3770.svg_3">) is
the cardinal number 2, while the class of all couples of the form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\uparrow\iotaʻy\)" src="images/4038.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.108ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4038.svg_2"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/3770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3770.svg_4">) is the ordinal number
2, to which, for the sake of distinction, we assign the symbol
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg_1">," where the suffix "<img alt="" data-tex="\(r\)" src="images/33.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.02ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_33.svg_48">" stands for "relational," because
the ordinal 2 is a class of relations. In the present and the following
numbers, we shall define 2 and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg_2"> as the classes of cardinal and
ordinal couples respectively, leaving it to a later stage to show that
2 and <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg_3">, so defined, are respectively a cardinal and an ordinal
number. An ordinal couple will also be called an <i>ordered</i> couple
or a <i>couple with sense</i>. Thus a couple with sense is a couple of
which one comes first and the other second.</p>

<p>We introduce here the cardinal number 0, defined as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/3979.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.729ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3979.svg_2">.
That 0 so defined is a cardinal number, will be proved at a later
stage; for the present, we postpone the proof that 0 so defined has the
arithmetical properties of zero.</p>

<p>Cardinal couples are much less important, even in cardinal arithmetic,
than ordinal couples, which will be considered in the two following
numbers (<a href="#_55" class="pginternal">*55</a> and <a href="#_56" class="pginternal">*56</a>). It is necessary, however, to prove some of the
properties of cardinal couples, and this will be done in the present
number. Some properties of cardinal couples which have been already
proved are here repeated for convenience of reference. The definitions
of 0 and 2 are:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*54·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(0=\iotaʻ\Lambda \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4137.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.56ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4137.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*54·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(2=\hat{\alpha}\{(\exists x,y).x\neq y.\alpha=\iotaʻx\cup\iotaʻy\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4138.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.1ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_4138.svg"></p>

following are among the most important.</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*52·46·1.*22·58}.\supset\vdash:\iotaʻx\cup \iotaʻy\in 1.&amp;\supset.\iotaʻx\cup \iotaʻy=\iotaʻx.\iotaʻx\cup \iotaʻy=\iotaʻy.\\ [\text{*20·23}] &amp;\supset.\iotaʻx=\iotaʻy &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*22·56}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\iotaʻx=\iotaʻy.\supset.\iotaʻx\cup \iotaʻy=\iotaʻx.\\ [\text{*52·22}] &amp;\supset.\iotaʻx\cup \iotaʻy\in 1 &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2)}.\supset\vdash:\iotaʻx\cup \iotaʻy\in 1.&amp;\equiv.\iotaʻx=\iotaʻy.\\ [\text{*51·23}] &amp;\equiv.x=y:\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4151.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.484ex; width: 84.078ex; height: 18.1ex;" id="img_images_4151.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition shows that a class contained in a couple is either the
null-class or a unit class or the couple itself, whence it will follow
that 0 and 1 are the only numbers which are less than 2.</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*54·53.Exp}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha\in 2.\supset:x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset.\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*54·26}.  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha\in 2.\supset:\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y.\supset.x\neq y &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*51·16}.  &amp;\supset\vdash:\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y.\supset.x,y\in\alpha &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(3)}.  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha\in 2.\supset:\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y.\supset.x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(4)}.  &amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4186.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 72.16ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_4186.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the above proposition, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset_{x,y}.\alpha=\iotaʻx\cup \iotaʻy\)" src="images/4189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 33.851ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_4189.svg">"
secures that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_186"> has not <i>more</i> than two members, while
"(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists x,y).x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y\)" src="images/4190.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.601ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4190.svg">" secures that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_187">
has not <i>fewer</i> than two members.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*54·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.0\cup 1\cup 2=\hat{\alpha}{x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset_{x,y}.\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y}\)" src="images/4191.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 49.379ex; height: 2.5ex;" id="img_images_4191.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*4·42}.  &amp;\supset\vdash\colon\colon x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset_{x,y}.\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y:\equiv\colon\ldotp\\ &amp;   x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset_{x,y}.\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y:{\sim}(\exists x,y).x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y\colon\ldotp \\ &amp; \lor\colon\ldotp x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset_{x,y}.\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y:(\exists x,y).x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*11·63}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp{\sim}(\exists x,y).x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset:x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset_{x,y}.\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*4·71}] &amp; \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset_{x,y}.\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y:{\sim}( \exists x,y).x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y:\equiv:\\  &amp;{\sim}(\exists x,y).x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y:\\ [\text{*11·521}] &amp;   \equiv:x,y\in\alpha.\supset_{x,y}.x=y:\\ [\text{*52·4}]    &amp;\equiv:\alpha\in 0\cup 1 &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).*54·54}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\supset_{x,y}.\alpha=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y:&amp;\equiv:\alpha\in 0\cup 1.\lor.\alpha\in 2:\\ [\text{*22·34}]     &amp;\equiv:\alpha\in 0\cup 1\cup 2\colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4192.svg" style="vertical-align: -16.759ex; width: 118.351ex; height: 34.649ex;" id="img_images_4192.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_382">[Pg 382]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*54·56.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha{\sim}\in 0\cup 1\cup 2.\equiv.(\exists x,y,z).x,y,z\in\alpha.x\neq y.x\neq z.y\neq z\)" src="images/4193.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.211ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4193.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*54·55.*11·52}.&amp;\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha{\sim}\in 0\cup 1\cup 2.&amp;\equiv:(\exists x,y).x,y\in\alpha.x\neq y.\alpha\neq \iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y:\\ [\text{*51·2.*22·59}]  &amp;\equiv:(\exists x,y).\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y\subset \alpha.x\neq y.\alpha\neq \iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y:\\ [\text{*24·6}]         &amp;\equiv:(\exists x,y).\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y\subset \alpha.x\neq y.\exists!\alpha-(\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y):\\ [\text{*51·232.Transp}]&amp;\equiv:(\exists x,y):\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y\subset \alpha.x\neq y:(\exists z).z\in\alpha.z\neq x.z\neq y:\\ [\text{*51·2.*22·59}]  &amp;\equiv:(\exists x,y,z).x,y,z\in\alpha.x\neq y.x\neq z.y\neq z\colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4194.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.484ex; width: 78.176ex; height: 18.1ex;" id="img_images_4194.svg"></span></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition, a class which is neither null nor a unit
class nor a couple contains at least three distinct members. Hence it
will follow that any cardinal number other than 0 or 1 or 2 is equal to
or greater than 3. The above proposition is used in *104·43, which is
an existence-theorem of considerable importance in cardinal arithmetic.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_54_6">*54·6</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha\cap \beta=\Lambda.x,xʻ\in\alpha.y,yʻ\in\beta.\supset: \iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y=\iotaʻ xʻ\cup \iotaʻ yʻ.\equiv.x=xʻ.y=yʻ\)" src="images/4195.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 79.586ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4195.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*51·2}.\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset:\iotaʻ x\subset \alpha.\iotaʻ x'\subset \alpha.\iotaʻ y\subset \beta.\iotaʻ yʻ\subset \beta.\alpha\cap \beta=\Lambda:\\ [\text{*24·48}]     &amp; \supset:\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y=\iotaʻ xʻ\cup \iotaʻ yʻ.&amp;\equiv.\iotaʻ x=\iotaʻ xʻ.\iotaʻ y=\iotaʻ yʻ.\\ [\text{*51·23}]      &amp;&amp;                     \equiv.x=x'.y=yʻ\colon\ldotp\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4196.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.753ex; width: 100.465ex; height: 8.638ex;" id="img_images_4196.svg"></span></p>

<p>The above proposition is useful in dealing with sets of couples
formed of one member of a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_188"> and one member of a class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_96">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_189"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_97"> have no members in common. It
is used in the theory of cardinal multiplication (*113·148).</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_383">[Pg 383]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_55">*55. ORDINAL COUPLES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *55.</p>

<p>Ordinal couples, which are now to be considered, are much more
important, even in cardinal arithmetic, than cardinal couples. Their
properties are in part analogous to those of cardinal couples, but
in part also to those of unit classes; for they are the smallest
existent relations, just as unit classes are the smallest existent
classes. The properties which are analogous to those of unit classes
do not demand that the two terms of the couple should be distinct,
<i>i.e.</i> they hold for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ x\downarrow \iotaʻ x\)" src="images/4197.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.293ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4197.svg"> as well as
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ x\uparrow \iotaʻ x\)" src="images/4198.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.293ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4198.svg"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\neq y\)" src="images/3770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_3770.svg_5">); on the other
hand, the properties which are analogous to those of cardinal couples
do in general demand that the two terms of the ordinal couple should be
distinct.</p>

<p>The notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ x\uparrow \iotaʻ x\)" src="images/4198.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.293ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4198.svg_1"> is cumbrous, and does not
readily enable us to exhibit the couple as a descriptive function of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_486"> for the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_220">, or vice versa. We therefore introduce
a new symbol, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4199.svg">," for the couple. In a couple
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4199.svg_1">, we shall call <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_487"> the referent of the couple, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_221"> the relatum. In virtue of the definitions in <a href="#_38" class="pginternal">*38</a>, this gives
rise to two relations, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow\)" src="images/4200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4200.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow y\)" src="images/4201.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.868ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4201.svg">; hence we
obtain the notations <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrowʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.678ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4202.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow yʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.031ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4203.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,}y\)" src="images/4204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.022ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_4204.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4205.svg"> and so
on, which will be much used in the sequel. It should be observed
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrowʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4202.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.678ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4202.svg_1"> means the class of ordinal couples in
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_488"> is referent and a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_98"> is relatum, while
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow yʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.031ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4203.svg_1"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,}y\)" src="images/4204.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.022ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_4204.svg_1"> denotes the
class of couples having <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_222"> as relatum and a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_190"> as
referent; <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4205.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 8.909ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4205.svg_1"> denotes all such classes
of couples as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow yʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4203.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 7.031ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4203.svg_2">, where y is any member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_99">; and in virtue of <a href="#_40_7" class="pginternal">*40·7</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 11.327ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4206.svg">
denotes all ordinal couples of which the referent is a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_191">, while the relatum is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_100">. This is a
very important class, which will be used to define the product of two
cardinal numbers; for it is evident that the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\alpha\downarrow_{,,}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4206.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 11.327ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4206.svg_1"> is the product of the number of
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_192"> and the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_101">.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_384">[Pg 384]</span></p>

<p>The first few propositions of the present number are immediate
consequences of the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4199.svg_2"> and the notations
introduced in <a href="#_38" class="pginternal">*38</a>. We then proceed to various elementary properties
of the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4199.svg_3">, of which the most used are the
following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:z(x\downarrow y)w.\equiv.z=x.w=y\)" src="images/4207.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.75ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4207.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{D}ʻ(x\downarrow y)=\iotaʻ x.\text{ᗡ}ʻ(x\downarrow y)=\iotaʻ y.Cʻ (x\downarrow y)=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y\)" src="images/4208.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 57.936ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4208.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{D}ʻ R=\iotaʻ x.\text{ᗡ}ʻ R=\iotaʻ y.\equiv.R=x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 38.932ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4209.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·202.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x\downarrow y=z\downarrow w.\equiv.x=z.y=w.\equiv.y\downarrow x=w\downarrow z\)" src="images/4210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 48.035ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4210.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition should be contrasted with <a href="#_54_22" class="pginternal">*54·22</a>, as giving one
reason why ordinal couples are more useful in arithmetic than cardinal
couples. In virtue of the above proposition, when two ordinal couples
are identical, their referents are identical, and their relata are
identical.</p>

<p>We proceed next to various properties of the relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow\)" src="images/4200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4200.svg_1">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow x\)" src="images/4211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4211.svg">. These relations play a great part in
arithmetic. It will be observed that if two terms have the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow\)" src="images/4200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4200.svg_2">, the referent is a couple whose relatum is the
relatum in the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow\)" src="images/4200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4200.svg_3">, <i>i.e.</i> when we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R(x\downarrow)y\)" src="images/4212.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.64ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4212.svg">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(R=x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4213.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.525ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4213.svg"> (cf. <a href="#_55_122" class="pginternal">*55·122</a>).
Similar remarks apply to the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow\)" src="images/4200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4200.svg_4">. The class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrowʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4214.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.845ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4214.svg">, consisting of all couples whose referent is a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_193">, while the relatum is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_489">, is important. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·232.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists!\downarrow xʻʻ\alpha\cap\downarrow yʻʻ\beta.\equiv.x=y.\exists!\alpha\cap\beta\)" src="images/4215.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 38.701ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4215.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is frequently useful.</p>

<p>We proceed next (*55·3—·51) to give various properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4199.svg_4"> which are analogous to the properties of unit
classes. Among the more important of these properties are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:xRy.\equiv.x\downarrow y\unicode{x2abd}R.\equiv.\dot{\exists}!(x\downarrow y)\dot{\cap}R\)" src="images/4216.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.834ex; height: 2.871ex;" id="img_images_4216.svg"></p>

<p>This is the analogue of <a href="#_51_31" class="pginternal">*51·31</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\dot{\exists}!R.R\unicode{x2abd}x\downarrow y.\equiv.R=x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4217.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 28.413ex; height: 2.769ex;" id="img_images_4217.svg"></p>

<p>This is the analogue of <a href="#_51_4" class="pginternal">*51·4</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·5.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash\colon\ldotp R &amp;\unicode{x2abd}x\downarrow y\unicode{x228d}z w.\equiv:\\ &amp;R=\dot{\Lambda}.\lor.R=x\downarrow y.\lor.R=z\downarrow w.\lor.R=x\downarrow y\unicode{x228d}z\downarrow w\end{align}\]" src="images/4218.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.365ex; width: 57.242ex; height: 5.862ex;" id="img_images_4218.svg"></span></p>

<p>This is the analogue of <a href="#_54_4" class="pginternal">*54·4</a>.</p>

<p>We then proceed to such properties of ordinal couples as are not
analogous to those of unit classes. For connecting the cardinal number
2 with the ordinal number <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg_4">, we have the proposition</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·54.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\colon x\neq y.\supset\colon\ldotp Cʻ R=\iotaʻ x\cup \iotaʻ y.R\dot{\cap}\breve{R}=\dot{\Lambda}.\equiv:R=x\downarrow y.\lor.R=y\downarrow x\)" src="images/4219.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 67.769ex; height: 2.9ex;" id="img_images_4219.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_385">[Pg 385]</span></p>

<p>This proposition shows that the only asymmetrical relations which
have a given cardinal couple <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\cup\iotaʻy\)" src="images/3926.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_3926.svg_5"> for their
field are the two corresponding ordinal couples <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow)y\)" src="images/4220.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.042ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4220.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\downarrow x\)" src="images/4221.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4221.svg">. We have next a set of propositions on the
relative products of couples and other relations, <i>i.e.</i> on
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid(x\downarrow y)\)" src="images/4222.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.154ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4222.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y)\mid S\)" src="images/4223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.016ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4223.svg">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid(x\downarrow y)\mid S\)" src="images/4224.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.499ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4224.svg">. These propositions are very
useful in arithmetic. The chief of them is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*55·61.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\text{E}!Rʻ z.\text{E}!Sʻ w.\supset.(R\Arrowvert\breve{S})ʻ (z\downarrow w)=(Rʻ z)\downarrow(Sʻ w)\)" src="images/4225.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 52.055ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4225.svg"></p>

<p>Finally we have four propositions which belong, by their subject, to
<a href="#_43" class="pginternal">*43</a>, but could not be given there, because the proofs make use of
ordinal couples.</p>

<p>The above propositions are frequently useful in arithmetic. Their
use arises as follows. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_194">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_102">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_4">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/4322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4322.svg"> be classes of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_195"> is correlated with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_5"> by the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_198">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_103"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/4322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4322.svg_1">
by the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_39">. Then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\gamma.y\in\delta\)" src="images/4323.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 11.174ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_4323.svg">, the
couple consisting of the correlate of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_490"> and the correlate of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_223"> is (<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻx)\downarrow(Sʻy)\)" src="images/4324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.323ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4324.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>, by the above,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid(x\downarrow y)\mid\breve{S}\)" src="images/4325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.499ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4325.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\Arrowvert\breve{S})ʻ(x\downarrow y)\)" src="images/4326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.096ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4326.svg">. Thus the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\Arrowvert\breve{S}\)" src="images/4327.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.308ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_4327.svg"> correlates the couples, in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_196"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_104">, composed of the correlates of terms in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_6"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/4322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4322.svg_2">. The most useful form, in practice, of *55·583, is that
given below in *55·61.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_395">[Pg 395]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_56">*56. THE ORDINAL NUMBER <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg_5">.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *56.</p>

<p>In this number, we have to consider the class of those relations which
are each constituted by a single couple. In case the two members of
this couple are not identical, the class of such relations is (as will
be shown later) the ordinal number 2, which, to distinguish it from
the cardinal number 2, we denote by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg_6">." (Here the suffix
is intended to suggest "relational.") The class of all relations
consisting of a single couple, without the restriction that the
two members of the couple are to be distinct, will be denoted by
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{2}\)" src="images/4339.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 2.242ex;" id="img_images_4339.svg">." This is not an ordinal number. It will be observed that
there is no ordinal number 1, because ordinal numbers apply to series,
and series must have more than one member if they have any members.
This will appear more fully when we come to deal with series.</p>

<p>The properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{2}\)" src="images/4339.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 2.242ex;" id="img_images_4339.svg_1"> are largely analogous to those of 1,
while the properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg_7"> are more analogous to those of 2.</p>

<p>Most of the propositions of the present number are seldom referred to
in the sequel, but such references as occur are important. The most
useful propositions in the present number are the following.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*56·111.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in 2_{r}.\equiv.\text{D}ʻ R,\text{ᗡ}ʻ R\in 1.\text{D}ʻ R\cap \text{ᗡ}ʻ R=\Lambda\)" src="images/4340.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 44.04ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4340.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*56·112.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in 2_{r}.\equiv.\text{D}ʻ R,\text{ᗡ}ʻ R\in 1.Cʻ R\in 2\)" src="images/4341.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.394ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4341.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*56·113.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{2}-2_{r}=\hat{R}\{(\exists a).R=a\downarrow a\}\)" src="images/4342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.06ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_4342.svg"></p>

<p>Observe that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{C}ʻʻ2\)" src="images/4343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.566ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_4343.svg">" means "relations whose fields have two
terms."</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*56·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{2}-2_{r}=\hat{R}\{(\exists a).R=a\downarrow a\}\)" src="images/4342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.06ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_4342.svg_1"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*56·37.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in 2_{r}.\equiv.Cʻ R\in 2.R\dot{\cap}\breve{R}=\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/4344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 31.787ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_4344.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(2_{r}\)" src="images/3772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.041ex; height: 1.864ex;" id="img_images_3772.svg_8"> is the class of asymmetrical relations whose fields have two terms.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*56·381.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:Cʻ R=\iotaʻ x.\equiv.R=x\downarrow x\)" src="images/4345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.386ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4345.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*56·39.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\dot{2}-2_{r}=\breve{C}ʻʻ 1\)" src="images/4346.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.909ex; height: 2.916ex;" id="img_images_4346.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> the relations which are couples whose referent and relatum
are identical are the relations whose fields consist of a single term.</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*56·11.*11·52.Transp}.\supset \vdash:R{\sim}\in 2_{r}. &amp;\equiv:R=x\downarrow y.\supset_{x,y}.x=y  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*56·1}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp R\in \dot{2}-2_{r}.&amp;\equiv:(\exists a,b).R=a\downarrow b:R=x\downarrow y.\supset_{x,y}.x=y:\\ [\text{*11·45}]  &amp;\equiv:(\exists a,b):R=a\downarrow b:R=x\downarrow y.\supset_{x,y}.x=y:\\ [\text{*13·193}] &amp;\equiv:(\exists a,b):R=a\downarrow b:a\downarrow b=x\downarrow y.\supset_{x,y}.x=y:\\ [\text{*55·202}] &amp;\equiv:(\exists a,b):R=a\downarrow b:a=x.b=y.\supset_{x,y}.x=y:\\ [\text{*13·21}] &amp;\equiv:(\exists a,b).R=a\downarrow b.a=b:\\ [\text{*13·195}] &amp;\equiv:(\exists a).R=a\downarrow a\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/4370.svg" style="vertical-align: -12.178ex; width: 96.95ex; height: 25.488ex;" id="img_images_4370.svg"></span></p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{2}-2_{r}\)" src="images/4371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.937ex; height: 2.599ex;" id="img_images_4371.svg"> might be defined as the ordinal number 1, since it
is what we shall call a relation number (cf. *153). But we wish our
ordinal numbers to be<span class="pagenum" id="Page_398">[Pg 398]</span> classes of <i>serial</i> relations, and such
relations have the property of being contained in diversity. Hence if
we were to define <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{2}-2_{r}\)" src="images/4371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 5.937ex; height: 2.599ex;" id="img_images_4371.svg_1"> as the ordinal number 1, we should
introduce a tiresome exception, from which trivial complications would
be introduced into ordinal arithmetic. We have, therefore, not adopted
this course.</p>

the cardinal and ordinal 2. It shows that the ordinal 2 consists of
those asymmetrical relations whose fields have (cardinal) 2 terms. It
is used in the theory of well-ordered series (*250·44).</p>

in relation-arithmetic (*165·38) and in the theory of series (*205·4).</p>
