<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_404">[Pg 404]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_B_b">SECTION B.<br>
<br>
SUB-CLASSES, SUB-RELATIONS, AND RELATIVE TYPES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of Section B.</i></p>

<p>In this section, we consider first the classes contained in a given
class and the relations contained in a given relation. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_197">
is any class, the classes contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_198"> are the members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\beta}(\beta \subset \alpha)\)" src="images/4429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.786ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4429.svg">; these are also called the
sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_199">, or (sometimes) the "parts" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_200">.
In this last usage, they are called "proper parts" when they are not
coextensive with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_201">, this phrase being formed on the analogy of
"proper fractions." The sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_202"> are all the classes
that can be formed from members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_203">; they are the same thing
as the "combinations" of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_204"> taken any number at
a time. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_45"> is the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_205">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(2^{n}\)" src="images/545.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.279ex; height: 1.528ex;" id="img_images_545.svg_3"> is
the number of sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_206">, whether <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_46"> be finite or
infinite. The number of sub-classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_207"> is always greater
than the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_208">. On account of these and other
propositions, the class of sub-classes of a given class is an important
function of the class. If the class is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_209">, we denote the class
of its sub-classes by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.068ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4430.svg">." This is a descriptive
function, derived from the relation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}\)" src="images/4431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4431.svg">," defined as follows:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cl} = \hat{\kappa}\hat{\alpha}\{\kappa = \hat{\beta}(\beta \subset \alpha)\} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/4432.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.712ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4432.svg"></span></p>

<p>The sub-relations of a given relation are all the relations contained
in the given relation, <i>i.e.</i> all relations which imply the given
relation for all possible arguments. That is, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_31"> is the given
relation, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_199"> is a sub-relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_32"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \unicode{x2abd} P\)" src="images/4433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4433.svg">.
Thus denoting the class of sub-relations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_33"> by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rl}ʻP\)" src="images/4434.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4434.svg">,"
we are to have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Rl}ʻP = \hat{R}(R \unicode{x2abd} P)\text{;} \]" src="images/4435.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.248ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_4435.svg"></span>
hence we take as the definition of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rl}\)" src="images/4436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.294ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_4436.svg">" the following:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Rl} = \hat{\lambda}\hat{P}\{\lambda = \hat{R}(R \unicode{x2abd} P)\} \quad \text{Df}. \]" src="images/4437.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.491ex; height: 2.968ex;" id="img_images_4437.svg"></span>
Sub-relations have properties analogous to those of sub-classes, but
they are of somewhat less importance. It should, however, be observed
that when one series is contained in another, <i>i.e.</i> is obtained
by selecting some of the terms of the other series without changing
their order, then the generating relation of the one series is a
sub-relation of the generating relation of the other series. (It is not
the case that a sub-relation of the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_405">[Pg 405]</span> generating relation of a series
must generate a contained series, for its field may fall apart into
detached portions, or otherwise fail of being serial.)</p>

<p>We shall also consider in this section (<a href="#_62" class="pginternal">*62</a>) the relation of membership
of a class, <i>i.e.</i> the relation which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_491"> has to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_210"> when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_9">. This relation bears the same relation to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_10">"
as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(I\)" src="images/46.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.14ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_46.svg_2">" bears to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x = y\)" src="images/418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_418.svg_3">." Strictly speaking, we ought
to introduce a new notation for it, putting (say)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ A = \hat{x}\hat{\alpha}(x \in \alpha) \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/4438.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.036ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_4438.svg"></span>
But as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_3">, unlike "<img alt="" data-tex="\(=\)" src="images/99.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 1.76ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_99.svg_1">," is a letter, and capable of being
conveniently used alone, it seems more desirable, from the point of
view of avoiding unnecessary duplication of symbols, to put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \in = \hat{x}\hat{\alpha}(x \in \alpha) \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/4439.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.22ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_4439.svg"></span>
Strictly speaking, this definition is faulty, since it gives two
different meanings to "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_4">." But practically this does not matter,
since the above definition gives
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash: x\in \alpha .\equiv. x \in \alpha\text{,} \]" src="images/4440.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 18.057ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4440.svg"></span>
where the first <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_5"> has the meaning just defined, while the second
has the old meaning. Thus all that is really required of the above
definition, namely to give a meaning to formulae in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_6">
occurs without referent or relatum, is effected without the danger of
any confusion that could lead to errors.</p>

<p>The chief importance of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_7"> as a relation arises from the fact
that relations contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_8"> play a very important part in
arithmetic. Take, for example, the problem of selecting one term out of
each member of a class of classes: in this case we require a selecting
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_200"> which is such that whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(x R \alpha\)" src="images/3754.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.459ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_3754.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_492"> is
a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_211">, <i>i.e.</i> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \unicode{x2abd} {\in}\)" src="images/4441.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.584ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4441.svg">. (This condition is only part of the definition of a selecting
relation; the complete definition is given in <a href="#_80" class="pginternal">*80</a>.)</p>

<p>Three numbers in this section (<a href="#_63" class="pginternal">*63</a>, <a href="#_64" class="pginternal">*64</a>, <a href="#_65" class="pginternal">*65</a>) are devoted to the
discussion of <i>relative types</i>. Given a variable <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_493">, we
often want to define the relative types of other variables, or of
ambiguous symbols, occurring in the same context; that is, we wish to
express the types of these other symbols in terms of that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_494">.
We use "<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_2">" for the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_495">, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4442.svg">" for the
type in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_212"> is contained. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha = \alpha \cup -\alpha\)" src="images/4443.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.798ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4443.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx = \iotaʻx \cup -\iotaʻx = t_{0}ʻ\iotaʻx\)" src="images/4444.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.297ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4444.svg">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha = t_{0}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻ\alpha = \text{Cl}ʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4445.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 26.116ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4445.svg">. Also we
introduce a notation (*65) for giving typical definiteness, relatively
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_496">, to typically ambiguous symbols. This notation is very useful
in cardinal and ordinal arithmetic, since numbers are typically
ambiguous, and the failure to take account of this fact has led to
the contradictions concerning the greatest cardinal and the greatest
ordinal.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_406">[Pg 406]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_60">*60. THE SUB-CLASSES OF A GIVEN CLASS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *60.</p>

<p>Our definitions in this number are as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}=\hat{\kappa}\hat{\alpha}{\kappa=\hat{\beta}(\beta\subset\alpha)} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 25.821ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4446.svg"></p>

<p>This defines the relation to a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_213"> of the class of all its sub-classes.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl ex}=\hat{\kappa}\hat{\alpha}\{\kappa=\hat{\beta}(\beta\subset \alpha.\exists !\beta)\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4447.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.021ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4447.svg"></p>

<p>This defines the relation to a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_214"> of the class of all its
<i>existent</i> sub-classes, <i>i.e.</i> of all its sub-classes except
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_41">. This is often required, as, for example, in the statement
of Zermelo's axiom: "Given any class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_215">, there is a relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_201"> such that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_105"> is any existent sub-class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_216">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\beta\)" src="images/4448.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.355ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4448.svg"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_106">," <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}(\exists R):\beta\in\text{Cl ex}ʻ\alpha.\supset_{\beta}.Rʻ \beta\in\beta.\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/4449.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 35.036ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4449.svg"></span>
This axiom, or its equivalent the multiplicative axiom, plays (as
will appear hereafter) an important part as the hypothesis to many
propositions in cardinal arithmetic.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}=\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cls} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4450.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.616ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_4450.svg"></p>

<p>A <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\)" src="images/4451.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.142ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_4451.svg"> is a class whose members are classes.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{3} = \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cls}^{2} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4452.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.603ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_4452.svg"></p>

<p>A <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{3}\)" src="images/4453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.142ex; height: 2.089ex;" id="img_images_4453.svg"> is a class whose members are classes whose members
are classes, <i>i.e.</i> a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{3}\)" src="images/4453.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.142ex; height: 2.089ex;" id="img_images_4453.svg_1"> is a class of classes of
classes.</p>

<p>Apart from propositions which merely embody the definitions, the most
useful propositions in this number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\Lambda\in\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha\)" src="images/4454.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.792ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4454.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cl}ʻ\Lambda=\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/4455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.324ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4455.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·34.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\alpha\in\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha\)" src="images/4456.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.67ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4456.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·362.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cl}ʻ \iotaʻ x=\iotaʻ\Lambda\cup \iotaʻ \iotaʻ x\)" src="images/4457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.332ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4457.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_42"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ x\)" src="images/4458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4458.svg"> are the only sub-classes of a
unit class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ x\)" src="images/4458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4458.svg_1">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.sʻ\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha=\alpha\)" src="images/4459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.34ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4459.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·57.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\kappa\subset\text{Cl}ʻsʻ \kappa\)" src="images/4460.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.05ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4460.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·6.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:x\in\alpha.\supset.\iotaʻ x\in\text{Cl ex}ʻ \alpha\)" src="images/4461.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 25.971ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4461.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_407">[Pg 407]</span></p>

<p>The propositions of this number are chiefly useful in cardinal and
ordinal arithmetic, but uses also occur in the theory of series; hardly
any uses occur before cardinal arithmetic.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*60·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}=\hat{\kappa}\hat{\alpha}\{\kappa=\hat{\beta}(\beta\subset \alpha)\}     \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4462.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.083ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4462.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl ex}=\hat{\kappa}\hat{\alpha}\{\kappa=\hat{\beta}(\beta\subset \alpha.\exists !\beta)\}     \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4463.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.021ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4463.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}=\text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cls}      \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.616ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_4464.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{3} = \text{Cl}ʻ\text{Cls}^{2}      \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/4465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.603ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_4465.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\,\text{Cl}\, \alpha.\equiv.\kappa=\hat{\beta}(\beta\subset \alpha)      \quad\text{[*21·3.(*60·01)]}\)" src="images/4466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.636ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4466.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\,\text{Cl ex}\, \alpha.\equiv.\kappa=\hat{\beta}(\beta\subset \alpha.\exists !\beta)    \quad\text{[*21·3.(*60·02)]}\)" src="images/4467.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.574ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4467.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha=\hat{\beta}(\beta\subset \alpha)      \quad\text{[*30·3.*60·1]}\)" src="images/4468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.717ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4468.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cl ex}ʻ \alpha=\hat{\beta}(\beta\subset \alpha.\exists !\beta) \quad\text{[*30·3.*60·11]}\)" src="images/4469.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.786ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_4469.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\exists !\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha      \quad\text{[*60·12.*14·21]}\)" src="images/4470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.063ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4470.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\beta\in\text{Cl ex}ʻ \alpha.\equiv.\beta\in\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha.\exists !\beta      \quad\text{[*60·2·21]}\)" src="images/4474.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.145ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4474.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\beta\in\text{Cl ex}ʻ \alpha.\equiv.\beta\in\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha-\iotaʻ \Lambda      \quad\text{[*60·22.*53·52]}\)" src="images/4475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.619ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4475.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cl ex}ʻ \alpha=\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha-\iotaʻ\Lambda      \quad\text{[*60·23.*20·43]}\)" src="images/4476.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.52ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4476.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\Lambda\in\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha     \quad\text{[*24·12.*60·2]}\)" src="images/4477.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 27.381ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4477.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\exists !\text{Cl}ʻ \alpha      \quad\text{[*60·3.*10·24]}\)" src="images/4478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.931ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4478.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*60·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cl}ʻ\Lambda=\iotaʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/4455.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.324ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4455.svg_1"></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_61">*61. THE SUB-RELATIONS OF A GIVEN RELATION.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *61.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number (except that *61·371·372·373
imperfectly correspond to <a href="#_60_371" class="pginternal">*60·371</a>) are the analogues of those with
the same decimal part in <a href="#_60" class="pginternal">*60</a>. Proofs are omitted, as they are exactly
analogous to those in *60. There are very few subsequent references to
the propositions of this number.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_414">[Pg 414]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_62">*62. THE RELATION OF MEMBERSHIP OF A CLASS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *62.</p>

<p>When "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\alpha\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg_3">" was defined, in <a href="#_20" class="pginternal">*20</a>, it was defined as a
propositional function; and this mode of definition was necessary,
because we had to treat of this function before treating of relations.
But for many purposes it is desirable to regard <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_9"> as a relation,
so that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\alpha\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg_4">" becomes an instance of the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(uRv\)" src="images/4571.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.109ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_4571.svg">."
This requires, strictly speaking, a change in the meaning of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\alpha\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg_5">," but it is a change which does not falsify any of the
previous propositions in which "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in\alpha\)" src="images/1768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_1768.svg_6">" occurs; for if we call
the new meaning "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\unicode{x03AD}\alpha\)" src="images/4572.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.1ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4572.svg">," <i>i.e.</i> if we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\unicode{x03AD} = \hat{x}\hat{\alpha}(x\in\alpha) \quad\text{Df},\\ \text{we have}\qquad &amp;\vdash: x\unicode{x03AD}\alpha . \equiv . x\in\alpha. \end{array} \]" src="images/4573.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.217ex; width: 34.276ex; height: 5.566ex;" id="img_images_4573.svg"></span></p>

<p>Hence it is unnecessary in practice to have a new notation for the new
meaning, and we put simply
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \epsilon = \hat{x}\hat{\alpha}(x\in\alpha) \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/4574.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.258ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_4574.svg"></span>
This definition, though strictly incorrect, is recommended by its
convenience, and by the fact that it cannot lead to any harmful
confusions. The new meaning of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\epsilon\)" src="images/48.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.919ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_48.svg_2"> may be taken as replacing
the old throughout the remainder of this work.</p>

<p>The uses of the propositions of the present number occur almost
exclusively in the theory of selections from a class of classes
(<a href="#_83" class="pginternal">*83</a>, <a href="#_84" class="pginternal">*84</a>, <a href="#_85" class="pginternal">*85</a> and <a href="#_88" class="pginternal">*88</a>). Such selections are effected by means of
selective relations, part of whose definition is that they are
contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\epsilon\)" src="images/48.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.919ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_48.svg_3">. Hence the uses of the present number.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_57"> is the class of classes from which a selection
is to be made, a selective relation will in fact be contained
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\epsilon\upharpoonright\kappa\)" src="images/4575.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.422ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4575.svg">; hence the properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\epsilon\upharpoonright\kappa\)" src="images/4575.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.422ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4575.svg_1"> become important. Some of these
properties are given in <a href="#_62_4" class="pginternal">*62·4</a> ff.</p>

<p>The most important propositions of the present number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*62.2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\overrightarrow{\epsilon}ʻ \alpha = \alpha\)" src="images/4576.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.577ex; height: 3.097ex;" id="img_images_4576.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*62.231.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \kappa\subset\text{ᗡ}ʻ \epsilon . \equiv . \Lambda{\sim}\epsilon\kappa\)" src="images/4577.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.918ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4577.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*62.26.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . R = \epsilon \mid \overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/4578.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 11.644ex; height: 3.753ex;" id="img_images_4578.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*62.3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . \epsilonʻʻ \kappa = sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4579.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.064ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4579.svg"></p>

<p>Note that, since <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg"> is not a homogeneous relation, <i>i.e.</i>
not one in which referent and relatum belong to the same type,
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}^{2}\)" src="images/4604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 2.497ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_4604.svg"> is strictly meaningless. For if we have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha.\alpha \in\kappa\)" src="images/4605.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.031ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4605.svg">, the two <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg_1">'s have different
meanings, and do not therefore properly give <img alt="" data-tex="\(x{\in}{^{2}}\kappa\)" src="images/4606.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.094ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_4606.svg">. But
it is convenient to allow <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}^{2}\)" src="images/4604.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 2.497ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_4604.svg_1">, on the understanding that the
ambiguity of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg_2"> is to be differently determined for the two
factors in the product <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\mid {\in}\)" src="images/4607.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 4.904ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_4607.svg">, namely the second <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg_3">
must make both referent and relatum belong to the next type above that
to which they respectively belong for the first <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg_4">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_419">[Pg 419]</span></p>

<h2 class="nobreak" id="_63">*63. RELATIVE TYPES OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>

<p><i>Summary of</i> *63.</p>

<p>The notations introduced in this and the two following numbers serve to
express the type of one variable in terms of the type of another. They
are very useful in arithmetic, where it is necessary to take account
of types in order to avoid contradictions. The two chief notations are
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4442.svg_1">," for the type in which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_218"> is contained, and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_3">," for the type of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_498"> is a member. We put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha = \alpha \cup -\alpha \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/4639.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.481ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4639.svg"></p>

<p>This defines "the type of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_219">," or "the type which is
of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_220">." The characteristic of a type is that
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_548.svg_1"> is a type, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (x) . x \in \tau\text{,} \]" src="images/4640.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.919ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4640.svg"></span>
and conversely, if <img alt="" data-tex="\((x) . x \in \tau\)" src="images/4641.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.29ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4641.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_548.svg_2"> is a type. For
in that case, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \tau\)" src="images/4642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.23ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4642.svg">" is true whenever it is significant,
<i>i.e.</i> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_499"> belongs to the type which is the range of
significance of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_500"> in "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \tau\)" src="images/4642.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.23ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4642.svg_1">." Consequently <img alt="" data-tex="\(\tau\)" src="images/548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.029ex; width: 1.17ex; height: 1.005ex;" id="img_images_548.svg_3"> is
this range of significance, <i>i.e.</i> is a type.</p>

<p>Since we have (<img alt="" data-tex="\(x) . x \in (\alpha \cup -\alpha)\)" src="images/4643.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.171ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4643.svg">, it follows that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cup -\alpha\)" src="images/4644.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 7.171ex; height: 1.538ex;" id="img_images_4644.svg"> is a type. It is not "the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_221">,"
but "the type of the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_222">." (In case <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_223"> is
null, "the type of the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_224">" may be interpreted as
meaning "the type to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_501"> belongs when '<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \alpha\)" src="images/273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_273.svg_11">' is
significant.") "The type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_502">," <i>i.e.</i> the type of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_503">
is a member, is defined as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx = \iotaʻx \cup -\iotaʻx \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/4645.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.348ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4645.svg"></p>

<p>By what was said above, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\iotaʻx\)" src="images/4646.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.614ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4646.svg">" is the type of the members
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\)" src="images/401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_401.svg_5">, <i>i.e.</i> the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_504">. By combining the
definitions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_4"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4442.svg_2">, we obtain
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash . tʻx = t_{0}ʻ\iotaʻx\text{.} \]" src="images/4647.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.117ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4647.svg"></span>
Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash . x \in tʻx \quad \text{and} \quad \vdash : y \neq x .\supset. y \in tʻx. \]" src="images/4648.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 38.521ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_4648.svg"></span></p>

<p>In short, <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_5"> consists of everything either identical or not identical with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_505">,
that is, every <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_224"> for which there is such a proposition, whether true or false,
as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(y = x\)" src="images/4649.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_4649.svg">." We put "<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_6">" here instead of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4650.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.622ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4650.svg">," because <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_506"> need not be a
class, and is in fact subject to no limitation whatever, whereas "<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻx\)" src="images/4651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.456ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4651.svg">" is
not significant unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_507"> is a class, and therefore we write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4442.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4442.svg_3">" rather
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_420">[Pg 420]</span>than "<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻx\)" src="images/4651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.456ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4651.svg_1">."</p>

<p>We put also</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·011.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{1}ʻx = tʻx \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/4652.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.625ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4652.svg"></p>

<p>This definition serves merely to bring <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_7"> notationally into line
with <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻx\)" src="images/4651.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.456ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4651.svg_2"> and the types <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{2}ʻx, t^{3}ʻx, \ldots t_{2}ʻx, t_{3}ʻx, \ldots\)" src="images/4653.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.528ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4653.svg">
defined below.</p>

<p>In virtue of <a href="#_20_8" class="pginternal">*20·8</a>, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash: {\phi}a \lor {\sim}{\phi}a .\supset. \hat{x}({\phi}x \lor {\sim}{\phi}x) = tʻa\text{,} \]" src="images/4654.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 35.408ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_4654.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> if "<img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}a\)" src="images/145.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.545ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_145.svg_4">" is significant, then the range of
significance of the function <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}\hat{z}\)" src="images/4655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_4655.svg"> is the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_121">. It
follows that two ranges of significance which overlap are identical,
and two different ranges of significance have no member in common.</p>

<p>It will be seen that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx\)" src="images/401.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.452ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_401.svg_6"> is always of the next type above that
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_508">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_11"> (if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_60"> is a class of classes) is of
the next type below that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_61">. We put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{1}ʻ\kappa = t_{0}ʻsʻ\kappa \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/4656.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4656.svg"></p>

<p class="nind">
so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{1}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.465ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4657.svg"> is the type next below that in which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_62"> is contained. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_63"> is a class of classes of
individuals, <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{1}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4657.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.465ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4657.svg_1"> is the class of individuals. We put also</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·04.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{2}ʻx = tʻtʻx \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/4658.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.799ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4658.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·041.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{3}ʻx = tʻt^{2}ʻx \quad \text{Df} ~ \text{and so on}\)" src="images/4659.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.542ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4659.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·05.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{2}ʻ\kappa = t_{1}ʻt_{1}ʻ\kappa \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/4660.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.792ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4660.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·051.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{3}ʻ\kappa = t_{1}ʻt_{2}ʻ\kappa \quad \text{Df} ~ \text{and so on}\)" src="images/4661.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.548ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4661.svg"></p>

<p>Thus given any two objects which are members of any one of the
following: the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_509">, the type of the classes to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_510">
belongs, the type of the classes to which these classes belong, and so
on, we can express the type of either of our two objects by means of
its relation to the other object.</p>

<p>The propositions of this and the two following numbers will hardly ever
be used until we come to cardinal arithmetic. They are used constantly
in the first section on cardinal arithmetic, and they are constantly
relevant in the first section on relation-arithmetic. Moreover they are
usually required for cardinal and ordinal existence-theorems.</p>

<p>Among the most useful propositions of the present number are the
following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·103.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. x \in tʻx\)" src="images/4662.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.917ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4662.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·105.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \alpha \subset t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4663.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.463ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4663.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_63_11">*63·11</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: x \in t_{0}ʻ\alpha .\supset. tʻx = \alpha \cup -\alpha = t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4664.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.365ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4664.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_511"> either is or is not a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_225">,
then the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_512"> is the type which contains <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_226">. This
proposition uses <a href="#_20_8" class="pginternal">*20·8</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: {\phi}x . {\phi}y .\supset. y \in tʻx\)" src="images/4665.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 19.86ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4665.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if there is any function satisfied by both <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_513"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_225">,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_226"> is of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_514">. It is necessary to the use of
this proposition that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi\hat{z}\)" src="images/187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_187.svg_29"> is a typically<span class="pagenum" id="Page_421">[Pg 421]</span> ambiguous
function, it should receive the same typical determination for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_515">
and for <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_227">. For example, we have always <img alt="" data-tex="\(x = x\)" src="images/2212.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.605ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_2212.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y = y\)" src="images/4666.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.234ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_4666.svg">;
but we must not regard these as values of one function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z} = \hat{z}\)" src="images/4667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.121ex; height: 2.018ex;" id="img_images_4667.svg">,
because such a function is typically ambiguous. On the other
hand, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x = a\)" src="images/192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.505ex;" id="img_images_192.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y = a\)" src="images/4668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.323ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_4668.svg"> are values of one function <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{z} = a\)" src="images/4669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.266ex; height: 2.018ex;" id="img_images_4669.svg">,
because here the presence of a renders the function typically
determinate.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. t_{0}ʻtʻx = tʻx\)" src="images/4670.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.504ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4670.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·19.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. tʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha = tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.812ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4671.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: x \in tʻy .\equiv. y \in tʻx .\equiv. \exists! tʻx \cap tʻy .\equiv. tʻx = tʻy\)" src="images/4672.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 49.563ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4672.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition, which depends upon <a href="#_63_11" class="pginternal">*63·11</a>, and thence upon <a href="#_20_8" class="pginternal">*20·8</a> and
<a href="#_13_3" class="pginternal">*13·3</a>, and thence upon *9·14·15, is vital to the whole theory of types.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. t_{1}ʻ\kappa = sʻt_{0}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4673.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.754ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4673.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·371.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \beta \subset t_{0}ʻ\alpha .\equiv. \beta \in tʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4674.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.988ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4674.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·383.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. tʻt_{1}ʻ\kappa = t_{0}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4675.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.51ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4675.svg"></p>

<p>We shall have generally <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{m}ʻt^{n}ʻ\kappa = t^{m+n}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4676.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.683ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_4676.svg">, where
we may count suffixes as negative indices, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{m}ʻt_{n}ʻ\kappa = t^{m-n}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4677.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.683ex; height: 2.206ex;" id="img_images_4677.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{n-m}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4678.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.471ex; width: 7.274ex; height: 2.167ex;" id="img_images_4678.svg"> according as <img alt="" data-tex="\(m\)" src="images/446.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.986ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_446.svg_9"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_47"> is the greater.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: x \in t_{0}ʻ\alpha .\equiv. \alpha \in t^{2}ʻx .\equiv. \alpha \subset tʻx .\equiv. tʻx = t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4679.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 50.325ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4679.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is used constantly.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \alpha \in t_{0}ʻ\kappa .\equiv. \alpha \subset t_{1}ʻ\kappa .\equiv. \kappa \subset tʻ\alpha .\equiv. tʻ\alpha = t_{0}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/4680.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 50.612ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4680.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \alpha \in t_{1}ʻ\lambda .\equiv. \alpha \subset t_{2}ʻ\lambda .\equiv. \lambda \subset t^{2}ʻ\alpha .\equiv. tʻ\alpha = t_{1}ʻ\lambda     .\equiv. t^{2}ʻ\alpha = t_{0}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/4681.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 67.543ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4681.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·53.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: x \in t_{0}ʻ\alpha .\equiv. t^{2}ʻx = tʻ\alpha .\equiv. tʻx = t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4682.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 41.045ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4682.svg"></p>

<p>The above four propositions, together with four similar ones
(*63·54·55·56·57), give transformations which enable us to express any
relation of type, as between class and members or members of members or
etc., that is likely to occur in practice.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*63·64.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. tʻ\beta = t_{0}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/4683.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.818ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4683.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is often used in the first section on cardinal
arithmetic.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_429">[Pg 429]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_64">*64. RELATIVE TYPES OF RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *64.</p>

<p>In the present number, we introduce notations defining the type of a
relation relatively to the types of its domain and converse domain,
when these types are given relatively to some fixed class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_227">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_202"> is any relation, it is of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\text{D}ʻR \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/4797.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.947ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4797.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_10"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_13"> are both of the
same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_228">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_203"> is of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\uparrow t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4798.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.608ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4798.svg">,
which is of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\uparrow \alpha\)" src="images/4799.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.437ex; width: 5.284ex; height: 2.007ex;" id="img_images_4799.svg">.
The type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4800.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.608ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4800.svg">
we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{00}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.41ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4801.svg">, and the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{m}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t^{n}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4802.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.373ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4802.svg">
we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{mn}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4803.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.174ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4803.svg">, and the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{m}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{n}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4804.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.373ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4804.svg">
we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{mn}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4805.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.174ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4805.svg">, and the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{m}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t^{n}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4806.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.373ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4806.svg"> we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{m}^{n}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4807.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.576ex; width: 5.215ex; height: 2.273ex;" id="img_images_4807.svg">,
and the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(t^{m}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{n}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4808.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.373ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4808.svg"> we call
<img alt="" data-tex="\({}^{m}t_{n}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4809.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.362ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4809.svg">. We thus have a means of expressing the type of
any relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_204"> in terms of the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_229">, provided the
types of the domain and converse domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_205"> are given relatively
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_230">.</p>

<p>The most useful propositions of the present number are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*64·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : R \unicode{x2abd} t_{0}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\beta .\equiv. R \in tʻ(t_{0}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\beta)\)" src="images/4810.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.785ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4810.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*64·201.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : R \unicode{x2abd} S .\supset. R \in tʻS . tʻR = tʻS\)" src="images/4811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.611ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4811.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*64·231.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R \in tʻQ .\supset. \text{D}ʻR \in tʻ\text{D}ʻQ . \text{ᗡ}ʻR \in tʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻQ .CʻR \in tʻCʻQ\)" src="images/4812.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 59.968ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4812.svg"></p>

<p>Here "<img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR \in tʻCʻQ\)" src="images/4813.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.601ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4813.svg">" will only be significant if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_206"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_6">
are homogeneous relations, which is not required by the rest of the
proposition. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_207"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_7"> are homogeneous relations we have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*64·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : R \in tʻQ .\equiv. CʻR \in tʻCʻQ .\equiv. t_{0}ʻCʻR=t_{0}ʻCʻQ\)" src="images/4814.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 52.234ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4814.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is useful in connecting ordinal and cardinal existence-theorems.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*64·312.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. t^{22}ʻx = t^{11}ʻtʻx = t_{00}ʻt^{2}ʻx\)" src="images/4815.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.526ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4815.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*64·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \text{Rl}ʻ(t_{0}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\beta) = tʻ(t_{0}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\beta) = tʻ(\alpha \uparrow \beta)\)" src="images/4816.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.701ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4816.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is frequently used. It states that the class of
relations whose referents are of the type of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_231">
while its relata are of the type of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_107"> (<i>i.e.</i>
the class of all relations contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/4817.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.44ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4817.svg">)
is the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{0}ʻ\alpha \uparrow t_{0}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/4817.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.44ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4817.svg_1"> and
is also the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \uparrow \beta\)" src="images/2877.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.117ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2877.svg_1">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*64·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: CʻP \subset t_{0}ʻ\alpha .\equiv. P \in t_{00}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4818.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4818.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_430">[Pg 430]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*64·57.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : CʻP \subset tʻx .\equiv. P \in t^{11}ʻx\)" src="images/4819.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 27.394ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_4819.svg"></p>

<p>The propositions of the present number are mostly obvious, though
formal proofs are sometimes not very easily found. The use of the
propositions of this number occurs chiefly in the first section on
relation-arithmetic and in the proofs of existence-theorems in ordinal
arithmetic and the theory of ratio.</p>

<p>By putting <img alt="" data-tex="\(t_{s}^{i}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/4843.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.575ex; width: 4.56ex; height: 2.454ex;" id="img_images_4843.svg"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(i\)" src="images/4844.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.781ex; height: 1.52ex;" id="img_images_4844.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/40.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_40.svg_11"> are some
index and suffix which have been defined) for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_232"> and

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*64·5}.\supset\vdash:tʻP=tʻ(\alpha\uparrow\beta).&amp;\supset.tʻP=tʻ(t_{0}ʻ\alpha\uparrow t_{0}ʻ\beta).\\ [\text{*64·231.*35·85·86}]   &amp; \supset.\text{D}ʻP\in tʻt_{0}ʻ\alpha.\text{ᗡ}ʻ P\in tʻt_{0}ʻ\beta.\\ [\text{*63·19}]              &amp; \supset.\text{D}ʻP\in tʻ\alpha.\text{ᗡ}ʻP\in tʻ\beta &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*64·61.*63·16}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4887.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 73.993ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_4887.svg"></span></p>
