<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_434">[Pg 434]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_65">*65. ON THE TYPICAL DEFINITION OF AMBIGUOUS SYMBOLS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *65.</p>

<p>In this number we are concerned with definitions and propositions in
which an ambiguous symbol is determined as belonging to some assigned
type. If "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_233">" is an ambiguous symbol representing a class
(such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_45"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_26"> for example), "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha_{x}\)" src="images/4888.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.551ex; height: 1.357ex;" id="img_images_4888.svg">"
is to denote what <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_234"> becomes when its members are determined
as belonging to the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_516">, while "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha(x)\)" src="images/4889.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.502ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4889.svg">" denotes what
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_235"> becomes when its members are determined as belonging to the
type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_8">. Thus <i>e.g.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda_{x}\)" src="images/4890.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.673ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_4890.svg">" will be everything
of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_517">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_9">; <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}(x)\)" src="images/4891.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.751ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4891.svg"> will
be <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻtʻx\)" src="images/4892.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.643ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4892.svg">. Similarly if "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_209">" stands for a relation of ambiguous
type, such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_46"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{V}\)" src="images/4893.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.74ex; height: 2.33ex;" id="img_images_4893.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{x}\)" src="images/4894.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.82ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_4894.svg"> will denote
what <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_210"> becomes when its domain is confined within the type of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_518">; <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{x,y}\)" src="images/4895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 4.049ex; height: 2.213ex;" id="img_images_4895.svg"> will denote what <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_211"> becomes when its domain and
converse domain are confined respectively within the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_519"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_228">; <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(x,y)\)" src="images/4896.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.886ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4896.svg"> will have the domain and converse domain confined
respectively to the types of <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_10"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻy\)" src="images/4897.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 3.283ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4897.svg">; with analogous
meanings for <img alt="" data-tex="\(R(x)\)" src="images/4898.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.771ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4898.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{x,y}\)" src="images/4895.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 4.049ex; height: 2.213ex;" id="img_images_4895.svg_1">. Throughout this number, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_212">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_236"> do not stand for proper variables, but for typically
ambiguous symbols.</p>

<p>The notations of the present number are used in the elementary parts of
the theory of cardinals and ordinals, <i>i.e.</i> in Part III, Section
A, and in Part IV, Section A. The only <i>proposition</i>, however,
which is much used, is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*65·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \alpha = \beta_{x} . \equiv . \alpha = tʻ x \cap \beta . \equiv . \alpha \subset tʻ x . \alpha = \beta\)" src="images/4899.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 43.446ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4899.svg"></p>

<p>Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_109"> is supposed to be a typically ambiguous symbol. The
first equivalence, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = \beta_{x} . \equiv . \alpha = tʻ x \cap\beta\)" src="images/4900.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.349ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4900.svg">,"
merely embodies the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta_{x}\)" src="images/4901.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 2.383ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4901.svg"> (<a href="#_65_01" class="pginternal">*65·01</a>). It
is the second equivalence that is important. Let us, for the sake of
illustration, put 1 in place of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_110">. Then we are to have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha = tʻ x \cap 1 . \equiv . \alpha\subset tʻ x . \alpha = 1. \]" src="images/4902.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.516ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4902.svg"></span>
(Since 1 is a class of classes, we shall have to suppose that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_520">
is a class.) Consider <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in\alpha\)" src="images/4903.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.323ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_4903.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = tʻx\cap 1\)" src="images/4904.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.579ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4904.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in\alpha.\equiv. y\in tʻx . y\in 1\)" src="images/4905.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 22.449ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4905.svg">. But we have <img alt="" data-tex="\((y) . y\in tʻx\)" src="images/4906.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.218ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_4906.svg">. Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in\alpha.\equiv. y\in 1\)" src="images/4907.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 14.101ex; height: 1.971ex;" id="img_images_4907.svg">, whence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = 1\)" src="images/4908.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.596ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_4908.svg">.
Also if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = tʻx\cap 1\)" src="images/4904.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.579ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4904.svg_1">, of course <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\subset tʻx\)" src="images/4909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.933ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4909.svg">.
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = tʻx\cap 1.\supset.\alpha\subset tʻx.\alpha = 1\)" src="images/4910.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.139ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4910.svg">.
The converse implication follows from <a href="#_22_621" class="pginternal">*22·621</a>. The reason for the
proposition is that a symbol such as "1," if it occurs in such a
proposition as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = tʻx\cap 1\)" src="images/4904.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.579ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4904.svg_2">, must, for significance, be
determined as meaning that 1 which is of the same type as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_237">,
<i>i.e.</i> the class of all<span class="pagenum" id="Page_435">[Pg 435]</span> unit classes which are of the same type
as members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_238">. And similarly, when we put <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha=1\)" src="images/4911.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.596ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_4911.svg">,
that does not mean that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_239"> is the class of all unit classes,
but only that it is the class of all unit classes of the appropriate
type, which, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\subset tʻx\)" src="images/4909.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.933ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4909.svg_1">, will be <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ x\cap 1\)" src="images/4912.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.114ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4912.svg">. The
proposition "<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻ x\cap 1=1\)" src="images/4913.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.262ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4913.svg">" is true whenever it is significant, but
<img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻc x\cap 1\)" src="images/4914.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.094ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4914.svg"> is typically definite when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_521"> is given, whereas 1
is typically ambiguous. The use of the above proposition lies in its
enabling us to substitute typically definite symbols for such as are
typically ambiguous.</p>

<p>Another useful proposition is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*65·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{sg}ʻ \{R_{(x,y)}\}=\overrightarrow{R}(x_{y})\)" src="images/4915.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 22.085ex; height: 3.99ex;" id="img_images_4915.svg"></p>

<p>Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_213"> is supposed to be a typically ambiguous symbol; the proposition
states that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_214"> is typically defined as going from objects of type <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_522"> to objects
of type <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_229">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_349.svg_12"> must go from objects of type <img alt="" data-tex="\(tʻx\)" src="images/3752.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.468ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3752.svg_11"> to objects of type <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_230">. This
proposition is only used twice (*102·3 and *154·2), but both uses are of great
importance, the one in cardinal and the other in ordinal arithmetic.</p>

<p>The only other proposition of this number which is subsequently used is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*65·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.R_{\beta}ʻʻ \mu=(Rʻʻ\mu)_{\beta}=Rʻʻ\mu\cap tʻ \beta\)" src="images/4916.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 35.728ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_4916.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is used in *102·84.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*4·2.(*65·01)}. &amp;\supset\vdash:\alpha=\beta_{x}.\equiv.\alpha=tʻ x\cap\beta &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*22·621.*13·13}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\alpha\subset tʻ x.\alpha=\beta.\supset.\alpha=tʻx\cap\beta &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*22·43}.  &amp;\supset\vdash:\alpha=tʻx\cap\beta.\supset.\alpha\subset tʻx.\alpha\subset\beta. &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ [\text{*63·13}]  &amp;\supset.\beta\in tʻtʻx.\\ [\text{*63·371·15}] &amp;\supset.\beta\subset tʻx.\\ [\text{*22·621}]  &amp;\supset.\beta=tʻ x\cap\beta &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(3).(4)}.    &amp;\supset\vdash:\alpha=tʻx\cap\beta.\supset.\alpha\subset tʻx.\alpha=\beta &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).(5)}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4925.svg" style="vertical-align: -11.652ex; width: 64.504ex; height: 24.434ex;" id="img_images_4925.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*32·1·23.(*65·1)}.\supset\\ \vdash:\alpha[\text{sg}ʻ\{R_{(x,y)}\}]w.&amp;\equiv.\alpha=\hat{z}\{z\in tʻ x.w\in tʻ y.zRw\}.\\ [\text{*22·39.*20·42}]      &amp;\equiv.\alpha=tʻ x\cap \hat{z}(w\in tʻ y.zRw).\\ [\text{*65·13}]             &amp;\equiv.\alpha\subset tʻ x.\alpha=\hat{z}(w\in tʻ y.zRw)&amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*20·33}.\supset\vdash\colon\colon \alpha=\hat{z}(w\in tʻ y.zRw).\equiv\colon\ldotp z\in\alpha.\equiv_{z}.w\in tʻ y.zRw\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*63·108}]     &amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp w\in tʻ y:z\in\alpha.\equiv_{z}.w\in tʻ y.zRw\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*4·73}]       &amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp w\in tʻy:z\in\alpha.\equiv_{z}.zRw\colon\ldotp\\ [\text{*20·33.*32·1}]&amp;\equiv\colon\ldotp w\in tʻ y.\alpha\overrightarrow{R}w &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).*63·5}.\supset\vdash:\alpha[\text{sg}ʻ\{R_{(x,y)}\}]w.\equiv.\alpha\in t^{2}ʻx.w\in tʻ y.\alpha\overrightarrow{R}w.\\ [\text{*35·102.(*65·11)}]                   \equiv.\alpha{\overrightarrow R\{_{(x_{y})}}\}w:\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4929.svg" style="vertical-align: -17.718ex; width: 114.559ex; height: 36.566ex;" id="img_images_4929.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_65_21">*65·21</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.R_{(x,y)}=\{R_{(x,y)}\}_{(x,y)}\)" src="images/4930.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.8ex; width: 21.831ex; height: 2.497ex;" id="img_images_4930.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*21· 2.(*65·1)}.\supset\vdash.\{R_{(x,y)}\}_{(x,y)}&amp;=tʻ x\upharpoonleft\{tʻ x\upharpoonleft R\upharpoonright tʻ y\}\upharpoonright tʻ y\\ [\text{*35·33·34}]  &amp;=tʻ x\upharpoonleft R\upharpoonright tʻ y\\ [\text{(*65·1)}]                             &amp;=R_{(x,y)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop}\\ \end{array} \]" src="images/4931.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.967ex; width: 62.872ex; height: 9.066ex;" id="img_images_4931.svg"></span></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_437">[Pg 437]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_C_b">SECTION C.<br>
<br>
ONE-MANY, MANY-ONE, AND ONE-ONE RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of Section C.</i></p>

<p>In the present section we have to consider three very important
classes of relations, of which the use in arithmetic is constant. A
<i>one-many</i> relation is a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_215"> such that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_231"> is any
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻ R\)" src="images/4938.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4938.svg">, there is one, and only one, term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_523"> which
has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_216"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_232">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻ y\in 1\)" src="images/4939.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.08ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_4939.svg">.
Thus the relation of father to son is one-many, because every
son has one father and no more. The relation of husband to wife is
one-many except in countries which practise polyandry. (It is one-many
in monogamous as well as in polygamous countries, because, according
to the definition, nothing is fixed as to the number of relata for a
given referent, and there <i>may</i> be only one relatum for each given
referent without the relation ceasing to be one-many according to the
definition.) The relation in algebra of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x^{2}\)" src="images/2421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.912ex;" id="img_images_2421.svg_1"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_524"> is one-many,
but that of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_525"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x^{2}\)" src="images/2421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.912ex;" id="img_images_2421.svg_2"> is not, because there are two different
values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_526"> that give the same value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x^{2}\)" src="images/2421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 2.282ex; height: 1.912ex;" id="img_images_2421.svg_3">.</p>

<p>When a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_217"> is one-many, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_55"> exists whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in\text{ᗡ}ʻ R\)" src="images/4940.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.307ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4940.svg">, and vice versa; <i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in \text{one-many}.\equiv:y\in\text{ᗡ}ʻ R.\supset_{y}.\text{E}!Rʻ y. \]" src="images/4941.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 38.155ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_4941.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus relations which give descriptive functions that are existent
whenever their arguments belong to the converse domains of the
relations in question are one-many relations. Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}\)" src="images/2507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.086ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2507.svg_4">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_7">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\)" src="images/2637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2637.svg_7">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(C\)" src="images/42.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.719ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_42.svg_9">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_349.svg_13">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}\)" src="images/350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.451ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_350.svg_11">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sg}\)" src="images/353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_353.svg_5">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{gs}\)" src="images/354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_354.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\epsilon}\)" src="images/4942.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.357ex; width: 2.554ex; height: 1.902ex;" id="img_images_4942.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(p\)" src="images/39.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 1.439ex;" id="img_images_39.svg_281">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(s\)" src="images/40.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_40.svg_12">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{p}\)" src="images/3429.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.138ex; height: 2.174ex;" id="img_images_3429.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}\)" src="images/3430.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.061ex; height: 1.758ex;" id="img_images_3430.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\)" src="images/46.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.14ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_46.svg_3">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_6">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}\)" src="images/3958.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.891ex;" id="img_images_3958.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}\)" src="images/4431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4431.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rl}\)" src="images/4436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.294ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_4436.svg_1"> are all of them
one-many relations.</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_218"> is a one-many relation, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_56"> is a one-valued function;
conversely, every one-valued function is derivable from a one-many
relation. A <i>many</i>-valued function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_233"> is a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_343.svg_10">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_343.svg_11"> is not a
unit class, and any one of its members is regarded as a value of the
function for the argument y; but a <i>one</i>-valued function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_234">
is the single term <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_57"> which is obtained when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_219"> is one-many.
Thus for example the sine would, in our notation, appear as a relation,
<i>i.e.</i> we should put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} \text{sin} &amp;= \hat{x}\hat{y}\left\{x=y - \frac{y^{3}}{3!} + \frac{y^{5}}{5!} - \ldots\right\} \qquad\text{Df},\\ \text{whence}\qquad\text{sin}ʻy &amp;= y - \frac{y^{3}}{3!} + \frac{y^{5}}{5!} - \ldots, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/4943.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.065ex; width: 56.249ex; height: 11.261ex;" id="img_images_4943.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_438">[Pg 438]</span>
so that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin ʻy\)" src="images/329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.621ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_329.svg_3">" has the usual meaning of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin y\)" src="images/328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.264ex; height: 1.977ex;" id="img_images_328.svg_3">. Then
instead of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin^{-1}x\)" src="images/2559.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 6.682ex; height: 1.986ex;" id="img_images_2559.svg_3">, we should have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{\sin}ʻx\)" src="images/2558.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.807ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_2558.svg_2">,
which would be the class of values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\sin^{-1}x\)" src="images/2559.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 6.682ex; height: 1.986ex;" id="img_images_2559.svg_4">; and instead of
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(y = \sin^{-1}x\)" src="images/4944.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.807ex; height: 2.425ex;" id="img_images_4944.svg">," which is a misleading notation because
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y = \sin^{-1}x\)" src="images/4944.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.807ex; height: 2.425ex;" id="img_images_4944.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z = \sin^{-1}x\)" src="images/4945.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 10.751ex; height: 2.147ex;" id="img_images_4945.svg"> do not imply <img alt="" data-tex="\(y = z\)" src="images/4946.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.178ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_4946.svg">, we should
have <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \overleftarrow{\sin}ʻx\)" src="images/4947.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.681ex; height: 3.946ex;" id="img_images_4947.svg">. Similar remarks would apply to
any of the other functions that occur in analysis.</p>

<p>A relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_220"> is called <i>many-one</i> when, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_527"> is any member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_11">, there is one, and only one, term <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_235"> to which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_528"> has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_221">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx \in 1\)" src="images/4948.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4948.svg">. Thus many-one relations are the converses of one-many relations.
When a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_222"> is many-one, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻx\)" src="images/2882.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_2882.svg_2"> exists whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/4949.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4949.svg">.</p>

<p>A relation is called <i>one-one</i> when it is both one-many and
many-one, or, what comes to the same, when both it and its converse are
one-many. Of the one-many relations above enumerated, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}\)" src="images/2507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.086ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2507.svg_5">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{sg}\)" src="images/353.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_353.svg_6">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{gs}\)" src="images/354.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 2.023ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_354.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\)" src="images/46.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.14ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_46.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iota\)" src="images/49.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.023ex;" id="img_images_49.svg_7">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}\)" src="images/3958.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 0.801ex; height: 1.891ex;" id="img_images_3958.svg_2">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}\)" src="images/4431.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.262ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4431.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rl}\)" src="images/4436.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 2.294ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_4436.svg_2"> are one-one.</p>

<p>Two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_240">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_111"> are said to be <i>similar</i> when
there is a one-one relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_223"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR = \alpha . \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \beta\)" src="images/4950.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.004ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4950.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> when their terms can be connected one to one,
so that no term of either is omitted or repeated. We write "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \mathop{\text{ sm }} \beta\)" src="images/4951.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.39ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4951.svg">" for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_241"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_112">."
When two classes are similar, the cardinal numbers of their terms are
the same; it is this fact chiefly that makes one-one relations of
fundamental importance in cardinal arithmetic.</p>

<p>According to the above, a relation is one-many when
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ y \in \text{ᗡ}ʻR .\supset_{y}. \overrightarrow{R}ʻy \in 1\text{,} \]" src="images/4952.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 21.76ex; height: 3.857ex;" id="img_images_4952.svg"></span>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \textit{i.e.} ~ \text{when} \quad \overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR \subset 1. \]" src="images/4953.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.847ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4953.svg"></span></p>

<p>Similarly a relation is many-one when
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overleftarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻR \subset 1\text{,} \]" src="images/4954.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.746ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4954.svg"></span>
and a relation is one-one when both conditions are
fulfilled. The classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/4955.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.864ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4955.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/4956.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.969ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4956.svg">, which appear here, are often
important; some of their properties have already been given in
*37·77·771·772·773 and in <a href="#_53_61" class="pginternal">*53·61</a> to <a href="#_53_641" class="pginternal">*53·641</a>.</p>

<p>It is convenient to regard one-many, many-one and one-one relations
as particular cases of relations which, for some given <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_242"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_113">, have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR \subset \alpha . \overleftarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻR \subset \beta\text{.} \]" src="images/4957.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.231ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4957.svg"></span>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{We put} \quad \alpha \rightarrow \beta = \hat{R}\{\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR \subset \alpha.\overleftarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻR \subset \beta\} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/4958.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.713ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_4958.svg"></span></p>

<p>Hence, without a new definition, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_4959.svg">" becomes the
class of one-one relations; also, as will be shown, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/4960.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4960.svg">" becomes the class of one-many relations, and
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4961.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4961.svg">" becomes the class of many-one relations.
Although it is chiefly these three special values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\rightarrow \beta\)" src="images/4962.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.248ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4962.svg">
that are important, we shall begin by a general study of classes of
relations of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \rightarrow \beta\)" src="images/4963.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.248ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4963.svg">.</p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_439">[Pg 439]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_70">*70. RELATIONS WHOSE CLASSES OF REFERENTS AND OF RELATA
BELONG TO GIVEN CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *70.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_243"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_114"> are two given classes of classes, a
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_224"> is said to belong to the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \rightarrow\beta\)" src="images/4964.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.248ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4964.svg">
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy \in \alpha\)" src="images/4965.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.397ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_4965.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/4966.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.307ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_4966.svg">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx \in \beta\)" src="images/4967.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.149ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4967.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/4968.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.863ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4968.svg">.
If only one of these conditions is to be imposed, this result is
secured by replacing the class involved in the other condition by
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/2002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2002.svg_5">," since "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy \in \text{Cls}\)" src="images/4969.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 10.103ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_4969.svg">"
always holds, and so does "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx \in \text{Cls}\)" src="images/4970.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.022ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4970.svg">,"
and therefore neither imposes any limitation on <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_225">. In the most
important cases, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_244"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_115"> are either both cardinal
numbers, or one is a cardinal number while the other is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/2002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2002.svg_6">.</p>

<p>In virtue of *37·702·703, the conditions above mentioned as imposed
upon <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_226"> by membership of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \rightarrow \beta\)" src="images/4963.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.248ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4963.svg_1"> are equivalent
to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR \subset \alpha.\overleftarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{D}ʻR \subset \beta\text{.} \]" src="images/4971.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 29.231ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_4971.svg"></span></p>

<p>This form is used in the definition (<a href="#_70_01" class="pginternal">*70·01</a>).</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number are hardly ever used except
in <a href="#_71" class="pginternal">*71</a>, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_245"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_116"> are both replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_17"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\)" src="images/2002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 3.154ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2002.svg_7">. The most useful propositions are</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_446">[Pg 446]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_71">*71. ONE-MANY, MANY-ONE, AND ONE-ONE RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *71.</p>

<p>In this number we shall be concerned with the more elementary
properties of one-many, many-one, and one-one relations. These
properties are very numerous and very important. The properties of
many-one relations (<i>i.e.</i> of relations belonging to the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4961.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4961.svg_1">) result from those of one-many relations
by means of <a href="#_70_5" class="pginternal">*70·5</a>, whence it follows that many-one relations are
the converses of one-many relations. It is thus only necessary to
interchange <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_227"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}\)" src="images/335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_335.svg_4">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_8"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\)" src="images/2637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2637.svg_8">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}\)" src="images/349.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_349.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}\)" src="images/350.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.451ex; height: 3.238ex;" id="img_images_350.svg_12"> in order to obtain
a property of a many-one relation from a property of a one-many
relation. Or we may repeat the various steps of any proof, making the
above interchanges at every step, and the analogous proposition will
result. For this reason, in what follows, we shall omit all proofs of
properties of many-one relations, confining ourselves to proving the
analogous properties of one-many relations.</p>

<p>In virtue of <a href="#_70_42" class="pginternal">*70·42</a>, one-one relations (<i>i.e.</i> relations belonging
to the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_4959.svg_1">) are the relations which are both
one-many and many-one; hence their properties result from combining the
properties of one-many and many-one relations. We shall omit the proofs
when they consist merely in such combinations.</p>

<p>A one-many relation gives rise to a descriptive function which is
existent whenever its argument belongs to the converse domain of
the relation. That is, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5040.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5040.svg">, we
have <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.353ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_332.svg_6"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/5041.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.307ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5041.svg">. Conversely, if
a descriptive function <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_58"> exists for the argument <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_236">, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_228"> is one-many so far as that argument is concerned, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy \in 1\)" src="images/5042.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.08ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5042.svg">. Thus we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls} .\equiv. \text{E}‼Rʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\text{.} \]" src="images/5043.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.451ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5043.svg"></span></p>

<p>The descriptive function <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_59"> derived from a one-many relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_229"> has thus a definite value whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/5041.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.307ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5041.svg_1">, and
not otherwise. Thus the class of arguments for which such a function
exists is the converse domain of the relation which gives rise to the
function, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls} .\supset. \hat{y}\{\text{E}!Rʻy\} = \text{ᗡ}ʻR\text{,} \]" src="images/5044.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.862ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_5044.svg"></span>
and the converse implication also holds.</p>

<p>It often happens that a relation which is not in general
one-many becomes so when its domain, converse domain, or field
is subjected to some limitation. For example, let <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_230"> be the
relation of parent to child, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_246"> the class of males, and<span class="pagenum" id="Page_447">[Pg 447]</span>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_117"> the class of females. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_231"> is not one-many, but
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/3328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.366ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_3328.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/5045.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5045.svg"> are one-many,
and in fact (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft R)ʻy\)" src="images/5046.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.712ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5046.svg"> = the father of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_237">,
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\upharpoonleft R)ʻy\)" src="images/5047.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.544ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5047.svg"> = the mother of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_238">. We shall often
have occasion to deal with relations obtained by limitations imposed
on <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_9"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\)" src="images/2637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2637.svg_9">; thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha(\text{D}\upharpoonright\lambda)R.\equiv.R\)" src="images/5048.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.663ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5048.svg">
belongs to the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_21">, and has
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_247"> for its domain. The class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_22"> may be so constituted
that only one relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_232"> fulfils this condition; in that
case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5049.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.818ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5049.svg">.
Since <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D} \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5050.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.299ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5050.svg">, we find
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\equiv.\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda \in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5051.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 33.638ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5051.svg">.
This type of condition, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright \lambda \in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5052.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 13.796ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5052.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\upharpoonright \lambda \in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5053.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.425ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5053.svg">
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(C\upharpoonright \lambda \in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5054.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 13.787ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5054.svg">, is one which
frequently occurs in subsequent work. Another condition which often
occurs is <img alt="" data-tex="\(F\upharpoonright \lambda \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5055.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.784ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5055.svg">.
When this condition is realized, a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_529"> which belongs to the
field of one relation of the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_23"> does not belong to the
field of any other relation of this class, <i>i.e.</i> the fields of
relations of this class are mutually exclusive.</p>

<p>For purposes of realizing imaginatively the properties of one-many
relations, it is often convenient to picture their structure as in the
accompanying figure.</p>

<figure class="figcenter width500" style="width: 471px;" id="i_447">
<img alt="Diagram showing vector transformations R and R' under rotations about the x, y and z axes, illustrating changes in direction between reference frames." height="500" src="images/i_447.jpg" width="471" id="img_images_i_447.jpg">
</figure>

<p class="nind">
Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_530">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_239">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_35">, ... form the domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_233">, and all the
points in the oval marked <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.102ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_344.svg_8"> are such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_531">
has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_234"> to each of them, with similar conditions
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_240"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_36">. What characterizes <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_235"> as a <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow\text{Cls}\)" src="images/5056.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_5056.svg">
is the absence of overlapping in the ovals. For if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.102ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_344.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/5057.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.917ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5057.svg"> had a point in
common, this would be a relatum both to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_532"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_241">, and both
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_533"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_242"> would be referents to it; whereas in a <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5058.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_5058.svg">, no term has more than one referent.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_448">[Pg 448]</span></p>

<p>The above figure illustrates a very important property of one-many
relations, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls} . \equiv . R \mid  \breve{R} = I\upharpoonright \text{D}ʻR. \]" src="images/5059.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 33.17ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_5059.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the above figure, <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/5060.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.144ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5060.svg"> is the relation of
identity confined to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_534">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_243">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_37">,.... If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_236"> were not a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5061.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_5061.svg">, we could sometimes go from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_535"> to some term
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx \cap \overleftarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/5062.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 12.534ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5062.svg"> by the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_237">, and thence back to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_244"> by the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}\)" src="images/335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 2.462ex;" id="img_images_335.svg_5">. But when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5040.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5040.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid \breve{R}\)" src="images/5063.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.32ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_5063.svg"> must bring us
back to the point from which we started.</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5064.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 10.265ex; height: 1.636ex;" id="img_images_5064.svg">, each of the ovals
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.102ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_344.svg_10">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/5057.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.917ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5057.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻz\)" src="images/5065.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.86ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5065.svg">, ... in the above figure shrinks to a single
point, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}ʻx = \iotaʻ\breve{R}ʻx\)" src="images/5066.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.647ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5066.svg">. Thus
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_238"> is given as a <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5067.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_5067.svg">, it will be
a <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_4959.svg_2"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy = Rʻz . \supset_{y, z} . y = z\)" src="images/5068.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 22.437ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_5068.svg">.
This proposition is constantly used, and so is the consequence that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/5069.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5069.svg"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_4959.svg_3"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(y, z \in \beta . Rʻy = Rʻz . \supset_{y, z} . y = z\)" src="images/5070.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 30.657ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_5070.svg">.
(These propositions are *71·54·55 below.)</p>

<p>The hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5040.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5040.svg_2"> is equivalent to the
hypothesis
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ xRz . yRz . \supset_{x, y, z} . x= y \]" src="images/5071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 21.659ex; height: 2.213ex;" id="img_images_5071.svg"></span>
(cf. <a href="#_71_17" class="pginternal">*71·17</a>, below), and the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in  \text{Cls} \rightarrow  1\)" src="images/5072.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5072.svg"> is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ xRy . xRz . \supset_{x, y, z} . y = z. \]" src="images/5073.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 22.288ex; height: 2.213ex;" id="img_images_5073.svg"></span></p>

<p>These are for many purposes the most convenient hypotheses to use.</p>

<p>The most useful propositions in the present number are the following.
(We omit here propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4961.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4961.svg_2"> or
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_4959.svg_4"> which are mere analogues of propositions concerning
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5061.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_5061.svg_1">.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : R \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls} . \equiv . \text{E} ‼ Rʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/5074.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.462ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5074.svg"></p>

<p>This gives the connection of one-many relations with descriptive
functions. We have also</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·163.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  R \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls} . \equiv : y \in  \text{ᗡ}ʻR . \equiv_{y} . \text{E} ! Rʻy\)" src="images/5075.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 39.109ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_5075.svg"></p>

<p>For many of the constant relations defined from time to time, such as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}\)" src="images/2507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.086ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_2507.svg_6"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_10">, the following proposition is useful:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·166.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : (y) . \text{E} ! Rʻy . \supset . R \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5076.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.927ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5076.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_71_17">*71·17</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  R \in  1  \rightarrow   \text{Cls} . \equiv : xRz. yRz. \supset_{x, y, z} . x = y\)" src="images/5077.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 41.365ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5077.svg"></p>

<p>This might have been taken as the definition of one-many relations,
if we had not wished to derive them from the more general notion of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \rightarrow \beta\)" src="images/4963.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.248ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4963.svg_3">. In proving that a relation is one-many,
*71·17 is more often employed than any other proposition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : R \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls}. S \unicode{x2abd} R . \supset . S \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5078.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.269ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5078.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash . R,\,S \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls} . \supset . R\mid S \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5079.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 36.924ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_5079.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·36.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  R \in  1 \rightarrow  \text{Cls} . \supset : x = Rʻy . \equiv . xRy\)" src="images/5080.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 36.092ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5080.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·381.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : R \in  \text{Cls} \rightarrow  1 . \supset . Rʻʻ(\alpha - \beta) = Rʻʻ\alpha - Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/5081.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.762ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5081.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_449">[Pg 449]</span></p>

<p>(This proposition is more useful than the corresponding property of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\)" src="images/5082.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.433ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_5082.svg">)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·55.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\colon R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\supset\colon\ldotp R\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow 1.\equiv:y,z\in \beta.Rʻy=Rʻz.\supset_{y,z}.y=z\)" src="images/5083.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 69.138ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_5083.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is constantly used. For example, putting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\)" src="images/2637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2637.svg_10">
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_239">, it gives
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash\colon\ldotp \text{ᗡ}\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow 1.\equiv:P,\,Q\in \beta.\text{ᗡ}ʻP=\text{ᗡ}ʻQ.\supset_{P,Q}.P=Q. \]" src="images/5084.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 56.923ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5084.svg"></span></p>

<p>Most of the relations used to establish correlations in arithmetic are
obtained from a one-many relation, such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}\)" src="images/2637.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2637.svg_11">, by imposing
some limitation on the converse domain which makes the relation one-one.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·571.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp y\in \beta.\supset_{y}.\text{E}!Rʻy:\equiv.R\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\beta\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/5085.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 49.174ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_5085.svg"></p>

<p>Here "<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in \beta.\supset_{y}.\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/5086.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 16.252ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_5086.svg">" is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{E}‼Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.611ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3092.svg_5">, which has already played a large part as a
hypothesis, <i>e.g.</i> in <a href="#_37_6" class="pginternal">*37·6</a> ff.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·7.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp Q\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\supset:xP\mid Qz.\equiv.xP(Qʻz)\)" src="images/5087.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.223ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5087.svg"></p>

<p>Thus for example we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(x(P\mid\text{Cnv})R.\equiv.xP(\text{Cnv}ʻR)\)" src="images/5088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.129ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5088.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·132.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\colon R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\equiv\colon\ldotp (y):\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\in 1.\lor.\overrightarrow{R}ʻy=\Lambda\colon\ldotp (x):\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\in 1.\lor.\overleftarrow{R}ʻx=\Lambda \quad[\text{*70·14}]\)" src="images/5105.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 82.03ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5105.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\equiv:\exists !\overrightarrow{R}ʻy.\supset_{y}.\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\in 1 \quad[\text{*70·47}]\)" src="images/5106.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 48.406ex; height: 3.857ex;" id="img_images_5106.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·141.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\equiv:\exists !\overleftarrow{R}ʻx.\supset_{x}.\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\in 1 \quad[\text{*70·471}]\)" src="images/5107.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 51.758ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_5107.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*71·142.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\equiv:\exists !\overrightarrow{R}ʻy.\supset_{y}.\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\in 1:\exists !\overleftarrow{R}ʻx.\supset_{x}.\overleftarrow{R}ʻx\in     1 \quad[\text{*70·15}]\)" src="images/5108.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 69.384ex; height: 3.857ex;" id="img_images_5108.svg"></p>
