<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_462">[Pg 462]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_72">*72. MISCELLANEOUS PROPOSITIONS CONCERNING ONE-MANY,
MANY-ONE, AND ONE-ONE RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *72.</p>

<p>In this number we shall prove various propositions involving <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5261.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_5261.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4961.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4961.svg_3">, or <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5262.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_5262.svg">, but not embodying fundamental properties of these
classes of relations.</p>

<p>The present number begins with various propositions (<a href="#_72_1" class="pginternal">*72·1</a>-<a href="#_72_191" class="pginternal">·191</a>)
showing that various special relations are one-many or one-one. The
most useful of these are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·182.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. x \downarrow y \in 1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 15.727ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5263.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·184.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash .x\downarrow, \downarrow x \in 1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5264.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 18.05ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5264.svg"></p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions concerning <img alt="" data-tex="\(RʻSʻz\)" src="images/5265.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.943ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5265.svg"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_240"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_40"> are one-many, or <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\breve{R}ʻz\)" src="images/5266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.201ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5266.svg"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_241"> is one-one, and
kindred matters. The most useful of these is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·241.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp R \in 1 \rightarrow 1 .\supset: y \in \text{ᗡ}ʻR .\equiv. y = \breve{R}ʻRʻy\)" src="images/5267.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 41.146ex; height: 2.878ex;" id="img_images_5267.svg"></p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions (<a href="#_72_3" class="pginternal">*72·3</a>-<a href="#_72_341" class="pginternal">·341</a>) concerning products and
sums of classes of relations; of these the one most used is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  \lambda \subset 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}: P,Q \in \lambda. \exists! \text{ᗡ}ʻP \cap \text{ᗡ}ʻQ .\supset_{P,Q}.     P = Q :\supset.\dot{s}ʻ\lambda \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5268.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 72.036ex; height: 2.385ex;" id="img_images_5268.svg"></p>

<p>which is an extension of <a href="#_71_24" class="pginternal">*71·24</a>.</p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions (<a href="#_72_4" class="pginternal">*72·4</a>—<a href="#_72_481" class="pginternal">·481</a>) giving various
relations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5269.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5269.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_3566.svg_1"> when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5270.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5270.svg">, or of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/390.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.88ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_390.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/3088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.713ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3088.svg_23">
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5271.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5271.svg">. The more useful propositions
of this set are those that have the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5272.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5272.svg">;
these are occasionally useful in arithmetic. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·401.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1 .\supset. Rʻʻ\alpha \cap Rʻʻ\beta = Rʻʻ(\alpha \cap \beta)\)" src="images/5273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.259ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5273.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·411.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1 . \alpha \cap \beta = \Lambda .\supset. Rʻʻ\alpha \cap Rʻʻ\beta = \Lambda\)" src="images/5274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 48.231ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5274.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_463">[Pg 463]</span></p>

<p>For example, the relation of son to father is many-one. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_248">
= Cabinet Ministers, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_118"> = fools; then assuming <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \cap\beta = \Lambda\)" src="images/5275.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.83ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_5275.svg">,
it will follow that the sons of Cabinet Ministers and the sons of
(male) fools have no common member. If we make <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_242"> the relation of
son to parent (which is not many-one), it no longer follows that the
sons of Cabinet Ministers and the sons of fools have no common member.</p>

<p>We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·451.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset.R_{{\in}}\upharpoonright \text{Cl}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR \in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5276.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 40.723ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5276.svg"></p>

<p>The effect of this proposition is that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_249"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_119"> are both contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_14">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\alpha=Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/5277.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.61ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5277.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha=\beta\)" src="images/5278.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5278.svg"> (using <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{{\in}}ʻ\alpha=Rʻʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/5279.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.555ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5279.svg">.</p>

<p>We next have a set of propositions concerned with the relations
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{{\in}}\)" src="images/5280.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.403ex; width: 2.972ex; height: 1.949ex;" id="img_images_5280.svg"> and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R})_{{\in}}\)" src="images/5281.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 3.852ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5281.svg">, or, what
comes to the same thing, with the circumstances under which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha=Rʻʻ\beta.\equiv.\beta=\breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5282.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.128ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5282.svg"> and under which
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻ\breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha=\alpha\)" src="images/5283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 14.777ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5283.svg">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·502.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\alpha\subset \text{D}ʻR.\supset.Rʻʻ\breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha=\alpha\)" src="images/5284.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 43.751ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5284.svg"></p>

<p>Thus for example the fathers of the children of wise fathers are the
class of wise fathers; but the fathers of the children of wise parents
are not all wise, and the parents of the children of wise parents are
not all wise—the first because "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\subset \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/5285.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.268ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5285.svg">" fails,
the second because "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5286.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5286.svg">" fails.</p>

<p>We have also</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·52.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp R \in 1\rightarrow 1.\alpha\subset \text{D}ʻR.\beta\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR.\supset:\alpha=Rʻʻ\beta.\equiv.\beta=\breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5287.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 61.444ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_5287.svg"></p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions (<a href="#_72_59" class="pginternal">*72·59</a>—<a href="#_72_66" class="pginternal">·66</a>) in which the
relative product <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid \breve{R}\)" src="images/5063.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.32ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_5063.svg_1"> occurs if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1\rightarrow\text{Cls}\)" src="images/5288.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5288.svg">,
or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}\mid R\)" src="images/5289.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.32ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_5289.svg"> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5272.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5272.svg_1">.
The most useful propositions in this set are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·591.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset.S\mid \breve{R}\mid R=S\upharpoonright \text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/5290.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 38.725ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_5290.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·601.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR.\supset.S\mid \breve{R}\mid R=S\)" src="images/5291.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 44.094ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_5291.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·66.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:S^{2}\unicode{x2abd}S.S=\breve{S}.\equiv.(\exists R).R \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.S=R\mid \breve{R}\)" src="images/5292.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.189ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_5292.svg"></p>

<p>This is the "principle of abstraction." It shows that every relation
which has the formal properties of equality, <i>i.e.</i> which is
transitive and symmetrical, is equal to the relative product of a
many-one relation into its converse; <i>i.e.</i> whenever the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_41"> holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_536"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_245">, there is a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_250"> such
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(xR\alpha.yR\alpha\)" src="images/5293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.739ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5293.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_243"> is a many-one relation;
and <a href="#_72_64" class="pginternal">*72·64</a> shows that this term <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_251"> may be taken to be
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{S}ʻx\)" src="images/5294.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.157ex; height: 3.692ex;" id="img_images_5294.svg">, which is equal to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{S}ʻy\)" src="images/5295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.971ex; height: 3.704ex;" id="img_images_5295.svg">.
This principle embodies a great part of the reasons for our definitions
of the various kinds of numbers; in seeking these definitions, we
always have, to begin with, some transitive symmetrical relation which
we regard as sameness of number; thus by *72·64, the desired properties
of the numbers of the kind in question are secured by taking the number
of an object to be the class of objects to which the said object has
the transitive symmetrical relation in question. It is in this way
that we are led to define cardinal numbers as classes of classes, and
ordinal numbers as classes of relations.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_464">[Pg 464]</span></p>

<p>The remaining propositions of this number are of less importance, with
the exception of</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·92.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.S\unicode{x2abd}R.\supset.S=R\upharpoonright \text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/5296.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.808ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5296.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition shows that every relation contained in a one-many
relation is obtainable by a limitation of the converse domain. Thus
<i>e.g.</i> every relation contained in that of father to son can be
specified by specifying the class of sons who are to be its converse
domain; for then all the fathers of these sons must be included to
provide referents. But if we take the relation of parent and child,
which is not one-many or many-one, a contained relation is not
determinate even when both its domain and its converse domain are
given; for the relation may relate some of the children in any one
family to the father and some to the mother, and so long as all the
children and both parents are each related to some one by the relation,
the domain and converse domain remain unchanged by permutations within
the family.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*32·22·221.*71·166}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{sg},\,\text{gs} \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*32·14·15·21·211.*71·54}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5303.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 61.631ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_5303.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·131.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{ᗡ} \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} \quad[\text{*33·121.*71·166}]\)" src="images/5305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.298ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5305.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·132.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:C \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} \quad[\text{*33·122.*71·166}]\)" src="images/5306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.912ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5306.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.x\unicode{x2640},\unicode{x2640}x \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} \quad[\text{*38·12.*71·166}]\)" src="images/5307.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 37.119ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5307.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition applies to a great many of the relations we have to
deal with, for example <img alt="" data-tex="\(\upharpoonleft P\)" src="images/5308.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5308.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\upharpoonright\)" src="images/5309.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.271ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5309.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x0294f}\)" src="images/5310.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.057ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5310.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\mid\)" src="images/5311.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.957ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_5311.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid P\)" src="images/5312.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.957ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_5312.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow\)" src="images/4200.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4200.svg_5">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow x\)" src="images/4211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4211.svg_1">, etc.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*72·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.P_{{\in}}\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} \quad[\text{*37·111.*71·166}]\)" src="images/5313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.648ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5313.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_465">[Pg 465]</span></p>

not represent a variable proposition. Similarly s in *72·161 has the

<p class="nind"><b>*72·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.p\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 14.097ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5314.svg"></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*52·22.(*51·01)}.&amp;\supset\vdash.(x).\overrightarrow Iʻx\in 1.\\ [\text{*71·12}] &amp;\supset\vdash.I\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*71·21.*50.2}.&amp;\supset\vdash.I\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1 &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5320.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.063ex; width: 47.24ex; height: 13.258ex;" id="img_images_5320.svg"></span></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_476">[Pg 476]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_73">*73. SIMILARITY OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *73.</p>

<p>Two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_252"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_120"> are said to be <i>similar</i>
when there is a one-one relation whose domain is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_253"> and whose
converse domain is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_121">. We express "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_254"> is similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_122">" by the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \mathop{\text{ sm }} \beta\)" src="images/5464.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.39ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5464.svg">."
When two classes are similar, they have the same cardinal number of
terms: it is this fact which gives importance to the relation of
similarity.</p>

<p>We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \mathop{\text{ sm }} \beta .\equiv. (\exists R) . R \in 1 \rightarrow 1 . \alpha = \text{D}ʻR . \beta = \text{ᗡ}ʻR\text{.} \]" src="images/5465.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.807ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5465.svg"></span></p>

<p>The relation of similarity is that of the domain of a <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_4959.svg_5">
to the converse domain, <i>i.e.</i> it is the relative product of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D} \upharpoonright (1 \rightarrow 1)\)" src="images/5466.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.471ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5466.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\((1 \rightarrow 1)\upharpoonleft \breve{\text{ᗡ}}\)" src="images/5467.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.1ex; height: 3.131ex;" id="img_images_5467.svg">,
or, what comes to the same thing, it is the relative product of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D} \upharpoonright 1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5468.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 9.711ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5468.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\text{ᗡ}}\)" src="images/5469.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 3.018ex;" id="img_images_5469.svg">.</p>

<p>Most of the properties of similarity result immediately from those of
one-one relations and offer no difficulty of any kind.</p>

<p>When there are relations which correlate <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_255">'s with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_123">'s
so as to make <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_256"> similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_124">, we denote the class of
such relations by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \mathop{\overline{\text{ sm }}} \beta\)" src="images/5470.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.39ex; height: 2.17ex;" id="img_images_5470.svg">."
Thus we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp;\alpha \mathop{\overline{\text{ sm }}} \beta = 1 \rightarrow 1 \cap \overleftarrow{\text{D}}ʻ\alpha \cap \overleftarrow{ᗡ}ʻ\beta \quad &amp;\text{Df}\\ \text{and} \quad &amp;\text{ sm } = \hat{\alpha}\hat{\beta}\{\exists! \alpha \mathop{\overline{\text{ sm }}} \beta\} \quad &amp;\text{Df} \\ \end{align} \]" src="images/5471.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.224ex; width: 46.304ex; height: 7.579ex;" id="img_images_5471.svg"></span></p>

<p>When, as in this case, we have a descriptive double function closely
connected with a relation, we shall make it a practice to distinguish
the descriptive double function by a bar.</p>

<p>It is to be observed that "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/5472.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_5472.svg">," like <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_47"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{V}\)" src="images/304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.697ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_304.svg_27"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(1\)" src="images/395.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.131ex; height: 1.507ex;" id="img_images_395.svg_18"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4959.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 5.782ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_4959.svg_6">, is ambiguous as to
type, and only acquires a definite meaning when the types of its domain
and converse domain are specified. The domain and the converse domain
may or may not be of the same type, <i>i.e.</i> "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ sm }\)" src="images/5472.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 3.907ex; height: 1.038ex;" id="img_images_5472.svg_1">" may
or may not be a homogeneous relation. This enables us to speak of two
classes of different types as having the same number of terms. We
shall return to this point in connection with cardinal numbers (cf.
especially *102—*106).</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number are important, and are very
frequently referred to throughout cardinal arithmetic. In order to
prove that two classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_257"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_125"> have the same cardinal
number of terms, it is<span class="pagenum" id="Page_477">[Pg 477]</span> generally necessary, in the fundamental
arithmetical propositions with which we are concerned, actually to
construct a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_246"> such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in \alpha\,\overline{\text{sm}}\,\beta\)" src="images/5473.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 10.743ex; height: 2.17ex;" id="img_images_5473.svg">.
Such relation will be called a <i>correlator</i> of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_258"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_126">. It will usually be obtained by taking some
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_42"> for which we have (<img alt="" data-tex="\(y).\text{E}!Sʻy\)" src="images/5474.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.09ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5474.svg">, and limiting the
converse domain to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_127">, so that <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/5475.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.94ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5475.svg"> is the
required correlator. Very frequently we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in 1\rightarrow\text{Cls}\)" src="images/5476.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.03ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5476.svg">,
not <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5477.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 10.007ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5477.svg">, but <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_128"> will be such
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5478.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 13.488ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5478.svg">.</p>

<p>Among the more important propositions of the present number are the
following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·142.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\upharpoonright \beta\in \alpha\overline{\text{ sm }}\beta.\equiv.R\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow 1.\beta\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR.\alpha=Rʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/5479.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 55.3ex; height: 2.183ex;" id="img_images_5479.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/5069.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5069.svg_1"> is a correlator of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_259">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_129"> if (1) <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/5069.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5069.svg_2"> is one-one, (2)
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_130"> is contained in the converse domain of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_247">, (3) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_260">
is the class of those terms which have the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_248"> to members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_131">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\supset.\text{D}ʻR \text{ sm } \text{ᗡ}ʻR.\text{ᗡ}ʻR \text{ sm } \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/5480.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 44.219ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5480.svg"></p>

<p>This results immediately from the definition.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\beta\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR.\supset.Rʻʻ\beta \text{ sm } \beta.R\upharpoonright \beta\in (Rʻʻ\beta)\overline{\text{ sm }}\beta\)" src="images/5481.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.567ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5481.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\alpha \text{ sm } \alpha.I\upharpoonright \alpha\in \alpha\overline{\text{ sm }}\alpha\)" src="images/5482.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 24.555ex; height: 2.17ex;" id="img_images_5482.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·31</b>. <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha \text{ sm } \beta.\equiv.\beta \text{ sm } \alpha\)" src="images/5483.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 19.684ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5483.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha \text{ sm } \beta.\beta \text{ sm } \gamma.\supset.\alpha \text{ sm } \gamma\)" src="images/5484.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 27.054ex; height: 2.084ex;" id="img_images_5484.svg"></p>

<p>The above three propositions show that similarity is reflexive,
symmetrical and transitive.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·36.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha \text{ sm } \beta.\supset:\exists !\alpha.\equiv.\exists !\beta\)" src="images/5485.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 24.328ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_5485.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\iotaʻʻ\alpha\text{ sm }\alpha.\iota\upharpoonright \alpha\in (\iotaʻʻ\alpha)\overline{\text{ sm }}\alpha\)" src="images/5486.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.008ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5486.svg"></p>

<p>Thus every class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_261"> is similar to a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.964ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5487.svg"> of
higher type, and consisting wholly of unit classes.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·45.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.1=\hat{\beta}(\beta \text{ sm } \iotaʻx)\)" src="images/5488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.469ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_5488.svg"></p>

<p>Thus 1 is the class of all classes similar to any unit class.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·48.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.0=\hat{\beta}(\beta \text{ sm } \Lambda)\)" src="images/5489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.587ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_5489.svg"></p>

<p>Thus 0 is the class of all classes similar to the null-class.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·611.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\downarrow xʻʻ\alpha \text{ sm } \alpha.(\downarrow x)\upharpoonright \alpha\in (\downarrow xʻʻ\alpha)\overline{\text{ sm }}\alpha\)" src="images/5490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 41.527ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5490.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is very often useful. For arithmetical purposes,
we often wish to obtain mutually exclusive classes. Now whether or
not <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_262"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_132"> be mutually exclusive, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow xʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.217ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5491.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow yʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/5492.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 6.864ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5492.svg"> are mutually exclusive provided
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x \neq y\)" src="images/2001.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2001.svg_1">. Thus by means of the above proposition we can always
construct mutually exclusive classes each similar to a given class,
<i>i.e.</i> each having some assigned number of members.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha \text{ sm }\beta.\gamma \text{ sm }\delta.\alpha\cap \gamma=\Lambda.\beta\cap \delta=\Lambda.\supset.(\alpha\cup \gamma)\text{ sm }(\beta\cup \delta)\)" src="images/5493.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.79ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5493.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is fundamental in the theory of addition.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_478">[Pg 478]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·88.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha \text{ sm } \gamma.\beta \text{ sm } \delta.\gamma\subset \beta.\delta\subset \alpha.\supset.\alpha \text{ sm } \beta\)" src="images/5494.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 39.838ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_5494.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> "if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_263"> is similar to a part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_133">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_134"> is similar to a part of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_264">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_265"> is
similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_135">." This is the Schröder-Bernstein theorem. The
proof given below is due to Zermelo.</p>

<p>The following propositions, down to <a href="#_73_241" class="pginternal">*73·241</a>, are deduced from
preceding propositions of this number just as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\text{ sm }\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/5514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.143ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5514.svg">"
was deduced in <a href="#_73_2" class="pginternal">*73·2</a> from <a href="#_73_1" class="pginternal">*73·1</a>. The proofs are therefore merely
indicated by references to the previous propositions of this number
which are used.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*71·166}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*33·431}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\beta\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2)}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset:R\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\beta\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR:y,z\in \beta.Rʻy=Rʻz.\supset_{y,z}.y=z:\\ [\text{*73·24}]&amp;\supset:Rʻʻ\beta\text{ sm }\beta\colon\ldotp \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5522.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.368ex; width: 90.331ex; height: 11.866ex;" id="img_images_5522.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition will be convenient in such cases as the following: Let
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_136"> be a class of relations whose domains are mutually exclusive,
<i>i.e.</i> such that no two members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_137"> have domains which
have a member in common, and suppose we wish to prove that the class
of these domains is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_138">.<span class="pagenum" id="Page_481">[Pg 481]</span> The class of domains is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ\beta\)" src="images/5523.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.724ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5523.svg">, and we have (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P).\text{E}!\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/5524.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.54ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5524.svg">. Hence
we have only to prove (putting <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\)" src="images/2636.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.729ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_2636.svg_11"> in place of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_249"> of
<a href="#_73_25" class="pginternal">*73·25</a>)
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P,\,Q\in \beta.\text{D}ʻP=\text{D}ʻQ.\supset_{P,Q}.P=Q, \]" src="images/5525.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 36.609ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5525.svg"></span>
which, in the case supposed, is proved immediately.</p>

<p>This is the <i>reflexive</i> property of similarity. The conditions of
significance require that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_266"> should be a class of some type,
but impose no restriction as to the type of class.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·301.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in \alpha\overline{\text{ sm }}\beta.\equiv.\breve{R}\in \beta\overline{\text{ sm }}\alpha\)" src="images/5533.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 28.65ex; height: 2.853ex;" id="img_images_5533.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition shows that similarity is a <i>symmetrical</i> relation.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·311.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in \alpha\overline{\text{ sm }}\beta.S\in \beta\overline{\text{ sm }}\gamma.\supset.R\mid S\in \alpha\overline{\text{ sm }}\gamma\)" src="images/5536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 43.59ex; height: 2.294ex;" id="img_images_5536.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha\text{ sm }\beta.\beta\text{ sm }\gamma.\supset.\alpha\text{ sm }\gamma \quad[\text{*73·311·04}]\)" src="images/5538.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.882ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5538.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition shows that similarity is a <i>transitive</i> relation.
Thus we have now proved that similarity is reflexive, symmetrical, and
transitive.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·4.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{Cnv}ʻʻ\lambda\text{ sm }\lambda.\text{Cnv}\upharpoonright \lambda\in (\text{Cnv}ʻʻ\lambda)\overline{\text{ sm }}\lambda \quad[\text{*73·26.*72·11.*31·13}]\)" src="images/5548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.852ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5548.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_483">[Pg 483]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\iotaʻʻ\alpha\text{ sm }\alpha.\iota\upharpoonright \alpha\in (\iotaʻʻ\alpha)\overline{\text{ sm }}\alpha \quad[\text{*73·26.*72·18.*51·12}]\)" src="images/5549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 56.641ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_5549.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is useful, because it gives a class
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/5550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.844ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5550.svg"> similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_267"> but of higher type. Thus if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_4"> is a cardinal number, and it is known that in a certain type
there are classes having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_5"> terms, it follows that there will be
classes having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_6"> terms in the next higher type, and therefore in
the next type above that, and so on. No corresponding means exist for
lowering the type.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*73·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha\subset 1.\supset.\alpha\text{ sm }\breve{\iota}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.579ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_5551.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\vdash.\text{*52·13}.\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\alpha\subset\text{D}ʻ\iota &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ &amp;\vdash.\text{(1).*73·21.*72·18}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5552.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 41.1ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_5552.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition gives a means of lowering the type without altering
the cardinal number, provided our class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_268"> is composed wholly of
unit classes; for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5553.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.964ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_5553.svg"> is of the type next below
the type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_269">. But when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_270"> is not composed wholly of
unit classes, this construction fails.</p>

<p>The following propositions give the proof of the Schröder-Bernstein
theorem, namely: If one class is similar to part of another, and the
other is similar to part of the one, then the two classes are similar.
The proof here given is due to Zermelo<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_60" id="FNanchor_60">[60]</a>. An explanation of the
following proof is given in connection with another proof in the
summary of <a href="#_94" class="pginternal">*94</a>.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_73_87">*73·87</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R,\,S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset \text{D}ʻS.\text{ᗡ}ʻS\subset \text{D}ʻR.\supset.\text{D}ʻR\text{ sm }\text{D}ʻS\)" src="images/5614.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 58.4ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5614.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*71·252}.\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset.R\mid S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\\ [\text{*73·86·85}]&amp;\supset.\text{ᗡ}ʻS\text{ sm }\text{D}ʻR.\\ [\text{*73·2}] &amp;\supset.\text{D}ʻS\text{ sm }\text{D}ʻR:\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5615.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.733ex; width: 47.301ex; height: 8.597ex;" id="img_images_5615.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_73_88">*73·88</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\alpha\text{ sm }\gamma.\beta\text{ sm }\delta.\gamma\subset \beta.\delta\subset \alpha.\supset.\alpha\text{ sm }\beta\)" src="images/5616.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 39.838ex; height: 2.111ex;" id="img_images_5616.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*73·1}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.(\exists R,\,S).R,\,S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻR=\alpha.\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\gamma.\\ &amp;\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{D}ʻS=\beta.\text{ᗡ}ʻS=\delta.\gamma\subset \beta.\delta\subset \alpha.\\ [\text{*73·87}] &amp;\supset.(\exists R,\,S).\text{D}ʻR=\alpha.\text{D}ʻS=\beta.\text{D}ʻR\text{ sm }\text{D}ʻS.\\ [\text{*13·22}] &amp;\supset.\alpha\text{ sm }\beta:\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5617.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 64.74ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_5617.svg"></span></p>

<p>This is the Schröder-Bernstein theorem.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_490">[Pg 490]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_74">*74. ON ONE-MANY AND MANY-ONE RELATIONS
WITH LIMITED FIELDS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *74.</p>

<p>The purpose of the present number is to collect together various
propositions in which we have such hypotheses as
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \upharpoonright \lambda \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}, \kappa \upharpoonleft R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\text{, etc.} \]" src="images/5618.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 37.317ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5618.svg"></span>
or in which such hypotheses are shown to be deducible from others.
Hypotheses of this kind occur very frequently, and it is important to
be able to deal with them easily. For the sake of completeness, we
shall here repeat propositions previously proved on this subject.</p>

<p>The propositions of this number are mostly of the nature of
lemmas, to be used in the theory of selections (Part II, Section
D), and in cardinal and ordinal arithmetic. The most useful of
them are *74·772·773·774·775. These propositions are concerned
with circumstances under which <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \parallel \breve{R}\)" src="images/5619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.895ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5619.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid\breve{R}\)" src="images/5620.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.975ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_5620.svg">,
with or without some limitation of the converse domain,
is a one-one relation. The reason they are important is that the
correlators by means of which many of the fundamental theorems of
cardinal and ordinal arithmetic are proved are such relations as
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\parallel \breve{R}\)" src="images/5621.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.895ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5621.svg"> (with the converse domain limited) for
suitable values of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_250">. The above-mentioned propositions
are as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*74·772.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  (x). \text{E}!Qʻx:(y).\text{E}!Rʻy:Q,\,R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1 :\supset. Q \parallel \breve{R} \in 1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5622.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.992ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5622.svg"></p>

<p>The hypothesis of this proposition will be verified if we put, for
example, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q = R = \downarrow x\)" src="images/5623.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 11.966ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5623.svg">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\((\downarrow x) \parallel (\text{Cnv}ʻ\downarrow x) \in 1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5624.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.636ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5624.svg">. This proposition is
used in *116·531, which is used in proving one of the formal laws of
exponentiation, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^{\varpi} \times \nu^{\varpi} = (\mu \times \nu)^{\varpi}\)" src="images/5625.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.09ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5625.svg">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_74_773">*74·773</a>.</b>
    <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash: &amp;Q \upharpoonright \alpha, R \upharpoonright \beta \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1 . \alpha \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻQ.\beta \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR.sʻ\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda \subset \alpha.sʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\lambda \subset \beta .\supset.\\ &amp;(Q \parallel \breve{R}) \upharpoonright \lambda \in 1 \rightarrow 1 . (Q \parallel \breve{R}) \upharpoonright \lambda \in \{(Q \parallel \breve{R})ʻʻ\lambda\}\mathop{\overline{\text{ sm }}} \lambda \end{align}\]" src="images/5626.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.395ex; width: 74.096ex; height: 5.921ex;" id="img_images_5626.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition is used in connection with both cardinal and ordinal
multiplication and exponentiation. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \upharpoonright \alpha\)" src="images/5627.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.438ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_5627.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \upharpoonright \beta\)" src="images/2870.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_2870.svg_1"> correlate <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_7"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_271">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/4322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4322.svg_3"> with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_139">, then if we take for <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_24"> the
class of all ordinal couples that can be formed of an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_272"> and
a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_140">, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \parallel \breve{R})ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/5628.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.809ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5628.svg"> will be the class
of all couples<span class="pagenum" id="Page_491">[Pg 491]</span> that can be formed of a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_8"> and a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/4322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4322.svg_4">.
Thus in virtue of the above proposition, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_9"> is similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_273"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/4322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4322.svg_5"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_141">, the class of ordinal
couples formed of a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_10"> and a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\delta\)" src="images/4322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.005ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_4322.svg_6"> is similar to the class
of ordinal couples formed of an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_274"> and a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_142">. This result
is useful because we define the product of the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_275"> and the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_143"> as the number of
ordinal couples formed of an <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_276"> and a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_144">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*74·774.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1:(y).\text{E}!Rʻy:\supset.\mid \breve{R}\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5629.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.342ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5629.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is useful when, for example, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_251"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow x\)" src="images/4211.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 3.054ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_4211.svg_2">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*74·775.</b>
    <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash:Q\upharpoonright &amp;sʻ\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda,R\upharpoonright sʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\lambda\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.sʻ\text{D}ʻʻ\lambda\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻQ.sʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\lambda\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻR.\supset.\\ &amp;(Q\Arrowvert \breve{R})\upharpoonright \lambda\in 1\rightarrow 1.(Q\Arrowvert \breve{R})\upharpoonright \lambda\in \{(Q\Arrowvert \breve{R})ʻʻ\lambda\}\overline{\text{ sm }}\lambda\end{align}\]" src="images/5630.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.395ex; width: 73.478ex; height: 5.921ex;" id="img_images_5630.svg"></span></p>

<p>This is a particular case of *74·773, and has similar uses.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*74·1.</b>
    <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\colon R\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}.\supset\colon\ldotp R\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow 1.\equiv:y,\,z\in \beta.Rʻy=Rʻz.\supset_{y,z}.y=z\)" src="images/5631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 72.996ex; height: 2.364ex;" id="img_images_5631.svg"></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.*71·55.\supset\vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.\\ \supset\colon\ldotp (R\upharpoonright \beta)\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow 1.\equiv:y,\,z\in \beta.(R\upharpoonright \beta)ʻy=(R\upharpoonright \beta)ʻz.\supset_{y,z}.y=z\colon\ldotp     \\ [*35·31·7] \supset\colon\ldotp R\upharpoonright \beta\in 1\rightarrow 1.\equiv:y,z\in \beta.Rʻy=Rʻz.\supset_{y,z}.y=z\colon\colon \supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5632.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.835ex; width: 75.37ex; height: 8.801ex;" id="img_images_5632.svg"></span></p>
