<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_500">[Pg 500]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_D_b">SECTION D.<br>
<br>
SELECTIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of Section D.</i></p>

<p>The subject to be considered in this section is important chiefly
in connection with multiplication, both cardinal and ordinal. In
order to get a definition of multiplication which is not confined
to the case where the number of factors is finite, we have to seek
a construction by which, from a given class of classes, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_64">
say, we construct another class which, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_65"> is finite,
has that number of terms which, in the usual elementary sense, is
the product of the numbers of terms in the various classes which are
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_66">, and which, whether <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_67"> is finite or not,
obeys as many as possible of the formal laws of multiplication. The
usual elementary sense of multiplication is derived from addition;
that is to say, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu \times \nu\)" src="images/5743.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.329ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_5743.svg"> is to be the number of terms in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_12">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_68"> is a class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_7"> mutually exclusive
classes each having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/5744.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_5744.svg"> members, or vice versa. This sense can be
extended to any finite number of factors, but not to an infinite number
of factors; hence for a number of factors which may be infinite we
require a different definition, and this is derived from the theory of
<i>selections</i>.</p>

<p>Selections are of two kinds, selections from classes of classes, and
selections from relations. The latter is the more general notion, from
which the former is derived. But as the former is an easier notion, we
will begin by explaining selections from classes of classes.</p>

<p>Given a class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_69">, a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_8"> is called a
<i>selected class</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_70"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_9"> is formed by choosing
one term out of each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_71">. For example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_72">
consists of two members, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_277"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_145">, and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \in\alpha\)" src="images/240.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.508ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_240.svg_1">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \beta\)" src="images/3091.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.155ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_3091.svg_3">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻx \cup \iotaʻy\)" src="images/5745.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.234ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5745.svg"> is a
selected class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_73">. If every constituency elects a local man,
Parliament is a selected class of the constituencies. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_74"> is
a class of mutually exclusive classes, <i>i.e.</i> a class no two of
whose members have any member in common, then a selected class consists
of only one term from each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_75">; <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_10"> is
a selected class if
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu \subset sʻ\kappa : \alpha \in \kappa .\supset_{\alpha}. \mu \cap \alpha \in 1. \]" src="images/5746.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 30.343ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5746.svg"></span>
But if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_76"> is not a class of mutually exclusive classes, this
does not hold necessarily; for a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_537"> which is a member of
both <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_278"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_146"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha, \beta \in \kappa\)" src="images/5747.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5747.svg">)
may be chosen as the representative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_279">, while some other
term may be<span class="pagenum" id="Page_501">[Pg 501]</span> chosen as the representative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_147">, so that two
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_148"> may belong to the selected class. Again, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_77"> is a class of mutually exclusive classes, the relation of
the representative to its class must be one-one, because, since no
term belongs to two classes which are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_78">, no term
can be the representative of two classes. But when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_79"> is not
a class of mutually exclusive classes, a term which belongs to two
classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_280"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_149"> may be chosen as the representative of
both. Thus the relation of the representative to its class may be only
one-many, not one-one.</p>

<p>The relation of the representative to its class may be called a
<i>selective relation</i>. A selective relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_80"> is
one which selects, from every class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_281"> which is a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_81">, a certain member <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_538"> as the <i>representative</i> of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_282">; that is, we have, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_252"> is the selective relation,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha\in \kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.Rʻ\alpha\in \alpha:\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\kappa. \]" src="images/5748.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.505ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5748.svg"></span>
This condition is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in 1\rightarrow\text{Cls}.R\unicode{x2abd}\in .\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\kappa. \]" src="images/5749.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.893ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5749.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_253"> is a selective relation, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_12"> is a selected class;
and if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_11"> is a selected class, there is a selective relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_254">
such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu=\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/5750.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.185ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5750.svg">. Thus the study of selections from classes
of classes is wholly contained in the study of selective relations.</p>

<p>The class of selective relations from a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_82"> is called
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg">. Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.&amp;\equiv.R\in 1\rightarrow\text{Cls}.R\unicode{x2abd}\in .\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\kappa,\\ \text{and}\qquad\quad {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa&amp;=(1\rightarrow\text{Cls})\cap \text{Rl}ʻ\in \cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻ\kappa. \end{align} \]" src="images/5752.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.859ex; width: 48.412ex; height: 6.848ex;" id="img_images_5752.svg"></span>
Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.134ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5753.svg"> is the class of selected
classes.</p>

<p>It will be seen that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\in \kappa\)" src="images/5754.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.517ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_5754.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3753.svg_1"> may be any
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_283">, and we get a different <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_255"> for each different
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_284">. Thus if we keep the representatives of all
the other members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_83"> unchanged, the number of selective
relations to be obtained by varying the representative of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_285">
is the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_286">. Hence the number of selective
relations altogether may be fitly defined as the product of the
numbers of terms possessed by the various members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_84">. In
case <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_85"> is finite, this agrees with the usual definition of
multiplication; and whether <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_86"> is finite or infinite, the
product so defined obeys all the formal laws of multiplication.</p>

<p>To illustrate the notion of selective relations, let us take a very
simple case, the case where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_87"> consists of two classes
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_287"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_150">, each of which has two members. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_539"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_246"> be the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_288">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_38"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_13"> the members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_151">. We assume <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \neq \beta\)" src="images/5755.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.746ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_5755.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \neq y\)" src="images/2001.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_2001.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z \neq w\)" src="images/5756.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 5.689ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_5756.svg">.
Then the selective relations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_88"> are the following:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x\downarrow\alpha\unicode{x228d} z\downarrow\beta,\\ x\downarrow\alpha\unicode{x228d} w\downarrow\beta,\\ y\downarrow\alpha\unicode{x228d} z\downarrow\beta,\\ y\downarrow\alpha\unicode{x228d} w\downarrow\beta. \]" src="images/5757.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 49.245ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5757.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_502">[Pg 502]</span>
Thus they are four in number, <i>i.e.</i> the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_1"> is the product of the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_289"> and the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_152">. A similar process
would show that our definition of the product agrees with the usual
definition in any case in which all the numbers concerned are finite.</p>

<p>Selections from <i>relations</i> are an obvious generalization of
selections from classes of classes. We had above
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa = (1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}) \cap \text{Rl}ʻ{\in} \cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻ\kappa\text{.} \]" src="images/5758.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.014ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_5758.svg"></span>
We put, generally,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa = (1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}) \cap \text{Rl}ʻP \cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻ\kappa\text{,} \]" src="images/5759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 34.147ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_5759.svg"></span>
which we derive from the definition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P_{\Delta}=\hat{\lambda}\hat{\kappa}\{\lambda = (1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}) \cap \text{Rl}ʻP \cap \overleftarrow{\text{ᗡ}}ʻ\kappa \} \quad \text{Df}\text{.} \]" src="images/5760.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.39ex; height: 3.907ex;" id="img_images_5760.svg"></span>
This is the fundamental definition in the subject of selections. We
have, in virtue of this definition,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash: R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa .\equiv. R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls} . R \unicode{x2abd} P . \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \kappa \text{.} \]" src="images/5761.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 44.983ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5761.svg"></span>
When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa = \text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/5762.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.734ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5762.svg">, we may call <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg"> the
class of selections from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_34">. Thus generally, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_1">
is the class of selections from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \upharpoonright \kappa\)" src="images/5764.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.203ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5764.svg">
provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/5765.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.734ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5765.svg">; and if this condition is not
fulfilled, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa = \Lambda\)" src="images/5766.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.221ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5766.svg">. We may call the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_2"> the class of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_35">-selections from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_89">."
The class of "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_12">-selections from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_90">" will be what we
previously called the class of "selective relations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_91">."
It will be observed that we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa . y \in \kappa .\supset. Rʻy \in \overrightarrow{P}ʻy\text{.} \]" src="images/5767.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 31.816ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5767.svg"></span>
Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.717ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5768.svg"> is a class of mutually exclusive
classes, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_13"> selects one from each of these classes, and is
therefore a selective class of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.717ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5768.svg_1">; hence in
this case
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa = \text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa\text{.} \]" src="images/5769.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.271ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5769.svg"></span></p>

<p>In Cardinal Arithmetic, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_2"> is the important
notion, and the more general notion <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_3"> is seldom
required. In Ordinal Arithmetic, <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.636ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5770.svg"> is the important
notion. It will be seen that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in F_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa .\equiv. R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls} . R \unicode{x2abd} F . \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \kappa\text{.} \]" src="images/5771.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 42.341ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5771.svg"></span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.636ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5770.svg_1"> is only significant when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_92"> is a
class of relations; in this case we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in F_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa . Q \in \kappa .\supset. RʻQ \in CʻQ\text{.} \]" src="images/5772.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 33.882ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5772.svg"></span>
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_503">[Pg 503]</span>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_256"> chooses a representative member of the field of every
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_93">. The most important case is when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_94"> is of
the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg_4">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_36"> is a serial relation whose field consists
of serial relations. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta}ʻCʻP\)" src="images/5773.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5773.svg"> becomes the field of a
relation which may be defined as the ordinal product of the relations
composing <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg_5">; in this way we get an infinite ordinal product
analogous to the infinite cardinal product. This will be explained at a
later stage (*172).</p>

<p>Although it is chiefly <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_3"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.636ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5770.svg_2"> that will be required in the sequel, we shall
treat <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_4"> generally, because this introduces
little extra complication, and most of the theorems which hold for
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_4"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(F_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5770.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.636ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5770.svg_3"> have exact analogues
for <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_5">.</p>

<p><img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_6">, as above defined, is the class of one-many
relations contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_37"> and having <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_95"> for their converse
domain. We know of no proof that there always are such relations when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/5774.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.734ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5774.svg">. In fact, the proposition
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻP.\supset_{P,\kappa}.\exists !P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa \]" src="images/5775.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 22.782ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_5775.svg"></span>
is equivalent to the "multiplicative axiom," <i>i.e.</i> to the axiom
that, given any class of mutually exclusive classes, none of which is
null, there is at least one class formed of one member from each of
these classes. (This equivalence is proved in <a href="#_88_36" class="pginternal">*88·36</a>, below.) It is
also equivalent to Zermelo's axiom<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_61" id="FNanchor_61">[61]</a>, which is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\alpha).\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Cl ex}ʻ\alpha; \]" src="images/5776.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.95ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5776.svg"></span>
hence also it is equivalent to the proposition that every class can be
well-ordered. In the absence of evidence as to the truth or falsehood
of these various propositions, we shall not assume their truth, but
shall explicitly introduce them as hypotheses wherever they are
relevant.</p>

<p>In the present section, we shall begin (<a href="#_80" class="pginternal">*80</a>) by considering such
properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_7"> as do not depend upon any
hypothesis as to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_38">. We shall then (<a href="#_81" class="pginternal">*81</a>) proceed to consider
such further properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_8"> as result from
the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\upharpoonright \kappa\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5777.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.773ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5777.svg">.
This hypothesis is important, because it is verified in many
of the applications we wish to make, and because it leads to
important properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_9"> which are not true in
general when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_39"> is not subject to any hypothesis. These special
properties are mostly due to the fact that when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\upharpoonright\kappa\)" src="images/5778.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.203ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5778.svg">
is a many-one relation, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_10"> consists of
one-one relations (not merely of one-many relations, as it does in
the general case). This is proved in <a href="#_81_1" class="pginternal">*81·1</a>. We then (<a href="#_82" class="pginternal">*82</a>) proceed
to consider the case of relative products, <i>i.e.</i> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/5779.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.452ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5779.svg">.
It will appear that, with a suitable hypothesis,
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda=\mid QʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻQʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/5780.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.756ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5780.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ(P\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda=DʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻQʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/5781.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.534ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5781.svg">.
In the following number (<a href="#_83" class="pginternal">*83</a>) we apply the results of <a href="#_80" class="pginternal">*80</a> to the
particular case where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_40"> is replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg_5">, which is
the important case for cardinal arithmetic. In <a href="#_84" class="pginternal">*84</a> we apply the
propositions of <a href="#_81" class="pginternal">*81</a> to the case where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_41"> is replaced by <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg_6">,
and where, therefore, we have the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\upharpoonright \kappa\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5782.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.583ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5782.svg">.
This hypothesis is equivalent to the hypothesis that no two members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_96"> have any members in common, <i>i.e.</i> that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha,\beta \in \kappa.\alpha \neq \beta.\supset_{\alpha,\beta}.\alpha\cap \beta=\Lambda. \]" src="images/5783.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 31.349ex; height: 2.27ex;" id="img_images_5783.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_504">[Pg 504]</span>
When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_97"> fulfils this hypothesis, it is a class of
mutually exclusive classes. For classes of mutually exclusive
classes we adopt the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/5784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_5784.svg">."
It is shown in <a href="#_84_14" class="pginternal">*84·14</a> that a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/5784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_5784.svg_1">
is one for which we have <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\upharpoonright \kappa \in\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5785.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.583ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5785.svg">.
When <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_98"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\text{excl}\)" src="images/5786.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.974ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_5786.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}\upharpoonright P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5787.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.562ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5787.svg">
is a one-one relation, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\,\text{ sm }\, {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5788.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.487ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5788.svg">.
Also in this case <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.134ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5753.svg_1"> consists of
all classes formed of one member from each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_99">,
<i>i.e.</i> all classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_12"> such that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu\subset sʻ\kappa:\alpha \in \kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\mu\cap \alpha \in 1. \]" src="images/5789.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 30.343ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_5789.svg"></span>
In <a href="#_85" class="pginternal">*85</a>, we prove various important propositions, of which the chief is
a form of the associative law<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_62" id="FNanchor_62">[62]</a>, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash:\kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} \text{excl}.\supset.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻsʻ\kappa\, \text{ sm }\, {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa. \]" src="images/5790.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 43.29ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_5790.svg"></span>
Finally, in <a href="#_88" class="pginternal">*88</a>, we consider the question of the existence of
selections. This cannot in general be proved when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_100"> is an
infinite class. The assumption that <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_5"> is never
null unless one member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_101"> is null is equivalent to various
other assumptions, for example to the assumption that every class can
be well-ordered. One of these equivalent assumptions is called the
"multiplicative axiom." This axiom is equivalent to the assumption that
an arithmetical product cannot be zero unless one of its factors is
zero, and is regarded by some mathematicians as a self-evident truth.
This can be proved when the number of factors is finite, <i>i.e.</i>
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_102"> is a finite class, but not when the number of factors
is infinite. We have not assumed its truth in the general case where
it cannot be proved, but have included it in the hypotheses of all
propositions which depend upon it.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_505">[Pg 505]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_80">*80. ELEMENTARY PROPERTIES OF SELECTIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *80.</p>

<p>In this number, we shall give such properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}\)" src="images/5791.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.345ex; width: 2.973ex; height: 1.891ex;" id="img_images_5791.svg"> as
follow most directly from the definition, without any restrictive
hypothesis as to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_42">.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5792.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.117ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5792.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_257"> selects one member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\)" src="images/5793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.165ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5793.svg">, whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \kappa\)" src="images/5794.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.178ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5794.svg">, as the
selected referent of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_247">. For, since <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1 \rightarrow\text{Cls} . \text{ᗡ}ʻR = \kappa\)" src="images/5795.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.046ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5795.svg">,
we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \kappa .\supset.\text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/5796.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 15.303ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5796.svg">; and since
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \unicode{x2abd} P\)" src="images/4433.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_4433.svg_1">, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \kappa .\supset.(Rʻy)Py\)" src="images/5797.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.701ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5797.svg">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \kappa .\supset. Rʻy \in \overrightarrow{P}ʻy\)" src="images/5798.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 20.064ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5798.svg">.
Calling <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_60"> the <i>selected referent</i> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_248">, it
is evident that we may replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻy\)" src="images/326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_326.svg_61"> by any other member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\)" src="images/5793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.165ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5793.svg_1">, and still have a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_11">. (This is proved in <a href="#_80_4" class="pginternal">*80·4</a>.) Thus if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_12"> has any members at all, we can get as many
members as there are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\)" src="images/5793.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.165ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5793.svg_2"> by merely
altering the selected referent of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_249">, leaving the other selected
referents unchanged.</p>

<p>In the present section, we first prove various simple properties of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_13">. Most of these are almost immediate consequences
of</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*80·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa .\equiv. R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}. R \unicode{x2abd} P.\text{ᗡ}ʻR = \kappa\)" src="images/5799.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 44.354ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5799.svg"></p>

<p>The most useful of them are</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_80_2">*80·2</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \exists! P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa .\supset. \kappa \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/5800.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.667ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5800.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*80·291.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa .\supset. R \unicode{x2abd} P \upharpoonright \kappa\)" src="images/5801.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.806ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5801.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*80·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa . y\in \kappa .\supset. \text{E}!Rʻy\)" src="images/5802.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 29.065ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5802.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*80·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa .\supset. \text{D}ʻR \subset Pʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5803.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.066ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5803.svg"></p>

<p>We then have various propositions (<a href="#_80_4" class="pginternal">*80·4</a>—<a href="#_80_46" class="pginternal">·46</a>) concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x \downarrow y\)" src="images/5804.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5804.svg"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x P y\)" src="images/5805.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5805.svg">. Of these the most important are the
following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*80·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa . y \in \kappa . x'Py .\supset. [\{R \dot{-} (Rʻy) \downarrow y\} \unicode{x228d}  x' \downarrow y] \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5806.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 60.061ex; height: 2.62ex;" id="img_images_5806.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> given a selective relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_258">, the selected referent of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_250"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(y \in \text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/5807.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 8.289ex; height: 2.161ex;" id="img_images_5807.svg">) may be replaced by any other term
having the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_43"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_251">, and we shall still have a selective
relation.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*80·45.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. P_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻy = \downarrow yʻʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\)" src="images/5808.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 22.123ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_5808.svg"></p>

<p>We then have a set of propositions (<a href="#_80_5" class="pginternal">*80·5</a>—<a href="#_80_54" class="pginternal">·54</a>) connecting
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x228d} Q)_{\Delta}ʻ(\kappa \cup \lambda)\)" src="images/5809.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.501ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5809.svg"> with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_14"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/5810.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.986ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5810.svg">. These are chiefly
useful as leading to the next set</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_506">[Pg 506]</span></p>

<p class="nind">
(*80·6—·69), connecting <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ(\kappa\cup \lambda)\)" src="images/5811.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.227ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5811.svg"> with

propositions are seldom used, but they would be useful in considering

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*51·36}. &amp; \supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.P_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa\subset -\iotaʻ\Lambda. &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ [\text{*37·42}]  &amp;\supset.P_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa=\{(-\iotaʻ\Lambda)\upharpoonleft P_{\Delta}\}ʻʻ\kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*80·12.*33·431}. &amp;\supset\vdash.\kappa\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻP_{\Delta}.\\ [\text{*37·51}]  &amp;\supset\vdash.\kappa\subset \breve{P}_{\Delta}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*37·2}.        \supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\breve{P}_{\Delta}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa&amp;\subset \breve{P}_{\Delta}ʻʻ(-\iotaʻ\Lambda)\\ [\text{*37·4}] &amp;\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\{(-\iotaʻ\Lambda)\upharpoonleft P_{\Delta}\} &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(3).(4)}.&amp; \supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\kappa\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\{(-\iotaʻ\Lambda)\upharpoonleft P_{\Delta}\} &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash.\text{(5).*80·83.*73·22}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\{(-\iotaʻ\Lambda)\upharpoonleft P_{\Delta}\}ʻʻ\kappa\text{ sm }\kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(6)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(6)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5952.svg" style="vertical-align: -13.952ex; width: 82.856ex; height: 29.036ex;" id="img_images_5952.svg"></span></p>

ordinal multiplication (*113 and *172).</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_80_9">*80·9</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp y \neq z.\supset:M\in P_{\Delta}ʻ(\iotaʻy\cup \iotaʻz).\equiv.(\exists u,v).uPy.vPz.M=u\downarrow y\unicode{x228d}v\downarrow z\)" src="images/5826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 70.059ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5826.svg_1"></p>

<p>80·9·91 can be extended, by precisely similar proofs, to any finite
number of variables <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_253">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_39">, .... They will, on occasion, be
assumed for three or four variables, without fresh proofs.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*80·92.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:y \neq z.\supset.\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ(\iotaʻy\cup \iotaʻz)=\hat{\xi}\{(\exists u,v).uPy.vPz.\xi=\iotaʻu\cup \iotaʻv\}\)" src="images/5956.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 68.001ex; height: 2.991ex;" id="img_images_5956.svg"></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_519">[Pg 519]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_81">*81. SELECTIONS FROM MANY-ONE RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *81.</p>

<p>When <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\upharpoonright \kappa\)" src="images/5961.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.203ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5961.svg"> is a many-one relation,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_17"> has many important properties which do not
hold in the general case. In the first place, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_18">
consists wholly of one-one relations. In the second place, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5792.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.117ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5792.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_14"> takes one term and
no more out of each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.717ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5768.svg_2">.
Again, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5792.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.117ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5792.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_259"> is determinate
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_15"> is given; <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(R,\,S \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\text{D}ʻR=\text{D}ʻS.\supset.R=S\)" src="images/5962.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.297ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5962.svg">.
It follows that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5963.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.077ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5963.svg"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_19">;
hence the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_20"> is the number
of ways of choosing one member out of each class belonging to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.717ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5768.svg_3">. It should be remembered that when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\upharpoonright \kappa\)" src="images/5961.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.203ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_5961.svg_1"> is many-one, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.717ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5768.svg_4">
is a class of mutually exclusive classes, <i>i.e.</i> no two different
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.717ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5768.svg_5"> have any common member. This
follows immediately from <a href="#_71_181" class="pginternal">*71·181</a>.</p>

<p>As explained in the introduction to this section, the propositions of
this number are chiefly useful on account of their application to the
case of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg_7">. This application is made in <a href="#_84" class="pginternal">*84</a>. The most important
propositions in this number are:</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_81_1">*81·1</a>.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset.P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\subset 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5964.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.869ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5964.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*81·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.R=(\text{D}ʻR)\upharpoonleft     P\upharpoonright \kappa=P\dot{\cap}\text{D}ʻR\uparrow \kappa\)" src="images/5965.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 66.351ex; height: 2.654ex;" id="img_images_5965.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition, by exhibiting <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_260"> as a function of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_16">,
leads immediately to</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*81·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset.\text{D}\upharpoonright P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa \in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\,\text{     sm }\,P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5966.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 61.549ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5966.svg"></p>

<p>This is the principal proposition of this number. The following also is
important:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*81·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset.\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=\hat{\mu}\{y \in \kappa.\supset_{y}.\mu\cap     \overrightarrow{P}ʻy \in 1:\mu\subset Pʻʻ\kappa\}\)" src="images/5967.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 73.004ex; height: 3.857ex;" id="img_images_5967.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*80·14}. &amp;\supset\vdash:R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.R \in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*80·291}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp R \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset:R\unicode{x2abd}P\upharpoonright \kappa:\\ [\text{*71·221}] &amp;\supset:P\upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset.R \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1 &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2)}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/5968.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 57.477ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_5968.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*81·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\upharpoonright \kappa\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.R\in P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.x\in \text{D}ʻR.\supset.\text{E}!\breve{R}ʻx.x(P\upharpoonright \kappa)\breve{R}ʻx\)" src="images/5969.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.97ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_5969.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is very important. The class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5963.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.077ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5963.svg_1">, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\upharpoonright \kappa\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5982.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.773ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5982.svg">, is formed, as we shall prove later, by
making every possible selection of one term out of each member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5768.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.717ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_5768.svg_6">, each such selection giving us one
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5963.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.077ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5963.svg_2">. The fact that, with the
above hypothesis, the class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5963.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.077ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5963.svg_3">
has the same number of terms as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_22"> (which results
from the above proposition), is of great utility in the theory of
cardinal multiplication and exponentiation.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_524">[Pg 524]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_82">*82. SELECTIONS FROM RELATIVE PRODUCTS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *82.</p>

<p>The propositions contained in this number are not much used except in
connection with the associative law for cardinal multiplication, but
they have a certain intrinsic interest. We prove in this number that,
with a suitable hypothesis, (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/5779.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.452ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_5779.svg_1"> results
from <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻQʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/6002.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.154ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6002.svg"> by multiplying each member by <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_10">,
<i>i.e.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*82·52}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.(P\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\breve{Q}ʻʻ\kappa\,\text{ sm }\,\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\\ [\text{*81·31}] &amp;\supset.(P\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\breve{Q}ʻʻ\kappa\,\text{ sm }\,DʻʻR_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\\ [\text{*82·52.*73·32}]&amp;\supset.(P\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\breve{Q}ʻʻ\kappa\,\text{ sm }\,(R\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\breve{Q}ʻʻ\kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*82·33}.\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset.\text{D}ʻʻ(P\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\breve{Q}ʻʻ\kappa=\text{D}ʻʻP_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ [\text{*81·31}] &amp; =\text{D}ʻʻR_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ [\text{*81·3.*40·5}] &amp;=\hat{\mu}\{\alpha\in \overrightarrow{P}ʻʻ\kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\mu\cap \alpha\in 1:\mu\subset Pʻʻ\kappa\} &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{*82·33}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\text{D}ʻʻ(R\mid Q)_{\Delta}ʻ\breve{Q}ʻʻ\kappa=\text{D}ʻʻR_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).(3).(4).(5)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6056.svg" style="vertical-align: -14.31ex; width: 86.041ex; height: 29.751ex;" id="img_images_6056.svg"></span></p>


<hr class="chap x-ebookmaker-drop">

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_531">[Pg 531]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_83">*83. SELECTIONS FROM CLASSES OF CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *83.</p>

<p>In this number, the general propositions which have been proved for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_23"> are to be applied to the important special case
where <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_45"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_13">. In this case, we have selections from classes
of classes: if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \in_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6057.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.173ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6057.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_262"> picks out a
<i>representative</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3753.svg_2"> from each class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_290"> which is
a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_103">; <i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \alpha \in \kappa .\supset_{\alpha}. Rʻ\alpha \in \alpha. \]" src="images/6058.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.866ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6058.svg"></span></p>

<p>The propositions of this number result from those of previous numbers
either immediately, by the substitution of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_14"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_46">, or by the
use of propositions of *62, notably <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{{\in}}ʻ\alpha = \alpha\)" src="images/6059.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.78ex; height: 3.319ex;" id="img_images_6059.svg">
(<a href="#_62_2" class="pginternal">*62·2</a>), and <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}ʻʻ\kappa = sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6060.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.266ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6060.svg"> (<a href="#_62_3" class="pginternal">*62·3</a>).</p>

<p>The propositions of the present number follow, in the main, the same
course as those of <a href="#_80" class="pginternal">*80</a>, with <img alt="" data-tex="\(\in\)" src="images/239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_239.svg_15"> substituted for <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_47"> (except
that the special forms of propositions before <a href="#_80_2" class="pginternal">*80·2</a> are not given).
We have first a set of propositions resulting immediately from early
propositions of *80. Of these the most used are:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \Lambda \in \kappa .\supset. {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa = \Lambda\)" src="images/6061.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.329ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6061.svg"></p>

<p>This leads to the proposition that an arithmetical product is null if
one of its factors is null. (We cannot prove the converse universally
without assuming the multiplicative axiom.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·15.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\Lambda = \iotaʻ\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/6062.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.091ex; height: 2.808ex;" id="img_images_6062.svg"></p>

<p>Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/6063.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.957ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6063.svg"> is a unit class. This is the source of
the proposition <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^{0} = 1\)" src="images/6064.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.5ex; height: 2.375ex;" id="img_images_6064.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_14"> is a cardinal (cf. note to
*83·15).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  R \in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa .\supset: \alpha \in \kappa .\equiv. \text{E}!Rʻ\alpha .\equiv. Rʻ\alpha \in \alpha\)" src="images/6065.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 46.082ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6065.svg"></p>

<p>Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻ\alpha\)" src="images/3753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.523ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3753.svg_3"> is the "representative" of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_291">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa .\supset. \text{D}ʻR \subset sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6066.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.127ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6066.svg"></p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions (<a href="#_83_4" class="pginternal">*83·4</a>—<a href="#_83_44" class="pginternal">·44</a>) on selections from unit
classes and classes of unit classes. We have</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_532">[Pg 532]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻ\alpha \mathop{\text{ sm }} \alpha\)" src="images/6067.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.491ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6067.svg"></p>

<p>This leads to the proposition that a product of one factor is equal to
that factor.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·43.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\subset 1.\supset.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=\iotaʻ(\breve{\iota}\upharpoonright \kappa)=\iotaʻ({\in}\upharpoonright \kappa)\)" src="images/6068.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.993ex; height: 2.434ex;" id="img_images_6068.svg"></p>

<p>This leads to</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·44.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\subset 1.\supset.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa \in 1\)" src="images/6069.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.702ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6069.svg"></p>

<p>whence it follows that a product of factors, each of which is one, is
one. This holds even if the number of factors is infinite or zero.</p>

<p>We have next a set of propositions (<a href="#_83_5" class="pginternal">*83·5</a>—<a href="#_83_58" class="pginternal">*·58</a>) on changing the
representative of a class, and on selections from a class of classes
some of which are unit classes. These propositions are seldom referred
to in the sequel.</p>

<p>We have next (<a href="#_83_6" class="pginternal">*83·6</a>—<a href="#_83_74" class="pginternal">·74</a>) a set of propositions on
the domains of selections, <i>i.e.</i> on the class
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.134ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5753.svg_2">. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·66.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.sʻ\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6070.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 33.28ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6070.svg"></p>

<p>(The hypothesis here cannot be dispensed with unless we assume the
multiplicative axiom.)</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·7.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻ\alpha=\iotaʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6071.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 22.806ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6071.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_83_71">*83·71</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha=\iotaʻ\alpha.\text{D}ʻ\alpha\upharpoonleft \breve{\iota}=\alpha\)" src="images/6072.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.812ex; height: 2.321ex;" id="img_images_6072.svg"></p>

<p>We have next two propositions (*83·8·81) on the types of
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.134ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5753.svg_3">. The
type of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.134ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5753.svg_4"> is the same as that of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_104"> (<a href="#_83_81" class="pginternal">*83·81</a>).</p>

<p>The last set of propositions in this number (<a href="#_83_9" class="pginternal">*83·9</a>—<a href="#_83_904" class="pginternal">·904</a>) deals with
the existence of selections. We have</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·9.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/6073.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.232ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6073.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·901.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻ\alpha.\equiv.\exists !\alpha\)" src="images/6074.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.627ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6074.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·904.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\kappa\cup \iotaʻ\beta).\equiv.\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\exists !\beta\)" src="images/6075.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.453ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6075.svg"></p>

<p>From these propositions we shall deduce by mathematical induction that
whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_105"> is a finite class, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_7"> exists
unless <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda \in\kappa\)" src="images/6076.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.639ex; height: 1.71ex;" id="img_images_6076.svg"> (cf. *120·62). Thus a product consisting
of a finite number of factors (which may themselves be either finite or
infinite) can only vanish if one of the factors vanishes.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*83·1.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.\Lambda{\sim}{\in}\kappa\)" src="images/6077.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.132ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6077.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*80·2}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\kappa\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ{\in}.\\ [\text{*62·231}] &amp;\supset.\Lambda{\sim}{\in}\kappa:\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6078.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 31.237ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_6078.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\Lambda \in \kappa.\supset.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=\Lambda \quad[\text{*83·1.Transp}]\)" src="images/6079.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.691ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6079.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_533">[Pg 533]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·12.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=({\in}\upharpoonright \kappa)_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa \quad[\text{*80·23}]\)" src="images/6080.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.855ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6080.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\Lambda{\sim}\in \kappa.Q=\in \upharpoonright \kappa.\supset.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=Q_{\Delta}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻQ \quad[\text{*80·24.*62·231}]\)" src="images/6081.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 59.11ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6081.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.Q=\in \upharpoonright \kappa.\supset.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=Q_{\Delta}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻQ \quad[\text{*83·1·13}]\)" src="images/6082.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 53.002ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6082.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_83_15">*83·15</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\Lambda=\iotaʻ\dot{\Lambda} \quad[\text{*80·26}]\)" src="images/6083.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.896ex; height: 2.921ex;" id="img_images_6083.svg"></p>

<p>In virtue of this proposition, the product of 0 cardinal numbers is
1—a proposition of which a particular case, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu^{0}=1\)" src="images/5850.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 6.5ex; height: 2.375ex;" id="img_images_5850.svg_1">, is
familiar. This arithmetical proposition results from the above as
follows. We shall define the product of the numbers of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_106"> as the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_8">.
Thus when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa=\Lambda\)" src="images/3490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.89ex; height: 1.805ex;" id="img_images_3490.svg_3">, the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_9"> is a product of 0 factors. Now by the
above proposition, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\Lambda\)" src="images/6063.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.957ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6063.svg_1"> has one member, namely
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\Lambda}\)" src="images/35.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 2.355ex;" id="img_images_35.svg_5">. Hence a product of 0 factors is 1.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·16.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !\kappa.\supset.\dot{\Lambda}{\sim}\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa \quad[\text{*80·28}]\)" src="images/6084.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.194ex; height: 2.921ex;" id="img_images_6084.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·2.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset:\alpha\in \kappa.\equiv.\text{E}!Rʻ\alpha.\equiv.Rʻ\alpha\in \alpha \quad[\text{*80·32.*62·2}]\)" src="images/6085.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 61.67ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6085.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.\text{D}ʻR\subset sʻ\kappa \quad[\text{*80·33.*62·3}]\)" src="images/6086.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 43.715ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6086.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.\text{E}‼Rʻʻ\kappa.Rʻʻ\kappa=\text{D}ʻR \quad[\text{*80·34}]\)" src="images/6087.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 49.586ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6087.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.\text{D}ʻR=\hat{x}\{(\exists \alpha).\alpha\in \kappa.x=Rʻ\alpha\} \quad[\text{*80·35}]\)" src="images/6088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.597ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_6088.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·24.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\alpha\in \kappa.x\in \alpha.\supset.[\{R\dot{-}(Rʻ\alpha)\downarrow \alpha\}\unicode{x228d}x\downarrow \alpha]\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa     \quad[\text{*80·41}]\)" src="images/6089.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.488ex; height: 2.62ex;" id="img_images_6089.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.\dot{s}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=\in \upharpoonright \kappa \quad[\text{*80·42}]\)" src="images/6090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.676ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_6090.svg"></p>
