<p class="nind"><b>*83·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻ\alpha\text{ sm }\alpha \quad[\text{*83·4.*73·611}]\)" src="images/6099.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.456ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6099.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_534">[Pg 534]</span></p>

<p>This proposition shows that a cardinal product of one factor
is equal to that one factor. For the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6100.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.993ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6100.svg"> is the product of the numbers of
members of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.606ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6101.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> it is a product
whose only factor is the number of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_292">. By the
above proposition, this product is equal to the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_293">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*83·42.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha=\iotaʻ(\alpha\upharpoonleft \breve{\iota})=\iotaʻ(\breve{\iota}\upharpoonright \iotaʻʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/6102.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 38.025ex; height: 2.434ex;" id="img_images_6102.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*83·12}. &amp;\supset\vdash.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha=(\in \upharpoonright \iotaʻʻ\alpha)_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha\\ [\text{*62·56}]  &amp;\qquad\qquad\quad=(\breve{\iota}\upharpoonright \iotaʻʻ\alpha)_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*72·181.*71·26}.&amp;\supset\vdash.\breve{\iota}\upharpoonright \iotaʻʻ\alpha\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls} &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*37·15.*33·21}. &amp;\supset\vdash.\iotaʻʻ\alpha\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ\breve{\iota}.\\ [\text{*35·65}] &amp;\supset\vdash.\iotaʻʻ\alpha=\text{ᗡ}ʻ(\breve{\iota}\upharpoonright ʻʻ\alpha) &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(3).*82·21}.&amp;\supset\vdash.(\breve{\iota}\upharpoonright \iotaʻʻ\alpha)_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha=\iotaʻ\{(\breve{\iota}\upharpoonright     \iotaʻʻ\alpha)\upharpoonright \iotaʻʻ\alpha\}\\ [\text{*35·31}] &amp;\qquad\qquad\qquad =\iotaʻ(\breve{\iota}\upharpoonright \iotaʻʻ\alpha) &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ [\text{*62·56}] &amp;\qquad\qquad\qquad =\iotaʻ(\alpha\upharpoonleft \breve{\iota}) &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(4).(5)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6103.svg" style="vertical-align: -13.837ex; width: 80.276ex; height: 28.805ex;" id="img_images_6103.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition shows that a cardinal product whose factors
are all 1 is 1. For <img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5487.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.964ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5487.svg_1"> is a class whose members
are all unit classes, and thus the number of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6104.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6104.svg"> is the product of a number of 1's; and
by the above proposition, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\iotaʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6104.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6104.svg_1"> is a unit
class, its sole member being <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft \breve{\iota}\)" src="images/6105.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 4.449ex; height: 2.308ex;" id="img_images_6105.svg">.
This result is rendered more explicit by *83·43·44.</p>

<p>This proposition shows that in a product any number of factors each
equal to 1 may be omitted without altering the value of the product.</p>

<p>The following propositions, down to <a href="#_83_74" class="pginternal">*83·74</a>, are concerned with the
domains of selective relations, <i>i.e.</i> with the selected classes.</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*80·14.*83·21.*35·83}.&amp;\supset\vdash:R\in\in_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.R\unicode{x2abd}sʻ\kappa\uparrow \kappa.\\ [\text{*63·105.(*63·03)}] &amp;\supset.R\unicode{x2abd}t_{1}ʻ\kappa\uparrow t_{0}ʻ\kappa.\\ [\text{*64·201}]  &amp;\supset.R\in tʻ(t_{1}ʻ\kappa\uparrow t_{0}ʻ\kappa).\\ [\text{(*64·021)}] &amp;\supset.R\in t_{10}ʻ\kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*63·371}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6150.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.9ex; width: 64.7ex; height: 14.932ex;" id="img_images_6150.svg"></span></p>

<img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\in_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6158.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.834ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6158.svg"> whenever <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_109"> is a finite
class of classes none of which is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_48">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_540">[Pg 540]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_84">*84. CLASSES OF MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE CLASSES.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *84.</p>

<p>A class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_110"> of mutually exclusive classes is one such that,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_294"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_154"> are two different members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_111">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_295"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_155"> have no common members; <i>i.e.</i> it is
a class composed of non-overlapping classes. Classes of mutually
exclusive classes have many important properties. They are important
in cardinal arithmetic, among other reasons, because if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_112">
is a class of mutually exclusive classes, the cardinal number of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_13"> is the sum of the cardinal numbers of the members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_113">. Also if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_114"> is a class of mutually exclusive
classes, the number of selected classes of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_115"> (<i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5753.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.134ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5753.svg_5">) is the same as the number of
selective relations (<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_10">)</p>

<p>"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_116"> is a class of mutually exclusive classes" is written
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \in \text{Cls}^2 ~ \text{excl}\)" src="images/6159.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.609ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_6159.svg">."</p>

<p>An important case is when no member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_117"> is null; in this case
we write
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa \in \text{Cls} ~ \text{ex}^2 ~ \text{excl}\text{.} \]" src="images/6160.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 16.003ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_6160.svg"></span></p>

<p>For a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^2 ~ \text{excl}\)" src="images/6161.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.54ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_6161.svg"> which is contained in a class of
classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_11">, we write
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cl} ~ \text{excl}ʻ\gamma\text{,} \]" src="images/6162.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 9.876ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_6162.svg"></span>
on the analogy of the notation <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/6163.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 4.848ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_6163.svg">.</p>

<p>The definitions are as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^2 ~ \text{excl} = \hat{\kappa}(\alpha, \beta \in \kappa . \alpha \neq \beta .\supset_{\alpha, \beta}.     \alpha \cap \beta = \Lambda) \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/6164.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 50.023ex; height: 2.693ex;" id="img_images_6164.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl} ~ \text{excl}ʻ\gamma  = \text{Cls}^2 ~ \text{excl} \cap \text{Cl}ʻ\gamma \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/6165.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 32.85ex; height: 2.532ex;" id="img_images_6165.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls} ~ \text{ex}^2 ~ \text{excl} = \text{Cls}^2 ~ \text{excl} - \overleftarrow{{\in}}ʻ\Lambda \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/6166.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.5ex; height: 3.319ex;" id="img_images_6166.svg"></p>

<p>The propositions of this number begin (<a href="#_84_1" class="pginternal">*84·1</a>—<a href="#_84_14" class="pginternal">·14</a>) with various
equivalent forms for the definitions. Of these the most useful are:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp  \kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} ~ \text{excl} .\equiv: \alpha, \beta \in \kappa . \exists! \alpha \cap \beta .\supset_{\alpha,\beta}.\alpha     = \beta\)" src="images/6167.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 48.046ex; height: 2.693ex;" id="img_images_6167.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·13.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \kappa \in \text{Cls} ~ \text{ex}^2 ~ \text{excl} .\equiv. \kappa \in \text{Cls}^2 ~ \text{excl} . \Lambda \mathrel{{\sim}{\in}} \kappa\)" src="images/6168.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 42.8ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_6168.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_84_14">*84·14</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash : \kappa \in \text{Cls}^2 ~ \text{excl} .\equiv. {\in} \upharpoonright \kappa \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/6169.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 34.604ex; height: 2.482ex;" id="img_images_6169.svg"></p>

<p>The last of these is specially important, because it renders the
propositions of <a href="#_81" class="pginternal">*81</a> applicable to <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_11"> when
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_541">[Pg 541]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \in \text{Cls}^2 ~ \text{excl}\)" src="images/6159.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.609ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_6159.svg_1">.</p>

<p>We have next (<a href="#_84_2" class="pginternal">*84·2</a>—<a href="#_84_28" class="pginternal">·28</a>) a set of propositions dealing with various
special cases, such as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\Lambda\)" src="images/34.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.57ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_34.svg_49"> and 1. The most useful of these are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·23.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\iotaʻ\alpha\in \text{Cls}^2\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/6170.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.113ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_6170.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·241.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash.\iotaʻʻ\alpha\in \text{Cls}^2\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/6171.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.47ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_6171.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·25.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\in \text{Cls}^2\, \text{excl}.\lambda\subset \kappa.\supset.\lambda\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/6172.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 37.915ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_6172.svg"></p>

<p>We next have a set of propositions (<a href="#_84_3" class="pginternal">*84·3</a>—<a href="#_84_37" class="pginternal">·37</a>) which are immediate
consequences of propositions in <a href="#_81" class="pginternal">*81</a>, by means of <a href="#_84_14" class="pginternal">*84·14</a>. The most
useful of these is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·3.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}.\supset.\in _{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\subset 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/6173.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 33.951ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_6173.svg"></p>

<p>We next have a set of propositions (<a href="#_84_4" class="pginternal">*84·4</a>—<a href="#_84_43" class="pginternal">·43</a>) dealing with the
domains of selections from a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/5784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_5784.svg_2">. These are
for the most part still immediate consequences of propositions in *81,
in virtue of *84·14. The most useful are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}.\supset.\text{D}\upharpoonright \in _{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻʻ\in _{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\text{     sm }\in _{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6174.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 59.873ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_6174.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_84_412">*84·412</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}.\supset.\text{D}ʻʻ\in_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=\hat{\mu}\{\alpha\in \kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\mu     \cap \alpha\in 1:\mu \subset sʻ\kappa\}\)" src="images/6175.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 66.581ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_6175.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_84_43">*84·43</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha,\,\beta\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}.sʻ\alpha=sʻ\beta.\supset:\alpha\subset \text{D}ʻʻ\in _{\Delta}ʻ\beta.\equiv.\beta\subset     \text{D}ʻʻ\in _{\Delta}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6176.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 69.675ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_6176.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition applies to such cases as the relations of rows and
columns. Imagine any set of terms arranged in rows and columns so as to
form a rectangle. Then each column is a selection from the rows, and
each row is a selection from the columns. This is a particular case of
the above proposition.</p>

<p>We next have a set of propositions on <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6177.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.735ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6177.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Rʻʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.093ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3101.svg_4">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6178.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.991ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6178.svg"> (<a href="#_84_5" class="pginternal">*84·5</a>—<a href="#_84_55" class="pginternal">·55</a>). The most
important of these are</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\upharpoonright \kappa\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\supset.\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/6179.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 39.308ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6179.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·53.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}.\supset.Rʻʻʻ\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/6180.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 49.96ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_6180.svg"></p>

<p>Finally we have a set of propositions (<a href="#_84_59" class="pginternal">*84·59</a>—<a href="#_84_62" class="pginternal">·62</a>) showing
circumstances under which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\cup \lambda\)" src="images/6181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 5.137ex; height: 1.62ex;" id="img_images_6181.svg"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}\)" src="images/6182.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_6182.svg">.
The only one of these which is used subsequently is</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·62.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha \neq \beta.\supset:\iotaʻ\alpha\cup \iotaʻ\beta\in \text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}.\equiv.\alpha\cap \beta=\Lambda\)" src="images/6183.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 47.444ex; height: 2.529ex;" id="img_images_6183.svg"></p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*84·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^2\, \text{excl}=\hat{\kappa}(\alpha,\beta\in \kappa.\alpha \neq \beta.\supset_{\alpha,\beta}.\alpha\cap \beta=\Lambda) \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/6184.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 49.835ex; height: 2.693ex;" id="img_images_6184.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cl excl}ʻ\gamma=\text{Cls}^2\, \text{excl}\cap \text{Cl}ʻ\gamma \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/6185.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 32.662ex; height: 2.532ex;" id="img_images_6185.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^2\, \text{excl}=\text{Cls}^2\, \text{excl}-\overleftarrow{\in}ʻ\Lambda \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/6186.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 32.611ex; height: 3.319ex;" id="img_images_6186.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_84_1">*84·1</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp \kappa\in \text{Cls}^2\, \text{excl}.\equiv:\alpha,\beta\in \kappa.\alpha \neq \beta.\supset_{\alpha,\beta}.\alpha\cap     \beta=\Lambda\\ &amp;[\text{*20·3.(*84·01)}]\end{align}\]" src="images/6187.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.251ex; width: 51.187ex; height: 5.634ex;" id="img_images_6187.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_542">[Pg 542]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·11.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp \kappa\in \text{Cls}^2\,\text{excl}.\equiv:\alpha,\,\beta\in     \kappa.\exists !\alpha\cap \beta.\supset_{\alpha,\beta}.\alpha=\beta\\ &amp;[\text{*84·1.Transp}]\end{align}\]" src="images/6188.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.251ex; width: 48.865ex; height: 5.634ex;" id="img_images_6188.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·12.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash\colon\ldotp \kappa\in \text{Cl excl}ʻ\gamma.&amp;\equiv:\alpha,\beta\in \kappa.\alpha \neq \beta.\supset_{\alpha,\beta}.\alpha\cap     \beta=\Lambda:\kappa\subset \gamma:\equiv:\\ &amp;\kappa\in \text{Cls}^2\,\text{excl}.\kappa\subset \gamma [\text{*20·3.(*84·02).*22·33.*84·1}]\end{align}\]" src="images/6189.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.251ex; width: 64.098ex; height: 5.634ex;" id="img_images_6189.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·121.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash\colon\ldotp \kappa\in \text{Cl excl}ʻ\gamma.\equiv:\alpha,\beta\in \kappa.\exists !\alpha\cap \beta.\supset_{\alpha,\beta}.\alpha=\beta:\kappa\subset     \gamma\\ &amp;[\text{*20·3.(*84·02).*22·33.*84·11}]\end{align}\]" src="images/6190.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.078ex; width: 56.816ex; height: 5.288ex;" id="img_images_6190.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following propositions are concerned with selections from
a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/5784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_5784.svg_3">. In virtue of <a href="#_84_14" class="pginternal">*84·14</a>, the
propositions of <a href="#_81" class="pginternal">*81</a> which have the hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\upharpoonright\kappa\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/6223.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 15.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_6223.svg">
become applicable when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_263"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}\)" src="images/4603.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 1.509ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_4603.svg_9"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_118"> is a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\, \text{excl}\)" src="images/5784.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_5784.svg_4">. Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_13"> has
many important properties when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_119"> is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}\)" src="images/6182.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_6182.svg_1">
which it does not have in the general case.</p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*84·13}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\Lambda{\sim}\in \kappa.\\ [\text{*62·42}] &amp;\supset.\text{ᗡ}ʻ\in \upharpoonright \kappa=\kappa  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*71·103.*80·14}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset:R\in 1\rightarrow 1.R\unicode{x2abd}\in \upharpoonright \kappa.\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\text{ᗡ}ʻ\in \upharpoonright \kappa.\supset.R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa     &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*80·14}.&amp;\supset\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset:R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\text{ᗡ}ʻ\in \upharpoonright \kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(3).*80·291.*84·3}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset:R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.R\in     1\rightarrow 1.R\unicode{x2abd}\in \upharpoonright \kappa.\text{ᗡ}ʻR=\text{ᗡ}ʻ\in \upharpoonright \kappa &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(4)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6232.svg" style="vertical-align: -11.652ex; width: 87.073ex; height: 24.434ex;" id="img_images_6232.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_84_37">*84·37</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}.\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset.\kappa\in \text{Cls ex}^{2}\,\text{excl}      \quad[\text{*83·1.*84·13}]\)" src="images/6233.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 58.19ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_6233.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_84_4">*84·4</a>.</b>  <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}.R,\,S\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa.\supset:\text{D}ʻR=\text{D}ʻS.\equiv.R=S  \quad[\text{*81·2.*84·14}]\)" src="images/6234.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.781ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_6234.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·41.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}.\supset.\text{D}\upharpoonright {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{D}ʻʻ\in _{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\text{     sm }{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa \quad[\text{*81·21.*84·14}]\)" src="images/6235.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 75.336ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_6235.svg"></p>

<p>This is an important proposition, since it shows that, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_120">
is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}\)" src="images/6182.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_6182.svg_2">, the number of classes that can be
selected from <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_121"> is the product of the numbers of the various
classes that are members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_122">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·411.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \alpha\in \kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\mu\cap \alpha\in 1:\mu\subset sʻ\kappa:\supset.\mu\in \text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa      \quad[\text{*81·212.*62·2·3}]\)" src="images/6236.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 69.875ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6236.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*84·412.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash:\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}.\supset.\text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=\hat{\mu}\{\alpha\in \kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\mu\cap     \alpha\in 1:\mu\subset sʻ\kappa\}\\ &amp;[\text{*81·22.*84·14.*62·2·3}]\end{align}\]" src="images/6237.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.209ex; width: 65.953ex; height: 5.55ex;" id="img_images_6237.svg"></span></p>

<p>This proposition gives what might be taken as the definition of the
class of selected classes, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{\mu}\{\alpha\in \kappa.\supset_{\alpha}.\mu\cap \alpha\in 1:\mu\subset sʻ\kappa\}. \]" src="images/6238.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.97ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_6238.svg"></span></p>

<p>We might, starting with this as our definition, deal with the class
of selected classes without first considering selective relations.
The disadvantages of this method would be, first, that it requires
that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_123"> should be a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}\)" src="images/6182.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.352ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_6182.svg_3"> if it is
to give the results desired in arithmetic; secondly, that it is much
more cumbrous technically than the method which proceeds by selective
relations; thirdly, that it does not enable us to deal with selection
from a class of classes as a particular case of selection from a
relation (namely from <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in} \upharpoonright \kappa)\)" src="images/6239.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.893ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6239.svg">, and therefore
does not yield theorems of such generality as those obtained by the
method adopted above.</p>

<p>It might be supposed that the converse of the above
would also hold. But this is not the case; for although
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\in\text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}\)" src="images/6247.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.982ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6247.svg">
secures that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻx\)" src="images/3115.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.369ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_3115.svg_2"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_343.svg_12">
cannot overlap when they are unequal, yet we may have
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻx=\overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/6248.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.569ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_6248.svg"> without having
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x = y\)" src="images/418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.42ex; height: 1.783ex;" id="img_images_418.svg_4">, so that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻx = \alpha= \overrightarrow{R}ʻy\)" src="images/6249.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 16.034ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_6249.svg">,
we shall have <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\in \alpha.\supset.zRx.zRy\)" src="images/6250.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 17.985ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6250.svg">,
whence, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\exists !\alpha.x \neq y\)" src="images/6251.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 9.761ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_6251.svg">, it follows that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_264"> is not a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}\,\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/6252.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.182ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_6252.svg"> even if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\in \text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}\)" src="images/6253.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.982ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6253.svg">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_549">[Pg 549]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_85">*85. MISCELLANEOUS PROPOSITIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *85.</p>

<p>In this number certain important propositions are proved, and the other
propositions of this number are mainly lemmas. The most important
propositions are the following:</p>

<p><a href="#_85_1" class="pginternal">*85·1</a> and <a href="#_85_14" class="pginternal">*85·14</a>, which show that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q \upharpoonright\lambda\)" src="images/6271.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_6271.svg">
is a <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/4961.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 7.804ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_4961.svg_4">, then the
domains of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/5810.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.986ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5810.svg_2"> are the same as the
domains of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\overrightarrow{Q}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/6007.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.21ex; height: 3.69ex;" id="img_images_6007.svg_1">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/5810.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.986ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5810.svg_3"> is similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\overrightarrow{Q}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/6007.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.21ex; height: 3.69ex;" id="img_images_6007.svg_2">, thus reducing the
problem of selections from many-one relations to that of selections
from classes of classes.</p>

<p><a href="#_85_27" class="pginternal">*85·27</a> and <a href="#_85_43" class="pginternal">*85·43</a>, which show that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} ~ \text{excl}\)" src="images/6272.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.609ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_6272.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.052ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6273.svg"> consists of the relational sums
of the domains of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻP_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.378ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6274.svg"> and is similar
to <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻP_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.378ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6274.svg_1">; <i>i.e.</i> the class of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_48">-selections from <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_14"> is similar to the class obtained
as follows: take the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_124"> one by one, and form the
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_49">-selections of each; we thus obtain a class of classes, each class
being of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5820.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.778ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5820.svg_1">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \in \kappa\)" src="images/6275.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 5.517ex; height: 1.312ex;" id="img_images_6275.svg">;
we then make a selection from this class of classes; this selection is
a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻP_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6274.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.378ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6274.svg_2">; the number of such
selections is the same as the number of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6273.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.052ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6273.svg_1">.</p>

<p><a href="#_85_28" class="pginternal">*85·28</a> and <a href="#_85_44" class="pginternal">*85·44</a>, which are special cases of *85·27 and *85·43,
but more useful than these. *85·44 is the source of the associative
law in cardinal multiplication; it states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_125"> is a
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2} ~ \text{excl}\)" src="images/6276.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 8.54ex; height: 2.09ex;" id="img_images_6276.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6277.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6277.svg"> has the
same number of members as <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6278.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.434ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6278.svg">.
(On associative laws in general, see the notes to *42·1·11.)
That is to say, if we form the class of selective relations
(<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha)\)" src="images/6279.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.715ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6279.svg"> for every <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_297"> which is a member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_126">, and then form the class of selective relations
for <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6280.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.048ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6280.svg">, we get the same number of terms
as if we proceeded to form the class of selective relations for
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6277.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6277.svg_1">. The way in which this proposition yields
the associative law of multiplication may be explained as follows.
We shall define the product of the numbers of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_298">
as the number of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6281.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.835ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6281.svg">. Thus <i>e.g.</i> if the
numbers of the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_299"> are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu_{\alpha 1}, \mu_{\alpha 2}, \mu_{\alpha 3}\)" src="images/6282.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 12.139ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_6282.svg">,
the number of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6281.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.835ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6281.svg_1"> is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu_{\alpha 1} × \mu_{\alpha 2} × \mu_{\alpha 3}\)" src="images/6283.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 13.648ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_6283.svg">. Suppose the
other members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_127"> are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_156"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_12">, and that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_157"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_13"> again have three members each. Then the
number of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6278.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.434ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6278.svg_1"> is the product of
the numbers of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6281.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.835ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6281.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\beta\)" src="images/6284.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.667ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6284.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\gamma\)" src="images/6285.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 5.615ex; height: 2.186ex;" id="img_images_6285.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> it is the product of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu_{\alpha 1} \times \mu_{\alpha 2} \times \mu_{\alpha 3}\)" src="images/6286.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 15.659ex; height: 1.6ex;" id="img_images_6286.svg">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu_{\beta 1} \times \mu_{\beta 2} \times \mu_{\beta 3}\)" src="images/6287.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 15.304ex; height: 1.761ex;" id="img_images_6287.svg"> and
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_550">[Pg 550]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu_{\gamma 1} \times \mu_{\gamma 2} \times \mu_{\gamma 3}\)" src="images/6288.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 15.193ex; height: 1.796ex;" id="img_images_6288.svg">.</p>

<p>But the numbers of the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3424.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.722ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3424.svg_15"> are
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu_{\alpha 1}, \mu_{\alpha 2}, \mu_{\alpha 3}, \mu_{\beta 1}, \mu_{\beta 2}, \mu_{\beta 3}, \mu_{\gamma 1}, \mu_{\gamma 2},     \mu_{\gamma 3}. \]" src="images/6289.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 38.239ex; height: 1.685ex;" id="img_images_6289.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus the number of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻsʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6277.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.109ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6277.svg_2"> is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \mu_{\alpha 1}×\mu_{\alpha 2}×\mu_{\alpha 3}×\mu_{\beta 1}×\mu_{\beta 2}×\mu_{\beta 3}×\mu_{\gamma 1}×\mu_{\gamma 2}×\mu_{\gamma 3}. \]" src="images/6290.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 44.272ex; height: 1.796ex;" id="img_images_6290.svg"></span></p>

<p>Hence <a href="#_85_44" class="pginternal">*85·44</a> enables us to conclude that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} (\mu_{\alpha 1}×\mu_{\alpha 2}×\mu_{\alpha 3})×(\mu_{\beta 1}×\mu_{\beta 2}×\mu_{\beta 3})×(\mu_{\gamma 1}×\mu_{\gamma 2}×\mu_{\gamma 3}) \\ =\mu_{\alpha 1}×\mu_{\alpha 2}×\mu_{\alpha 3}×\mu_{\beta 1}×\mu_{\beta 2}×\mu_{\beta 3}×\mu_{\gamma 1}×\mu_{\gamma 2}×\mu_{\gamma 3},\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/6291.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.156ex; width: 48.923ex; height: 5.442ex;" id="img_images_6291.svg"></span>
which is a case of the associative law. In fact *85·44 gives us this
law in its general form, when the number of brackets, and of factors in
each bracket, may be infinite or finite indifferently.</p>

<p>Another important pair of propositions is *85·53·54. These enable us to
reduce the problem of selections for <i>any</i> relation to the problem
of selections from a class of classes. The method is as follows: Given
any term <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_542">, form the class of ordered couples of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_543"> is
relatum while the referent is a term having the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_50"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_544">. Call this class of couples <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x21a7} x\)" src="images/6292.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.351ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6292.svg">. Form this
class for every <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_545"> which is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_300">; we thus obtain a
class of classes, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \unicode{x21a7}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.219ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6293.svg">. Then the number
of selections from this class of classes is the same as the number of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5820.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.778ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5820.svg_2">.</p>

<p>We have one other important pair of propositions in this number,
namely *85·61·63. These show that what is called "Zermelo's axiom" is
equivalent to what is called the "multiplicative axiom." Zermelo's
axiom<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_63" id="FNanchor_63">[63]</a> is to the effect that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_301"> is any class,
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Cl ex}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6294.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.22ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6294.svg"> is never null, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\((\alpha).\exists! {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Cl ex}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6295.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.321ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6295.svg">. The
"multiplicative axiom" is to the effect that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa \in \text{Cls ex}^{2} ~ \text{excl}\)" src="images/6296.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 15.374ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_6296.svg">,
there is at least one class formed by taking one representative
from each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_128">, which is equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa \in \text{Cls ex}^{2} ~ \text{excl} .\supset_{\kappa}.\exists! {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa. \]" src="images/6297.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.461ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_6297.svg"></span></p>

<p>In <a href="#_85_63" class="pginternal">*85·63</a>, these two axioms are shown to be equivalent. From Zermelo's
theorem<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_64" id="FNanchor_64">[64]</a> it follows that both are equivalent to the assumption that
every class can be well-ordered. This will be proved later (*258).</p>

<p>The above-mentioned propositions, stated symbolically, are as follows:</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_85_1">*85·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: Q \upharpoonright \lambda \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1 .\supset. \text{D}ʻʻQ_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda = \text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\overrightarrow{Q}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/6298.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 50.392ex; height: 3.69ex;" id="img_images_6298.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_85_14">*85·14</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: Q \upharpoonright \lambda \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1 .\supset. Q_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda \mathop{\text{ sm }} {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\overrightarrow{Q}ʻʻ\lambda\)" src="images/6299.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 43.15ex; height: 3.69ex;" id="img_images_6299.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*85·27.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: \kappa \in \text{Cls}^{2} ~ \text{excl} .\supset. which latter are of fundamental importance, since they are the source
of the associative law in cardinal arithmetic.</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*85·44}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon \iotaʻ\kappa\cup\iotaʻ\lambda\in\text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl}.&amp;\supset.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻsʻ(\iotaʻ\kappa\cup\iotaʻ\lambda)\,\text{ sm }\,{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻʻ(\iotaʻ\kappa\cup\iotaʻ\lambda)     &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*24·57}.   \supset\vdash\colon\ldotp\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset:\kappa\neq\lambda.\lor.\kappa=\Lambda.\lambda=\Lambda:\\ [\text{*84·62·23}] &amp;\supset:\iotaʻ\kappa\cup\iotaʻ\lambda\in\text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{excl} &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*53·11·32}.&amp;\supset\vdash.sʻ(\iotaʻ\kappa\cup\iotaʻ\lambda)=\kappa\cup\lambda.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻʻ(\iotaʻ\kappa\cup\iotaʻ\lambda)=(\iotaʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\cup\iotaʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(2).(3)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6367.svg" style="vertical-align: -8.83ex; width: 101.553ex; height: 18.792ex;" id="img_images_6367.svg"></span></p>

<p>The purpose of the following propositions, down to <a href="#_85_55" class="pginternal">*85·55</a>, is to
show how to get from a class of classes a class of selections
having the same number of terms as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5763.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.634ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5763.svg_24">. For this
purpose we introduce a new notation, representing a rather important
analysis of the couples contained in a given relation. A couple
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\downarrow y\)" src="images/4199.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.791ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_4199.svg_5"> is contained in a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_53"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/6368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6368.svg">; thus
if, keeping <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_255"> fixed, we form the class of couples <img alt="" data-tex="\(\downarrow yʻʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻy\)" src="images/6369.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.748ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_6369.svg">,
all these couples are contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_54">. We put</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*85·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x21A7}y=\downarrow yʻʻ\overrightarrow{P}ʻy \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/6370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 20.985ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_6370.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_557">[Pg 557]</span></p>

<p>Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻP\in\text{Cls ex}^{2}\,\text{excl}\)" src="images/6371.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 24.068ex; height: 2.495ex;" id="img_images_6371.svg">.
Also <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻP\unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/6372.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.604ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6372.svg"> is the
class of all couples contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_55">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻsʻP\unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻP=P\)" src="images/6373.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.739ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_6373.svg">. We shall now prove that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha=\dot{s}ʻʻDʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻP\unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6374.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.766ex; height: 2.188ex;" id="img_images_6374.svg">,
so that every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5820.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.778ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5820.svg_4"> can be derived from a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻP\unicode{x21A7}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6375.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.606ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6375.svg">, and the problem
of the existence of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/5820.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.778ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5820.svg_5"> is reduced to that of the
existence of selections from a class of mutually exclusive existent
classes.</p>

<p><i>Note.</i> (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha).\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ \text{Cl}\,\text{ex}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6393.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.253ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6393.svg">
is "Zermelo's axiom." The above proposition shows that this is
true if
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa \in \text{Cls}\,\text{ex}^{2}\,\text{excl}.\supset _{\kappa }.\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ \kappa, \]" src="images/6394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.085ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_6394.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_559">[Pg 559]</span>
which again is true if
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \kappa \in \text{Cls}\,\text{ex}^{2}\,\text{excl}.\supset:(\exists \mu ):\alpha \in \kappa .\supset_{\alpha}.\mu \cap  \alpha \in 1 \]" src="images/6395.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 45.015ex; height: 2.565ex;" id="img_images_6395.svg"></span>
in virtue of <a href="#_84_412" class="pginternal">*84·412</a>. The last of these is the "multiplicative axiom,"
which is thus shown to imply "Zermelo's axiom."</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*85·701.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \beta \in \lambda .\supset _{\beta }.Rʻ \beta \subset \beta :\supset .\text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ     Rʻʻ \lambda \subset \text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ \lambda \quad[\text{*85·7}]\)" src="images/6398.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 62.724ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_6398.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*85·702.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}&amp;\vdash \colon\ldotp \beta \in \lambda .\supset _{\beta }.Rʻ\text{Cl}ʻ \beta \in\text{Cl}ʻ\beta :\supset .\text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ     Rʻʻ\text{Cl}ʻʻ \lambda \subset \text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ \lambda\\ &amp;\quad\left[\text{*85·701}\frac{R\mid \text{Cl}}{R}\right]\end{align}\]" src="images/6399.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.672ex; width: 66.644ex; height: 8.474ex;" id="img_images_6399.svg"></span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*85·71.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :R\in {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Cl}ʻʻ\lambda .\supset .\text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{D}ʻ R\subset \text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ     \lambda \quad[\text{*85·702.*83·2}]\)" src="images/6400.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 65.098ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6400.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition asserts that if we can select one sub-class out of
each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_25"> (where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_26"> is a class of classes),
then selections from the sub-classes so obtained are selections from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\lambda\)" src="images/2884.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.027ex; width: 1.319ex; height: 1.597ex;" id="img_images_2884.svg_27">.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_85_72">*85·72</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash \colon\ldotp (Sʻʻ \beta )\upharpoonleft S\in 1\rightarrow 1:\beta \in \lambda .\supset _{\beta }.Rʻ \beta &amp;\subset Sʻ \beta :\supset.\\ &amp;\text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ Rʻʻ \lambda \subset \text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ Sʻʻ \lambda\end{align}\]" src="images/6401.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.078ex; width: 71.211ex; height: 5.288ex;" id="img_images_6401.svg"></span></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash .\text{*14·21.*33·43}.&amp;\supset \vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Hp}.\supset :\beta \in \lambda .\supset .\beta \in \text{ᗡ}ʻ S  &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash .\text{*85·701}\, \frac{R\mid\breve{S},Sʻʻ \lambda}{R,\lambda} .\supset\\ \vdash \colon\ldotp \gamma \in Sʻʻ \lambda .&amp;\supset _{\gamma }.(R\mid \breve{S})ʻ \gamma \subset \gamma :\supset .\text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ     Rʻʻ \breve{S}ʻʻ Sʻʻ \lambda \subset \text{D}ʻʻ {\in}_{\Delta}ʻ Sʻʻ\lambda  &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash .\text{*37·63.*14·21}.\supset\\ \vdash\colon\colon \text{Hp}.\supset \colon\ldotp \gamma \in Sʻʻ \lambda .\supset _{\gamma }.(R\mid     \breve{S})ʻ \gamma \subset \gamma :&amp;\equiv :\beta \in \lambda .\supset _{\beta }.(R\mid\breve{S})ʻ Sʻ \beta \subset Sʻ \beta :\\ [\text{*74·53.(1)}] &amp;\equiv :\beta \in \lambda .\supset _{\beta }.Rʻ \beta \subset Sʻ \beta  &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash .\text{*74·171}.\supset \vdash: \text{Hp}.&amp;\supset .\breve{S}ʻʻ Sʻʻ \lambda =\lambda    &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash .\text{(2).(3).(4)}.\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6402.svg" style="vertical-align: -13.833ex; width: 114.068ex; height: 28.796ex;" id="img_images_6402.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_560">[Pg 560]</span></p>

<p>The following proposition is a lemma employed in the theory of double
similarity (*111·313).</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*85·81.</b>
    <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash\colon\ldotp \lambda\in \text{Cls}^{2}\text{excl}:\beta\in\lambda.\supset_{\beta}.sʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻTʻ&amp;\beta\subset\beta:R\in{\in}_{\Delta}ʻTʻʻ\lambda:\supset:\\ &amp;\beta\in\lambda.\supset_{\beta}.(\breve{s}ʻ\text{D}ʻR)\upharpoonright \beta=RʻTʻ\beta\end{align}\]" src="images/6403.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.379ex; width: 70.028ex; height: 5.89ex;" id="img_images_6403.svg"></span></p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_561">[Pg 561]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_88">*88. CONDITIONS FOR THE EXISTENCE OF SELECTIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *88.</p>


<p>The existence of selections cannot, so far as is known at present, be
proved in general. That is, we cannot prove any of the following:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} &amp;(P,\kappa):\kappa\subset\text{ᗡ}ʻP.\supset.\exists!P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\\ &amp;(P,\kappa):P\in\text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\kappa\subset\text{ᗡ}ʻP.\supset.\exists!P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\\ &amp;(P).\exists!P_{\Delta}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻ\\ &amp;(\kappa):\Lambda{\sim}\in\kappa.\supset.\exists!{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\\ &amp;(\kappa):\kappa\in \text{Cls ex}^{2}\text{excl}.\supset.\exists!{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\\ &amp;(\alpha).\exists!{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\text{Cl ex}ʻ\alpha\\ &amp;(\kappa)\colon\ldotp \kappa\in \text{Cls ex}^{2}\text{excl}.\supset:(\exists \mu):\alpha\in\kappa.\supset_\alpha.\mu\cap\alpha\in 1 \end{align} \]" src="images/6405.svg" style="vertical-align: -9.735ex; width: 49.9ex; height: 20.602ex;" id="img_images_6405.svg"></span></p>

<p>These various propositions can be shown to be all equivalent <i>inter
se</i>; and in virtue of Zermelo's theorem (cf. *258), they are
equivalent to the proposition "every class can be well-ordered." In
the present number we have to prove the above equivalences, as well
as certain propositions giving the existence of selections in various
particular cases.</p>

<p>The most apparently obvious of the above propositions is the last,
namely: "If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_129"> is a class of mutually exclusive classes, no
one of which is null, there is at least one class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_15"> which takes
one and only one member from each member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_130">." This we shall
define as the "multiplicative axiom."</p>

<p>We will call <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_56"> a <i>multipliable</i> relation (denoted by "Rel
Mult") if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P_{\Delta}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/6406.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.744ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6406.svg"> exists, or, what is equivalent, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\subset\text{ᗡ}ʻP.\supset_\kappa.\exists!P_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/6407.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.136ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6407.svg">
Thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Rel Mult}=\breve{P}\{\exists!P_{\Delta}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻP\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6408.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.628ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_6408.svg"></span></p>

<p>We will call <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_131"> a <i>multipliable</i> class of classes if
<img alt="" data-tex="\({\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\)" src="images/5751.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.69ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_5751.svg_14"> exists, <i>i.e.</i> we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Cls}^{2} \text{Mult}=\breve{\kappa}\{\exists!{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6409.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.455ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_6409.svg"></span></p>

<p>The multiplicative axiom will be denoted by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Mult ax}\)" src="images/6410.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 7.733ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_6410.svg">." Thus we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Mult ax}.=\colon\ldotp \kappa\in\text{Cls ex}^{2} \text{excl}.\supset_\kappa:(\exists \mu):\alpha\in \kappa.\supset_\alpha.\mu\cap\alpha\in 1 \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6411.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.758ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_6411.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the present number, we shall first give various equivalent forms
of the assumption that <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_57"> is a multipliable relation (<a href="#_88_1" class="pginternal">*88·1</a>—<a href="#_88_15" class="pginternal">·15</a>);
we shall then do the same for multipliable classes of classes
(<a href="#_88_2" class="pginternal">*88·2</a>—<a href="#_88_26" class="pginternal">·26</a>); next we shall give various equivalent forms of the
multiplicative axiom (<a href="#_88_3" class="pginternal">*88·3</a>—<a href="#_88_39" class="pginternal">·39</a>).<span class="pagenum" id="Page_562">[Pg 562]</span> (Some important equivalent forms
cannot be given at this stage, as they depend upon definitions not
yet given, such as the definitions of cardinal multiplication and
of well-ordered series. Cf. *114·26 and *258·37.) Finally we shall
give propositions showing that various special classes of classes
are multipliable. Most of these propositions will not be used in
the sequel, but they illustrate the nature of the difficulties
involved in proving that a class of classes is multipliable, and
some of them show that mere size does not prevent a class from
being multipliable. For example, <a href="#_88_48" class="pginternal">*88·48</a> shows that, given any class
of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_132">, if each member <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_302"> is replaced by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\iotaʻʻ\alpha\cup\iotaʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.085ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6412.svg">, the result is a multipliable class
of classes; but the only effect of this change is to increase the
number of members of each member of our class of classes by one.</p>

<p>The chief propositions in this number which are afterwards referred to
are the following:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·22.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\kappa\in \text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{Mult}.\lambda \subset \kappa.\supset .\lambda \in \text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{Mult}\)" src="images/6413.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 39.933ex; height: 2.133ex;" id="img_images_6413.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·32.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult}\,\text{ax}.\equiv :\kappa\in \text{Cls}\,\text{ex}^{2}\,\text{excl}.\supset_{\kappa}.\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ \kappa\)" src="images/6414.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 42.42ex; height: 2.339ex;" id="img_images_6414.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·33.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash :\text{Mult}\,\text{ax}.\equiv .(\alpha ).\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ \text{Cl}\,\text{ex}ʻ \alpha\)" src="images/6415.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.09ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6415.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·361.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult}\,\text{ax}.\equiv :\kappa\subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ R.\equiv_{R,\kappa}.\exists !R_{\Delta}ʻ \kappa\)" src="images/6416.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 38.041ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_6416.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·37.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult}\,\text{ax}.\equiv :\Lambda \in \kappa.\supset_{\kappa}.\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ \kappa\)" src="images/6417.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 33.061ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6417.svg"></p>

<p>The above is usually the most convenient form of the multiplicative
axiom.</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·372.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash \colon\ldotp \text{Mult}\,\text{ax}.\equiv:\Lambda \in \kappa.\equiv_{\kappa}.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=\Lambda \)" src="images/6418.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 35.761ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6418.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition is used in *114, to prove that the multiplicative
axiom is equivalent to the proposition that a cardinal product vanishes
when, and only when, one of its factors vanishes.</p>

<hr class="tb">

<p class="nind"><b>*88·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Rel}\,\text{Mult}=\hat{P}\{\exists!P_{\Delta}ʻ \text{ᗡ}ʻ P\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/6419.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.811ex; height: 2.943ex;" id="img_images_6419.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·02.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls}^{2}\,\text{Mult}=\hat{\kappa} \{\exists!{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ \kappa\} \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/6420.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 28.204ex; height: 2.609ex;" id="img_images_6420.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·03.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Mult ax}.=\colon\ldotp \kappa\in \text{Cls}\,\text{ex}^{2}\,\text{excl}.\supset_{\kappa}:(\exists \mu ):\alpha \in \kappa.\supset_{\alpha }.\mu     \cap \alpha \in 1 \quad\text{Df}\)" src="images/6421.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 63.319ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_6421.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_88_1">*88·1</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\in \text{Rel}\,\text{Mult}.\equiv .\exists !P_{\Delta}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻP \quad[\text{*20·3.(*88·01)}]\)" src="images/6422.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 47.375ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6422.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·11.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash:P\in \text{Rel}\,\text{Mult}.\lambda \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ P.\supset .\exists !P_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda\)" src="images/6423.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 36.688ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6423.svg"></p>

<p><i>Dem.</i></p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*80·6}. &amp;\supset\vdash:R\in P_{\Delta}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻP.\lambda \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ P.\supset .R\upharpoonright\lambda \in P_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda .\\ [\text{*10·24}] &amp;\supset.\exists!P_{\Delta}ʻ\lambda:\\ [\text{*10·11·23·35}]&amp;\supset \vdash :\exists !P_{\Delta}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻP.\lambda \subset \text{ᗡ}ʻ P.\supset .\exists !P_{\Delta}ʻ \lambda  \qquad\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).*88·1}.&amp;\supset \vdash .\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6424.svg" style="vertical-align: -5.317ex; width: 63.625ex; height: 11.765ex;" id="img_images_6424.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_563">[Pg 563]</span></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·371.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\equiv:\Lambda{\sim}\in \kappa.\equiv_{\kappa}.\exists !{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa \quad[\text{*88·37.*83·1}]\)" src="images/6457.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 50.597ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6457.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*88·372.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp \text{Mult ax}.\equiv:\Lambda\in \kappa.\equiv_{\kappa}.{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\kappa=\Lambda \quad[\text{*88·371.Transp}]\)" src="images/6458.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 54.574ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6458.svg"></p>

<p>This proposition shows that the multiplicative axiom is equivalent to
the assumption that a cardinal product is zero when, and only when, one
of its factors is zero.</p>
