<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_569">[Pg 569]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="SECTION_E_b">SECTION E.<br>
<br>
INDUCTIVE RELATIONS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of Section E.</i></p>

<p>The subjects to be treated in this section are certain general
ideas of which a particular instance is afforded by mathematical
induction. Mathematical induction is, in fact, the application to the
number-series of a conception which is applicable to all relations,
and is often very important. The conception in question is that
which we shall call the <i>ancestral relation</i> with respect to
a given relation. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_265"> is the given relation, we denote the
corresponding ancestral relation by "<img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6488.svg">"; the
name is chosen because, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_266"> is the relation of parent and
child, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6488.svg_1"> will be the relation of ancestor and
descendant—where, for convenience of language, we include <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_546"> among
his own ancestors if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_547"> is a parent or a child of anything.</p>

<p>It would commonly be said that <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_122"> has to <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_40"> the relation of
ancestor to descendant if there are a certain number of intermediate
people <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_38">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_20">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(d\)" src="images/838.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.176ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_838.svg_1">, ... such that in the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_123">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_39">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(c\)" src="images/319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.98ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_319.svg_21">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(d\)" src="images/838.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.176ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_838.svg_2">, ... <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_41"> each term has to the next the relation of
parent and child. But this is not an adequate definition, because the
dots in
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}a, b, c, d, \ldots z \unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/6489.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 14.691ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6489.svg"></span>
represent an unanalysed idea. We may then try to amend this definition
by saying that there is a finite class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_303"> of intermediate terms
such that one member (<img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_40">) of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_304"> is a child of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_124">, one
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_256">) is a parent of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_42">, every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_305"> except <img alt="" data-tex="\(b\)" src="images/181.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 0.971ex; height: 1.595ex;" id="img_images_181.svg_41">
is a child of one (and only one) member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_306">, and every member
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_307"> except <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_257"> is a parent of one (and only one) member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_308">. This definition is open to several objections. In the first
place, it is very complicated; in the second place, there will, in
regard to a general relation, be difficulty in securing the uniqueness
of the member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_309"> which is to be a parent (or a child) of a
given member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_310">; in the third place (and this is the really
fatal objection) the proposed definition states that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_311"> is
to be a <i>finite</i> class, and we shall find that finitude, in the
relevant sense, is only defined by means of the very conception of the
ancestral relation which we are here engaged in defining. In fact, if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(N\)" src="images/537.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.009ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_537.svg_9"> denotes the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/5744.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_5744.svg_1"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu + 1\)" src="images/6490.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.096ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_6490.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/5744.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_5744.svg_2"> is
a cardinal number, then a finite cardinal (in the sense we require) is
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_570">[Pg 570]</span>one to which 0 has the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(N_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6491.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.804ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6491.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>
one of which 0 is an ancestor with respect to the relation
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{\nu}\hat{\mu}\,(\mu=\nu+1). \]" src="images/6492.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.808ex; height: 2.398ex;" id="img_images_6492.svg"></span>
Hence we must not use the notion of finitude in defining the ancestral
relation. In fact, the ancestral relation is defined as follows.</p>

<p>Let us call <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_16"> a <i>hereditary class with respect</i> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_267"> if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻ\mu\subset\mu\)" src="images/6493.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.178ex; height: 2.903ex;" id="img_images_6493.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> if successors of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_17">'s
(with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_268">) are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_18">'s. Thus, for example, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_19"> is
the class of persons named Smith, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_20"> is hereditary with respect to
the relation of father to son. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_21"> is the Peerage, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_22"> is
hereditary with respect to the relation of father to surviving eldest
son. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_23"> is numbers greater than 100, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_24"> is hereditary with
respect to the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/5744.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_5744.svg_3"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu+1\)" src="images/6494.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.096ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_6494.svg">; and so on. If now
<img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_125"> is an ancestor of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_43">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_25"> is a hereditary class to
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_126"> belongs, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_44"> also belongs to this class. Conversely,
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_45"> belongs to every hereditary class to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_127"> belongs,
then (in the sense in which a is one of his own ancestors if <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_128"> is
anybody's parent or child) <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_129"> must be an ancestor of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_46">. For to
have <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_130"> for one's ancestor is a hereditary property which belongs
to <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_131">, and therefore, by hypothesis, to <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_47">. Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_132"> is an
ancestor of <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_48"> when, and only when, <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_133"> belongs to the field of
the relation in question and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_49"> belongs to every hereditary class to
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_134"> belongs. This property may be used to define the ancestral
relation; <i>i.e.</i> since we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ aR_{\unicode{x2217}}z.\equiv:a\in CʻR:\breve{R}ʻʻ\mu\subset \mu.a\in \mu.\supset_{\mu}.z\in \mu \]" src="images/6495.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 46.238ex; height: 3.099ex;" id="img_images_6495.svg"></span>
we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R_{\unicode{x2217}}=\hat{a}\hat{z}\{a\in CʻR:\breve{R}ʻʻ\mu\subset \mu.a\in \mu.\supset_{\mu}.z\in \mu\} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6496.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 52.806ex; height: 3.099ex;" id="img_images_6496.svg"></span>
We then have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash:a\in CʻR.\supset.\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻa=\hat{z}\{\breve{R}ʻʻ\mu\subset \mu.a\in \mu.\supset_{\mu}.z\in \mu\}. \]" src="images/6497.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 54.74ex; height: 3.875ex;" id="img_images_6497.svg"></span>
Here <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻa\)" src="images/6498.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.993ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6498.svg"> may be called "the
descendants of <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_135">." It is the class of terms of which <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_136"> is an
ancestor.</p>

<p>To make plain the relation of the above to mathematical induction, put
0 for <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_137">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\hat{\alpha}\hat{\beta}\,(\beta=\alpha+1)\)" src="images/6499.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.509ex; height: 2.993ex;" id="img_images_6499.svg"> for
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_269">. Then, since 1=0+1, we have <img alt="" data-tex="\(0\in CʻR\)" src="images/6500.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.691ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6500.svg">. Again
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \breve{R}ʻʻ\mu\subset \mu.\equiv:\alpha\in \mu.\supset_{\alpha}.\alpha+1\in \mu. \]" src="images/6501.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 34.868ex; height: 2.903ex;" id="img_images_6501.svg"></span>
Thus we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻ0=\hat{\beta}\{\alpha\in \mu.\supset_{\alpha}.\alpha+1\in \mu:0\in \mu:\supset_{\mu}.\beta\in \mu\}. \]" src="images/6502.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 50.888ex; height: 3.875ex;" id="img_images_6502.svg"></span>
Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_158"> is a descendant of 0, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_159"> belongs to every
class to which 0 belongs and to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha+1\)" src="images/6503.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.186ex; width: 5.345ex; height: 1.692ex;" id="img_images_6503.svg"> belongs whenever
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_312"> belongs. Hence mathematical induction, starting from 0,
will prove properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_160">. In elementary mathematics it is
customary to speak as if this held of <i>all</i> integers, <i>i.e.</i>
as if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻ0\)" src="images/6504.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.927ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6504.svg"> (as above defined)
included all integers; but in fact only <i>finite</i> integers (in<span class="pagenum" id="Page_571">[Pg 571]</span> one
of the two senses which the word <i>finite</i> may have) belong to the
class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻ0\)" src="images/6504.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.927ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6504.svg_1">, and they belong to it
<i>by definition</i>, being defined as the class
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \hat{\beta}\{\alpha\in \mu.\supset_{\alpha}.\alpha+1\in \mu:0\in \mu:\supset_{\mu}.\beta\in \mu\}, \]" src="images/6505.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 41.943ex; height: 3.113ex;" id="img_images_6505.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> as <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻ0\)" src="images/6504.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.927ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6504.svg_2"> in the above
sense. To infinite numbers, inductive proofs of this kind starting from
0 cannot be applied.</p>

<p>The study of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6488.svg_2"> will occupy <a href="#_90" class="pginternal">*90</a>. The
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6488.svg_3"> holds between <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_548"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_258"> if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x(I\upharpoonright C'R)y\)" src="images/6506.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.686ex; height: 2.283ex;" id="img_images_6506.svg"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(xRy\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_266.svg_10"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(xR^{2}y\)" src="images/6507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.108ex; height: 2.351ex;" id="img_images_6507.svg"> or etc. The
study of this "etc." occupies <a href="#_91" class="pginternal">*91</a>, "on the powers of a relation." We
may, for many technical purposes, regard <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻR\)" src="images/6508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.135ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6508.svg"> as
the 0th power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_270">; the other powers are <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_271">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{2}\)" src="images/6509.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 1.934ex;" id="img_images_6509.svg">, etc. If
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_43"> is a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_272">, so is <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid R\)" src="images/6510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6510.svg">. Now <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid R\)" src="images/6510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6510.svg_1"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid RʻS\)" src="images/6511.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.791ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6511.svg">,
according to the definition in <a href="#_38" class="pginternal">*38</a>. Thus if we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in \mu:S\in \mu.\supset_{S}.S\mid R\in \mu:\supset_{\mu}.P\in \mu, \]" src="images/6512.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 39.142ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_6512.svg"></span>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_58"> must be a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_273">, because the class of powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_274"> is
a value of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_26"> which satisfies the hypothesis
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in \mu:S\in \mu.\supset_{S}.S\mid R\in \mu. \]" src="images/6513.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 28.136ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6513.svg"></span>
Conversely, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_59"> is a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_275">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_60"> is reached by
repetitions of the process of turning <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_44"> into <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid R\)" src="images/6510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6510.svg_2">, starting
this process with <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_276">. Hence if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_61"> is a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_277">, we shall
have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in \mu:S\in \mu.\supset_{S}.S\mid R\in \mu:\supset_{\mu}.P\in \mu. \]" src="images/6514.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 39.142ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_6514.svg"></span></p>

<p>Consequently, if we denote the class of powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_278"> by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Pot}ʻR\)" src="images/6515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.627ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6515.svg">, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\in \text{Pot}ʻR.\equiv\colon\ldotp R\in \mu:S\in \mu.\supset_{S}.S\mid R\in \mu:\supset_{\mu}.P\in \mu. \]" src="images/6516.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 55.012ex; height: 2.382ex;" id="img_images_6516.svg"></span>
We might use this as the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Pot}ʻR\)" src="images/6515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.627ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6515.svg_1">; but we can
get a somewhat simpler form. For the above is shown, without much
difficulty, to be equivalent to
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\in \text{Pot}ʻR.\equiv.P(\mid R)_{\unicode{x2217}}R, \]" src="images/6517.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 24.632ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6517.svg"></span>
that is, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_62"> belongs to the ancestry of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_279"> with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mid R\)" src="images/3692.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 2.975ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_3692.svg_1">,
in other words, <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_63"> is reached from <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_280"> by proceeding along
the series
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R,\quad \mid RʻR,\quad \mid Rʻ\mid RʻR, \quad\text{etc}. \]" src="images/6518.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 32.1ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6518.svg"></span>
which is the same as the series
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R,\quad R^{2},\quad R^{3}, \quad\text{etc}. \]" src="images/6519.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 20.45ex; height: 2.439ex;" id="img_images_6519.svg"></span>
The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\((\mid R)_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6520.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.722ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6520.svg"> is important on its own
account. We put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R_{\text{ts}}=(\mid R)_{\unicode{x2217}} \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/6521.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.209ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6521.svg"></span>
and then we put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Pot}ʻR=\overrightarrow{R}_{\text{ts}}ʻR \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6522.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 21.188ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6522.svg"></span></p>

<p>We often want to include <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻR\)" src="images/6508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.135ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6508.svg_1"> among the powers
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_281">; the class consisting of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Pot}ʻR\)" src="images/6515.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.627ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6515.svg_2"> together with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻR\)" src="images/6508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.135ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6508.svg_2"> we call <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Potid}ʻR\)" src="images/6523.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.514ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6523.svg">. The definition is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Potid}ʻR=\overrightarrow{R}_{\text{ts}}ʻ(I\upharpoonright CʻR), \]" src="images/6524.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 26.57ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_6524.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_572">[Pg 572]</span>
whence we easily prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Potid}ʻR=\text{Pot}ʻR\cup \iotaʻ(I\upharpoonright CʻR). \]" src="images/6525.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 33.354ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6525.svg"></span>
The relation of being related by some power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_282"> (other than
<img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻR\)" src="images/6508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.135ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6508.svg_3">) is a very important one. We denote it by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/6526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_6526.svg">, and put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R_{\text{po}}=\dot{s}ʻ\text{Pot}ʻR \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6527.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 20.969ex; height: 2.385ex;" id="img_images_6527.svg"></span>
Thus when <img alt="" data-tex="\(xR_{\text{po}}y\)" src="images/6528.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.997ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_6528.svg">, we have one of <img alt="" data-tex="\(xRy\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_266.svg_11">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(xR^{2}y\)" src="images/6507.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.108ex; height: 2.351ex;" id="img_images_6507.svg_1">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(xR^{3}y\)" src="images/6529.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.108ex; height: 2.349ex;" id="img_images_6529.svg">, etc. It is easy to prove that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R_{\unicode{x2217}}=R_{\text{po}}\unicode{x228d}I\upharpoonright CʻR. \]" src="images/6530.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 19.437ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_6530.svg"></span>
In a series in which every term (except the first, if there is a first)
has an immediate predecessor, and every term (except the last, if there
is a last) has an immediate successor, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_283"> is the relation of a
term to its immediate successor, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/6526.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 3.594ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_6526.svg_1"> is the relation of
any earlier term to any later one.</p>

<p>The next number (<a href="#_92" class="pginternal">*92</a>) concerns itself with some special properties of
the powers of one-many, many-one and one-one relations.</p>

<p>The next number (<a href="#_93" class="pginternal">*93</a>) analyses the field of a relation into successive
<i>generations</i>; <i>e.g.</i> if the relation is that of parent
and child, the first generation will consist of Adam and Eve, the
second of their children, the third of their grandchildren, and so
on, taking always the longest route from Adam and Eve when there
have been intermarriages between generations. That is, taking any
relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_64">, the first generation is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP-\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/6531.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.965ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6531.svg">,
the second is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻP-\text{ᗡ}ʻ(P^{2})\)" src="images/6532.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 14.467ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_6532.svg">, the third is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻ(P^{2})-\text{ᗡ}ʻ(P^{3})\)" src="images/6533.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.34ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_6533.svg">, and so on. Generally, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_10"> is a
power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_65"> (including <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/6534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.117ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6534.svg">), the corresponding
generation is
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;\text{ᗡ}ʻT-\text{ᗡ}ʻ(T\mid P),\\ \textit{i.e.} &amp;\text{ᗡ}ʻT-\breve{P}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻT. \end{array} \]" src="images/6535.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.508ex; width: 22.842ex; height: 6.147ex;" id="img_images_6535.svg"></span></p>

<p>In order to express this more conveniently, we introduce a new
symbol <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/6536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.161ex; height: 1.853ex;" id="img_images_6536.svg">, which is required also on other grounds,
especially in series. "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/6536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.161ex; height: 1.853ex;" id="img_images_6536.svg_1">" may be read "minimum
with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_66">." We regard "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xPy\)" src="images/6368.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.102ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6368.svg_1">" as "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_549"> precedes
<img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_259">"; then in a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_313">, the "minima of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_314">" will
be those members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_315"> which belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg_6"> and are not
preceded by any other members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_316">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cap CʻP-\breve{P}ʻʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6537.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 17.366ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_6537.svg">.
We put therefore
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp; x\, \text{min}_{P}\,\alpha.\equiv.x\in \alpha\cap CʻP-\breve{P}ʻʻ\alpha,\\ \textit{i.e.} &amp; \text{min}_{P}=\hat{x}\hat{\alpha}(x\in \alpha\cap CʻP-\breve{P}ʻʻ\alpha) \quad\text{Df}. \end{array} \]" src="images/6538.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.867ex; width: 44.905ex; height: 6.864ex;" id="img_images_6538.svg"></span>
Hence we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha=\alpha\cap CʻP-\breve{P}ʻʻ\alpha, \]" src="images/6539.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 28.978ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_6539.svg"></span>
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6540.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.966ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_6540.svg"> consists of
those members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\cap CʻP\)" src="images/6541.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.739ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6541.svg"> which are not preceded by any other
members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_317">. (If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_318"> has a single first term, this
term is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}ʻ\alpha\)" src="images/6542.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.966ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6542.svg">.) Thus we have, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_11"> is a power of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_67">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻT=\text{ᗡ}ʻT-\breve{P}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻT. \]" src="images/6543.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 30.267ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_6543.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_573">[Pg 573]</span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻT\)" src="images/6544.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.826ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_6544.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_12"> is any
power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_68"> (including <img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻP\)" src="images/6534.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.117ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6534.svg_1">) is the generation
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_69"> corresponding to <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_13">; thus the whole class of generations is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Potid}ʻP\)" src="images/6545.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 20.444ex; height: 3.934ex;" id="img_images_6545.svg">. Hence we
put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{gen}ʻP=\overrightarrow{\text{min}}_{P}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Potid}ʻP \quad\text{Df}, \]" src="images/6546.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 35.223ex; height: 3.948ex;" id="img_images_6546.svg"></span>
where "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{gen}\)" src="images/6547.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 3.394ex; height: 1.491ex;" id="img_images_6547.svg">" stands for "generation."</p>

<p>The notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/6536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.161ex; height: 1.853ex;" id="img_images_6536.svg_2">" will not be much used until we come
to series, but then it will be constantly used. At present, we shall
only give such properties of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{min}_{P}\)" src="images/6536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.339ex; width: 5.161ex; height: 1.853ex;" id="img_images_6536.svg_3"> as are necessary for
our immediate purposes, but in Part V (on series) we shall devote a
number (*205) to its properties.</p>

<p>In this number we also introduce the notation "<img alt="" data-tex="\(xBP\)" src="images/6548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.71ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_6548.svg">" for "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\in \text{D}ʻP-\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/6549.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 16.025ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6549.svg">."
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(xBP\)" src="images/6548.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 4.71ex; height: 1.57ex;" id="img_images_6548.svg_1">" may be read "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_550"> begins <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_70">." If there is a single
beginning of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_71">, this is <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg">; otherwise the class of beginnings
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/6551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6551.svg">, which =<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻP-\text{ᗡ}ʻP\)" src="images/6531.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.965ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6531.svg_1">. Thus
if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_72"> is the relation of father and son, <img alt="" data-tex="\(BʻP\)" src="images/6550.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6550.svg_1"> = Adam; if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_73">
is the relation of parent and child, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/6551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6551.svg_1"> = Adam
and Eve. <img alt="" data-tex="\(Bʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/6552.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_6552.svg"> will be the end of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_74">, if there is one;
generally, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻ\breve{P}\)" src="images/6553.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6553.svg"> will be the class of ends,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻP-\text{D}ʻP\)" src="images/6554.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 11.965ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6554.svg">. The first generation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_75">
is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/6551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6551.svg_2">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\in 1\rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/6555.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.269ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_6555.svg">, any
generation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_76"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{T}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/6556.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 9.081ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6556.svg">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_14">
is the corresponding power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_77">.</p>

<p>The field of a relation consists, in general, not only of the
generations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_78">, but also of another part, the part in which,
however far we go backwards, we never reach a beginning. This part is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻP\)" src="images/6557.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.176ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6557.svg">. The two parts <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{gen}ʻP\)" src="images/6558.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 8.869ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_6558.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻP\)" src="images/6557.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.176ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6557.svg_1"> are mutually exclusive, and together
exhaust <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻP\)" src="images/3399.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.776ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3399.svg_7">.</p>

<p>The two next numbers, <a href="#_94" class="pginternal">*94</a> and <a href="#_95" class="pginternal">*95</a>, are hardly ever relevant in
subsequent propositions, and may therefore be omitted by any reader
who is not interested in their subject-matter. *94 deals with powers
of relative products. It is only used in the following number (*95),
on "equi-factor relations." The matter to be dealt with in this number
may be explained as follows. In dealing with correlations and similar
topics, we often wish to consider the series of relations
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R,\quad P\mid R\mid Q,\quad P^{2}\mid R\mid Q^{2},\quad P^{3}\mid R\mid Q^{3}, \quad\text{etc}. \]" src="images/6559.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 49.444ex; height: 2.563ex;" id="img_images_6559.svg"></span>
Now we have not yet at our command a definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{\nu}\)" src="images/6560.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.86ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_6560.svg">, where
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/5744.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_5744.svg_4"> is any finite number; thus we cannot define a general term
of this series as <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{\nu}\mid R\mid Q^{\nu}\)" src="images/6561.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 11.174ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6561.svg">. We need therefore a
different method of definition. We have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{aligned} P\mid R\mid Q=(P\Arrowvert Q)ʻR,\\ P^{2}\mid R\mid Q^{2}=(P\Arrowvert Q)^{2}ʻR, \end{aligned} \]" src="images/6562.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.188ex; width: 25.167ex; height: 5.507ex;" id="img_images_6562.svg"></span>
and so on. Thus if <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_15"> is any power of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\mid)\mid (\mid Q)\)" src="images/6563.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.53ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6563.svg">, a
general term of our series is <img alt="" data-tex="\(TʻR\)" src="images/6564.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.667ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6564.svg">. For convenience of notation, we
put
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P\unicode{x2217} Q=\text{sg}ʻ(P\Arrowvert Q)_\unicode{x2217} \quad\text{Df}. \]" src="images/6565.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 23.697ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6565.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_574">[Pg 574]</span>
Then our series consists of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x2217}Q)ʻR\)" src="images/6566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.575ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6566.svg">. The sum of all
relations of this class is considered in this number.</p>

<p>The principal propositions proved in <a href="#_94" class="pginternal">*94</a> and <a href="#_95" class="pginternal">*95</a> are two which have the
same hypothesis as the Schröder-Bernstein theorem, namely
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R,\,S\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻS\subset \text{D}ʻR.\text{ᗡ}ʻR\subset \text{D}ʻS. \]" src="images/6567.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 39.361ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6567.svg"></span>
These two propositions state that, with the above hypothesis,</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp;sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(R\mid S)\text{ sm }  sʻ{\text{gen}}ʻ(S\mid R)\\ \text{and} &amp;pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R\mid S)\text{ sm } pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ(S\mid R). \end{array} \]" src="images/6568.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 42.136ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_6568.svg"></span>
The two combined reconstitute the Schröder-Bernstein theorem, since
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} &amp; sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(R\mid S)\cup pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R\mid S)=\text{D}ʻR\\ \text{and} &amp; sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(S\mid R)\cup pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S\mid R)=\text{D}ʻS. \end{array} \]" src="images/6569.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.149ex; width: 48.907ex; height: 5.43ex;" id="img_images_6569.svg"></span>
Thus they present, so to speak, an itemized account of the equality
proved by the Schröder-Bernstein theorem.</p>

<p><a href="#_96" class="pginternal">*96</a>, on the posterity of a term, is concerned with the properties
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg">, chiefly when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/6571.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_6571.svg">. In this case, in general,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_1"> consists of two parts,
first an open series and then a cyclic series. Either of these may
vanish, or may reduce to a single term. If we call the two parts
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_161"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_14">, the whole of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_162"> precedes the whole
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_15">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/5045.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 5.198ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_5045.svg_1">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\upharpoonleft R\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/6572.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 13.694ex; height: 2.059ex;" id="img_images_6572.svg">.
Thus if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_163"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_16"> vanishes,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\upharpoonleft R\in 1\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/6573.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.555ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6573.svg">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_17"> vanishes, the series never returns into itself,
that is, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\upharpoonleft R_{\text{po}}\unicode{x2abd}J\)" src="images/6574.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 14.674ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_6574.svg">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_18"> exists, there is a definite power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_284">, say
<img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_16">, such that <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\in \gamma.\supset_{y}.yTy\)" src="images/6575.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.667ex; width: 13.657ex; height: 2.199ex;" id="img_images_6575.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_164"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_19"> both exist, there is one term, namely the successor
of the last term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_165">, which has just two immediate
predecessors, one in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_166"> and one in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\gamma\)" src="images/293.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.229ex; height: 1.486ex;" id="img_images_293.svg_20">; every other
term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\text{po}}ʻx\)" src="images/6576.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.98ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_6576.svg"> has only one immediate
predecessor in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_2">. Thus
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_3"> is shaped like a <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_12">, with
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_551"> at the tip of the tail.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_575">[Pg 575]</span></p>

<p><a href="#_97" class="pginternal">*97</a> deals with the analysis of the field of a relation into families.
Taking any member <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_552"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(CʻR\)" src="images/362.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.794ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_362.svg_8">, the family of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_553"> with
respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_285"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\cup \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6577.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.961ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6577.svg">,
which we write <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftrightarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6578.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6578.svg">. Thus the
class of families is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftrightarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻCʻR\)" src="images/6579.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.948ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6579.svg">.
Those families which contain a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻR\)" src="images/6580.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.792ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6580.svg">
are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻR\)" src="images/6581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.945ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6581.svg">.
If we regard <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻR\)" src="images/6582.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.212ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6582.svg">
as arranged in a rectangle, in which the
generations are the successive rows, then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻR\)" src="images/6581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.945ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6581.svg_1">
will be the columns. Thus the relation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{gen}ʻR\)" src="images/6583.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 6.468ex; height: 2.163ex;" id="img_images_6583.svg"> to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻR\)" src="images/6581.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.945ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6581.svg_2"> may be
regarded as a generalized form of the relation of rows and columns.
Under a suitable hypothesis, each row is a selection from the columns,
and each column a selection from the rows. This is expressed in the
following proposition:
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} \vdash:R\in 1\rightarrow 1.\overrightarrow{B}ʻ&amp;\breve{R}\in \text{gen}ʻR\cup \iotaʻ\Lambda.\supset.\\ &amp;\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻR\subset \text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ(\text{gen}ʻR-\iotaʻ\Lambda).\text{gen}ʻR-\iotaʻ\Lambda\subset     \text{D}ʻʻ{\in}_{\Delta}ʻ\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻR \end{align} \]" src="images/6584.svg" style="vertical-align: -3.529ex; width: 90.885ex; height: 8.19ex;" id="img_images_6584.svg"></span>
whence we derive existence-theorems for selections in the cases
concerned.</p>

<p>The importance of the ideas dealt with in the present section is very
great. These ideas dominate the treatment of finite and infinite,
the theory of progressions and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_536.svg_4">, and the transition
from series generated by one-one or many-one relations of consecutive
terms to series generated by transitive relations of <i>before</i>
and <i>after</i>. Wherever, in short, mathematical induction is used
the ideas treated in this section are required. The portions of our
subsequent work in which this section is most referred to are the two
sections on finite and infinite cardinals and ordinals (Part III,
Section C and Part V, Section E). In the general theory of cardinals,
<i>i.e.</i> in Part III, Sections A and B, before the distinction of
finite and infinite has been introduced, the present section will be
seldom if ever referred to<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_65" id="FNanchor_65">[65]</a>.</p>


<div class="footnotes"><h3>FOOTNOTES:</h3>

<div class="footnote">

<p class="nind"><a class="label pginternal" href="#FNanchor_65" id="Footnote_65">[65]</a>
The present section is based on the work of Frege, who
first defined the ancestral relation. See his <i>Begriffsschrift</i>
(Halle, 1879), Part <span class="allsmcap">III</span>., pp. 55-87. Cf. also his
<i>Grundgesetze der Arithmetik</i>, Vol. <span class="allsmcap">I</span>. (Jena, 1893), §§
45, 46 (pp. 59, 60). In this work the ancestral relation is used to
prove the properties of finite cardinals and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_536.svg_5">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_576">[Pg 576]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_90">*90. ON THE ANCESTRAL RELATION.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *90.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_286"> is any relation, "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x R_{\unicode{x2217}} y\)" src="images/6585.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.108ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6585.svg">" is to mean
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_554"> is an ancestor of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_260"> with respect to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_287">," where a term
counts as its own ancestor provided it belongs to the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_288">.
The definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6488.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 1.829ex;" id="img_images_6488.svg_4"> is as follows:</p>

<p><b>90·01.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(R_{\unicode{x2217}} = \hat{x}\hat{y}\{x \in CʻR:\breve{R}ʻʻ\mu \subset \mu . x \in \mu .\supset_{\mu}. y \in \mu\} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/6586.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.685ex; width: 52.582ex; height: 3.099ex;" id="img_images_6586.svg"></p>

<p>That is, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x R_{\unicode{x2217}} y\)" src="images/6585.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.108ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6585.svg_1"> is to hold when <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_555"> belongs to
the field of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_289">, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_261"> belongs to every hereditary class to
which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_556"> belongs; a hereditary class being a class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_27"> such that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻ\mu \subset \mu\)" src="images/6587.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 10.178ex; height: 2.903ex;" id="img_images_6587.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> such that all successors of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_28">'s are <img alt="" data-tex="\(\mu\)" src="images/3357.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.489ex; width: 1.364ex; height: 1.489ex;" id="img_images_3357.svg_29">'s.</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_90_02">*90·02</a>.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}_{\unicode{x2217}} = \text{Cnv}ʻR_{\unicode{x2217}} \quad \text{Df}\)" src="images/6588.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 18.554ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_6588.svg"></p>

<p>This definition serves merely to decide the ambiguity
between <img alt="" data-tex="\((\breve{R})_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6589.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 4.465ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_6589.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cnv}ʻR_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6590.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.148ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6590.svg">, either of which might be meant of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/6591.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.283ex; width: 2.705ex; height: 2.697ex;" id="img_images_6591.svg">. It will be shown, however, that the
two are equal (<a href="#_90_132" class="pginternal">*90·132</a>).</p>

<p>The most important propositions of this number are the following:</p>

<p><b>90·112.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash\colon\ldotp  x R_{\unicode{x2217}} y: {\phi}z . z R w .\supset_{z,w}.{\phi}w:{\phi}x :\supset. {\phi}y\)" src="images/6592.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 38.455ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_6592.svg"></p>

<p><i>I.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x R_{\unicode{x2217}} y\)" src="images/6585.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 5.108ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_6585.svg_2"> and if <img alt="" data-tex="\({\phi}\hat{z}\)" src="images/4655.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.296ex;" id="img_images_4655.svg_1"> is
a hereditary property belonging to <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_557">, then it belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_262">.</p>

gives <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_294">; also it is contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid \breve{R}\)" src="images/5063.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.32ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_5063.svg_2">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R^{2}\mid \breve{R}^{2}\)" src="images/6631.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 7.296ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_6631.svg">,
etc. I has properties, as regards relational multiplication,
analogous to those of 1 in ordinary multiplication; thus to regard
<img alt="" data-tex="\(I\upharpoonright CʻR\)" src="images/6508.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.135ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_6508.svg_5"> as the 0th power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_295"> is analogous to
regarding 1 as the 0th power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_48">, where <img alt="" data-tex="\(n\)" src="images/394.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.357ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_394.svg_49"> is a number.</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*90·15·16}.&amp;\supset\vdash.I\upharpoonright CʻR\unicode{x228d}R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R\unicode{x2abd}R_\unicode{x2217} &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ [\text{Fact}] &amp;\supset\vdash:x(I\upharpoonright CʻR\unicode{x228d}R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R)z.zRw.\supset.xR_\unicode{x2217}z.zRw.\\ [\text{*10·24.*34·1}] &amp;\supset.x(R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R)w.\\ [\text{*23·58}] &amp;\supset.x(I\upharpoonright CʻR\unicode{x228d}R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R)w &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*90·13.*50·3}.&amp;\supset\vdash:xR_\unicode{x2217}y.\supset.xIx.x\in CʻR.\\ [\text{*35·101}] &amp;\supset.x(I\upharpoonright CʻR)x.\\ [\text{*23·58}] &amp;\supset.x(I\upharpoonright CʻR\unicode{x228d}R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R)x.\\ [\text{*4·7}] &amp;\supset.xR_\unicode{x2217}y.x(I\upharpoonright CʻR\unicode{x228d}R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R)x &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(3).*90·112}\, \frac{x(I\upharpoonright CʻR\unicode{x228d}R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R)z}{\phi z} .\supset\\ &amp;\vdash:xR_\unicode{x2217}y.\supset.x(I\upharpoonright CʻR\unicode{x228d}R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R)y &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(4)}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/6666.svg" style="vertical-align: -17.01ex; width: 89.774ex; height: 35.152ex;" id="img_images_6666.svg"></span></p>

<p>In the last line of the above proof, the process is as
follows. Writing <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi z\)" src="images/1269.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 2.4ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_1269.svg_2"> for <img alt="" data-tex="\(x(I\upharpoonright CʻR\unicode{x228d}R_\unicode{x2217}\mid R)z\)" src="images/6667.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 19.906ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6667.svg">,
(2) becomes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\phi z.zRw.\supset.\phi w\)" src="images/6668.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 14.536ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_6668.svg">, while (3) becomes
<img alt="" data-tex="\(xR_\unicode{x2217}y.\supset.xR_\unicode{x2217}y.\phi x\)" src="images/6669.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 17.636ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_6669.svg">. Hence, by
(2) and (3),
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ xR_\unicode{x2217}y.\supset:xR_\unicode{x2217}y:\phi z.zRw.\supset_{z,w}.\phi w:\phi x. \]" src="images/6670.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 38.34ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_6670.svg"></span>
Hence, by <a href="#_90_112" class="pginternal">*90·112</a>, <img alt="" data-tex="\(xR_\unicode{x2217}y.\supset.\phi y\)" src="images/6671.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 11.337ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_6671.svg">, which is the
proposition to be proved.</p>
