<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_617">[Pg 617]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_94">*94. ON POWERS OF RELATIVE PRODUCTS.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *94.</p>

<p>In this number we shall be chiefly concerned with propositions
connecting powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_9"> with powers of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S \mid R\)" src="images/7087.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7087.svg">. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_104">
is a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_10">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(S \mid P \mid R\)" src="images/7088.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 8.647ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7088.svg"> will be a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid R\)" src="images/6510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6510.svg_4">.
If <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_105"> is a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_11">, it is a product of the
form
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (R \mid S) \mid (R \mid S) \mid \ldots \mid (R \mid S). \]" src="images/7089.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 29.406ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7089.svg"></span></p>

<p>If we transfer the initial <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_319"> to the end, we get a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S \mid R\)" src="images/7087.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7087.svg_1">.
Thus there is a power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S \mid R\)" src="images/7087.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7087.svg_2">, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(T\)" src="images/533.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.593ex; height: 1.532ex;" id="img_images_533.svg_19">, such that
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P \mid R = R \mid T\text{.} \]" src="images/7090.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 14.144ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7090.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls} . \text{ᗡ}ʻ(R \mid S) \subset\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/7091.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 30.651ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7091.svg">, we find
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \mid (S \mid R) \mid (S \mid R) \mid \ldots \mid (S \mid R) \mid \breve{R} = (R \mid S) \mid (R \mid S) \ldots (R \mid S) \]" src="images/7092.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 64.759ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7092.svg"></span>
by rearranging and observing that <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid \breve{R} = I \upharpoonright \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/7093.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 16.481ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_7093.svg">. Thus
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls} . \text{ᗡ}ʻ(R \mid S) \subset \text{D}ʻR . P \in \text{Pot}ʻR \mid S .\supset. (\exists T) . T \in \text{Pot}ʻS \mid R . P = R \mid T \mid \breve{R}\text{.} \]" src="images/7094.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 84.964ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7094.svg"></span></p>

<p>Expressions of the form <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid T \mid \breve{R}\)" src="images/7095.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 8.799ex; height: 2.977ex;" id="img_images_7095.svg"> are constantly
needed. They will be specially dealt with in *150, and will occur
constantly in the sequel.</p>

<p>The above connections of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Pot}ʻ(R \mid S)\)" src="images/7096.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.732ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7096.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R)\)" src="images/7097.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.732ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7097.svg"> are embodied in the following propositions:</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*94·14.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \mid Rʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R \mid S) = R \mid ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R)\)" src="images/7098.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.877ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7098.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*94·21.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. \text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R) = (S \parallel R)ʻʻ\{\text{Pot}ʻ(R \mid S) \cup \iotaʻI\}\)" src="images/7099.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 46.985ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7099.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*94·31.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls} . \text{ᗡ}ʻ(R \mid S) \subset \text{D}ʻR .\supset. \text{Pot}ʻ(R \mid S) = (R \parallel \breve{R})ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R)\)" src="images/7100.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 73.842ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7100.svg"></p>

<p>From <a href="#_94_4" class="pginternal">*94·4</a> to <a href="#_94_54" class="pginternal">*94·54</a>, the propositions are all concerned with <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ(R\mid S)\)" src="images/7101.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.39ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7101.svg">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ(S\mid R)\)" src="images/7102.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.39ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7102.svg">. We prove</p>

<p class="nind"><b>*94·5.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash. pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R) = pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻR \mid ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R)\)" src="images/7103.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 48.323ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7103.svg"></p>

<p class="nind"><b>*94·51.</b> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\vdash: R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls} .\supset. pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R) = \breve{R}ʻʻpʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R \mid S)\)" src="images/7104.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 62.749ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7104.svg"></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_618">[Pg 618]</span></p>

<p>Finally we prove (*94·53·54) that if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_320"> is one-one
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻ(R \mid S) \subset \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/7105.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.358ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7105.svg">, or <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_46">
is one-one and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻ(S \mid R) \subset \text{D}ʻS\)" src="images/7106.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.1ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7106.svg">,
then <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R \mid S)\)" src="images/7107.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.3ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7107.svg"> is similar to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R)\)" src="images/7108.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.3ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7108.svg">.</p>

<p>The only proposition of this number which is ever subsequently
referred to is the last, <a href="#_94_64" class="pginternal">*94·64</a>, which, owing to the fact that the
Schröder-Bernstein theorem has been already proved (<a href="#_73_88" class="pginternal">*73·88</a>), is only
used in <a href="#_95_23" class="pginternal">*95·23</a>. But *95·23 itself is never referred to again. The
reader may therefore omit the reading of the propositions of this
number (as also of <a href="#_95" class="pginternal">*95</a>) without detriment to the understanding of what
follows; he should, however, read the summaries.</p>

<p>The chief importance of the propositions in the present number is
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_321"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_47"> fulfil the hypothesis of the Schröder-Bernstein
theorem, <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R,\,S \in 1 \rightarrow 1 . \text{ᗡ}ʻR \subset \text{D}ʻS . \text{ᗡ}ʻS \subset \text{D}ʻR. \]" src="images/7109.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 39.738ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7109.svg"></span></p>

<p>In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_12"> gives what we may call a "reflexion" of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_19"> into part of itself; this part may be again reflected by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid S\)" src="images/7110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7110.svg"> into a part of itself, and so on. The terms in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_20">
which are eliminated sooner or later by this process of reflexion
constitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(R \mid S)\)" src="images/7111.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.992ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7111.svg">, since any one reflexion
eliminates terms which constitute one generation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \mid S\)" src="images/370.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_370.svg_13">.
The terms not eliminated by any number of reflexions constitute
<img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R \mid S)\)" src="images/7107.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.3ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7107.svg_1">. These two sets of terms together
constitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(R \mid S)\)" src="images/7112.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.908ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7112.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_21">. In
this number and *95 we shall prove that, with the Schröder-Bernstein
hypothesis,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(R \mid S) \mathop{\text{ sm }} sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(S \mid R).pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R \mid S) \mathop{\text{ sm }} pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S \mid R)\text{.} \]" src="images/7113.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 75.542ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7113.svg"></span></p>

<p>These two propositions together yield a proof of the Schröder-Bernstein
theorem, in virtue of *93·274·275. This proof is essentially the same
as Bernsteinʻs published originally by Borel<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_66" id="FNanchor_66">[66]</a>.</p>

<p>The nature of the two proofs of the Schröder-Bernstein theorem, namely
Zermelo's (that given in <a href="#_73" class="pginternal">*73</a>) and Bernstein's (that to be given in this
number and <a href="#_95" class="pginternal">*95</a>) will be best apprehended by means of figures.</p>

<figure class="figcenter width500" style="width: 525px;" id="i_618">
<img alt="Geometrical diagram which represents mathematical relationships between transformations." height="500" src="images/i_618.jpg" width="525" id="img_images_i_618.jpg">
</figure>

<p>In Zermelo's proof, we first prove that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_322"> is one-one, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_167"> is a class contained in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_22"> and containing
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_15">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_168"> is similar both to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_23">
and to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_16">. In the figure, the points of the outer
rectangle form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_24">, those of the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_619">[Pg 619]</span> inner rectangle form
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_17">, and those of the outer oval form <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_169">. Thus the
shaded portion of the figure is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta-\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/7114.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.478ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7114.svg">. We now define
a class of classes <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_133"> by the following characteristics:
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_334"> is a member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_134"> if (1) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_335"> is contained in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_25">, (2) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_336"> contains the whole of the shaded area,
(3) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻ\alpha\subset \alpha\)" src="images/7115.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.345ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7115.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> if <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_582"> is a
member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\)" src="images/209.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.448ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_209.svg_337">, so is any term to which <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_583"> has the relation
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_323">. Our proposition is obtained by considering <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_13">,
<i>i.e.</i> the area common to all the members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\kappa\)" src="images/619.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.303ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_619.svg_135">. We
prove (<a href="#_73_81" class="pginternal">*73·81</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\in \kappa\)" src="images/7116.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 7.868ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7116.svg"> and (<a href="#_73_811" class="pginternal">*73·811</a>) that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻpʻ\kappa\)" src="images/7117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.231ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7117.svg"> does not contain any of the shaded area. In
the figure, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻpʻ\kappa\)" src="images/7117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.231ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7117.svg_1"> is the smaller oval. We then
prove (<a href="#_73_83" class="pginternal">*73·83</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_14"> consists entirely of the shaded
portion and the smaller oval. Hence <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_170"> (the larger oval)
consists of two mutually exclusive parts, namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_15"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR-\breve{R}ʻʻpʻ\kappa\)" src="images/7118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.429ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7118.svg">, the latter being that part of the
inner rectangle which lies outside the inner oval. Assuming now that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_324"> is one-one, <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\kappa\)" src="images/3412.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 3.799ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_3412.svg_16"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻʻpʻ\kappa\)" src="images/7117.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 8.231ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7117.svg_2">;
hence, adding <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR-\breve{R}ʻʻpʻ\kappa\)" src="images/7118.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 15.429ex; height: 2.867ex;" id="img_images_7118.svg_1">, it follows that
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_171"> is similar to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_18">, and therefore to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_26">.</p>

<p>In order to obtain hence the Schröder-Bernstein theorem, it is
only necessary to replace <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_325"> by <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid S\)" src="images/7110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7110.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\beta\)" src="images/210.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.281ex; height: 2.034ex;" id="img_images_210.svg_172"> by
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/7119.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7119.svg">, and to assume further that <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_48"> is a one-one whose
domain contains <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻR\)" src="images/360.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.432ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_360.svg_19">. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR=\text{D}ʻ(R\mid S)\)" src="images/7120.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.729ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7120.svg">,
and we obtain (<a href="#_73_87" class="pginternal">*73·87</a>) <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻS \text{ sm } \text{D}ʻS\)" src="images/7121.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 12.627ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7121.svg">, and
therefore <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻS \text{ sm } \text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/7122.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.256ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7122.svg">, which was to be proved.</p>

<figure class="figcenter width500" style="width: 940px;" id="i_619">
<img alt="A schematic diagram showing two parallel systems each containing nested regions." height="500" src="images/i_619.jpg" width="940" id="img_images_i_619.jpg">
</figure>

<p>In Bernstein's proof, we have the two relations <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_326"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_49">
from the beginning. In the left-hand part of the figure, the
outer rectangle is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_27">, which = <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻ(R\mid S)\)" src="images/7123.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.908ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7123.svg">, the oval is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻS\)" src="images/7119.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.174ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7119.svg_1">, and the second rectangle is
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻ(R\mid S)\)" src="images/7124.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.537ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7124.svg">. Thus the points of the outer but not the
second rectangle form the first generation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid S\)" src="images/7110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7110.svg_2">. Within
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻ(R\mid S)\)" src="images/7124.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.537ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7124.svg_1"> we can form a third rectangle, which will
be <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{S}ʻʻ\breve{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻ(R\mid S)\)" src="images/7125.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.144ex; height: 3.029ex;" id="img_images_7125.svg">, <i>i.e.</i>
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{ᗡ}ʻ(R\mid S)^{2}\)" src="images/7126.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.525ex; height: 2.452ex;" id="img_images_7126.svg">. The points belonging to the second
rectangle but not to the third form the second generation of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid S\)" src="images/7110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7110.svg_3">. We can proceed in this way to continually smaller
rectangles. The points which sooner or later are left outside
some rectangle form <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(R\mid S)\)" src="images/7127.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.992ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7127.svg">; those which are
common to all the rectangles form <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R\mid S)\)" src="images/7128.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.3ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7128.svg">.
A similar analysis,<span class="pagenum" id="Page_620">[Pg 620]</span> exhibited in the right-hand part of the
figure, may be applied to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻS\)" src="images/2759.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.545ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_2759.svg_1">, which is thus divided
into <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(S\mid R)\)" src="images/7129.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 13.992ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7129.svg"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S\mid R)\)" src="images/7130.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.3ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7130.svg">.
We prove in this number (<a href="#_94_53" class="pginternal">*94·53</a>) that, with a hypothesis
which is part of the hypothesis of the Schröder-Bernstein
theorem, <img alt="" data-tex="\(pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(R\mid S) \text{ sm }pʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻʻ\text{Pot}ʻ(S\mid R)\)" src="images/7131.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 40.507ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7131.svg">;
in the next number (<a href="#_95_71" class="pginternal">*95·71</a>) we prove that with the hypothesis of the
Schröder-Bernstein theorem, <img alt="" data-tex="\(sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(R\mid S) \text{ sm } sʻ\text{gen}ʻ(S\mid R)\)" src="images/7132.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 31.892ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7132.svg">.
Hence by addition, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR \text{ sm }\text{D}ʻS\)" src="images/7133.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.256ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7133.svg">.</p>

<div class="chapter">
<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_626">[Pg 626]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_95">*95. ON THE EQUI-FACTOR RELATION.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *95.</p>

<p>The purpose of this number may be explained as follows. Consider the
series of relations
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R, P \mid R \mid Q,\, P^{2} \mid R \mid Q^{2},\, P^{3} \mid R \mid Q^{3}, \ldots\text{;} \]" src="images/7183.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 41.289ex; height: 2.563ex;" id="img_images_7183.svg"></span>
it is required to find a means of defining this series without the use
of numbers. If we used numbers, and had the definition given later
(*301) of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{\nu}\)" src="images/6560.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 2.86ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_6560.svg_1"> where <img alt="" data-tex="\(\nu\)" src="images/5744.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.199ex; height: 1ex;" id="img_images_5744.svg_5"> is any finite integer, the general
term of the series would be <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{\nu} \mid R \mid Q^{\nu}\)" src="images/7184.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 11.174ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7184.svg">. But we have
not yet defined numbers, and we therefore desire some means, not
involving numbers, of expressing what is intended when we say that,
in a given term of the series, the same power of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_106"> and of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_15">
is to be involved. This we do as follows. Using the definition of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\parallel Q\)" src="images/7185.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 5.877ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7185.svg">
in <a href="#_43" class="pginternal">*43</a>, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P \mid R \mid Q = (P \parallel Q)ʻR . P^{2} \mid R \mid Q^{2} = (P \parallel Q)^{2}ʻR . P^{3} \mid R \mid Q^{3} = (P \parallel Q)^{3}ʻR \ldots\text{.} \]" src="images/7186.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 80.343ex; height: 2.565ex;" id="img_images_7186.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus the general term of our series is got by taking any power <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_50"> of
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \parallel Q)\)" src="images/7187.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.757ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7187.svg">, and forming <img alt="" data-tex="\(SʻR\)" src="images/7188.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.534ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7188.svg">. The whole of the terms of the
series are therefore constituted by the terms which have to <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_327"> the
relation (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P \parallel Q)_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/7189.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 7.745ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7189.svg">; <i>i.e.</i> they are
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\{\text{sg}ʻ(P \parallel Q)_{\unicode{x2217}}\}ʻR\)" src="images/7190.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 17.342ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7190.svg">. For convenience
of notation we put<a class="fnanchor pginternal" href="#Footnote_67" id="FNanchor_67">[67]</a>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (P\unicode{x2217}Q) = \text{sg}ʻ(P \parallel Q)_{\unicode{x2217}} \quad \text{Dft} ~ \text{[*95]} \]" src="images/7191.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 32.182ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7191.svg"></span></p>

<p>Thus the class of relations we wish to consider is
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x2217}Q)ʻR\)" src="images/6566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.575ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6566.svg_1">.</p>

<p>To illustrate the nature of (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\unicode{x2217}Q)ʻR\)" src="images/6566.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 8.575ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_6566.svg_2">, suppose <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_328">
is the relation "first cousin," while <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_107"> is the relation of child
to parent and <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_16"> is the relation of parent to child. Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(P \mid R \mid Q\)" src="images/7192.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 8.978ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7192.svg"> is the relation "second cousin," <img alt="" data-tex="\(P^{2} \mid R \mid Q^{2}\)" src="images/7193.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 11.078ex; height: 2.45ex;" id="img_images_7193.svg"> is
the relation "third cousin," and so on. Thus (<img alt="" data-tex="\(P*Q)ʻR\)" src="images/7194.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.58ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7194.svg"> is the class
of all relations of cousinship which do not involve a difference of
generation; and "<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\{\dot{s}ʻ(P\unicode{x2217}Q)ʻR\}y\)" src="images/7195.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.538ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_7195.svg">" will mean
"<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_584"> is a cousin of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_280"> in the same generation."</p>

<p>Most of the propositions in this number are inserted because they are
required in the proof of <a href="#_95_52" class="pginternal">*95·52</a>, which states that, under suitable
circumstances, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{s}ʻ(P\unicode{x2217}Q)ʻR \in 1 \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/7196.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.421ex; height: 2.301ex;" id="img_images_7196.svg">.
This proposition itself is proved mainly because it is required in the
proof of <a href="#_95_63" class="pginternal">*95·63</a>, which states that, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_108">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_17"> are one-one's each
of which has its converse domain contained in its domain, and if the<span class="pagenum" id="Page_627">[Pg 627]</span>
first generation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_109"> is similar to the first generation of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_18">,
then the sum of the generations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_110"> is similar to the sum of the
generations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_19">. This leads immediately to a proposition (<a href="#_95_71" class="pginternal">*95·71</a>)
which is half of the Schröder-Bernstein theorem (the other half being
<a href="#_94_53" class="pginternal">*94·53</a> or <a href="#_94_54" class="pginternal">*94·54</a>), namely: "If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_329"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_51"> are one-one's each of
which has its converse domain contained in the domain of the other,
then the sum of the generations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\mid S\)" src="images/7110.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_7110.svg_4"> is similar to the sum of
the generations of <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\mid R\)" src="images/6510.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.563ex; width: 5.062ex; height: 2.26ex;" id="img_images_6510.svg_5">."</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_95_65">*95·65</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash:&amp;P,Q\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻP\subset \text{D}ʻP.\text{ᗡ}ʻQ\subset \text{D}ʻQ.\overrightarrow{B}ʻP \text{ sm }\overrightarrow{B}ʻQ.\\ &amp;CʻP=\breve{P}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻP.CʻQ=\breve{Q}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻQ.\supset.CʻP \text{ sm } CʻQ\\ &amp;[\text{*95·63.*93·36}]\end{align}\]" src="images/7284.svg" style="vertical-align: -5ex; width: 56.482ex; height: 11.131ex;" id="img_images_7284.svg"></span></p>

<p>The following example may illustrate the scope of <a href="#_95_65" class="pginternal">*95·65</a>. Let <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_330">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_52"> be the generating relations of two well-ordered series, neither
of which has a last term. Put <img alt="" data-tex="\(P=R\dot{-}R^{2}.Q=S\dot{-}S^{2}\)" src="images/7285.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 22.494ex; height: 2.493ex;" id="img_images_7285.svg">. Then
<img alt="" data-tex="\(P\)" src="images/384.svg" style="vertical-align: 0; width: 1.699ex; height: 1.545ex;" id="img_images_384.svg_111"> is the relation of immediately preceding in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_331">-series, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_20"> is the relation of immediately preceding in the <img alt="" data-tex="\(S\)" src="images/254.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.05ex; width: 1.459ex; height: 1.645ex;" id="img_images_254.svg_53">-series. We
shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ P,\,Q\in 1\rightarrow 1.\text{ᗡ}ʻP\subset \text{D}ʻP.\text{ᗡ}ʻQ\subset \text{D}ʻQ. \]" src="images/7286.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 40.298ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7286.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_636">[Pg 636]</span>
Also, except in certain exceptional cases, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\)" src="images/6551.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.774ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6551.svg_5">,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overrightarrow{B}ʻQ\)" src="images/7287.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.864ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7287.svg"> are the first derivatives of the two series
(including the first terms of the two series).
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \unicode{x201c}CʻP=\breve{P}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻʻ\overrightarrow{B}ʻP\unicode{x201d} \]" src="images/7288.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 19.984ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7288.svg"></span>
states that, starting from any term of the series and going backwards, a finite
number of steps will bring us to a member of the first derivative, which is
true. Hence, by <a href="#_95_65" class="pginternal">*95·65</a>, neglecting certain exceptional cases, we arrive at
the result that if the first derivatives of two well-ordered series have the
same cardinal number of terms, then the series themselves have the same
cardinal number of terms. This proposition can of course be proved otherwise;
the above is merely mentioned as an illustration of the results of
*95·65.</p>

<p><span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{array}{l} \vdash.\text{*93·101.*24·412.*37·16·321}.\supset\\ \vdash:\text{Hp}.&amp;\supset.\overrightarrow{B}ʻ(R\mid S)=(\text{D}ʻR-\text{ᗡ}ʻS)\cup (\text{ᗡ}ʻS-\breve{S}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR).\\ &amp;\overrightarrow{B}ʻ(S\mid R)=(\text{D}ʻS-\text{ᗡ}ʻR)\cup (\text{ᗡ}ʻR-\breve{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻS) &amp;\qquad \text{(1)}\\ \vdash.\text{*71·38.*37·32}. &amp; \supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\breve{R}ʻʻ(\text{D}ʻR-\text{ᗡ}ʻS)=\text{ᗡ}ʻR-\breve{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻS &amp;\qquad \text{(2)}\\ \vdash.\text{*71·381.*37·32}. &amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.Sʻʻ(\text{ᗡ}ʻS-\breve{S}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR)=\text{D}ʻS-Sʻʻ\breve{S}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR\\ [\text{*72·502}] &amp;\qquad\qquad\qquad =\text{D}ʻS-\text{ᗡ}ʻR &amp;\qquad \text{(3)}\\ \vdash.\text{(2).(3).*73·21·22}.&amp;\supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.\text{D}ʻR-\text{ᗡ}ʻS \text{ sm } \text{ᗡ}ʻR-\breve{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻS.\\ &amp;\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{ᗡ}ʻS-\breve{S}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR \text{ sm } \text{ᗡ}ʻS-\text{ᗡ}ʻR &amp;\qquad \text{(4)}\\ \vdash.\text{*24·21}.&amp; \supset\vdash:\text{Hp}.\supset.(\text{D}ʻR-\text{ᗡ}ʻS)\cap (\text{ᗡ}ʻS-\breve{S}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻR)=\Lambda.\\ &amp;\qquad\qquad\qquad(\text{ᗡ}ʻR-\breve{R}ʻʻ\text{ᗡ}ʻS)\cap (\text{ᗡ}ʻS-\text{ᗡ}ʻR)=\Lambda &amp;\qquad \text{(5)}\\ \vdash.\text{(1).(4).(5).*73·71}.\supset\vdash.\text{Prop} \end{array} \]" src="images/7290.svg" style="vertical-align: -20.122ex; width: 99.21ex; height: 41.376ex;" id="img_images_7290.svg"></span></p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_637">[Pg 637]</span></p>
<h2 class="nobreak" id="_96">*96. ON THE POSTERITY OF A TERM.</h2>
</div>


<p><i>Summary of</i> *96.</p>

<p>By the "posterity" of a term with respect to a relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_332">
we mean the class <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_6">.
In the present number, we shall be chiefly concerned with
the relation (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx) \upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/7297.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.888ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7297.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_333"> confined
to the posterity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_585">. We shall also be concerned with
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx) \upharpoonleft R_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/7298.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.875ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7298.svg">
and (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/7299.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 12.765ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_7299.svg">,
which, as is proved in <a href="#_96_13" class="pginternal">*96·13</a>, are respectively
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \{(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx) \upharpoonleft R\}_{\unicode{x2217}} ~\text{and}~ \{(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx) \upharpoonleft R\}_{\text{po}}. \]" src="images/7300.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 36.333ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_7300.svg"></span></p>

<p>The most interesting case is when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/7301.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_7301.svg">. In this case, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_7"> is in
general shaped like a <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_21">, with <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_586"> at the tip of the tail; that
is, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_8"> may be divided into two
parts, the first an open series, the second a closed series. If <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_281">
is the junction of the two, we shall have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ x R_{\unicode{x2217}} z .z R_{\text{po}} y .\supset. {\sim}(z R_{\text{po}} z)\text{,} \]" src="images/7302.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 25.432ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_7302.svg"></span>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ y R_{\unicode{x2217}} z .\supset. z R_{\text{po}}z\text{;} \]" src="images/7303.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 14.965ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_7303.svg"></span>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{in fact,} \quad (\exists P): P \in \text{Pot}ʻR : y R_{\unicode{x2217}} z .\supset_{z}. z P z\text{.} \]" src="images/7304.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 42.634ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7304.svg"></span></p>

<p>We have also, when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5271.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5271.svg_2">,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ y,\,z  \in \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx .\supset: y R_{\unicode{x2217}} z .\lor. z R_{\unicode{x2217}} y\text{.} \]" src="images/7305.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 30.305ex; height: 3.654ex;" id="img_images_7305.svg"></span></p>

<p>It thus appears that <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_9">
is divided into two parts, the first consisting of those terms
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_60"> for which <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}(z R_{\text{po}} z)\)" src="images/7306.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.219ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_7306.svg">, the second of those
for which <img alt="" data-tex="\(z R_{\text{po}} z\)" src="images/7307.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.698ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_7307.svg">. The first wholly precedes the
second; the first exists if <img alt="" data-tex="\({\sim}(x R_{\text{po}} x)\)" src="images/7308.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 9.703ex; height: 2.347ex;" id="img_images_7308.svg">, the
second if <img alt="" data-tex="\(\dot{\exists}!\{(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R_{\text{po}} \dot{\cap} I\}\)" src="images/7309.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 20.444ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_7309.svg">.
Every term in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\text{po}}ʻx\)" src="images/6576.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.98ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_6576.svg_1"> has one and only
one immediate predecessor, except the term (if it exists) at the
junction of the tail and circle of the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_22">; this term has just
two immediate predecessors, one in the tail and one in the circle.
But if either the tail or the circle is null, then every term in
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\text{po}}ʻx\)" src="images/6576.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.98ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_6576.svg_2"> has only one immediate predecessor,
and therefore
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ (\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx) \upharpoonleft R \in 1 \rightarrow 1\text{.} \]" src="images/7310.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 20.945ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7310.svg"></span><span class="pagenum" id="Page_638">[Pg 638]</span>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \text{Put} \quad (I_{R}ʻx = \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx \cap \hat{z}(z R_{\text{po}} z) \quad \text{Dft} \]" src="images/7311.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 37.566ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_7311.svg"></span>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ J_{R}ʻx = \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx \cup \hat{z}\{{\sim}(z R_{\text{po}} z)\} \quad \text{Dft} \]" src="images/7312.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 35.028ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_7312.svg"></span>
(these definitions being only to apply within <a href="#_96" class="pginternal">*96</a>). Then <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg"> is
the open part of the series <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_10">,
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg"> is the circular part. The open part wholly precedes the
circular part, provided <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5271.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5271.svg_3">; <i>i.e.</i>
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1 .\supset. J_{R}ʻx \supset pʻ\overrightarrow{R}_{\text{po}}ʻʻI_{R}ʻx\text{.} \]" src="images/7315.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 38.869ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_7315.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_1"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_1"> both exist, <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_2"> has a last
term, say <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_282">. The successor of this term, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻy\)" src="images/7316.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.878ex;" id="img_images_7316.svg">, is the
only term in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_11"> which has two
immediate predecessors in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_12">,
namely <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_283"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ(I_{R}ʻx \cap \overrightarrow{R}ʻ\breve{R}ʻy)\)" src="images/7317.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 18.74ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7317.svg">.</p>

<p>The most important applications of the propositions of the
present number are in the theory of finite and infinite, both
cardinal and ordinal. When <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_334"> is many-one, then if <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_2">
exists, or, more generally, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_3"> has a last term,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_13"> is a finite class,
<i>i.e.</i> what we shall call a "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Cls} ~ \text{induct}\)" src="images/7318.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 10.007ex; height: 1.643ex;" id="img_images_7318.svg">" (cf.
*120). That is, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \vdash: R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1 . \text{E}! ~ \text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx .\supset. \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx \in \text{Cls} ~ \text{induct}\text{.} \]" src="images/7319.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 54.212ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7319.svg"></span></p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_4"> exists, but has no last term,
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_14"> is a <i>progression</i> (cf.
*122) when its terms are arranged in the order generated by <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_335">.
That is, giving to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\aleph_{0}\)" src="images/536.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.375ex; width: 2.37ex; height: 1.945ex;" id="img_images_536.svg_6"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(\omega\)" src="images/52.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.407ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_52.svg_1"> the meanings given by
Cantor (cf. *123 and *263), and using "<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{Prog}\)" src="images/7320.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.466ex; width: 4.69ex; height: 2.011ex;" id="img_images_7320.svg">" for the class
of one-one relations which generate progressions, we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ \begin{align} \vdash: R \in \text{Cls} \rightarrow 1&amp;.{\sim}E! ~ \text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx.\exists! J_{R}ʻx .\supset.\\ &amp;\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx \in \aleph_{0} . (\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx) \upharpoonleft R \in \text{Prog} . (\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx)     \upharpoonleft R_{\text{po}} \in \omega.\\ \end{align} \]" src="images/7321.svg" style="vertical-align: -2.825ex; width: 65.837ex; height: 6.781ex;" id="img_images_7321.svg"></span></p>

<p>Another very important proposition in the proof of which the
present number is useful is *121·47, which proves that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_336">
is either one-many or many-one, and <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_138"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_61"> are any two
terms whatever, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻa \cap\overrightarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻz\)" src="images/7322.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 13.622ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7322.svg">
(which we call the "interval" from <img alt="" data-tex="\(a\)" src="images/144.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.023ex; width: 1.197ex; height: 1.02ex;" id="img_images_144.svg_139"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_62">) is always a finite
class. The proof that progressions are well-ordered series depends upon
the propositions of this number, since it uses *122·23, which depends
upon <a href="#_96_52" class="pginternal">*96·52</a>.</p>

<p>The present number begins with a series of propositions (ending with
<a href="#_96_16" class="pginternal">*96·16</a>) on <img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha \upharpoonleft R_{\text{po}}\)" src="images/7323.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 7.243ex; height: 2.22ex;" id="img_images_7323.svg"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha\upharpoonleft R_{\unicode{x2217}}\)" src="images/7324.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 6.353ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_7324.svg">, both in general and when
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\alpha = \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/7325.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 10.555ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_7325.svg">. We then proceed to a few
propositions (<a href="#_96_2" class="pginternal">*96·2</a>-<a href="#_96_25" class="pginternal">·25</a>) on (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/7326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.888ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7326.svg">
when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in 1 \rightarrow \text{Cls}\)" src="images/5040.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5040.svg_3">; with
the exception of <a href="#_96_24" class="pginternal">*96·24</a>, these propositions are all used in the
cardinal theory of finite and infinite. They are, however, less
important than the subsequent propositions, which are concerned with
<span class="pagenum" id="Page_639">[Pg 639]</span><img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_15"> when <img alt="" data-tex="\(R \in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1\)" src="images/5272.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.09ex; width: 12.288ex; height: 1.686ex;" id="img_images_5272.svg_2">.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_337"> is a many-one relation, and x is a member of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{D}ʻR\)" src="images/358.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 4.803ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_358.svg_28">, the relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_338"> in general arranges
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_16"> (<i>i.e.</i> the posterity
of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_587">) in a figure such as is here given. The relation <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_339"> holds
between each dot and the next, starting from <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_588">, and travelling
round the circle in the sense indicated by the arrow. The dots from
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_589"> to <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_284"> constitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_5">, and the dots in the circle
constitute <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_3">. <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_285"> is the last term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_6">,
<i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(\text{max}_{R}'J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7327.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.643ex; width: 10.922ex; height: 2.361ex;" id="img_images_7327.svg">; <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_18"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{R}ʻy\)" src="images/7316.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.183ex; height: 2.878ex;" id="img_images_7316.svg_1">, and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_63"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(\breve{\iota}ʻ(\overrightarrow{R}ʻw\cap I_{R}ʻx)\)" src="images/7328.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 16.177ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7328.svg">, or,
what comes to the same thing, <img alt="" data-tex="\(\{(I_{R}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R\}ʻw\)" src="images/7329.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 15.967ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7329.svg">.
<img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_19"> is the only term which has more than one immediate predecessor
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_17">; <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_20"> always exists if
neither <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_7"> nor <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_4"> is null, and conversely, if <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_21">
exists, neither <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_8"> nor <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_5"> is null. The proof of these
propositions is long; the following are useful stages in the proof.</p>

<p>If <img alt="" data-tex="\(xRx\)" src="images/7330.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 4.305ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_7330.svg">, the whole posterity of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_590"> is <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_591"> itself (<a href="#_96_33" class="pginternal">*96·33</a>); if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(xRy\)" src="images/266.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_266.svg_12"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(yRx\)" src="images/7331.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 4.12ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_7331.svg">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_592"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_286"> constitute the whole posterity of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_593"> (<a href="#_96_331" class="pginternal">*96·331</a>), and so on. The successors of members of <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_6">
belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_7"> (<a href="#_96_341" class="pginternal">*96·341</a>), and the predecessors of members of
<img alt="" data-tex="\(J_Rʻx\)" src="images/7332.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7332.svg">, if they belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_18">,
belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_9"> (<a href="#_96_351" class="pginternal">*96·351</a>). (It should be observed that,
since <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_340"> is only assumed to be many-one, not one-one,
every member of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_19">
may have any number of predecessors which do not belong to
<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx)\)" src="images/7333.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 6.97ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7333.svg">. We have a series
of propositions, beginning with <a href="#_96_4" class="pginternal">*96·4</a>, which deal with the
hypothesis <img alt="" data-tex="\(yRw.zRw\)" src="images/7334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.841ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_7334.svg">. We prove (<a href="#_96_42" class="pginternal">*96·42</a>) that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(yRw.zRw\)" src="images/7334.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 9.841ex; height: 2.009ex;" id="img_images_7334.svg_1"> and
<img alt="" data-tex="\(yR_{\text{po}}z\)" src="images/7335.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.755ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_7335.svg">, then <img alt="" data-tex="\(zR_{\text{po}}z\)" src="images/7336.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 5.698ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_7336.svg">, <i>i.e.</i> <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_64">
belongs to <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_8">. We prove (<a href="#_96_431" class="pginternal">*96·431</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_10"> wholly
precedes <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_9">; that (<img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/7337.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.107ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7337.svg"> and
(<img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/7338.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 9.847ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7338.svg"> are both one-one (<a href="#_96_45" class="pginternal">*96·45</a>), so that if
<img alt="" data-tex="\(yRw.zRw.y\neq z\)" src="images/7339.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.486ex; width: 16.025ex; height: 2.106ex;" id="img_images_7339.svg">, one of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_287"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_65"> must belong to <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_11">
and the other to <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_Rʻx\)" src="images/7340.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7340.svg"> (<a href="#_96_441" class="pginternal">*96·441</a>). Hence it follows (<a href="#_96_453" class="pginternal">*96·453</a>)
that if either <img alt="" data-tex="\(xR_{\text{po}}x\)" src="images/7341.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 6.183ex; height: 2.195ex;" id="img_images_7341.svg"> (in which case <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx={po})\)" src="images/7342.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 11.442ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7342.svg">
or (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R_{\text{po}}\unicode{x2abd}J\)" src="images/7343.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.65ex; width: 15.555ex; height: 3.84ex;" id="img_images_7343.svg">
(in which case <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx=\Lambda)\)" src="images/7344.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.516ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7344.svg">,
then (<img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R\)" src="images/7326.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 10.888ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7326.svg_1"> is
a one-one relation. (This proposition is used twice in the cardinal
theory of finite and infinite, namely in *121·43 and *122·17.) Hence we
arrive at the proposition (<a href="#_96_47" class="pginternal">*96·47</a>) that if two different members <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_288">
and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_66"> of <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_20"> both immediately
precede a term <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_22">, then one of <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_289"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_67"> (say <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_290">) is the
last term of <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_12">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_23"> is its immediate successor and <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_68"> is
the immediate predecessor of <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_24"> in <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_10">, <i>i.e.</i> we have
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ y=\text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx.w=\breve{R}ʻ\text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx.z=\{(I_{R}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R\}ʻ\breve{R}ʻ\text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx. \]" src="images/7345.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.806ex; height: 2.98ex;" id="img_images_7345.svg"></span>
Thus <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_291">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_69">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_25"> are unique if they exist. We prove next
(<a href="#_96_475" class="pginternal">*96·475</a>) that <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_292">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_70">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_26"> exist when, and only when, neither
<img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_11"> nor <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_13"> is null.</p>

<p>It follows from the above propositions that if <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_341"> is one-one, either
<img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_12"> or <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_14"> must be null (<a href="#_96_491" class="pginternal">*96·491</a>), <i>i.e.</i> the
posterity of a term is either an open series or a cycle, and cannot
have the <img alt="" data-tex="\(Q\)" src="images/2826.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.439ex; width: 1.79ex; height: 2.032ex;" id="img_images_2826.svg_23">-shape.</p>

<p><span class="pagenum" id="Page_650">[Pg 650]</span></p>

<p>The above proposition, since it exhibits <img alt="" data-tex="\(y\)" src="images/141.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.464ex; width: 1.109ex; height: 1.464ex;" id="img_images_141.svg_293">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(z\)" src="images/228.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.052ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_228.svg_71">, <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_27"> as
functions of <img alt="" data-tex="\(x\)" src="images/30.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.294ex; height: 1.025ex;" id="img_images_30.svg_594"> and <img alt="" data-tex="\(R\)" src="images/31.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.048ex; width: 1.717ex; height: 1.593ex;" id="img_images_31.svg_342">, shows that there is at most one <img alt="" data-tex="\(w\)" src="images/263.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.025ex; width: 1.62ex; height: 1.027ex;" id="img_images_263.svg_28">
in <img alt="" data-tex="\(\overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx\)" src="images/6570.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 6.09ex; height: 3.643ex;" id="img_images_6570.svg_21"> having more than one
immediate predecessor, and that this one has exactly one immediate
predecessor in <img alt="" data-tex="\(J_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7313.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.309ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7313.svg_15"> and one in <img alt="" data-tex="\(I_{R}ʻx\)" src="images/7314.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.452ex; width: 5.049ex; height: 2.149ex;" id="img_images_7314.svg_13">. (These results
require <a href="#_96_441" class="pginternal">*96·441</a>, in addition to <a href="#_96_462" class="pginternal">*96·462</a>.) Thus we arrive at the
following proposition:</p>

<p class="nind"><b><a id="_96_47">*96·47</a>.</b> <span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[\begin{align}\vdash\colon\ldotp R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow &amp;1.y,z\in \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx.yRw.zRw.y     \neq z.\supset:w=\breve{R}ʻ\text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx:\\ &amp;y = \text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx.z=\{(I_{R}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R\}ʻ\breve{R}ʻ\text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx.\lor.\\ &amp;z = \text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx.y=\{(I_{R}ʻx)\upharpoonleft R\}ʻ\breve{R}ʻ\text{max}_{R}ʻJ_{R}ʻx\\ \quad[\text{*96·441·462}]\end{align}\]" src="images/7458.svg" style="vertical-align: -6.441ex; width: 71.045ex; height: 14.014ex;" id="img_images_7458.svg"></span></p>

<p>We still have to prove
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\exists !J_{R}ʻx.\exists !I_{R}ʻx.\supset.(\exists y,z,w).y,z\in \overleftarrow{R}_{\unicode{x2217}}ʻx.yRw.zRw.y \neq z, \]" src="images/7459.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 71.326ex; height: 3.756ex;" id="img_images_7459.svg"></span>
or, what comes to the same thing because of <a href="#_96_441" class="pginternal">*96·441</a>,
<span class="align-center"><img alt="" data-tex="\[ R\in \text{Cls}\rightarrow 1.\exists !J_{R}ʻx.\exists !I_{R}ʻx.\supset.(\exists y,z,w).y\in J_{R}ʻx.z\in I_{R}ʻx.yRw.zRw. \]" src="images/7460.svg" style="vertical-align: -0.566ex; width: 72.176ex; height: 2.262ex;" id="img_images_7460.svg"></span>
This is effected in the following propositions.</p>
